en: The Bhāmatī: Śaṅkara’s Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.

We bow to that Brahma— the immortal, consisting of immeasurable bliss and knowledge— from whom these transformations of space, wind, fire, water, and earth proceed as his two-fold ministers, and from whom this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, high and low, has arisen. (1)

The two-fold [ignorance], namely the root-ignorance (*mūlavidyā*) and the secondary ignorance (*tūlāvidyā*), is the transformation [of reality] without the destruction of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). The Vedas are his breath; the five elements are his glance.
His smile is this world of moving and non-moving beings, and his sleep is the great dissolution. //2//
We pay homage to the Veda and to Bhava, who is endowed with six limbs, who possesses various imperishable [forms], and who is eternal. //3//
We pay homage to Mārtaṇḍa, Tilakasvāmin, and Mahāgaṇapati, who are worshipped by the universe and who bestow all spiritual accomplishments. //4//
Salutations to that Veda-vyāsa, the creator of the Brahma-sūtras, the architect of the Vedas, who is an incarnation of the power of knowledge of the Blessed Lord Hari. //5//
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, the treasury of compassion, whose consciousness is utterly pure, this commentary—clear yet profound—is now being expounded as composed by him. (6)
Even the speech of those like us, though devoid of the refined composition of a teacher, purifies like the falling current of the Gaṅgā purifies the water of a street. //7//
Now, that which is free from doubt and devoid of purpose is not an object of inquiry for a discerning person,
just like a jar situated in bright light and in contact with the sense organs and the mind,
or the teeth of a crow.
And thus, this Brahman is all-pervasive;

[wherever there is the state of being an object of inquiry (jijñāsyatva), there alone are the states of being doubtful (saṃdigdhatva) and having a purpose (saprayojanatva)]. Since being doubtful and having a purpose are pervaders of being an object of inquiry, the cognition here is the perception of their opposite—their absence—which is contradictory to them.

And thus, the meaning here is that in the absence of the pervader (the desire to know), there is an absence of the pervaded (the object of inquiry). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Brahman is not an object of inquiry for one who desires liberation, because it is not doubted by him and because it serves no purpose.
The meaning is that it is like the horn of a hare or the teeth of a crow in such a [non-existent] jar.
This is the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*).
For instance: because of its largeness, it is a nourisher (*bṛṃhaṇa*)... [and so forth].
Note: The form "brahman" is derived from the verbal roots *bṛh* and *bṛhi*, which signify growth (*vṛddhi*).
It should be understood that "expansion" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) consists in being the cause of the development and transformation of the body and other such entities.
Thus, because it possesses these qualities, the Self alone is celebrated as Brahman.

Moreover, this [Self]—from worms and insects up to the divine sages—is established for every living being through the direct, non-doubtful, and non-erroneous experience of "I," by means of its discrimination from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects which are the locus of the notion of "I-thus"; therefore, it is not an object of inquiry.
For no one at any time doubts in this regard, thinking, "Am I, or am I not?"
Nor does one fall into the error of thinking "I am not this," nor does one think "I am thin" or "I am fat."

It is correct [to hold] that this "I-conceit" (ahaṅkāra) has the body as its substrate, because we observe a grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the body and [the notion] "I go," etc., which means that they are known to convey a single referent.

For if that [body] were the objective support [of the self], there could be no recognition in the form: "I, who experienced my parents in childhood, am the very same one who now experiences my grandchildren in old age.
Indeed, there is not even the slightest recognition between the bodies of the child and the elder. (Note:
Recognition is a cognition that penetrates the identity of the individual entity directly perceived with a previously experienced one.)
There must be a fragrance by which oneness could be determined.
Therefore, that which persists when certain things are excluded is distinct from them, just as a thread is distinct from flowers.
Likewise, although the bodies of children and so forth undergo change, that which persists as the locus of the supreme ego is distinct from them.

Moreover, having assumed a divine body during the end of a dream and experiencing enjoyments appropriate to it, one who has awakened perceives oneself as having a human body and realizes, "I am not a god; I am merely a human. Thus, even while the divine body is sublated, one understands that the locus of the "I" is unsublated and distinct from the body.
Moreover, [the term] *yoga*—

[referring here to] having assumed a tiger-body through the power of yoga for the sake of sport and so forth by obtaining powers such as *aṇimā*, and thus possessing identification with that body; in this regard, it should be understood that no change of body is established in childhood or old age, which consist of the increase and decrease of bodily parts.
It should be understood that because the notion "this is the body" persists [in dreams], the example of "in a dream" (*svapnānte*) was cited out of dissatisfaction with that view.

Furthermore, it should be noted that for those who maintain that dreams are mere delusions, that notion is unestablished; therefore, the analogy of the "yogic tiger" is given to demonstrate [the persistence of the notion] even during the waking state.
Since even a tiger experiences itself as undivided despite the division of its body, the body is not the objective referent of the "I"-conception (ahaṅkāra).
For this very reason, the sense organs are also not its objective referent;
for even when there is a change of sense organs, there is a recognition of the object of the "I"-conception in the form: "I who saw that, I myself now touch it."
However, his discrimination regarding sense objects is indeed quite robust;

for, in the case of the two instruments—the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*)—there is the manifestation of the appearance of an agent in the form of "I. (Note: *prakhyāna* means "expression" or "word.")
The meaning is that it is logically untenable for instruments (*karaṇas*) to be denoted by the term "agent" (*kartṛ*).
[Furthermore,] there is an impossibility of [the self] being an object [of cognition].

And as for such usages as "I am thin" or "I am blind," even though there is no actual identity [between the self and the body], they are somehow [justified], just as in the case of "the platforms [are crying]."

Note: Since it has been established previously that the Self is distinct from the body and so forth, the sense is that because [the literal meaning] is untenable, a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) must be resorted to.
We consider it logical that [these expressions] are figurative, like the phrase "the banks cry out" (*krośanti*).

Therefore, it is proven that the Self—which is excluded from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects that are the locus of the notion of "this" (*idam*), and which is known through the very clear experience of "I" (*aham*)—is not an object of inquiry (*ajijñāsya*) due to the absence of doubt.
And because it is not purposeful. [Note: 1. He analyzes the second reason.]

For instance, liberation (apavarga), defined here as the cessation of saṃsāra, is intended as the goal. And saṃsāra, which is caused by the non-realization of the true nature of the self (ātman), must be brought to an end through the knowledge of the self's true nature.
If this [saṃsāra] is beginningless and persists alongside beginningless knowledge of the self's true nature, [then it cannot be removed].
Whence is its cessation? Because there is no contradiction. And whence is the non-experience of the true nature of the self?
For there is no knowledge of the true nature of the self other than the experience "I am."

Furthermore, the Self— which is established by the most vivid and universal experience as "I" and is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth— cannot be rendered otherwise even by thousands of Upaniṣads,
because that would contradict direct experience.
For not even a thousand scriptures have the power to turn a jar into a cloth.

Therefore, because this contradicts direct experience, we consider it logical that the Upaniṣads have only figurative meanings; with this intention, having raised the objection, he refutes it with the words "of the spheres of the notions of 'you' and 'I'. Here, the portion beginning with "yuṣmadasmad" and ending with "is fit to be false" constitutes the text of the objection;
the portion beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless) constitutes the text of the refutation.
Nevertheless, because of the connection with the word "tathāpi" (nevertheless), one should read "yadyapi" (even though) when expressing doubt.
Although it would have been sufficient to say "of these two [objects] within the scope of our own cognition," the use of the term "yuṣmad" (you/that) is intended to indicate absolute difference.
For the notion of "you" (*tvam-kāra*) is the counter-correlative of the notion of "I" (*aham-kāra*), whereas the notion of "this" (*idam-kāra*) is not.
The meaning is that although there is no difference between this word (*idam*) and that word (*adas*) in their capacity to indicate what is remote,

the expression "these we are" and so forth occurs very frequently; consequently, by virtue of such extensive usage, it appears as if it were the primary [referent], and thus its conventional power (*nirūḍha*) is established therein.
"Because it is observed through application":

the self (*ātman*) has consciousness as its intrinsic nature and is the subject; the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and the objects have insentience as their intrinsic nature and are the objects.
For these [attributes] confine and bind the conscious self (cidātman);
that is to say, they render it definable by their own form.
Regarding this extreme difference, which is the cause for the absence of mutual superimposition, the illustration is: "like darkness and light."
For indeed, no one ever [possesses] two modes of activity (*vṛtti*) that are perceived as distinct while they are actually occurring;
for superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is pervaded by the non-apprehension of distinction.
The intention here is that superimposition is not tenable because there exists the apprehension of their distinction;
for light and darkness cannot be perceived as having each other's nature.
This is what was stated: "because the existence of one in the other is impossible."
The state of being one in the other is "mutuality" (*itaretaratva*).
That is to say, identity;
[this refers to] "in the case of its impossibility.
This might be so.
Let there be no mutual identity between the two substrates;
however, there will be a mutual superimposition of their attributes, such as insentience and sentience, or permanence and impermanence.
For it is observed that even when the distinction between two substrates is grasped, there occurs a superimposition of their respective attributes.

Just as, even when a crystal gem is perceived as distinct from a flower, because of its extreme transparency it takes on the reflection of a *japā* flower, there arises the delusion that "the crystal is red"; therefore it is said: "of their properties as well.
The impossibility of the exchange—that is, the presence of properties in one another's substrates—is what is meant.

This is the intended meaning: for a material substance possessing color might, due to its extreme transparency, take on the shadow of another colored substance even while that other substance is being perceived with its distinction [from the first].
The conscious self (*cidātmā*), however, being formless and the subject, cannot receive the reflection of an object.
As they have said: "What kind of reflection could there be of sound, smell, or taste?

Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be that through the mutual interpenetration of the object and the subject, there occurs a reciprocal exchange consisting of the mutual interpenetration of their respective attributes.
If those two substrata, being apprehended with absolute distinction, are unmixed,
then their properties are all the more unmixed,
because they are far removed due to the intervention of their respective substrata.
This is what was stated by the words "all the more so" and "by its opposite";
the meaning is "by the reversal of the object."
The word "mithyā" (false) signifies concealment or negation.
This is what is meant: superimposition is pervaded by the non-apprehension of difference, whereas here there exists the apprehension of difference, which is its opposite.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "Even though it is logical that [the notion of 'I'] should be false because it would remove the non-apprehension of difference and thereby also remove the superimposition pervaded by that [non-apprehension], nevertheless...
The intention here is this: this would indeed be so if the true nature of the Self were revealed in the experience of "I."
But this is not the case;

for indeed, the reality of the Self is celebrated in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas as being one, non-dual, indifferent, and of the single essence of infinite bliss-consciousness, unconditioned by any limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Nor do these [texts] begin with...
FN: 1. *Upakrama* is the beginning; *parāmarśa* is the intermediate reference; and *upasaṃhāra* is the conclusion, which is the restriction of what was stated in general to a specific instance.
Here, the intention is as follows: having begun with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second,"...

Having instructed, "Seek the real root through the sprout of fire," and "Seek the real root through the sprout of food," and so forth, the passage concludes with, "That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That thou art, Śvetaketu.
This statement has the purport of imparting an undivided reality, as evidenced by the indications of its opening and concluding sections.
The passage read in an intermediate section, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," and so forth, is to be understood in connection with this [preceding statement].
Now, one might object: does it not also explain the sequence of creation beginning with fire and water? No;
for it is Brahman alone—single and without a second—that is intended to be established here.
Whatever a word intends as its primary goal, that alone is its meaning; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, since it can rightly be said that "whatever was uttered was for the sake of manifesting Brahman," these [scriptural passages] indeed establish the reality of the Self as free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); this is the direction of the argument.

Through references, summaries, and the repetition of actions, these texts—which have such a reality of the Self as their primary purport—cannot be made to have even figurative meanings even by Śakra himself.
For in repetition, there is an increase in the clarity of the object—as when one says, "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful!"—and not a diminution;
much less can it be said that the term is used figuratively.

But as for my own experience, it reveals a self that is partial and overwhelmed by the manifold proliferation of various sorrows, sufferings, and the like; how, then, could it have the true nature of the Self as its object, or how could it be free from such affliction?
[Note: 2] *Upaplava* means error (*viparyāsa*). The meaning is: how can there be an experience of "I" that is devoid of that [error]?

Furthermore, because it would contradict the most authoritative means of knowledge, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)—which depends upon that [perception]—would itself be invalidated.

FN: 3. Here, "dependence on that" should be understood as the state of depending upon its own validity by way of being a restatement of an object established by the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa). [Objection:
It is logical that [the Veda] has validity and that its meaning is figurative; for it is non-human (apauruṣeya)... [End of fragment]
FN: 4. Being possessed of a sequence dependent on a particular person’s cognition, independent of any prior sequence, is "human authorship" (*pauruṣeyatva*);
the meaning is "by virtue of being devoid of that.
[Thus, it refers to one] from whom all suspicion of defect has been dispelled by that [authorlessness].
By virtue of being a cognizer, it is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by itself;
for validity consists precisely in the cognition of an object not previously apprehended and not sublated,
and that [validity] is established through internal perception— this is the meaning.

Because an entity is independent with respect to its own effect— the cognition [of it]; and even if it is independent regarding cognition, it is dependent upon perception for its own production, and thus, due to contradiction with that [perception], its invalidity is characterized by non-production— if this is argued, we say no, because there is no opposition to its producer.

For conventional knowledge derived from scripture does not undermine the validity of perception, such that [perception] would cease to exist due to the absence of its cause; rather, it is [perception’s] ultimate validity [that is not undermined].

Nor is that [scriptural knowledge] the producer of that [ultimate perception], since we observe the arising of knowledge of reality even from conventional means of valid cognition that possess only non-ultimate validity.
And likewise, even other properties such as shortness and length, when superimposed upon a phoneme (*varṇa*), serve as causes for the comprehension of the [intended] reality.
For ordinary people, when understanding an elephant or a tree from the words "nāga" or "naga," do not become deluded.
Nor is it the case that—
FN: 1. He refutes what was previously stated regarding the figurative nature [of the meaning]:
"It is not logical for a sentence that has another purpose to have its own literal meaning be figurative;
for it has been said: 'In an injunction...'"
FN: It is established in the Śābara-bhāṣya that in an injunctive word, the secondary indicated meaning (lakṣya) is not the primary meaning of the word.

Nor [is this contradicted] by the acceptance of possessive indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*)—as in "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*)—where [the word *soma*] implies "that which possesses soma."

Furthermore, it should not be argued that this [interpretation] is incorrect because those who maintain the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in passages such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) accept a partial indication (*bhāgalakṣaṇā*).

This is because the intention is that a sentence possessing a specific purport— whether it be equal to an injunction or equal to that [identity statement]— cannot be led elsewhere to support some minor detail.
The intention here is that accomplishment [of the goal] must be accepted even without an intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Regarding the phrase "the other is the word-meaning" (*paraḥ śabdārthaḥ*):
being "senior" (*jyeṣṭhatva*) is the cause for that which is not required to be sublated, but it is not the cause for its being a sublater.
Because it is observed that the stronger cognition of silver is sublated by the weaker cognition of mother-of-pearl;
for if that [weaker cognition] were not sublated, the former could not have the nature of being a sublation of it.
[FN: 3. The cognition of mother-of-pearl consists in the sublation of the cognition of silver.]
Therefore, the meaning is that if it had not been sublated, then it would not have arisen;
for its non-arising follows from its arising [only as such].
And it has already been shown that the state of being a valid means of cognition in the ultimate sense does not depend [on anything else].
And likewise, there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage:

"In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when the officiating priests, having been mutually connected, exit the sacrificial hall, an expiation for the cause of separation is heard: 'If the Udgātṛ should be separated [from the others], one should perform the sacrifice without the sacrificial fee (adakṣiṇa).'"

If the *pratihartṛ* should be interrupted, [the rule states] "with a sacrifice where one's entire property is given as the sacrificial fee. In that case, when there is a sequential interruption by both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ*, and since a combination of two contradictory expiations is impossible, a doubt arises as to whether the former should be performed or the latter. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is:
"The former arises without subverting the latter, because it has not yet come into being."
"Because another [element] arises as non-different [from the preceding], it occurs without subverting the knowledge [of the former];
thus, 'the weakness of the preceding is like that of the original base' (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.2). Likewise: "In that case, let the superiority of the subsequent over the preceding indeed be recognized."
Where there might be the arising of cognitions that are mutually independent of one another.
Thus it is said. Furthermore,

even those who maintain that the self is the locus of the notion of "I" must not accept its ultimate reality, because there is the perception of it as localized— such as in the thought, "I am here in this very house, conscious"— despite [the claim that] it is all-pervading.
It is like the cognition of the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass appearing on the ground to one standing at the foot of great trees growing on high mountain peaks.
Nor is it correct to say that this limitation to a specific location is experienced as belonging to the body and not to the self;
for at that time, the cognition does not occur in the form "I [am limited]."
Or, if it were figurative, the term "not knowing" would not apply;

moreover, a word for one thing is used for another through connection with a quality perceived therein, and that is figurative where there is mutual agreement between the speaker and the listener, and that [figurative usage] is preceded by a cognition of difference.

For example, in the case of the *naiyamika-agnihotra*, the word *agnihotra* is used as a name for the ritual (*karman*) because it makes known the deity of the fire-oblation, as in the statement: "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati" (PMS 1.4.4).

In the case of the ritual belonging to the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana, whose distinction from other rites is established by a difference in context (*prakaraṇa*), the statement "He performs the Agnihotra for a month" (*māsam agnihotraṃ juhoti*) is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*) based on similarity with the goal (*sādhyasādṛśya*). [Note:

Since the distinction between rituals is established by the difference in context, and because it would be cumbersome to assume multiple primary powers (*śakti*) for the term *agnihotra*, the phrase "he offers like the Agnihotra" is figurative, based on similarity with the goal.]

In the case of a boy, the word "lion" [is applied] because of a difference established through experience; however, the primary referent of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is not one whose internal essence—the unique form—is clearly extracted and manifested. *FN:

2. "Nirluṭhita" means that which has been thoroughly extracted (*niṣkṛṣya*) and manifested (*luṭhitaḥ*), such that its internal essence (*garbhaḥ*), namely its unique form (*asādhāraṇākāraḥ*), is revealed; thus it is so described.*
And thus, the meaning is that there should be no dispute on this point:

[the self] is experienced as distinct from the body and so forth by virtue of being the embryo (garbha), such that the word "other" (*para*) would only be figurative (*gauṇa*) with respect to the body and the like.
And it is the established doctrine of the scriptures that,
because of the frequency of usage, a word appears as if it were its primary meaning; thus,
a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) is similar to the function of direct denotation (*śakti*).

It should be understood that even in a secondary (gauṇa) usage, there is no misconception of it being secondary due to its conventional rootedness (*nirūḍhatā*), just as in the case of the word "oil" (*taila*) applied to mustard seeds and the like.

Even in that case, once the difference between [the oil] and the oil produced from sesame is established, there is merely a misconception that mustard seeds and so forth are denoted by the word "oil";
however, there is no determination of non-difference between the two objects, namely, [sesame] oil and mustard oil.

Thus it is established that being secondary (gauṇatva) is pervaded by the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between the secondary and the primary for one who perceives both. Therefore, when this pervading discriminative knowledge is withdrawn, it also withdraws the state of being secondary. Furthermore, even though there is a difference between the bodies of a child and an old man, the recognition "I am that same person" regarding the single Self establishes its distinction from the body and other such things.
It should not be said that there is no experience of a self;
for this discussion indeed concerns investigators,
not ordinary people.
For even investigators, at the time of practical activity, do not transcend common worldly usage.
Indeed, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya will state immediately hereafter: "Because there is no distinction from cattle and the like.
Even outsiders have said: "Those who contemplate the scriptures indeed analyze in this manner, but not those who act upon them."

By process of elimination, we consider it logical that the common person, employing the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) whose object is the conscious self (*cidātman*) in the form "I am here in this house," imagines the self to be spatially limited due to the apprehension of its non-difference from the body and so forth—
just as space appears limited by adjuncts such as jars, water-pots, or flower-vessels. Furthermore,
it is not tenable to claim that the self is spatially limited like the body and other such things merely for the sake of validating the authority of the ego-sense.
In that case, would this [self] have the dimension of an atom or the dimension of the body?
If it had the dimension of an atom, then [the cognitions] "I am stout" and "I am tall" would not occur.
If, however, [the self] were of the same size as the body, it would follow that, being composed of parts, it is impermanent like the body itself.
Furthermore, in this view, would the collection of parts be conscious, or would each individual part be conscious?

If the position is that each part is conscious, then because there are many independent conscious entities, there would be no consensus; consequently, due to simultaneous actions in opposing directions, the body would be torn apart.
Alternatively, it would follow that there is no action [at all].
For if consciousness were inherent in the aggregate, then when one part is severed, a part of the conscious self would also be severed, and thus it would not perceive;
moreover, no such rule of mutual inseparability is observed among many parts.
If that very part which has disintegrated were absent at that time, then [the self] would not cognize;
even if the object of the "I"-conception (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is consciousness, its erroneous nature remains exactly as it was,
because that [self] appears as a stable entity while consciousnesses are unstable.
By this,
[the objection] that "I am fat," "I am another," "I am going," and so forth, are also explained as being cases of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Thus, when the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) has been rendered like a rotten gourd by the sequence of reasoning just described, the Blessed Śruti is able, without impediment, to negate the nature of the Self as consisting of agency, enjoyership, suffering, grief, and so forth— which had been attributed to it by that experience of "I.

Therefore, this is the detailed explanation of the nature, cause, and result of the notion of "I"— whose falsity is proclaimed by all disputants through the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa— beginning with the words "In one another," and so on.
And here, having superimposed "mutual identity" upon each respective substratum— such as the self and the body— one thinks, "I am this body," and so forth;
and the term "this" refers to the object in reality, not merely to its appearance.

Worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is the conventional practice of people; it consists of this designation "I am," as indicated by the word "iti," as well as the process of cognizing— by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— the various objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that are either conducive or adverse to the body and so forth, and subsequently engaging in their acquisition, avoidance, and so on.

"Having superimposed the attributes of one upon the other substratum"—that is, having superimposed the attributes of the body and so forth, such as birth, death, old age, and disease, upon the Self as the substratum (the locus) to which the body and so forth have been superimposed;

and likewise, having superimposed the attributes of the Self, such as consciousness and so forth, upon the body and so forth to which the nature of the Self has been superimposed—there arises the worldly usage and designation: "This is mine," [referring to] old age, death, sons, cattle, ownership, and so forth.
And that which is indicated by the word *iti*—namely, activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth—is consistent with that [superimposition].

Here, the agent who is inferred from the acts of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is the same; thus, it is logically established that "having superimposed [the object], one engages in empirical usage" (*adhyasya vyavahāraḥ*), by virtue of their having a common agent.
He clarifies that superimposition is the cause of empirical usage, as indicated by its occurring at a prior time: "empirical usage has false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) as its cause."
Superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); it has that [false knowledge] as its cause.
The meaning is that the existence or non-existence of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) follows the existence or non-existence of that [superimposition].
Having thus stated the nature and the result—empirical usage—of superimposition, he states its cause: "through the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) of one from the other."
The meaning is "due to the non-apprehension of distinction.
Now, one might ask: why not simply assume that there is no distinction at all, and thus no superimposition? To this he says: "Of the attribute and the substrate, which are absolutely distinct."

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the non-identity of two substrata (*dharmin*) is their distinction (*viveka*), and the non-confusion of their attributes (*dharma*) is their distinction.
This might be argued:
it is logical that there should be an illusion of identity based on the non-apprehension of the difference between two distinct, real entities.

Just as the delusion of identity with silver is based on the non-apprehension of the difference from the mother-of-pearl shell, here, however, there is no real entity such as the body that is absolutely distinct from the truly existent conscious self; therefore, how could there be a non-apprehension of difference from the conscious self, and how could there be a delusion of identity? To this he says: "having coupled the real and the unreal."
The construction is: "having superimposed [the one] due to a failure of discrimination.
The conscious self (*cidātman*) is real;
the intellect, the senses, the body, and so forth, are unreal.
Having coupled those two substrata— that is, having joined them into a pair— the meaning is that they are presented together as a pair.

Furthermore, since there is no ultimate union between that which exists conventionally and that which exists ultimately, the suffix *cvi* is employed in the sense of "the becoming of what was not [previously] so.

What is meant is this: because it is impossible to superimpose something that is not already perceived, the perception of the object to be superimposed is required, not its actual ontological existence.
This might be the case.

If there is a cognition of the object of superimposition, then there is the superimposition of what was previously seen; and if there is the cognition based on superimposition, then there is the cognition of the object of superimposition. Thus, a mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*) is unavoidable. To this, he says: "Innate" (*naisargika*). This conventional usage is natural and beginningless.
Because this conventional usage is beginningless, it is stated that its cause—superimposition—is also beginningless.

Furthermore, since the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and so forth—which are presented by each preceding false cognition—are utilized for each subsequent superimposition, there is no mutual dependence (parasparāśrayatva) because of this beginninglessness, just like the relationship between a seed and a sprout; such is the meaning.
This might be argued:
"Granted that mere prior cognition is indeed useful for a superimposition,"
But that which is being perceived does not possess ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*).
Indeed, perception itself is impossible for the body, the senses, and so forth, which are absolutely non-existent and comparable to a lotus in the sky.

For even the consciousness-self (*cidātman*) has existence solely insofar as it is manifest; its existence is not something distinct from that manifestation, nor is it the inherence in a universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya-samavāya*), nor is it the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*).
Because this would entail the consequence of duality;
and because, if one were to postulate another existence or another causal efficiency for existence and causal efficiency themselves, it would lead to an infinite regress,
existence must be admitted as nothing other than the state of being manifest.
And thus, the body and so forth are not non-existent because they are manifest, like the conscious self (cidātman).
Or, if they were non-existent, they would not be manifest; so how could there be a union between the real and the unreal?
Or, in the absence of that [non-apprehension of difference], for whom and from what source could there be non-apprehension of difference?
And in the impossibility of that, how could there be superimposition (*adhyāsa*)? Bearing this intention in mind, the objector says: "What is this so-called superimposition?
The word "what" (*kaḥ*) is used here in the sense of an objection.

The respondent, while explaining the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as established in common worldly experience, refutes the objection: It is said that superimposition is the appearance (*avabhāsa*) of something previously perceived in another [object], which is either obscured (*avasanna*) or disparaged (*avamata*).
Its obscuration or disparagement consists in its being sublated by another cognition.
By this much, it has been stated that this is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
This is its further explanation, beginning with the words "the appearance of what was previously seen" (*pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa*).
The appearance of what was previously seen is "the appearance of what was previously seen."

Furthermore, a false cognition does not occur without a pair consisting of the object of superimposition and that which is superimposed; thus, by the mention of "previously seen," it brings forward the unreal thing to be superimposed.
And for that [previously seen thing], its mere state of having been seen is what is required, not its actual existence as a real entity—this is the purpose of the term "seen.
Nevertheless, since a presently occurring "seen" or perception is not useful for superimposition, the word "previous" was used.
And that [silver], though existing as a real entity in its own nature when previously perceived, is unreal because it is indefinable (*anirvācya*) by virtue of being superimposed.
He states that the object of superimposition is real with the words "elsewhere" (*paratra*):
"elsewhere," namely in the mother-of-pearl and so forth, which is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Thus, by this, the pairing of truth and falsehood has been stated.
It might be argued that the definition— "the appearance of what was previously perceived elsewhere"— is not a valid definition.
Because it is over-extensive;
for there is indeed an appearance elsewhere, in a brindled cow, of the "cowness" previously perceived in a healthy cow.
There is [this point]: this example is intended when one wishes to express that the locus (*āśraya*) is the appearance of another's attributes (*paradharmāvabhāsa*);
however, it should be understood that the previous [example] was intended with reference to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of an attribute from a previously perceived object onto another locus.
Furthermore, the appearance (*avabhāsa*) of Devadatta—who was previously seen in Pāṭaliputra—in another place, namely Māhiṣmatī, is correct.

[Regarding the objection: "But surely, since the etymology of *avabhāsa* is 'an appearance that is disregarded' (*avamato bhāsaḥ*), how can you claim over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the examples cited?"—in response to one who says this, he states: "And the word *avabhāsa*... [etc.]
By this, the view of certain scholars—that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that because it was stated that the term "previously seen" (*pūrvadṛṣṭa*) refers to the indescribable falsehood (*anirvācyānṛta*), the mention of over-extension in that case is inconsistent;
for it should be understood that such a meaning is expressed by the word "recollection" (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, the term *pada* is well-established even in the sense of a "condition" (*pratyaya*), as in the expressions "the appearance of blue" or "the appearance of yellow"; therefore, he says "having the form of memory" (*smṛtirūpa*).
Its form is like that of memory; thus, it is "having the form of memory."
Furthermore, having a non-present object is the nature of memory,
whereas recognition (pratyabhijñāna) having a present object is valid; thus, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti),
nor is there any under-extension (avyāpti).
Dream-cognition, too, is an error regarding memory; that is to say,
it is the superimposition of another form upon that which is being remembered.
Because form (rūpa) is of such a nature;

for even here, when a father or the like is being remembered, due to the influence of a lapse in consciousness (nidropaplava), there is no awareness of their absence, and thus there is a superimposition (samāropa) upon them of the very proximity of place and time that was previously perceived.
This same definition should also be applied here to the cases: "the conch is yellow" and "jaggery is bitter.
For instance, one experiences yellowness—which resides in the bile-substance (pitta-dravya) that has come into contact with the clear rays of the eye issuing outward—as being devoid of bile;
and one experiences the conch as having its whiteness obscured by a defect, rather than experiencing it as a mere substance.
And not perceiving the connection between yellowness and the conch shell,

one superimposes the previously perceived grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— based on the similarity of not grasping that connection— upon yellowness and the nature of being a conch shell, as in cases such as "the mass of gold is yellow" or "the *bilva* fruit is yellow," and says, "The conch shell is yellow. By this, the cognition "the molasses is bitter" is also explained.

Thus, when clear surfaces such as mirrors or water are facing the perceiving person, the visual light, though it strikes them, is turned back against its current by the more powerful solar light; this [visual light], having come into contact with the face,
causes the face to be perceived, yet— due to a defect— it fails to perceive the face’s actual location and its non-facing orientation.
The state (*tattā*) of that whose location is precisely the same as the location of the previously perceived objects facing [the mirror], namely water and so forth;
thus, the meaning is that there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of those [objects] upon the face and so on.

Because it superimposes upon the face the state of being in the same region as the mirror-water and the quality of facing it, the delusion of a reflection (*pratibimba-vibhrama*) is also characterized.

By this, the definition should be applied accordingly to other delusions such as the double moon, confusion of directions, the fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), the city of the Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*), and the snake in a bamboo stalk.
What is meant is this: existence is not merely the state of appearing.
By means of which the body, the sense organs, and so forth would have existence through their being manifest;

for it is not the case that ropes and the like, or crystals and the like, do not appear as having the nature of snakes and so forth, or as possessing qualities such as redness; nor, when they do appear in such a way, do they become identical with or possess the properties of those [illusory appearances].

If that were so, one who proceeds with the conviction, "This is a mass of mirages in the desert," or "This is the Mandākinī descended near the ocean, with its garland of surging, high, and low waves," would quench his thirst by drinking that water.
Therefore, even against one's will, one must not admit that what is superimposed possesses real existence merely because it appears.

Nor is it correct to argue that water in the form of a mirage is non-existent while being ultimately real in its own nature, whereas the body, senses, and so forth are non-existent even in their own nature; for since they are beyond the range of experience, how could they be superimposed? For if that which is non-existent is not within the range of experience, then how is it that non-existent things such as mirages [appear]?
Nor do things exist by way of their own intrinsic nature even as the nature of water and so forth.

If it should be argued that there is no such thing as non-existence distinct from existence, but rather that existence itself is non-existence insofar as it has the nature of another entity, while it is existence in its own nature;

As they have said: "Non-existence is indeed another state of being (bhāvāntara), for [the absence of a jar] in such cases as 'there is no jar here' consists in the very nature of the locus, namely the bare ground; otherwise, it would be impossible to define."
Likewise, the non-existence of rays in the form of water is simply because they are rays;
it is with this in mind that it was said: "But by some particular perspective. [The phrase] "by some particular perspective" [is explained as follows].
Consequently, because it is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*),
it would be appropriate for this [object] to come within the scope of experience by way of being expressible.
Furthermore, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is absolutely non-existent, devoid of all capacity, and lacks any reality, how could it be an object of experience,
or how could it be superimposed upon the conscious self (*cidātman*)?
Nor is it the case that...
Note: By the passage beginning with "Furthermore, because the fivefold proliferation (*prapañca*) is absolutely non-existent," the doctrine of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) has been refuted.
Now, he refutes the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) with the words "nor [is it]...
For the proponents of emptiness indeed admit that even emptiness appears.
Furthermore, through the power of preceding cognitions possessing a similar form, cognition acquires a unique, specific nature; it is precisely this cognition that manifests the non-existent.

Nor should it be argued that, according to their view, there would be a consequence of universal distrust because even the cognition manifesting the non-existent is itself empty, for they accept that even cognition possesses its existence dependent upon a preceding cognition.

Even though the object lacks all causal capacity, it is cognition itself that—having arisen with a specific nature established through its own power of self-awareness and without requiring an external example—effects the manifestation of what is non-existent.

[Objection: If it is argued that, according to the Buddhist view, it is ignorance (*avidyā*) that manifests the non-existent, [we reply: that very power of cognition to manifest the non-existent is indeed what constitutes its ignorance; thus, it is the power to manifest the real (*sat*) that is its ignorance. This is correct.
Since this power of consciousness to manifest the non-existent exists, what, then, is its object?
If it is argued that it is "the non-existent," is this its product or its object of cognition?
It cannot first be an effect,
because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to have reality; nor can it be something to be made known.
Let there be no causal efficiency for that which is non-existent,
because it lacks the requisite capacity.

If it is asked, "Why then should [the object] not be that which is made known by the capacity (*śaktijñāpya*)?"—it must be stated that being made known by a capacity consists in possessing a state of being made known (*jñāpyatā*) as defined by a capacity-to-make-known (*jñāpakatā*) residing in the capacity.

And since no cognition other than the cognition of the substratum of the capacity is perceived, that [state of being made known] is impossible; thus he says: "because of the non-perception of another cognition. [Otherwise, there would be] an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

FN: 8—If it is argued that another cognition (*jñānāntara*) perceives [the first], even so, since that too must function as a cognizer, there would be a requirement for yet another cognition, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*); this is the meaning. And because of this [regress]:
if it is claimed that the very nature of consciousness itself is the manifestation of the non-existent, [then...]
But what is this relationship between the existent and the non-existent?
If it is argued that the relationship of the existent—namely, cognition—with the non-existent consists in its being defined in dependence upon the non-existent, then alas!
how utterly exhausted must this poor cognition be, since even when the object is non-existent, its definition still persists.
And the condition (pratyaya) does not impart anything to that [non-existent],
because it is impossible for what is non-existent to be a substratum.

If it is argued that the condition itself possesses this nature— namely, that a condition does not manifest without the non-existent— and that nothing of its own belongs to the condition dependent upon the non-existent;

Oh, how great is this partiality for the false! For this [invariable concomitance] is an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) that arises from what is not its cause and whose nature is not that [of the probandum].
[Note: 1. The basis of invariable concomitance must be stated as either the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or identity of nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*);
the meaning is that both are impossible according to the sequence already stated.]
"Conditioned by necessity.
Therefore, since the body, sense organs, and so forth are absolutely non-existent and devoid of reality, they cannot possibly be objects of experience.
To this we reply:
FN: 2—When the proponent of existence (sadvādin) has thus argued that in every case an object appears as something truly existent, the respondent says: "To this we reply.

If that which lacks reality (*nistattva*) were not within the range of experience, then would even mirage-rays (*marīcayaḥ*) possess reality (*satattva*) in the form of water, such that they could become objects of experience?

They do not exist as such; for, even if it were granted by the proponent of existence (*sadvādin*) that rays of light do not exist as water, this would not result in the abandonment of our own tenet (*siddhānta*). This is because— [Note: 3. Now, if it is argued that if the non-existence of rays of light as water is admitted by the proponent of existence, then there is a loss of one's own tenet, we say: no.]

The intention is that the form of a mirage is non-existent in the form of water; if the form of the mirage were existent as the water perceived by you, it would not be sublated because of its reality,
[but it is sublated] because of its non-existence.
The reality of entities is twofold: existence and non-existence.
Of these, the former is intrinsic, while the latter is extrinsic.
As they have said: "In an entity that is eternally of the nature of both being and non-being through its own form and the form of others, some aspect is known by some at some time, and not [others]."
Thus [it is said].
Now, why is this?— the proponent of the established doctrine raises this doubt with the words "tat kiṃ" (why is this?).

The intention is that, because it would be apprehended as having such a cognition [of water] as its object, the form of the non-existent mirage-water would not be sublated by its being real. [Objection:
The cognition appearing as water in mirages has reality as its object;
and thus, being correct, it is neither erroneous nor subject to sublation.
The proponent of the theory of the six real entities (ṣaḍsadvādī) replies:
"In this case," the water in its true nature does not appear in the illusion;
rather, it appears as something else that has the nature of water.
Therefore, the acceptance that its sublation is logically established is justified.
Indeed, it would not be sublated if one were to perceive the rays of light—which do not have the nature of water—as having the nature of non-water;
but perceiving them as having the nature of water, how could one be non-deluded?

Or how is it not to be contradicted?—the proponent of the theory of the appearance of the indeterminable (anirvacanīyakhyāti) replies: As for what you said—that the rays of light appear as something else through the nature of a superimposed entity—that is now examined as follows: that [appearance] must be either real...
He says "no" with the word "hanta": "Alas!
The nature of water in mirages, which are essentially the absence of water, is certainly not real;
for since they are non-different from the absence of water, it is logically impossible for them to possess the nature of water."
Nor is it non-existent.
If you argue that it is not existent but rather simply non-existent (*asat*), then it must be stated whether that non-existence is a mere void (*tuccha*) or something distinct from existence.
It cannot be the first case, because that would contradict your own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case]: "For it is indeed another entity... Therefore, the theory of real manifestation (*satkhyāti*) is not accepted. For those who assert that "the non-existence of one entity is simply another entity," saying, "Non-existence is a distinct absence; there is no other [non-existence], because it cannot be defined."
Moreover, a superimposed form is not a separate entity;
for it must be either the mirage itself or the water found in the Ganges and other such rivers.
In the former case, the cognition would be "rays," not "water";
but in the latter case, it would be "water in the Ganges."
But it is not "here" [in this specific place].

When the distinction of location is not remembered, there may be the cognition "water," but not "here. [This refutes the theory of *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent). "Not this" [refutes the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (the apprehension of something as otherwise)].
Nor is it appropriate to claim that this [object] is absolutely non-existent, being a mere falsehood whose entire nature has been discarded;
for, as was stated above, such a thing cannot possibly be an object of experience.
[The proponent of the established doctrine concludes: "Therefore... [as indicated by the footnote].

Therefore, because of their mutual contradiction, it cannot be real, nor unreal, nor both real and unreal; thus, one must accept that the water superimposed upon the rays of light is simply indeterminable (anirvācya).
Thus, by this sequence, the water superimposed [upon the mirage] appears like real water;
for that very reason, it seems as if previously seen.
But in reality, it is neither water nor was it previously seen.
However, falsehood is that which is indefinable (*anirvācya*).
And thus, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, is also indefinable;
it is logical that even though it is unprecedented, it is superimposed upon the other—the conscious Self—as if presented by previous false cognitions.

This is because it possesses the characteristics of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Furthermore, the sublation of the phenomenal world consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, will be established later.

The conscious Self (*cidātman*), however, is the object of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas; its nature is determined as pure, awakened, and liberated by means of reasoning that is rooted in and not opposed to them. It is to be defined as existing (*sattvena*) alone.

Its existence is simply its own uncontradicted self-luminosity; and that is the very nature of the conscious self, not something distinct from it such as the inherence in the universal of existence or causal efficiency— thus all is clear.

Moreover, this superimposition (*adhyāsa*) characterized in such a manner is accepted as being indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) by all investigators; there is disagreement only regarding its specific nature. To confirm its indeterminability, he says: "Some describe it as the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another. [The phrase] "of the attributes of another" [is used].
Of the silver that is the nature of cognition—
that is, of the form of cognition—
there is a superimposition elsewhere, namely, upon the external object.
In the Sautrāntika system, an external object exists as a reality, and the form of cognition is superimposed upon it;
even for the Vijñānavādins, although no external object exists as a reality, [the same applies].
Nevertheless, the external world is false, being superimposed by the impressions of beginningless ignorance;
therein, the form of cognition is superimposed.
And the justification is this: it is a general rule that whatever form is established through experience must be accepted as being exactly of that nature.
Furthermore, its alteration occurs by virtue of a powerful subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*);

the point is this: in the [erroneous] perception "this is silver," an identity (*tādātmya*) having silver as its relatum (*anuyogika*) and "this-ness" (*idantva*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) appears;
when it is stated "this is not silver," that very [identity] becomes subverted.
This is because of the rule: "The counter-positive and its absence share the same status regarding presence and absence.

When there is no co-occurrence with the negative particle (*nañ*), whatever possession of a property delimited by a certain attribute and delimited by a certain relation exists in a locus delimited by that attribute;

when there is co-occurrence with the negative particle, there is the absence of that very thing, characterized by a counter-positiveness delimited by that same attribute and delimited by that same relation, in that locus delimited by that same attribute.
The meaning is that it is "cognized";
therefore, in the case of the cognition "this is not silver," it is only the "this-ness" (*idantā*) appearing as silver that is sublated, and not the silver itself.
Thus, according to this view, the cognition "I am silver" is a valid cognition (*pramā*); such is the intended sense.

Furthermore, since the subverting cognition "this is not silver" is adequately accounted for by the sublation of the mere "this-ness" (idantā) alone, it is not appropriate for it to have silver as its object.
For if the substrate (dharmin), namely silver, were sublated, both the silver and its attribute—this-ness—would have to be sublated;
therefore, it is better that only this-ness, which is its attribute, be sublated, rather than the silver itself, which is the substrate.
And thus, since silver, though sublated externally, is established by implication within internal cognition, the superimposition of the form of cognition upon the external world is proven.

However, some, dissatisfied with the theory of the manifestation of the form of cognition (*jñānākārakhyāti*), say: "Error consists in the non-apprehension of the distinction between that which is superimposed and that upon which it is superimposed.

They state the reason for their dissatisfaction as follows: "The fact that silver and so forth possess the nature of a cognition's form must be established either through direct experience (*anubhava*) or through inference (*anumāna*)."
In that regard, the inference [is as follows]:
"Because they are perceived together, the non-difference of the means of cognition (*mīti*) and the object of cognition (*meyya*) is not established. [End of footnote 2]
The meaning is that [the cognition] is established otherwise because it is caused by the relationship between the means and the end (*upāyopeyabhāva*).
This will be refuted later.
Furthermore, the experience would have to be either a cognition of silver, or—
Or it is a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).
First of all, it is not the experience of silver;
for that [experience] makes known the silver as the locus of the notion "this," but not as something internal.
For at that time, there would be the thought "I," because [the cognition] is not distinct from the cognizer's own awareness;
the erroneous consciousness determines its own internal form as being external.

And if it is argued that, in this way, it is not the object of the locus of "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra), but rather its status as having the form of cognition is to be understood through a subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya), then, alas, let your honor examine that subverting cognition!
Does the subverting cognition distinguish the substance present before one from silver, or does it also demonstrate that this [silver] has the nature of a form of cognition?
In this regard, the "Beloved of the Gods" (the fool), whose wisdom is truly praiseworthy, asserts that the function of the subverting cognition is to demonstrate its being a form of cognition.
As for its being present before one...

[Note: It has already been stated that [the cognition] does not manifest the form of the object directly (*sākṣāt*). He further states—beginning with the words "purovartitve" (if it were present before one)—that even the form of the object as belonging to the cognition is not established.
[Objection: If it is argued that the cognition possesses the form of the object by implication (*arthāt*) because of its negation [of the external object], [we reply: no.
Regarding what was stated—that which is sublated externally is established in another object—that too is possible through another means; thus he says, "due to non-proximity" (*asaṃnidhānāt*).
The meaning is that it may also exist in another location.

Because it is denied that [the object] is grasped, it does not exist in proximity; moreover, how could there be an absolute proximity of this [object] to the cognizer, given that its nature consists of the cognizer? [The Mīmāṃsaka replies to the argument regarding] "lightness" (lāghava) with the words "And not... (na ca).
The underlying intention is that, since the sublation of mere conventional usage is possible, there is no parsimony [of assumptions] resulting from the sublation of the object itself.
Furthermore, this is neither a negation of the silver nor of its "this-ness" (idantā).
Rather, it is the practical activity regarding silver that is occasioned by the non-apprehension of the distinction [between the two].
Nor is it the case that silver itself is superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl by the cognition of silver;
for it is not logical that the manifestation of silver should have the mother-of-pearl as its objective support, because that would contradict experience.
Indeed,
an object of cognition is not such by its mere existence alone.
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
for since all objects are indistinguishable in terms of their existence, it would follow that they must all equally serve as cognitive objects (*ālambana*).
Nor is it the cause...
FN: This means "by way of awakening the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of the cognition of silver.
Because the sense faculties and so forth are also causes [of cognition], the meaning of the "objective support" (*ālambana*) is simply the state of appearing [in consciousness].

And since it is not the case that mother-of-pearl appears in the cognition of silver— given that [the opponent] accepts two cognitions, namely one having "this" as its object and one having silver as its object—
how then can [mother-of-pearl] be the objective support?
FN: 9. By this, the superimposition of an object (*arthādhyāsa*) is refuted.
Or, if its manifestation is admitted, how could there not be a contradiction with experience? FN: 10.
He says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that the cognition "this is silver" is not false.
Moreover, since the capacity of the sense organs and other factors to produce correct cognition has been observed, how could false cognition arise from them?
If it is argued that these same factors, when accompanied by defects (*doṣa*), possess the capacity for false perception, we say no;
for defects function merely as causes that obstruct the capacity to produce the [intended] effect.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that a banyan sprout could arise even from a defective *kuṭaja* seed.
Furthermore, if cognitions were to deviate from their own objects, there would be the consequence of a total lack of confidence in all cognition whatsoever.
Therefore, one must maintain that all cognition is valid.
FN: If it is argued that if all cognitions were valid, there would be no error at all in the case cited, he states his own view in response: "And thus...
And thus, "silver" and "this" are two cognitions consisting of memory and direct experience, respectively.
In this context, "this" refers to the apprehension of the mere substance present before one;
because, due to a defect, the specific universal of "mother-of-pearl-ness" residing therein is not apprehended,
that mere [substance], once grasped, produces a memory of silver through the process of awakening latent impressions by virtue of its similarity.
And that [cognition] has the nature of manifesting as "this is what was grasped";
the point is that recollection has as its object a previous experience.
Although its nature is that of apprehension, due to the influence of a defect and the loss of the aspect of "having been apprehended," it remains as mere apprehension.

Thus, because there is a non-apprehension of the mutual difference— both in terms of essential nature and object— between the memory of silver and the apprehension of the mere substance present before one, [the error arises] through its similarity to a cognition whose object is nearby silver.

In this case, the similarity of that cognition is as follows: just as the cognition "this is silver" does not grasp the non-relation between "this" and the "silver," because the two are [in fact] related;
so too these two—recollection and perception—[do not grasp] the difference residing within themselves.
They do not indicate their own non-connection with their respective objects. Rather,
by virtue of their similarity to a cognition whose object is silver,
both the memory and the perception— though distinct as "this" and "silver"— bring about the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In some cases, however, there is indeed the apprehension of a mutual superimposition of difference,

as in the case of "the conch is yellow. For here, the yellowness of the bile-substance— which exists within the ocular rays as they exit externally— is apprehended, just like the transparency of glass, while the bile itself is not apprehended.

Even a conch shell, due to the influence of defects, is perceived merely in its own form, devoid of its white quality. Therefore, because there is a similarity consisting in the non-apprehension of the non-connection between these two—the quality and the possessor of the quality—there arises, through no distinction from the cognition of a yellow mass of gold, the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, since this non-difference is brought about by the non-apprehension of difference, it is logical that the corrective cognition "this is not [that]" functions as a sublater of that [erroneous] usage.
And once that [validity] is established, it is also proven— just as is well known in the world— that the preceding cognition was erroneous.
Therefore, [cognitions] correspond to their objects.
All cognitions are erroneous and characterized by doubt and delusion, because they are cognitions, like the cognition of a jar or similar objects.
This has been stated as "the superimposition of one thing upon another" (*yatra yadadhyāsaḥ*).

The common worldly understanding that there is a superimposition of silver and the like upon mother-of-pearl and the like is not based on the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), but rather on the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between the perceived silver and its recollection— once the aspect of having been perceived has been lost— and the mere object standing before one, characterized simply by "this-ness," and between the cognition of those two.
Error is based on the non-apprehension of that [difference].
And "erroneousness" consists in the designation of mutual coreferentiality between apprehension and recollection, as well as the practical activity regarding silver.
Others, however, being dissatisfied even with this [explanation], [state as follows:]...
Wherever there is a superimposition of one thing upon another, they describe that as the attribution of contrary attributes to the very object [upon which it is superimposed].

Here, the underlying intention is this: it is a matter of common experience for everyone that a person seeking silver acts toward a substance standing before them and employs a grammatical co-referential designation (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on the cognition "this is silver.
This [phenomenon] cannot possibly arise merely from the non-apprehension of the mutual difference between perception and memory, and between their respective objects.
For the linguistic usage and designation of a conscious being are based on apprehension; how could these arise from mere non-apprehension?

But was it not said that they do not arise from mere non-apprehension, but rather from apprehension and recollection themselves when their difference—both in terms of intrinsic nature and object—is not grasped?

They bring about the linguistic usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by means of their similarity to the cognition of silver that stands before one in a veridical manner.
Now, is this similarity to the veridical cognition the cause for the engagement in such linguistic usage when it is being apprehended,
or even when it is not being apprehended, but exists merely by its presence?

Even if there is apprehension, it is either the apprehension that "there is a similarity between these two cognitions, namely the cognition of this [shell] and the cognition of silver," or the apprehension that "there is a non-apprehension of the mutual difference between these two [cognitions] themselves, both in their own nature and in their objects. In that case,
the cognition "it is similar to a correct cognition" does not, like a correct cognition, prompt practical activity.
The cognition "the gavaya is not like a cow" does not prompt one who seeks a cow toward the gavaya;
however, the cognition "there is a non-apprehension of the difference between these two" is contradicted,
for when there is a non-apprehension of difference, the thought "between these two" cannot occur.

In the case of these two, there is the apprehension [of the object] and the non-apprehension of difference; therefore, it must be said that the non-apprehension of difference, by its mere existence, serves as the cause for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) even while remaining unapprehended.

In this regard, is this [non-apprehension] the cause of worldly transaction through the process of generating a superimposition (*āropa*), or rather, is it so by itself without having generated a superimposition?

We, however, observe that because it is untenable for the activity of volition (*cetanā*) to be preceded by [actual] knowledge, it occurs precisely through the sequence of generating a superimposed cognition (*āropa-jñāna*).
[Objection: It is true that the activity of volition is not preceded by ignorance; rather, it is preceded by the grasping and recollection of distinctions that were not previously cognized.
Not so;
for the mere recollection of the referent of the nominal stem "silver" (rajata) is not what is required for purposeful action.
Indeed, there is no dispute that the activity of those seeking silver is directed toward that which is the locus of the notion "this" (idam).
And how could this [person] proceed toward the locus of the notion "this" if he did not desire it?
To desire one thing and do another is a contradiction.
Furthermore, if he did not know that the locus of the notion "this" was silver, how could one desiring silver desire it?

If one were to say, "Because it is not apprehended as being otherwise," he should be answered: "Then, because it is not apprehended as being such [as it is], why would one not remain indifferent toward it?

Thus, this person, being pulled from both sides by grasping (*upādāna*) and indifference (*upekṣā*), is unsettled; yet, through the superimposition (*samāropa*) of silver upon that which is the locus of the notion "this," he is established precisely in grasping. Therefore, the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) is the cause for the engagement of a conscious agent by way of producing a superimposition.
For instance, having superimposed silverness upon the locus of the "this" through the non-apprehension of their difference,
and having reflected upon the fact that what belongs to that class is a cause of assistance,
one infers silverness in the locus of the "this" by virtue of its belonging to that same class.
Thus, the sequence— that one acts because of that [desire for silver]— is established.
Furthermore, a memory of silver standing apart [from the object] cannot lead to the inference that the substrate of the "this" (the shell) is the cause of assistance [to the silver],
because the reason (silver-ness) lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Indeed, it is the perception of one part that leads to inference, not the perception of many parts. As Śabarasvāmin has said: "For a person who knows the relationship between the probandum and the probans, the cognition of the mark—which is one part of the qualified property—arising from the perception of one part of the subject which possesses that qualified property, is inference."
"Because of the perception of one part of that which has a known connection.
However, in the case of superimposition (*samāropa*), there is indeed the perception of one part.
Thus it is established that this cognition of silver and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, [is a case of superimposition].
It has as its object the thing present before one, because it invariably induces activity toward silver or the like in one who desires such;

for whatever cognition invariably induces a person desiring a certain object toward a particular locus, that cognition has that object as its domain, just like the well-established cognition of real silver acknowledged by both parties.
And this is so; therefore, it is thus.
As for what was said—that because it does not appear [as such], the mother-of-pearl is not the objective support (ālambana)—[that is incorrect].

In this regard, may your honor be asked to explain: does the cognition "this is silver" lack an objective basis (*anālambanatva*) with respect to the shell-nature (*śuktikatva*), or rather with respect to the mere substance standing before one, which is white and lustrous?
If it is the shell-nature that lacks an objective basis, then that is certainly true.
For you, who assert that the subsequent [cognition] lacks an object, there is a contradiction with experience itself.
For instance, an experiencer perceiving "this is silver" points to the object present before him with his finger and so forth.
Moreover, it is observed that defective causes possess the capacity to produce a different effect by obstructing their usual effect.
Just as the seeds of cane burnt by a forest fire produce the stalks of plantains, and just as fire corrupted by *bhasmaka* bile causes the digestion of vast amounts of food; so too,
the inference of the reality of errors— which has its object sublated by direct perception— is a fallacy.
It is like the inference of heat from fire.
As for the objection that if false cognition were to deviate [from truth], there would be no confidence in any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
we have already refuted this by demonstrating— through the *nyāya*— that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) by virtue of being informative (*bodhakatva*), and not by virtue of non-deviation.

Note: It has been stated therein [in the *Kaṇikā*] that even for those [senses] that are errant—such as the eye and so forth with respect to white, blue, and other colors—their status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) exists by virtue of their being cognizers; this is not elaborated upon here. Furthermore, only a mere indication of the refutation of the "loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*) theory has been stated.
The detailed account, however, is to be understood from the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā*;
thus it has been said: "But others explain that where there is a superimposition of X upon Y, it is the attribution of contrary properties to that very [Y] itself.

The construction is as follows: where there is a superimposition of silver and so forth upon mother-of-pearl and so forth, it is the attribution of contrary properties—that is, the attribution of the property of being silver—to that very mother-of-pearl and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be disagreements among investigators, but what does this have to do with the present case? To this, he says: "In every respect, however, the attribution of the properties of one thing to another does not fail [to apply here].
The attribution of the properties of one thing to another...

FN: 1. The meaning of the term *avabhāsa* is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). This unreality of conceptual construction, which is its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*), shall be demonstrated below.

The meaning is that, because all investigators agree that the conceptualization of one thing as having the attributes of another necessarily involves being inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*), this inexpressibility is an established tenet (*siddhānta*) across all systems.

The point is that even those who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*) must accept this out of necessity, due to their attachment to the rules governing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), designation, and practical activity.
This unreality is not only established for investigators; [it is also accepted by others].
Moreover, he says that this applies even to worldly people: "And thus there is experience in the world—namely, that a mother-of-pearl shell appears like silver.
The remainder of the sentence is: "but it is not [actually] silver.
This might be so.
The delusion that one thing has the nature of another is established in common experience;

however, since the delusion of difference in that which is single and non-different is not observed, [the author] says—referring to how there could be a delusion of difference among individual souls (jīvas) who are non-different from the Self—"as the single moon appears as if accompanied by a second. Furthermore, he raises an objection regarding superimposition upon the conscious Self: "But how can there be a superimposition of objects and their attributes upon the inner Self, which is not an object?"

The meaning is this: does the conscious self (cidātman) manifest or not? If it does not manifest, how can there be a superimposition (adhyāsa) upon it of the object and its attributes? Indeed, the attribution of silver or its attributes to a substance standing before one is not possible if that substance is not appearing [to consciousness].
Or, even if it appears [in cognition], it is not tenable that this self is insentient (*jaḍa*) like a jar or other objects, having its manifestation dependent on something else.
Indeed, it cannot be both the agent and the object of an action, because of the contradiction involved.

Note: If it were stated that "the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root," then in cases such as *gacchati* ("he goes"), since the result of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) inheres not only in the village but also in Caitra, the undesirable consequence would follow that one could say *caitraścaivaṃ gacchati* ("Caitra himself goes [as an object]").
Therefore, the meaning is that the state of being an object consists precisely in possessing a result of an action that inheres in another (*parasamavetakriyāphalaśālitvam*).
For an object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit of an action inhering in another;
however, the action of knowing does not inhere in another, so how could there be an object in this case?
Nor can that very [action] be both self and other, because of contradiction.
But if one accepts that [the self] inheres in another self, it follows that the self which is the object of cognition would itself be non-self;
