thus, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of "that [self] belonging to that [other self].
This might be argued:
The self, although insentient and appearing in all cognitions of objects, is only the agent and not the object,

because it lacks the possession of a fruit of action inhering in another, just like Caitra. For instance, when Caitra reaches a city through an action inherent in Caitra— an action that inheres in both [agent and object]— the city alone possesses the status of the object (*karman*).
This is because it possesses the fruit of an action inherent in another,
and not because Caitra possesses the fruit of his own action, since the action of going is inherent in Caitra; therefore, that [objection] is not valid.
Because it contradicts scripture (*śruti*).

For it is heard [in scripture]: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*). And this is logically consistent; for instance, as for this result which is the manifestation of an object—in which both the object and the Self shine forth—is that [result] insentient or self-luminous?

If the object and the self were both insentient (*jaḍa*), then because there would be no distinction between them, what could manifest in what? Consequently, the entire world would fall into blindness.
And thus goes the proverb:
"Like one blind person clinging to another who is blind, there is a fall at every step.
Nor should it be argued that consciousness, like the eye and other sense organs, makes known both the object and itself by remaining hidden within.
For making known is the production of knowledge; and knowledge, once produced, being insentient, cannot avoid the aforementioned defect.
Thus, each subsequent cognition would likewise be insentient, leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, consciousness must be understood as having a manifestation that is not dependent on another. [Regarding the objection: "Let consciousness have a manifestation independent of another;
why might the self not be insentient?"—the proponent of the self's self-luminosity says: "Even so... [End of footnote].
Even so, what follows from this regarding the object and the self, both of which are insentient by nature?
This follows: that their consciousness is non-insentient. [Note:

Even though consciousness pertaining to the relation between the object and the self is non-insentient, the establishment of the manifestness of the object and the self is not achieved; it is like a father’s lack of learning despite having a learned son. To address this, he asks: "What then? [This refers to the objection that the manifestness of the object and the self is not established merely by the non-insentience of their consciousness.]
If it is argued that "just as the son is learned, so too must the father be learned," and that this is the very nature of consciousness—
which is self-luminous— to be related to both the object and the self, then alas! It would follow that for the learned son as well, it is his very nature to be related to his father.

FN: 2. The point is this: just as consciousness is connected by its very nature [to the object], so too is the state of being produced (janyatva) residing in the son connected to the state of being a progenitor (janakatva) residing in the father.
It is the same.

If it is argued that the illumination of consciousness occurs simultaneously with the illumination of the object and its self, and not without the illumination of the object and its self—that is its very nature—then...
In that case, are the manifestation of consciousness and the manifestation of the object-self distinct from consciousness?
And if so, it follows that consciousness is not self-luminous,
nor is there a manifestation of the object-self within consciousness.
Now, as for the claim that "the manifestation of consciousness and the manifestation of the object are not distinct from consciousness,"

They two are consciousness itself. If this is so, then what is meant by saying that consciousness, the self, and the object arise together is precisely what is meant by saying that consciousness, the object, and the self are manifested together. [Note: If one does not admit a manifestation distinct from consciousness, it would amount to saying that consciousness, the object, and the self manifest together; and in that case, the logic of the "son's scholarship" maxim would apply.]
And thus, the intended meaning is not established.
[The author] says "nor" (*na ca*) because the coexistence of cognition and its object is subject to deviation;
for there is no coexistence with the object even in the case of cognitions whose objects are past or future.
If it is argued that there is a coexistence with the object because they produce cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference regarding that object, we say no;
for, just as in the case of the cognition of the object itself, it is untenable for the cognitions of avoidance and so forth to have that [external] object as their domain.
If it is claimed that the cognitions of avoidance and so forth have the object as their domain because they produce avoidance and so forth, [we reply...]
If it is argued that the cognition of an object has that [object] as its domain because it generates cognitions such as the apprehension or loss of the object,
then why should not the contact between the body and the active self be the cause of the body’s engagement with or withdrawal from the object, and thus there be the manifestation of the object?
If it is argued that the contact between the body and the self does not manifest the object because of its insentience (*jāḍya*), [then...]

But has it not been established that even though this [consciousness] is self-luminous, its manifestation occurs only within itself like that of a firefly, whereas with respect to an object it is insentient?
Moreover, objects are not of the same nature as luminosity, for they are experienced as being distinct, long, and gross.
And this internal light manifests as neither gross, nor subtle, nor short, nor long. Therefore,
we consider it logical that— just as when the moon is being perceived, a second moon appears— any object other than self-luminous consciousness is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
FN: He states its non-duality in order to establish that the seven consciousnesses are the Self—“not...”.
@---------------------- Nor is there [any other] for this light, which is by nature unborn (ajānataḥ) from its own essence.
For one who knows, the distinction between individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is experienced;
however, an indefinable distinction of objects cannot make a manifest, definable [entity] distinct, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, it will be demonstrated later that even the mutual distinction between objects does not abide within the path of valid knowledge. Therefore, this very Light—self-luminous, one, immutable, eternal, partless, and the inner self (pratyagātman)—approaches (añcati) and knows itself as distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, which are indescribable; because it approaches [itself] inwardly, it is "inner" (pratyaṅ), and being the self, it is the "inner self" (pratyagātman).
And because it does not depend on another for its manifestation and because it is partless,
it is not an object.
In that [Self], there is a superimposition (adhyāsa) of the attributes of objects—that is, the attributes of the body, senses, and so forth. How?
This is an objection (*ākṣepa*); the objection is that this superimposition is untenable.
Why is this [position] untenable? To this he says: "For everyone superimposes one object upon another object that is situated before them.

What is meant by this is as follows: that which has a manifestation dependent on something else and which possesses parts, manifests otherwise when its general aspect is grasped but its specific aspects are not grasped due to a defect in the cause;
however, the inner self (pratyagātman), because its manifestation is independent of anything else, does not depend upon causes for its own cognition.
It is not defiled by those defects which reside in its substratum;
nor does it possess parts, such that some part of it might be grasped.
Nothing could be apprehended;

for it is impossible that the very same thing, at that very same time, could be both apprehended and unapprehended by that same [cognition]. Thus, there can be no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) on the view that consciousness is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). Furthermore, even if [consciousness] were eternally present, since it would lack the state of being situated before one (*puro 'vasthitatva*) and the quality of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), there could be no superimposition.

FN: If it is asked, "Since the apprehension and non-apprehension of a single object—just as in the case of mother-of-pearl—are established [by their own nature], why is its being an object proven to be merely conditional (*aupādhika*)?", [the author] replies with "Indeed not" (*na hi*), stating that while this might be so for a thing consisting of parts, it is not so for the Self because of its partlessness.
Indeed, one does not superimpose silver upon mother-of-pearl when it is not standing before one, thinking "this is silver."
Therefore, it is established that there is no superimposition (adhyāsa) in the case of either absolute apprehension or absolute non-apprehension.
This might be argued:
since the conscious self (cidātmā) is not an object, there can be no superimposition upon it.
But the conscious self (*cidātman*) is indeed the object of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*);
so how can there be no superimposition? To this he says: you maintain that the inner self (*pratyagātman*), being free from the notion of "thou" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*), is not an object;
for if the conscious self were an object, there would have to be another subject (*viṣayin*).
And thus, that which is the subject is precisely the conscious self (cidātman);
the object, however, must be admitted as distinct from that, being the sphere of the notion of "you" (yuṣmat-pratyaya).

Therefore, because it would otherwise follow that [the self] is not the self, and in order to avoid an infinite regress, one must state that the self is devoid of the notion of "you" and, for that very reason, is non-objective.
And thus, the meaning is that there is no superimposition [of the Self upon the body].
He refutes this: It is said—in reply—that this [Self] is not, first of all, an object in an absolute sense.
Why? Because it is the object of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*).
This is the meaning: it is true that the inner self (*pratyagātman*), being self-luminous, is not an object of cognition and is partless;

nevertheless, although it is in reality unconditioned, it appears as if conditioned, and although it is non-different, it appears as if different—due to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), and the subtle and gross bodies along with the sense organs, which are imagined by beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyānādyavidyā*).

Though it is not an agent, it appears as if it were an agent; though it is not an enjoyer, it appears as if it were an enjoyer; though it is not an object, it appears as if it were the object of our cognition (*asmat-pratyaya*).

Having attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), it manifests as if divided by various distinctions—just as the sky appears divided by the differences of delimitations such as jars, water-pots, and bowls—and as if possessing manifold attributes.
For when the aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa) of the Self, whose sole essence is consciousness, is apprehended, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unapprehended.
Indeed, bliss, eternity, omnipresence, and so forth do not in reality differ from its conscious nature;
for if they did, they would not be apprehended when that [consciousness] is apprehended.

However, although they are indeed grasped, because they are not distinguished by means of an imagined difference, they appear as if ungrasped. Furthermore, the difference of the Self from the intellect and so forth is not real,
such that when the conscious Self is grasped, that [difference] would also be grasped.
Since the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties are indeterminable (*anirvācya*), their distinctions are likewise indeterminable.

Therefore, because the unconditioned Self, which is consciousness itself and self-luminous, fails to grasp its distinction from the conditioned intellect and so forth, the state of being a living individual (*jīvabhāva*) arises through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon them. Consequently, it is logically consistent for that Self—which is not "this" (*anidam*)—to be the object of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*).
For instance, the conscious self (cidātman) appears as the agent and the enjoyer in the notion of "I.
Yet, for that [self] which is indifferent (udāsīna), neither the power of action nor the power of enjoyment is possible.
And as for that aggregate of causes and effects, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, in which the powers of action and enjoyment reside, it does not possess consciousness.

Therefore, the conscious self alone— strung together by the aggregate of causes and effects, having acquired the power for action and experience, and though self-luminous— is, through its intermingling with objects such as the intellect and so forth, somehow becomes the object of the notion of "I," the locus of the ego,
and is designated as the *jīva*, the "creature," and the *kṣetrajña*, the "knower of the field."
Indeed, the individual soul (jīva) is not distinct from the conscious self (cidātman);
for thus says the Śruti: "By this living self.
Therefore, because it is non-different from the conscious self, the jīva, although self-luminous, [is perceived] through the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya).

Note: 1. That contradiction previously stated regarding [the self] being both the agent and the object of action should also be understood as refuted by this, because it pertains to the realm of adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*).
It is called the objective support (*ālambana*) of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), insofar as it is made fit for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by way of being the agent and the enjoyer.

Nor is it correct to argue that there is a circularity—wherein superimposition exists only when there is objectivity, and objectivity exists only when there is superimposition—because, like the seed and the sprout, the process is beginningless; for there is no contradiction in an object being the locus of subsequent superimpositions once it has been made an object by preceding superimpositions and their impressions. This has been stated in the Bhāṣya passage: "This worldly transaction is innate."
Therefore, it has been well said: "This [self] is not, then, absolutely an objectless entity.

For the individual soul (*jīva*), while being an objectless entity by virtue of its nature as consciousness and its self-luminosity, is nonetheless an object in its conditioned (*aupādhika*) form; this is the intended meaning.
This might be so.
We do not reject superimposition on the grounds that [the inner self] is not an object because its manifestation is not dependent on anything else;

rather, we say that the inner self is not an object because it is manifested neither by itself nor by another. And so, since the inner self is not manifested in any way whatsoever, how can there be superimposition upon it? To this, he says: "And because the inner self is well-known through its immediacy."
The manifestation (*prathā*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is its establishment (*prasiddhi*), because it is immediately evident (*aparokṣatva*).
Although there is no manifestation other than that which exists within the inner self, [it is nevertheless established].
Nevertheless, there is a figurative designation of difference, as in the expression "consciousness of a person.

What is meant is this: it must necessarily be admitted that the conscious self is immediate; for it has been stated that if it were not manifest, everything would fail to be manifest, resulting in the undesirable consequence of universal blindness.
And there is a scriptural text on this point: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.

Having thus stated the solution from the perspective of ultimate reality, he now offers another solution as a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*), even while conceding the mediacy (*parokṣatā*) of the conscious self: "Nor is there this rule that [an object] must be situated in front, or must be immediately present (*aparokṣa*)."
One object must be superimposed upon another object.
Why is this not a fixed rule? To this he says: "For even though space is imperceptible, children superimpose its surface, impurity, and so forth upon it.
The word "hi" (for) is used in the sense of "because."
For space, though it exists as a substance, is not perceptible by the external sense-faculties due to its lack of color and tangibility; nor is it perceptible by the mind,
since the mind, being without assistance, does not operate with respect to external objects.
Therefore, it is imperceptible. Nevertheless, there, the ignorant and undiscriminating— those who see only what is shown by others— sometimes superimpose a dark color, belonging to earth,
and sometimes superimpose a white color, belonging to fire.
They perceive it as being dark like the petals of a blue lotus, or white like a row of royal swans;

even there, it is the appearance of a previously seen form—whether luminous or dark—that manifests in the sky in the form of a memory. Thus, they superimpose that very surface upon it, meaning they regard it as resembling a great cauldron made of sapphire turned upside down.

He concludes: "In this manner"—that is, by the way already stated, through the refutation of all objections—the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of non-self entities, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not contradictory.
Now, one might object: "Surely there are thousands of instances of superimposition."

For what purpose, then, has this specific superimposition (adhyāsa) alone been explained through objection and resolution, rather than mere superimposition in general? To this he says: "The learned consider this very superimposition, characterized in this way, to be ignorance (avidyā). For it is well known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇas, and so forth, that ignorance is indeed the seed of all misfortune.
He will state later that the Vedāntas have set forth for the sake of its eradication.

The superimposition of the non-self upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) alone is the cause of all evil, and not merely errors such as [mistaking] mother-of-pearl for silver; therefore, that [superimposition] itself is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since its true nature cannot be destroyed if it remains unknown, it is that very thing which must be explained, and not mere superimposition in general.
And here, by the phrase "having such a characteristic," its status as the cause of evil has been stated.

Since the superimposition of the internal organ and other things endowed with hunger and so forth upon the inner self— which is devoid of hunger and the like— renders that painless inner self painful,
it is therefore the cause of misfortune.
Nor do ordinary people conceive of such a superimposition in this manner.

To show that [ignorance] is not something that cannot be dispelled, it is said: "The wise consider... Now, one might think: "Indeed, this ignorance, which is bound by extremely deep and dense latent impressions (vāsanā) from beginningless time, cannot be ceased because there is no means [to do so].

To such a person, he states the means for its cessation: "And the determination of the true nature of reality through discrimination from that [ignorance]—the wise call such doubt-free knowledge 'vidyā'. The wise consider this.

Indeed, in the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is absolutely distinct from the intellect and other faculties, there occurs a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the nature of the intellect and its attributes, caused by the non-apprehension of the distinction between the intellect and so forth. In that regard, when the non-apprehension of the distinction is removed by the discriminative knowledge (*viveka-vijñāna*) attained through hearing, reflection, and so on, there follows the sublation of the superimposition, which consists in the negation of that [superimposed] nature.
FN: It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the nature of the object" (*vastusvarūpa*) and "its ascertainment" (*tadavadhāraṇa*).

The meaning is that the ascertainment of the nature of the object is *vidyā* (knowledge), which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmarūpa*), and it abides in its own nature (*svarūpe vyavatiṣṭhate*).
This might be so.

Even though ignorance (*avidyā*), which is permeated by extremely deep and dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*), has been sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), it may arise again due to the force of its own latent impressions and will bring about its appropriate effects, such as further impressions; therefore, he says:

"In that very case—when there is such ascertainment of the reality of things—the Self, which is consciousness, is not connected even in the slightest degree with any defect or quality produced by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of one thing upon another—for instance, the defects of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, or hunger and thirst."
The internal organ and so forth are not connected with the quality of the conscious self, such as consciousness, bliss, and the like.

This is what is meant: the very nature of the practice of discerning reality is such that it removes false cognitions, even those that are beginningless and possess deeply entrenched, dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For it is the very nature of cognitions to side with reality, as even the outsiders (Bāhyas) have said: "The nature of reality, which is free from affliction and is the true state of things,
cannot be subverted by erroneous cognitions, even if one does not exert effort, because the intellect has a natural bias toward that [reality]."
Thus [it is said].

Specifically, however, how could there be a sublation by indefinable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*) of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which has the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*) as its essence and is the most intimate internal factor?
As it has been stated: "Having coupled the real and the unreal..."

"Due to the non-apprehension of discrimination, one superimposes [the notion of] 'I', 'this', and 'mine', and thus worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) occurs"—in this regard, the transaction characterized by verbal designation has been explicitly stated.
He demonstrates the worldly transaction indicated by the word "thus" (*iti*) with the words: "This very thing called ignorance.
This is explained by the literal reading itself (*nigadavyākhyātam*).
[The opponent] objects: But how can the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as direct perception and the rest, have as their object that which is possessed of ignorance?
For valid knowledge (pramā) is the discernment of reality, which is itself knowledge (vidyā);
how then can its instruments (pramāṇas) have as their object that which is possessed of ignorance?
The meaning is that the means of valid cognition do not rely upon one who possesses ignorance, because their effect, which is knowledge, is the opposite of ignorance.
Or, let the means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth exist in whatever way they may according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti).

But since the scriptures are devoted to instructing men in what is beneficial and serve as the antidote to ignorance, they cannot possibly have as their object one who is possessed of ignorance; thus he says: "And the scriptures... He provides the answer: It is said that for one who is devoid of the conceits of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body, senses, and so forth—that is, for one who is devoid of the superimposition of identity and its attributes—since the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) would be untenable, the operation of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would likewise be untenable.
The meaning is as follows: the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is indeed agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the act of knowing (*pramā*), and that [agency] is sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
Sovereignty, moreover, is the capacity of the knower—who is not impelled by other causal factors (*kāraka*)—to employ all causal factors.
Therefore, by this [agency], the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is the instrument of knowing (*pramākaraṇa*), must be employed.
Furthermore, an instrument cannot be employed without its own activity;
nor can the conscious self (*cidātman*), which is immutable and eternally constant, possess activity by itself, as it is non-transforming (*apariṇāmī*).
Therefore, [the self appears active] due to the superimposition of identity with the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, which do possess activity.

Since it is capable of being presided over as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of possessing activity, it follows that the means of valid cognition have as their object the person possessed of ignorance (*avidyāvat-puruṣa*), and thus they have as their locus the person possessed of ignorance.

Now, one might ask: "Even if the means of valid cognition do not function, what is lost for us? To this he replies: "For the empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting of perception and so forth is not possible without employing the sense organs.
"Empirical usage" (*vyavahāra*) is that by which something is used; it is the result (*phala*).
The meaning is that it is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as direct perception (pratyakṣa) and the rest.
Regarding the term "senses" (indriyāṇi),
it should be understood as referring to the senses, inferential marks (liṅga), and so forth.
It is like the expression "the staff-bearers are going.

In this way, the term "perception and so forth" (pratyakṣādi) becomes logically consistent. Furthermore, because the agent of the conventional usage is implied by the act of that usage, there is a commonality of agent (samānakartṛkatā).
The construction is: "conventional usage which occurs without grasping.

Why, then, does the knower grasp the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*), and why does he not simply proceed by himself? To this he says: "And without a basis, the activity of the sense organs—that is, the activity of the means of valid cognition—is not possible."
Instruments never engage in their own respective functions unless presided over by an agent;
let it not be that cloth is produced from the loom and other tools when they are devoid of a weaver.
Now, why should the body itself not be the presiding agent?

Since it has been established that there is superimposition of the Self here [upon the body], he says: "And no one acts by means of a body whose nature as the Self has not been superimposed," because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of activity even during deep sleep; such is the sense.
This might be so.

Just as a weaver, employing a loom and other tools upon which he has not superimposed his own self-nature, is the maker of a cloth, so too one who employs the body, senses, and so forth upon which he has not superimposed his own self-nature will become a knower of them and thus a valid cognizer (pramātṛ). To this, [the author] says: "And not in all this"—meaning, in the absence of this mutual superimposition of self-natures.
The status of being a cognizer is untenable for the Self, which is unattached and eternally and in every way dissociated from all phenomena;
for we observe that weavers and others, possessing activity, exercise their agency by presiding over and operating with looms and other tools.

But for one who has not superimposed the nature of a self upon the body and so forth, there can be no connection with activity because of the self’s lack of attachment; this is the meaning. Furthermore, he states that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) depend upon superimposition: "And there is no operation of the means of valid cognition without the status of being a knower (pramātṛtva)."
Indeed, the knower (pramātṛ) is independent with respect to the fruit that is valid cognition (pramā).

And valid cognition is a specific transformation of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-pariṇāma-bheda) which is directed toward the object of knowledge (prameya-pravaṇa), yet resides in the agent (kartṛ-stha) and has consciousness as its essential nature (cit-svabhāva).
How, moreover, could the transformation of the insentient internal organ be of the nature of consciousness?
If the conscious self were not superimposed upon that [body],
how could this body have the conscious self as its agent?
And if the internal organ, which possesses activity, were not superimposed upon the conscious self, how could it function as such?

Therefore, through this mutual superimposition, the fruit of valid cognition (pramā-phala), which resides in the conscious self as the agent, is established; and upon its establishment, the status of being a knower (pramātṛtva) is established,
and it is with reference to that very valid cognition that the operation of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) occurs.
And by means of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), valid cognition (*pramā*) is indicated;
for in the absence of the result that is valid cognition, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not function.
And thus, the meaning is that the means of valid cognition would become a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
He concludes: Therefore, the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, have as their objects only those things associated with ignorance.
This may be so for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Since the linguistic conventions of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are observed even among those men who are highly proficient and who have realized the reality of the inner self through scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*upapatti*), how can it be said that the means of knowledge have as their sole object those possessed by ignorance (*avidyā*)?
To this he says: "And because there is no distinction from animals and the like.
Let them indeed know, by means of scripture and reasoning, the inner self as distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth.
In the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), however, they do not transcend the characteristics common to all living beings.
For the kind of behavior seen in animals, birds, and the like—whose state of ignorance is undisputed—is also observed among men who are highly proficient in learning.
Therefore, by virtue of that similarity, their possession of ignorance (*avidyāvatva*) at the time of such conventional usage can be inferred.
The word "ca" (and) signifies a conjunction.

The meaning is that the previously stated reasoning, together with the removal of the aforementioned doubt, establishes that the means of valid cognition have as their object the person possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*).
He analyzes this very point [with the words]: "For just as cattle and so forth... and so on.
And here, by the words "when there is a connection with sound and so forth" [via] the ear and other senses, perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is shown;
by the phrase "in the cognition of sound and so forth," its result is stated;
and by the word "adverse," the result of inference (*anumāna*) is indicated.

For instance, having perceived the nature of sound and so forth, and having recollected the disagreeableness of that which belongs to its class, one infers the disagreeableness of what is being perceived as belonging to that same class. He provides an example: "just as [in the case of] a staff," and so on.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
This might be so:
let it be that perception and the other means of knowledge have as their objects those possessed of ignorance;
however, the scripture—such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—cannot function on the basis of the superimposition of the body upon the Self.
In this context, indeed, an eligible person (adhikārī) capable of enjoying the fruit pertaining to the next world is understood.
And likewise, there is the aphorism of the Great Sage (Pāramarṣa-sūtra):

"Because the purpose [of the scripture] has that as its characteristic, since it has verbal testimony as its means of valid cognition... [FN: 1—because the purpose has that as its characteristic, i.e., because it has verbal testimony as its means of valid cognition].

The fruit of the scripture—the result accessible through the scripture—is understood to reside in the performer; therefore, in the performance—that is, the execution—the sacrificer himself should be the agent. This is the meaning of the Sūtra:
"The fruit resides in the performer, because that [fruit] is his characteristic; therefore, he should perform it himself" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.7.18).
Furthermore, since the body and so forth, once reduced to ashes, are not fit for a fruit belonging to another world, the scripture implies an agent who is a Self distinct from the body and its like.

Anticipating the objection—"If the realization of that [Self] is indeed *vidyā* (knowledge), how can the scripture have as its subject matter one who possesses *avidyā* (ignorance)?"—he says: "But regarding what pertains to the scripture" (*śāstrīye tu*).
The word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes what pertains to the scripture from ordinary worldly transactions such as perception and so forth.

For the scripture concerning qualification (*adhikāra-śāstra*) cannot be established without a person desiring heaven having a connection to the next world; thus, it would imply only that much [the existence of the next world].
However, it does not follow that he is beyond *saṃsāra*,
because that state would be useless for his qualification;
on the contrary, for the person of the Upaniṣads— who is neither an agent nor an enjoyer— such a qualification would be contradictory.
For the agent of an action is the one who partakes in the enjoyment of the fruit produced by that action; he is the one entitled to it and its master.
In that case, how can one who is not an agent be the instigator, or how can one who does not enjoy be a partaker in the enjoyment of the fruit produced by the action?

Therefore, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions proceeds by taking as its subject the person who, due to beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being an agent, an enjoyer, a Brahmin, and so forth.
Likewise, the Vedāntas also have as their object only the person possessed of ignorance;
for indeed, there can be no comprehension of their meaning apart from the distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the rest.
However, their distinction is this: while instructing those possessed of ignorance, they establish the instructed person—whose entire ignorance has been wiped away—in his true nature.
Therefore, it is established that the scriptures have as their sole object the person possessed of ignorance.
This may be so.

Although the person described in the Upaniṣads is not required for ritual qualification because of contradiction and lack of utility, nevertheless, as understood from the Upaniṣads, he is capable of obstructing that qualification.
Furthermore, since their meanings would thus mutually cancel each other out, the entire Veda would lose its authority; therefore, [the author] says: "And prior to such a Self... [and so forth].

It is true that the realization of the person taught in the Upaniṣads is opposed to [the eligibility for] ritual action; nevertheless, the injunctions for ritual action that precede it, while effecting their own appropriate worldly transactions, cannot be obstructed by a knowledge of Brahman that has not yet arisen. Nor is there a mutual annulment between them.
This is because the systematic arrangement [of rules] is established through the distinction between persons possessing knowledge and those lacking it.

For example, although there is a prohibition regarding the object to be accomplished in the injunction "One shall not harm any living beings," the scripture "One who practices malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena" operates without contradicting the rule "One shall not harm.
Why is that?
Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction between persons":
those persons who have conquered anger and malice are qualified for the prohibition [of violence],
whereas those who are under the sway of anger and malice are qualified for the *Śyena* sacrifice and other such scriptural injunctions.
He elucidates what was stated—that [the Vedic injunctions] do not transcend having as their object persons possessed of ignorance—as follows: "For instance":

the superimposition of caste is seen in such [injunctions] as "A king shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya"; the superimposition of the stage of life (āśrama) is seen in such [injunctions] as "A householder shall take a suitable wife."
Superimposition of age includes such injunctions as, "One with black hair should establish the sacred fires.
Superimposition of state includes such rules as, "Those with incurable diseases should abandon their lives by entering water, etc.

The inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi) is for the purpose of encompassing superimpositions regarding the great sins (mahāpātaka), minor sins (upapātaka), those that cause mixture of castes (saṃkarīkaraṇa), those that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), those that cause impurity (malinīkaraṇa), and so forth.

Thus, having established the mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the Self and the non-Self through objection and resolution, and having strengthened it by demonstrating the operation of the empirical transactions of means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavahāra*),

[the author] recalls its previously stated nature in order to demonstrate its status as the cause of all that is undesirable through an elaboration of examples: "We have already stated that superimposition is the cognition of something as that which it is not."
This is a concise statement of the definition: "An appearance elsewhere of something previously seen, having the form of memory.
In that context, the mere superimposition (adhyāsa) of identity with the substrate (*dharmin*) as "I" is not the cause of evil;

rather, the superimposition of attributes (*dharmādhyāsa*), which has not yet been produced [in the form of "mine"], is the cause. Therefore, he describes through an elaborate series of examples the superimposition of attributes—specifically the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*)—as the direct cause of the entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and all its evils: "For example, in the case of son, wife, and so forth."

Having superimposed identity with the body upon the Self, and having attributed the attributes of the body—such as sonship, wifehood, and ownership—as well as thinness and so forth, one says: "I myself am incomplete" or "I am complete.
Indeed, through the completeness of one's own possessions, the master or lord becomes complete and whole.
Thus, through its own deficiency, because the owner is not deficient, the owner— the Lord— becomes deficient or incomplete.
The meaning is that one superimposes upon the self those external factors, such as deficiencies and so forth, which have entered the body by way of the channel of the owner.

And when such is the case regarding ownership—a property of the body dependent on external conditions—then what need is there to speak of emaciation and other bodily attributes which are not dependent on conditions? Intending this, he says: "Likewise, the properties of the body.
This refers to the properties of the senses—which are more internal than the body itself and upon which the notion of self is superimposed—such as muteness and so forth.

The construction is as follows: from that [superimposition of the body], one superimposes upon the Self the attributes—such as desire, volition, and so forth—of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is more proximate [to the Self] and upon which the nature of the Self has been superimposed. Having thus explained the superimposition of attributes (*dharmādhyāsa*) through this elaboration, he states its root, the superimposition of the substrate (*dharmyadhyāsa*): "In this way, the object of the notion of 'I' (*ahampratyayinam*)"—that is, that internal organ and so forth in which the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the notion of 'I' resides is called "the object of the notion of 'I'."

Having superimposed [the world] upon the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the witness of its own mental modifications— that is, the witness of the activities of the internal organ— by means of both consciousness and neutrality.
Thus, having established [the soul's] status as agent and enjoyer,
he establishes its consciousness by means of its being the opposite of that— that is, the opposite of the internal organ and so forth— with respect to that inner self which is the witness of all.
The internal organ and so forth are non-conscious;
their opposite is consciousness (caitanya).
The instrumental case ending (tṛtīyā) is used here in the sense of "characterized by" (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe).
[It] superimposes [itself] upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth.
Thus, by this, the inner self (pratyagātman), delimited by the internal organ and so forth— possessing both the nature of "this" and "not-this," being conscious, the agent and enjoyer,

the substratum of the two-fold ignorance consisting of effect and cause, the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the transmigrating being (saṃsārī), and the vessel for the accumulation of all evils— is the individual self (jīvātman).

It has been stated that because mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) takes [the other] as its material cause, and superimposition likewise takes that [other] as its material cause, there is no fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), as they are beginningless like the seed and the sprout.

Although this has been firmly established through the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), for the benefit of the student, he further solidifies the nature of superimposition by first describing its essential form and then demonstrating its universal perceptibility: "Thus, this [superimposition] is beginningless and endless, and impossible to eradicate except through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)."
The reason for its being without beginning or end has been stated: it is "intrinsic" (*naisargika*).
It is "of the nature of false cognition" (*mithyāpratyayarūpa*); that is, the nature of false cognitions is their indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), and that which possesses this is so described.
The meaning is that it is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*). He concludes the subject at hand: "For the abandonment of this cause of evil.
To the question, "How can there be its abandonment without a contrary condition? he says: "For the realization of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self" (*ātmaikatvavidyāpratipattaye*).
It is for the sake of practice and attainment, and not merely for the purpose of recitation, nor for engagement in ritual actions.

The Vedāntas, cultivating an unshakeable realization of the oneness of the Self—which is the state where the entire phenomenal world has dissolved within the Being whose nature is Bliss—uproot superimposition (adhyāsa) by striking it down at its very root. This is what is meant: if the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*), which has the Self as its object, were valid, there would be no desire to know (*jijñāsā*), because Brahman would already be known and thus devoid of any further purpose.
And in the absence of that [purpose], the Vedāntas would not be studied for the sake of knowledge of Brahman;
rather, with their meaning unintended, they would be useful merely for recitation.
For then the cognition of the self derived from the Upaniṣads would not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Moreover, even if practiced, that [false cognition] which is not a valid means of knowledge cannot remove the real agency, enjoyership, and so forth of the self;
for it is only a superimposed form that is sublated by the knowledge of reality, whereas a real thing is not sublated by the absence of knowledge of reality.
For even a thousand perceptions of a snake-stream cannot succeed in subverting the rope-nature of a rope;
and a nature projected by false cognition can indeed be subverted by the knowledge of reality.

Furthermore, even the most firmly established latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of false cognition is overcome by the latent impression of the knowledge of reality, which is born from the practice of that knowledge for a long time, with devotion and without interruption.
This might be so:

since meditations on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such things are also frequently found in the Vedāntas, how can it be that the purpose of all the Vedāntas is the teaching of the unity of the Self? To this he says: "And how this is the meaning of all the Vedāntas, so we have [explained] in this Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā..."
We shall demonstrate this.
"Śarīraka" means the body itself; the one dwelling therein is the "śārīraka," namely the individual soul (jīvātman).
The inquiry into that [soul], which is denoted by the term *tvam* (thou), as having the nature of the Supreme Self denoted by the term *tat* (that) is what is thus described.
This is the summary of the meaning here: although, by means of the injunction for the private study (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) of one's own Veda—

which establishes that the entire mass of the Vedas denoted by the term *svādhyāya* is intended for the comprehension of fruitful meanings— it has been established that even the Vedāntas, being denoted by the word *svādhyāya*, are intended for the comprehension of fruitful meanings just like the injunctions and prohibitions regarding ritual actions (*karma*).

And although it might be argued that since the entire Veda is intent upon making known what is to be done (*kārya*), the Vedāntas would lack authority regarding the established (*siddha*) Brahman—to this he says: "But [the meaning] is not different.
For there is no difference in the meaning of sentences between common worldly usage and the Veda.
The meaning is that, just as mantras possess authority regarding deities and so forth, so too do the Vedāntas possess authority regarding Brahman.
Furthermore, as he will state later, the claim that the Veda is directed toward action (kārya) should be understood as pertaining specifically to the domain of dharma.

This is because, according to the maxim "the meaning of a sentence [is its primary purport]," it is the natural rule that the Vedāntas, like the mantras, have as their primary purpose the expression of an existing reality.

Although from the Vedāntas it is understood that the inner self (pratyagātman) is a single, undifferentiated mass of consciousness and bliss, devoid of agency and enjoyership, and free from the phenomenal world (niṣprapañca), nevertheless, the Vedāntas— being contradicted by the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), which is free from doubt or sublation and which apprehends the self as consisting of agency, enjoyership, suffering, grief, and delusion— are either deprived of their own meaning, possess a figurative meaning, or are useful only for recitation; thus, their literal sense is not intended.

And thus, the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, consisting of four chapters and having the investigation of that [Self] as its essence, need not be commenced. Furthermore, the Self—established through the "I-consciousness" (*ahamanubhava*) common to all people—is neither doubtful nor possesses a purpose for which it could be an object of inquiry; therefore, being already known, it does not prompt the application of investigation. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: this would indeed be so if the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) were a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

But since, in the manner already stated, it is impossible for that notion to sublate the Śruti and other authorities, and since its validity is not accepted by the Śruti and other authorities nor by any of the founders of philosophical systems (tīrthakara), it is merely a case of superimposition (adhyāsa).
Thus, the Vedāntas do not have unintended meanings, nor do they have figurative meanings; rather,
they possess the characteristics already described.
The primary meaning of those [words] is the inner self (pratyagātman) itself.

And since that self is subject to doubt according to the sequence to be explained, and because [the inquiry] possesses a purpose, the author of the Sūtras, intending this, formulated the desire to know it (taj-jijñāsā) in the form of a sūtra:
*athāto brahmajijñāsā* || 1.1.1 || Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. || 1.1.1 ||

Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. By the phrase "now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," [the author] indicates the doubt and the purpose through the very expression of the desire to know.
In this context, the knowledge of Brahman is explicitly stated as the purpose, because it is directly pervaded by the desire [for liberation].

Furthermore, there is nothing subsequent to the knowledge of Brahman— unlike the performance of ritual action which follows the knowledge of rituals— by virtue of which this [knowledge] could be considered a subordinate purpose.

However, it is precisely the knowledge of Brahman—induced by the Vedāntas, whose subject matter is authorized by the methodological procedure of the inquiry known as Brahmamīmāṃsā—that is our supreme goal; for that knowledge alone is free from doubt, consists in the cessation of all suffering, and has the singular essence of bliss.
Indeed, it is with reference to that end that discerning people exert themselves most intensely.
And although that [Self] has been attained, it remains as if unattained due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*); thus, it becomes an object of desire.
Just as one who, through some delusion, thinks a necklace (*graiveyaka*) already on his own neck does not exist, obtains—as if it were unobtained—that which has been pointed out by another;
so too, *jijñāsā* (the desire to know), being the effect of doubt (*saṃśaya*), indicates its own cause, namely doubt.

And doubt prompts the commencement of inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*). Thus, because this aphorism indicates both the doubt and the purpose—which are the causes for the engagement of discerning persons in the treatise—it is appropriate that this aphorism constitutes the beginning of the treatise; so says the venerable author of the Commentary: "This is the first aphorism of the Vedānta-mīmāṃsā-śāstra."

The word *mīmāṃsā* denotes a revered investigation (*vicāra*). And the reverence of that investigation consists in its having as its fruit the determination of the most subtle meanings, which serve as the cause for the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). The *śāstra* is the treatise of that *mīmāṃsā*.
For it is by means of this [sūtra] that the teaching is instructed and properly imparted to the disciples.
Furthermore, a sūtra exists because it indicates many meanings,
as they have said:
FN: 1. Brevity (*laghutva*) consists in having a meaning that is free from doubt;
for that which is subject to doubt becomes "heavy" due to its capacity to suggest multiple meanings. [As it is said:
"Brevities (*laghu*) are those whose meanings are indicated, consisting of few syllables and words."
The wise say that the sūtras are the essence of everything.
Thus, having explained the purport of the sūtra in this manner, he explains its first word, *atha*: "In that context, the word *atha* is understood to signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
The construction is as follows: among those words of the sūtra, this word *atha* has the meaning of immediate succession.

Is it not observed that the word *atha* also serves the purpose of indicating a new topic (*adhikāra*), as in the Veda: "Now this is the Jyotis [sacrifice]," or as in common usage: "Now begins the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) and "Now begins the instruction on yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*)?
Why, then, is the sense of "heading" (adhikāra) not accepted here? To this he says: it is not for the purpose of a heading.
Why? Because the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not something that can constitute a heading.
For, in this aphorism, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), as well as Brahman and its knowledge, are [all] expressed by the words themselves.

Objection: Since the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not what is to be propounded by the treatise (*śāstra*), let the word *atha* not be for the purpose of propounding that; however, it may be for the purpose of indicating the commencement of Brahman and the knowledge thereof. Reply: This is not so. For a primary element connects with a primary element. Here, because suffixes generate an understanding of their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), the desire directed toward the knowledge of Brahman is indeed the primary element; and in that case, no such connection is possible. This is the sense.
The primary [meaning] is understood.

And it cannot be argued that, just as in the case of "the staff-bearer recites the injunctions" (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*), where the staff—the subordinate element—is intended for emphasis, so too here the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman and its subordinate elements may be intended; for this is not the case.

For in that case, regarding the injunction "The Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the *praiṣa*," since the recitation of the *praiṣa* is already established by the mantra, there is no intention to express it as being connected to the injunction; rather, [the staff] is intended even though it is subordinate and not otherwise established, as in the case of taking up the staff.
One should infer that here, however, there is no reason for the desire to express the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) to be unintended.
In this context, even though the meaning of the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is subordinate, it is intended to be expressed.
Thus, here too, it is appropriate that [the inquiry] concerns Brahman and the knowledge thereof;

for it is precisely the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that is intended, as it serves to indicate the doubt and the purpose which are necessary factors for the commencement of the treatise on the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*). If that were not intended, then by failing to indicate those two, discerning people would not engage in the inquiry into Brahman, just as they do not engage in an investigation of a crow’s teeth.

For at that time, neither Brahman nor the knowledge thereof can constitute the subject matter (*abhidheya*) or the purpose (*prayojana*), because it is impossible for the Vedāntas to possess authority regarding such a subject when it contradicts the non-superimposed notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).

Furthermore, even those [Vedic passages] whose meanings are figurative for the sake of engaging in ritual action, or those used for recitation (*japa*)—such as "Aum Phat"—which do not intend to convey a literal meaning, are nevertheless grasped due to the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*). [The same applies to the Vedāntas.]
Because it is possible [for such a desire to arise],

therefore, *jijñāsā* (the desire to know), which indicates the doubt and the purpose, must be intended here as the primary element, both from the standpoint of the word and the sentence. And yet, it does not possess the status of being the subject qualified for the inquiry (*adhikārī*), because it has not been introduced [as such].

[Note: Because it is not being propounded with respect to each individual subject (*pratyadhikaraṇa*), that by which the word *atha*—occurring in grammatical co-utterance (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with it—could have the sense of "commencement of a topic" (*adhikāra*) [is lacking]. Rather, Brahman and the knowledge thereof, as qualifiers of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), would be the subject matter (*adhikārya*).
And even that [word "desire to know"] is not connected with the word "atha," because it lacks primacy;
nor is "jijñāsā" (the desire to know) the same as "mīmāṃsā" (investigation).
By which [definition] it would be governed like the *Yogānuśāsana* [of Patañjali].

Alternatively, the word *mīmāṃsā*—derived from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*) or from the root *māna* in the sense of "reverence" (*pūjāyām*), formed with the suffix *san* (intensive) in the sense of non-desire according to the rule *mānbadha-* etc.—denotes "venerated inquiry" (*pūjitavicāra*).
Indeed, its status as a term for venerated inquiry must be accepted on the strength of its established usage.
Because it is a word;
for the term *jijñāsā* denotes both knowledge (*jñāna*) and desire (*icchā*),
and it is indeed that which impels one toward *mīmāṃsā*.
FN: The reading is "5-mīmāṃsayā". [Otherwise] there would be a desire to know (jijñāsā). Nor, however, can there be identity between that which is to be incited and the inciter.
Because if they were identical, the existence of that [distinction] would be untenable;
and when it is possible for [the Veda] to have its own meaning as its primary purpose, it is not reasonable to assume that its primary purpose is something else,
for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, it has been well said: "Because the desire to know (jijñāsā) is not something that requires an agent.

Now, why should the word *atha* not have the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*)? For in that case, since it would be the cause of auspiciousness, the meaning of the Sūtra would result in the conclusion that the inquiry into Brahman must be performed every day; to this he replies: "And because auspiciousness lacks syntactical connection with the meaning of the sentence."
For it is only a word-meaning that is connected with the sentence-meaning, and that [meaning] must be either the expressed (vācya) or the indicated (lakṣya) sense;
however, in this case, auspiciousness is neither the expressed nor the indicated sense of the word *atha*.
However, the meaning is that the hearing of the word *atha* has as its sole effect [producing] an awareness of the action, like the sound of a drum or a conch shell.
Furthermore, it is not observed in linguistic usage that there is a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) between an effect and a signified object within the meaning of a sentence.
[Objection: In that case, should the word *atha*, when used for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), not be employed in various contexts?
And so it is said: "In ancient times, these two—the syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*—issued forth from Brahman after piercing his throat; therefore, both are auspicious."
To the objection that this contradicts traditional usage (*smṛti*), he says: "For the word *atha*, when employed in another sense, becomes auspicious by its very sound (*śruti*).

When the word *atha* is employed in senses other than [immediate] sequence and so forth, it brings about auspiciousness merely by being heard, like the sound of a flute or a lute, and thus serves the purpose of auspiciousness."
It is like seeing a water-pot being carried for another purpose;
therefore, there is no contradiction with memory.
Nor does it mean that because the meaning of "immediacy" exists here, it cannot serve as an auspicious sign merely by being heard.
This might be the case:
the word *atha* may refer back to what was previously mentioned, even without having the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
For example, with reference to this very word *atha*, it is deliberated whether this word *atha* signifies immediate succession or a new topic (*adhikāra*).
In this deliberative statement, the word *atha* refers back to the previously mentioned *atha* and serves to introduce an alternative position following the presentation of the first position.
Nor does it signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*), because the previously mentioned subject matter has been interrupted by the presentation of the first position.

Nor can it be independent of the subject under discussion, because for that which is independent of it, there is no possibility of being its object; and since their objects would not be the same, an alternative (vikalpa) between them is untenable.
Indeed, it never occurs that one asks: "Is the self eternal? [and then answers something else].
Now, [one might argue] that cognition is impermanent;

therefore, why does the word *atha* here not depend on what was previously mentioned, rather than signifying immediate succession? To this he says: "Because dependence on what was previously mentioned is, in effect, not distinct from immediate succession. The meaning of this is: we do not favor the interpretation of it as signifying immediate succession out of mere whim.
However, for the sake of establishing the previously mentioned subject matter that serves as the cause for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*),

and since this is established even if the word *atha* depends upon a previously mentioned topic, our insistence on determining that it signifies "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is redundant. This is what was meant by the phrase "in effect" (*phalataḥ*).
In ultimate reality, however, when another alternative is introduced, there is a dependence upon what was previously under discussion.
Since no other alternative is introduced here, it is logical by the method of exhaustion that [the particle *tu*] has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Let it be that it has the sense of immediate succession.
To the question "What follows from this being so?", he says: "And since it has the sense of immediate succession.
It cannot be said that the immediate succession here belongs to just anything, because that would already be established even without its being explicitly stated.
For a person necessarily performs one thing after having performed another;
yet we do not perceive any purpose—whether seen or unseen—for this immediate succession alone.
Therefore, its immediate succession must be stated here as that without which the inquiry into Brahman does not occur.
But when that which exists, [the effect] necessarily comes to be;
this is what was stated: "that which, having occurred previously, is invariably required.
This might be so.
Just as the inquiry into Dharma is appropriate, so too is the inquiry into Brahman; for the term *svādhyāya*—
referring to the study (*adhyayana*) concerning one's own Vedic text— is intended by the word *svādhyāya*,
since such study is obligatory (*nitya*).
There is no interval between meditation [and realization],
because Brahman, like the Dharma, is accessible through the single means of valid cognition that is scripture (āmnāya);
and because that [Brahman], if not grasped [through scripture], does not produce knowledge regarding its own object.

Furthermore, since the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is already established as a prerequisite by the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied," the meaning of the word *atha* for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must therefore be its immediate succession to the study of the Veda. To this, he says: "But the immediate succession to the study of one's own Veda is common to both the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman."
And here, by means of the object, namely *svādhyāya* (the Vedic text), he indicates the study which has that as its object.
And since this is already covered by the very [sūtra] "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), this [present] sūtra need not be commenced.
[This is because] the word "Dharma" (*dharma*)—@----------------------

FN: 2—Anticipating the objection, "Since Brahman is not mentioned in the sūtra *athāto dharmajijñāsā*, how can this [present inquiry] be considered a repetition of what has already been established? he says: "Of the word *dharma*... The meaning is that, because the word *dharma* serves as an indicator for the entire subject matter of the Veda, Brahman—as well as *dharma*—is equally the subject matter of the Veda; thus, there is a commonality in the instruction that [the inquiry] follows immediately after the study of the Veda. He raises an objection: "But surely, the distinction here is that [the inquiry into Brahman] follows immediately after the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*)."

The inquiry into Brahman [proceeds] from the inquiry into Dharma; the meaning of this is as follows: because, by the scriptural statement "they desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), sacrifices and the like are enjoined as subordinate members (*aṅga*) for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman—since it is knowledge itself, as the object of the action, that holds primacy with respect to the desire [to know].
And because of the connection with the primary [element], the other subordinate constituent elements [also become auxiliaries].
Even so, sacrifices and the like do not function as auxiliaries for the production of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning,
since the knowledge of the sentence-meaning arises from the sentence itself.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that a sentence depends upon ritual actions as its auxiliary cause;

for even in the case of those who have not performed rituals, provided they understand the relationship between words and their meanings, have mastered the principles of verbal logic, and possess the capacity to discern the expectancy, proximity, and semantic fitness of preceding and succeeding word-meanings— whether primary or subordinate— the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises without obstruction.

Alternatively, if there were no arising [of cognition], there would follow the consequence that there could be neither the performance nor the avoidance of those meanings, due to the absence of any cognition of the meaning of sentences involving injunctions and prohibitions. If, however, there is cognition of them, then the performance and avoidance of those meanings and the cognition of them would involve mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*): namely, that when the performance and avoidance exist, there is cognition of them; and from that cognition, the performance and avoidance arise.
Nor is it correct to claim that only the Vedānta passages require ritual action for the communication of their own meaning, while other passages do not,
for there is no specific reason [to make such a distinction].
Now, [it may be argued] that from the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the referent of the term *tvam* (the individual self)...

If it is argued that the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*), which consists of the nature of agent and enjoyer, with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—the referent of the term *tat* (That), whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and indifferent—is impossible to realize immediately because those of impure being (*asuddhasattva*) lack the certainty of such fitness (*yogyatā*) at first sight; and that only those of purified being (*viśuddhasattva*), whose internal impurities have been attenuated by sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting, will realize this identity after first ascertaining their fitness through faith;
then, do you intend to claim that the determination of fitness—the very cause of valid knowledge—is derived from ritual action (*karman*), which is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*)?
Alternatively, even ritual action (*karman*) might be a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the other [means].
However, once the determination of compatibility has been made by the power of reasoning rooted in the Vedānta and not contradicted by it, there is no further need for ritual actions.

Therefore, having grasped the identity of the individual self with the supreme self through knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), [one proceeds].

Having established this through reasoning rooted therein, the utility of sacrifices and other rites lies in their application toward the meditation—also termed *bhāvanā*—of that [Brahman], which is characterized by long duration and uninterrupted practice, and which results in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman.

FN: "The practice of the cessation of mental fluctuations, when cultivated for a long time and with uninterrupted devotion, becomes firmly grounded"—the meaning is that its object cannot be overcome by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
"'But that [practice], when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes firmly grounded.
Here, "reverence" (*satkāra*) refers to celibacy, austerity, faith, sacrifice, and so forth.
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Having known that alone, the wise Brāhmaṇa should cultivate wisdom (prajñā).
The meaning is that, having known [it] through verbal testimony aided by reasoning (tarka), he should cultivate wisdom, which is to say, meditative realization (bhāvanā).

In this regard, some maintain that sacrifices and other such acts are useful by way of destroying the impurities that obstruct the highest good (*śreyas*). Others hold that they are useful by way of purifying the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*).

For a person purified by sacrifices and the like, when practicing the contemplation of Brahman with earnestness, continuity, and over a long period of time, eradicates the beginningless latent impressions of ignorance along with their very roots.
Thereupon, his inner self becomes perfectly serene, solitary, and clear.

For this very reason, the Smṛti says: "By the great sacrifices and by the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman," and also, "He for whom these forty-eight purificatory rites [have been performed]."
Others, however, state that actions are useful for the knowledge of Brahman insofar as they discharge the three debts;
for there is a Smṛti text: "Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation."

Others, however, [hold that] based on such scriptural passages as "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas and through sacrifice," even those ritual acts enjoined for the sake of various specific fruits may, by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), serve the purpose of the meditation on Brahman—just as the quality of being made of *khadira* wood serves both the purpose of the sacrifice and the desire for vigor, as in the texts: "One binds the animal to a *khadira* post" and "One should make the sacrificial post of *khadira* wood for one desiring vigor. (Note 2: Regarding the single act of using *khadira* wood, there are two injunctions.)

The meaning is that, just as the quality of being made of *khadira* wood serves both the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), so too actions may serve both purposes; this is according to the principle:
"But when one thing serves two purposes, there is a distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvam*)," [which establishes] its being for the sake of vigor (*vīryārthatā*).

And on this point, there is the aphorism of the Great Sage: "There is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26).
The meaning is that the meditation on Brahman depends upon everything, including sacrifice, austerity, charity, and the like.

Therefore, whether the scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth are the authority, or the aphorism of the Great Sage (*pāramarṣa-sūtra*), in every case, the meditation on Brahman conjoined with rituals such as sacrifice— characterized by [the qualities of] long duration, reverence, and uninterruptedness— is capable of producing the direct realization of Brahman, which is synonymous with liberation, through the gradual eradication of beginningless ignorance and its latent impressions; for that purpose, ritual actions must be performed.
And these [effects] are not seen;
for while the removal of husks and the like is seen,
that which arises from sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth is unseen— that is, the inherent (*sāmavāyika*) effect which inheres in the very nature of the sacrifice (*kratusvarūpa*).
At a distance, regarding the unprecedented accomplishment (*apūrvasiddhi*) which conforms to its fruit,

there is assistance consisting of the group (*grāma*)— the collection— of subsidiaries (*aṅga*), including those prescribed directly (*aupadeśika*) and those obtained through extension (*ātideśika*) by the rule "the modification is to be performed like the archetype" (*prakṛtivadvikṛtiḥ kartavyā*), extending as far as the order of performance; together with these, there is the nature of the ritual action itself, distinct in each case, and the specific qualified agent required for it.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) here is that without knowledge of these two, ritual actions cannot be performed.
In this context, the consideration regarding the seen and the unseen (*dṛṣṭādṛṣṭa*) belongs to the second chapter;
from the beginning of the third chapter onwards, there is an investigation of the instructions (*upadeśa*) across four chapters.
Following that, an investigation of the four types of extended application (*atideśa*) was conducted.

[This consists of] the thorough knowledge of the distinct natures of the various ritual acts and their respective substrates— ranging from those accompanied by the entire collection of primary and subsidiary factors (including both directly taught and extended ones, as well as those involving the sequence of visible,
inherent, and remote auxiliary causes)— which cannot be performed without such knowledge.

And that thorough knowledge [of Brahman] does not occur without the cultivation of the inquiry into Dharma; therefore, it was rightly said that "the distinction is the immediate succession to the understanding of karma. For by the understanding of karma, there arises for the meditation on Brahman a concomitance with the performance of karma—this is the meaning.
He refutes this as follows: "No."
Why? Because even prior to the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*), the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is possible for one who has already studied the Vedānta.
This is the underlying intention here: it was stated that ritual actions are required by the meditation on Brahman, which is also termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*);
to this we reply: where, then, is its requirement for ritual action?

Is there a requirement for the *samidh* and other subsidiaries with respect to the *kārya* (the task), such as the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result) which is to be produced by the *āgneya* and other sacrifices and is conducive to a fruit that occurs after a long interval;
or with respect to their own essential form (*svarūpa*), such as those same sacrifices requiring the substance of the twice-offered sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the fire, the deity, and so forth?
It cannot be with respect to the *kārya*.
This is because that [position] cannot withstand critical analysis.

For instance, if the direct realization— which is accomplished through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the nature of Brahman during the meditation on Brahman— were to depend upon ritual action (*karman*), then that [realization] would not be the very nature of Brahman, since it would be something yet to be produced.
And because Brahman is eternal,
direct realization must be accepted as the effect;
and that [realization] must be either something produced, or...
Just as the lump of dough is the product of kneading— as prescribed by the rule "one kneads the flour"—
or as the rice grains are the object to be modified by threshing.
Or it may be something to be refined (*saṃskārya*),
such as the mortar and other implements for sprinkling;
or it may be something to be attained (*prāpya*), such as the milk for milking.
First of all, it is not something to be produced.

Indeed, unlike the direct perception of a jar or similar objects, a direct realization of Brahman—which is distinct from the insentient jars and so forth—cannot possibly be produced by meditation as something bestowed by the senses and other means.

This is because Brahman possesses a self-luminous nature; since the direct realization of Brahman is of the same nature as Brahman itself, it is eternal, and thus its being produced is logically untenable.

The point is this: if the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) were distinct from Brahman—which is already distinct [from the world]—then Brahman would become insentient (*jaḍa*), and since verbal testimony is a cause of indirect knowledge (*parokṣapramā*), the realization produced solely by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) would be invalid. Alternatively, because a realization produced by cultivation is susceptible to doubt—just like a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*)—it cannot possess the status of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).
For it is frequently observed that even for one who possesses such [a cognition] and the requisite causal complex, there is deviation;

indeed, for one suffering from cold whose body is sluggish with the weight of frost and who meditates upon fire known through inference, there is no direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a fire dense with flickering flames, because such a perception is frequently found to be contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, since there is no effect characterized by the direct realization that is authoritative, ritual action is not required for the production of meditation; nor is it required because [the Self] is immutable (*kūṭastha*). (Note 4: Because of its immutable eternity.)

The meaning is that there can be neither *vikāra* (modification), which consists in the disappearance of a previous form, nor *saṃskāra* (refinement), which consists in the emergence of a new quality,
for that which is eternal and all-pervading.
FN: By this it has been stated that there is no attainment [of Brahman].
Furthermore, from the meditation upon Brahman as possessing form (*mūrta*), the attainments of modification (*vikāra*) and refinement (*saṃskāra*) are possible.
This might be so.
Let it not be that the direct realization of Brahman is something to be produced or otherwise brought into being by meditation;

rather, it is to be purified (*saṃskārya*). [The term] "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*) is used to indicate that even though it is to be purified through the removal of the covering of indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no loss of its immutable eternity (*kūṭasthanityatva*).
