It will come to pass through the removal of the concealment of the two-fold ignorance,
like a dancer veiled by a curtain who appears on the stage through the removal of that curtain.
It is by means of that [activity];
therein lies the utility of the ritual actions.
However, this much is the distinction: upon the removal of the curtain, the members of the assembly obtain a direct perception of the dancer.
In this case, however, there is nothing else to be produced, but merely the removal of the veil of ignorance;
for the direct realization of Brahman, being of the very nature of Brahman, is eternal and thus not something to be produced.
To this it is replied: What, then, is this meditation on Brahman?
Is it a mere continuity of verbal cognition,
or rather a continuity of verbal cognition free from doubt?
If it is a mere continuity of verbal cognition, [then...]
How can this ignorance be destroyed even by being practiced?
It is the ascertainment of reality or its repeated practice that uproots error along with its latent tendencies,
not the practice of doubt.
Or it is the practice of perceiving only the common features [of an object].

For even if one practices the cognition "it is either a post or a person" or "it is a substance possessing height and girth" a hundred times, it is not sufficient for the certain determination that "it is indeed a person."
Except through the perception of the distinction [between the two].

But was it not said that, having grasped the state of the individual self as the Supreme Self by means of knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*), it is established by means of knowledge consisting of reasoning (*yuktimaya-jñāna*)?

Therefore, meditation (*upāsanā*)—which consists of a continuous stream of verbal knowledge free from doubt—is the cause for the destruction of the two-fold ignorance when acting in conjunction with ritual action (*karman*).
Moreover, she [the ignorance] has not yet produced the experience of Brahman, and thus she is not capable of being destroyed by it;
for an error consisting of direct perception is destroyed only by a knowledge of reality that is itself of the nature of direct perception, and not by a cognition appearing as something indirect.

For it is observed that errors such as the confusion of directions, the circle of a whirling firebrand, moving trees, and the water of a mirage—which appear as direct perceptions—are removed only by cognitions of the true nature of direction and so forth that likewise appear as direct perceptions.

Indeed, for those who have ascertained the true nature of direction and the rest through the words of a reliable authority, inferential signs, and so on, the confusion of directions and other such errors do not cease.
Therefore, the direct realization of the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you") as being identical with the referent of the term *tat* (the "That") must be sought.
For it is by this much alone that the direct realization of the "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) as being subject to suffering, grief, and so forth, is removed, and not otherwise. [Note:
Although Brahman is inherently immediate, its remoteness is grasped through error;
that [remoteness] is not removed by the word alone.]
Because that [scriptural testimony] is a cause of indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*),
its direct realization must be admitted to arise from direct means of knowledge alone (*aparokṣapramāṇa*).

And since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) produces the mental modification of "I" (*ahaṃvṛtti*) with respect to the Self when it is associated with limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), its status as a cause of direct cognition is established.

With the intention that this [realization] perfumed by a continuous stream of cognition of the identity with the Śabda-Brahman brings about for the individual soul (*jīva*) the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of its nature as Brahman—the reality denoted by the term "That" (*tat-pada-lakṣaṇa-brahmātmatā*)—he says: "And this is not...

"And this direct intuition is not the fruit of the means of knowledge consisting of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*), even when accompanied by philosophical inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*); rather, it is the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
Because it is a fixed rule that only that [cause] has that specific result;
otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a banyan sprout arising even from a *kuṭaja* seed.

Therefore, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), accompanied by the ripening of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of the sentence free from doubt, experiences the identity of the referent of the word "Thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*)—which is immediate—with the referent of the word "That" (*tatpadārtha*) by negating the forms of their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
This is logical;
moreover, this experience is not of the nature of Brahman such that it would not be produced,
but rather it is a specific modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having Brahman as its object.
Nor does this much [viz., being made known by verbal cognition] imply that Brahman lacks self-luminosity;
for it is not the case that Brahman, though made manifest by verbal knowledge, ceases to be self-luminous.
Indeed, it is proclaimed to be self-effulgent when free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
But it is not so even when [the self] is superimposed.
As the venerable author of the Bhāṣya said: "This is not an absolute non-object.
Nor is it...
Note 9: Regarding the phrase "by the internal organ":

the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that takes as its object Brahman devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) arises as the cause for the cessation of itself and all other adjuncts, because it too is an adjunct.

And thus, the meaning is that for that which is not limited by adjuncts (*anupahita*), there is the status of being the object, and there is no requirement for another means to remove the adjuncts. Furthermore,
even in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) through a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), there is liberation from all adjuncts.
This is because that very limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), while in a state of perishing, still exists as something that opposes both its own form and the forms of others.

Otherwise, since the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) is itself insentient, it would be impossible for it to be self-luminous without the reflection of consciousness; and if it were not self-luminous, it could not constitute direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
Nor can this [perception] be considered invalid on the grounds of being a mere "intuition" (*pratibhā*), like the intuition of fire that has been inferred or will yet to be produced.
In that case, because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire is beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*),

whereas here, even prior [to realization], the individual soul (*jīva*), whose true nature is Brahman but which is defiled by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). For indeed—

Objection: Although the individual soul (*jīva*) was previously non-manifest (*aparokṣa*), its realization is not true [in this case] because purity, enlightenment, and so forth are manifest (*pārokṣya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
Purity, enlightenment, and so forth do not, in reality, exceed that [the *jīva*].
Rather, it is the *jīva* itself, when devoid of those respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which is proclaimed as Brahman, whose very nature is purity, enlightenment, and so forth.
Nor does the absence of those respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) exceed [the nature of] that [Self].

Therefore, just as one perceives directly through the sense of hearing the distinctions among the scales (*grāma*), modulations (*mūrcchanā*), and notes such as *ṣaḍja* by means of the auditory faculty aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the repeated study of the knowledge of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*),

so too the individual soul (*jīva*), possessing the latent impressions produced by the repeated study of the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedāntas, perceives its own state of being Brahman through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

FN: The proponent of the cumulative theory (samuccayavādī) raises an objection: "In the case of the function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) producing the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), there is a dependence upon ritual action for that meditation. FN:
He refutes that view: "No."
No;
[is the utility of ritual actions] in the realization that is the effect of meditation, or rather in the essential nature of meditation itself?
He says that it is not an effect, stating "of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
This is because, since it lacks coexistence with the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), it is impossible for it to be an auxiliary (*sahakārin*) to such action.

Indeed, from a statement such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there arises a non-doubting [realization] of one whose nature is pure, awakened, and indifferent, endowed with non-agency (*akartṛtva*) and so forth.
One who realizes the single Self—transcending the body and other such things, and devoid of castes such as Brahminhood—is capable of understanding his qualification for ritual actions (*karma*).
And how could one who is unqualified be either an agent or an eligible performer?
If it should be argued that even when reality has been ascertained, worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is seen to continue due to the persistence of error;

Just as, even when the sweetness of molasses has been determined, those whose sense faculties are afflicted by bile continue to perceive it as bitter— since they spit it out and discard it after tasting it—
so too, the performance of ritual action continues due to the persistence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).
And by that [knowledge], acting as a cooperative cause for wisdom (*vidyā*), the destruction of that [ignorance] will be established.
Nor should it be asked: "How can karma, which is of the nature of ignorance, destroy ignorance? Or, how is the destruction of that karma which effects such destruction itself brought about?"
Because entities that are opposed to themselves or to others of their own kind are frequently observed;
for example, milk causes other milk to curdle and it itself curdles as well.

Just as one poison neutralizes another poison and is itself neutralized, or just as the powder of the *kataka* nut, when thrown into water turbid with other sediments, breaks up those sediments while itself dissolving, thereby making the water clear; so too is this case.
In this way, even that which consists of karma and ignorance, by causing other forms of ignorance to depart, departs of its own accord.
To this it is replied: True;

for from the beginning, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," up to the end, "That thou art," there is the verbal testimony of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*), accompanied by its auxiliary means, which has been practiced repeatedly.

Even when the realization of the reality of the inner Self— which is distinct from the body and so forth that are the substrate of beginningless ignorance— has arisen and all doubt has ceased, worldly cognitions and their corresponding activities continue due to the persistence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance.

Although the wise man considers such activities and cognitions to be false, he does not place faith in them, just as one whose sense organ is afflicted by bile spits out molasses and discards it, yet still perceives its bitterness.
And thus, how could this person—who has ascertained that the expansion of action, agent, instrument, procedure, and fruit is not ultimately real—be considered qualified?
For qualification belongs to the knower;
otherwise, the qualification of even animals, Śūdras, and the like would be unavoidable.
In this context, the one intended as "the wise person" (*vidvān*) in the *karmakāṇḍa* is one who understands the distinction between the essential natures of action, agent, and so forth;
for this very reason, the venerable commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) described the scripture as having the wise person as its subject.

Therefore, just as in the *rājasūya* sacrifice, which has as its performer one who identifies with the royal caste (*rājanya*), there is no entitlement for those who identify with the brahmin or vaiśya castes.
Thus, in an action performed by an agent who conceives of the distinctions between the castes, the acts, the instruments, and so forth, one who lacks such conceit has no entitlement.
Nor does a Vedic rite performed by one who lacks entitlement— even if capable— lead to its fruit, just as the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice does not do so for Brāhmaṇas or Kṣatriyas.

Therefore, while one who is capable may engage in actions with visible results and obtain their fruit—since those results are directly perceived—it is not logical for a result that is to be understood solely through scripture to accrue to one who lacks the qualification [for such actions]. Thus, there is no dependence on ritual action (*karman*) regarding the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*).
This might be so.

Just as one who lacks the conceit of being human has no entitlement to ritual acts prescribed for those with such a status, so too prohibitions have humans as their subject; therefore, one devoid of that conceit would have no entitlement even to them, like an animal.
And thus, performing what is prohibited, he would incur no sin.
[If it were] like that of animals and so forth, there would follow the consequence of having distinct karma;
but this is not so.

Indeed, he is not entirely devoid of the conceit of being human; rather, through the persistence of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance, that conceit continues to follow him to a certain extent.
It has been stated that one who considers even what is being followed to be false does not have faith. What follows from this?
If this is so, then this is the consequence: one who possesses faith is the qualified person for injunctions, not one who lacks faith.
Furthermore, one who lacks faith in the conceit of being a human being and so forth is not qualified for the scriptural injunctions;
as the Smṛti says: "That which is offered or given without faith," and so on.
However, the scripture of prohibitions does not depend upon faith.
Rather, a person proceeds only with an inclination toward the action being prohibited;
and thus, just like one involved in worldly life, even one who has understood the reality of Brahman through the Word, if he transgresses the prohibition and acts, he incurs sin.
Therefore, there is no acceptance of a separate ritual action [for the knower], and consequently, there is no dependence on ritual action for the result of meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
FN: 4. To address the lack of opportunity for a second [type of] kalpa, he says "for this very reason.

For this very reason, it has been stated that even regarding the arising of meditation (*upāsana*), there is no qualification for ritual action (*karman*) after the time when indubitable verbal knowledge (*nirvicikitsa-śābdajñāna*) has arisen.
And thus says the Śruti: "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality.
Now, does this mean that actions are entirely useless here?
If so, then Śrutis such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" would be contradicted.
They are not contradictory; for,

as it is said [in the commentary], "from afar," because sacrificial acts such as the *yajña* and others are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) to the arising of knowledge through the purification of the inner being (*sattvaśuddhi*)— this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding how karma in this life serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge in another birth.

For it is thus: by means of the recitation of the Vedas—that is, by the constant study of one's own portion of the Veda—the Brahmins desire to know (vividiṣanti) this very Self; they do not, however, [already] know it.
In reality, although the root meaning *vedana* (feeling) is primary, it is grammatically subordinate as the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*),
whereas the desire (*icchā*) is primary as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*); and since the comprehension of the action is achieved through the primary element [the suffix].

For when it is said, "Bring the king's man," although the king is in fact the principal, he is brought as a subordinate by virtue of being a qualifier of the man; rather, it is the man alone who is brought, because he is the primary element according to the word.
In the same way, there is an injunction for the sacrifice as a means of fulfilling the desire, just as there is for the recitation of the Vedas.
Thus it is with austerity consisting of fasting. Austerity is indeed the non-indulgence in desires;
for it is in one who eats what is wholesome, moderate, and pure that the desire to know Brahman arises.
But it is not because of dying from total fasting,
nor for one whose habit is asceticism such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, because of the resulting imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu).
And these obligatory rites purify the person by destroying the accumulated evil;
thus says the Śruti:
"By this rite, this limb of mine—the internal organ—is purified."

The meaning of the Śruti is this: having understood that "it is piled up"—meaning it is accumulated through merit—he who performs action for the sake of self-purification is a *ātmayājī* (a sacrificer unto the Self). He is superior to the *devayājī* (sacrificer unto the gods), who performs actions for the sake of desire.
Or, the *ātmayājī* is he who knows: "By this [act], this limb of mine is refined; by this, this limb of mine is built up.
For the word "by this" refers back to the sacrifice and other such acts under discussion.
And the Smṛti states: "He for whom these forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) [have been performed]...

Furthermore, the Ātharvaṇa Śruti shows that knowledge arises only in one who is not yet a knower, but whose impurities have been destroyed by the performance of obligatory and occasional duties, whose being is purified, and who has developed the desire to know (vividiṣā): "Then, with a purified being, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless."
And there is the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful karma," and so forth.

Since the status of the obligatory (*nitya*) rites as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) to the arising of knowledge is established by their very nature—acting as a means to destroy previously acquired evil through the purification of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) which is always beneficial—it is not necessary to assume a [separate] connection (*saṃyoga*). [Note: It should be understood here that even though their status as auxiliary factors is established by the principle of "separation of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), the direct auxiliary status favored by the proponent of simultaneous performance (*samuccaya-vādin*) is not tenable; rather, it is through a mediated sequence.]
Because of the complexity of the assumption (*kalpanā-gaurava*).

Just as there is complexity in assuming a benefit (*upakāra*) in excess of those already established for the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) when applied to the modified rite (*vikṛti*), so too, since there would be the fault of complexity in assuming a destruction of sin (*pāpa-kṣaya*) in addition to that which is already established for sacrifices (*yajña*) and other acts enjoined upon knowledge (*jñāna*), the intention is that their combination (*samuccaya*) should not be assumed.
It is logical that the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) exists directly through distinctness, because otherwise there would be the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
For instance, from the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), there arises merit (*dharma*).

Thereupon, evil ceases; for it is that [evil] which, through the perversion characterized by the perception of permanence, purity, and pleasure in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) that is actually impermanent, impure, and painful, defiles the essence of the mind.

When evil has ceased and the doors to perception and logical proof have been opened, one understands without obstruction—by means of both perception and logical proof—the nature of the cycle of existence as being impermanent, impure, and painful.
Then, in this regard, a dispassion characterized by a lack of delight arises in him; from that, the desire to abandon it occurs; and from that, he seeks the means for its abandonment.

Seeking the knowledge of the reality of the Self, one hears that action is the means for this; desiring that knowledge, one then attains it through the sequence of hearing and so forth. Thus, it is logical that actions serve as remote auxiliaries toward the production of the knowledge of reality by way of purifying the essence of the mind (*citta-sattva*).
The *Bhagavadgītā* restates this very point: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the cause."
"For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means."
And thus, even for one who has not performed ritual actions, if he is a pure being who has developed detachment by perceiving the worthlessness of saṃsāra,

there is no need for him to perform ritual actions that serve as a means for generating detachment, since that [detachment] is already accomplished through the performance of ritual actions in a previous life.
And it is with reference to this very distinction among the foremost of men that the Śruti declares: "Or otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) itself.

This has been stated [by the author]: because the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is possible even for one who has studied the Vedānta prior to the comprehension of ritual action (*karma*). For this very reason, the religious debts (*ṛṇa*) do not exist for a student.
On account of this [debt], one should perform the ritual actions for the purpose of discharging it.
And in accordance with this, the scriptural passage, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born burdened with three debts," should be explained as referring to one who has become a householder;
otherwise, it would contradict the Śruti text, "Or else, in another way, [one may depart] from studenthood itself."
Even for a householder, the discharge of debts is solely for the purpose of purifying the inner being (*sattva*).
The doctrine that life ends with old age, the doctrine that it ends in ashes, and the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) are intended for those who are ignorant and dull-witted regarding ritual action,
but not for those who are learned in the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).
Therefore, its immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is the meaning of the word *atha*:
that without which the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) does not arise, but when which it exists, it necessarily comes to be.

Since the comprehension of ritual action (*karmāvabodha*) is not such [a prerequisite], the meaning of the word *atha* is not merely immediate succession to the comprehension of ritual action; thus all is clear.
This might be so:
let it be that the Agnihotra is not [the primary act], for it is recorded in the sacred tradition as "One performs the Agnihotra; one cooks the gruel."

In that context, regarding the doubt concerning the sequence: since the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without a substance, and because bringing in another substance would render the scriptural injunction meaningless, and because it is improper to assume a remote auxiliary function (*ārādupakārakatva*) when a visible purpose exists, the sequence is established by the sense of the text as "having cooked the gruel, he offers it.
The point is that such a situation is not possible here.

The sequence of meaning is like the cooking of gruel, whereas the scriptural [sequence] will be as follows: "Having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce"—this Jābāla Śruti indicates that the performance of sacrifices and other rites occurs through the state of a householder.

And they remember: "Having studied the Vedas according to rule, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having performed sacrifices as far as one is able, one should direct the mind toward liberation."
And they censure him, saying: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downwards."

To this he says: And just as there is a rule of immediate succession regarding the portions of the heart and so forth—for what reason? Because the sequence is intended to be expressed by the two words "first" (*agre*) and "then" (*atha*) in the passage, "He cuts off first from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest"—in the same way, no rule of sequence is intended to be expressed here.
For that very scripture demonstrates the absence of a fixed rule, stating:
"Or else, in another way, one may renounce from the stage of studentship itself, or from the house, or from the forest.
By this much, it indicates the presence of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

For this very reason, there is the Śruti text: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce. And the statement of censure is intended for those whose inner nature (*sattva*) is unpurified.

The meaning is that one whose *sattva* is unpurified, desiring liberation but failing to engage in its means due to indolence, falls downward moment by moment through the accumulation of sin while neglecting even the obligatory and occasional duties of a householder.
This might be so:
let there be neither a scriptural nor an implied sequence;
[for instance,] the five *prayāja* offerings, such as "He offers to the *samidhs*," are enjoined as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
The sequence for them is according to their textual recitation.
In the Sādyaskra sacrifice, which is a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma, three animals are obtained through extended application (atideśa): the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya.

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because of the scriptural injunction "one should immolate the animals together," the original order (*prakṛta-krama*) is set aside. And this "togetherness" occurs in the place of the *savanīya* animal;
such being the case, both of the other two [animals] undergo an equal displacement from their positions.

In this regard, since simultaneity characterized by identity of time is impossible, the priority of the *savanīya* offering is determined by its position; this is the order based on position (*sthānakrama*). Regarding the scriptural injunction, "There are two [deities] belonging to Sarasvatī; for Sarasvatī and Sarasvant constitute a divine pair," two rites are heard of as being performed simultaneously.
Here, first the pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the deity Sarasvatī is recited, and thereafter that for the deity Sarasvant.
Therefore, it is understood that this is the sequence of the two rites by way of this order, because [the sequence] is supplementary to the application of the mantras.

When there is a requirement for a sequence regarding specific subsidiary acts such as the pouring out (nirvāpa), the sequence is determined precisely by the sequence of the principal acts; this is what is meant by "sequence of the principal" (mukhyakrama).
It should be understood that this is also an illustration of the "sequence of performance" (pravṛttikrama).

Since the sequence of the acts beginning with the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) is established by the order of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, only a mere indication has been shown here for fear of prolixity. [Objection: Why then does the sequence not arise from the evidence of textual position (*pāṭha*), physical location (*sthāna*), primary purpose (*mukhya*), or procedure (*pravṛtti*)? [Response: He says: "Because there is no evidence for the relationship of subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and principal (*śeṣin*). For there is no single fruit [common] to the subsidiaries, such as the *samid*-offerings, and the principals, such as the *āgneya*-offerings.

FN: 2–The "subsidiaries" (*śeṣa*) and the "principals" (*śeṣin*) are those things connected as means toward that single benefit which belongs to the fruit-bearing *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice and so forth.
By this, it is established that they are embraced by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavacana*).
[This applies to] those things connected with the benefit, delimited by a single result, and embraced by a single injunction of performance.

FN: 3. By this, it is indicated that because there is no difference in the agent (*kartṛ*), there is necessarily a dependence on sequence (*krama*). FN: 4. By this, it is stated that there is simultaneous performance (*yugapadanuṣṭhāna*) for those [acts] having a single authorized agent (*ekādhikārikartṛka*), such as a single full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*); and since that cannot be established without sequence, there is a dependence on sequence everywhere. However, the point here is that because they are distinct (*pṛthaktva*), there is no dependence on sequence in the present case.
Since it is impossible to perform simultaneously those rites connected with the time of the new moon (amāvāsyā),

and since a sequence is established by implication, when there is a requirement for its specific determination, the order of recitation and other factors are capable of regulating that particular sequence.

However, where there is neither a relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣi-bhāva*) nor a delimitation by a single qualification— as in the case of the *Saurya*, *Āryamṇa*, [and *Prājāpatya* sacrifices]—

such as "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," "One desiring heaven should offer a *caru* to Aryaman," and "One desiring a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces should offer a *caru* to Prajāpati"—
there is no sequence (*krama*) among these sacrifices which have distinct results.
Because there is no connection [between them],
and because simultaneous recitation is impossible, the order of recitation— which would otherwise be unavoidable— would serve merely for the purpose of study,
as in the case of the *prājāpatya* and other [rites].

In that case, since there is no dependence on a distinction of sequence, the order of recitation and so forth is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for determining a specific sequence, because such an order is understood therein only as something unavoidable. Furthermore, in this instance, regarding the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman, none of the means of valid knowledge— such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the rest— is present.
FN: 6. The reading is "nanu.
[Objection: This might be so;
even in the absence of a relationship between the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin), a fixed order is observed.
Just as the *godohana* vessel, which serves a human purpose, stands in relation to the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;

or as in the case of the relationship between the entirety and the subordinate part in the injunction "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma," between the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Soma sacrifices—therefore he says: "Or because there is no evidence for an entitlement based on a prior entitlement. The construction is as follows:

for one who desires heaven is entitled to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and being one who subsequently desires cattle, he has an entitlement to the *godohana* used for milking, which is dependent upon the water-carrying (*praṇayana*) that serves the purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual.
Indeed, the substance used for milking cannot directly produce cattle while remaining inactive;

nor is it heard in scripture as being engaged in any other operation by which it might bypass the sequence of its subsidiary parts; rather, it is understood as being dependent upon the carrying forward of the water (*appraṇayana*).

From the co-utterance [of the texts], "One should lead forward the water with a *camasa* (ladle)," and "One desiring cattle [should lead it] with a *godohana* (milk-pail)," and because of the suitability of this [pail] for the leading forward of the water,

it follows that since the *godohana* rests upon the leading forward of water which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the *godohana*— though serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*)— is established as possessing sequence according to the sequence of that [leading forward].
By the very refutation of [the authority of] the *Śruti*, it should be understood that even the sequence—such as that between the *iṣṭi* and the *Soma* sacrifices—is discarded.

Even in the absence of the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*), of qualification and the qualified (*adhikṛta-adhikāra*), a sequence might be intended if there were a delimitation by a single result, as in the case of the six sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya*, which are delimited by the single result of heaven; or if Dharma were a part of Brahman, the object of inquiry.

Just as Brahman, which is to be defined by the four characteristics, is defined by each characteristic one by one through its various aspects—and in that case, since the four characteristics are interconnected because they do not differ in their object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), a specific sequence is intended—so too here, because there is a single object of inquiry, a sequence between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman might be intended. Yet, he says that neither of these two conditions exists: "And because of the difference in fruit and the object of inquiry."
He distinguishes the difference in results: "The result of dharma is knowledge.
Since, in reality, the desire to know (jijñāsā) is dependent upon knowledge, the meaning is that the result of knowledge is the result of the desire to know.
Not only is there a difference in results by way of their essential nature, [but also...]
He states that there is also a distinction between them based on the difference in the manner of their production: "And that [knowledge] depends upon practice;
whereas the knowledge of Brahman does not depend upon another practice.
Through the repeated cultivation of the knowledge derived from scripture, it does not require another practice."
The meaning is that the coexistence [of the two] with the performance of obligatory and occasional rites has been rejected.
He states the absolute difference between the objects of inquiry: "And dharma is that which is to be produced" (*bhavya*).
That which is to come into being is *bhavya*.

The *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). And because that which is to come into being (*bhavitā*) is dependent upon the activity of the agent (*bhāvaka-vyāpāra*) for its accomplishment, it does not exist prior to that—at the time of cognition; this is the meaning. "Bhūtam" means "the real" (*satyam*).
"Always exclusively" means that [the object] is never non-existent.

Not only is there a difference between the two objects of inquiry in terms of their own nature (*svarūpa*), but there is also a difference due to the difference in the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that makes them known; thus he says: "And because of the difference in the operation of the injunction (*codanā*)."
The term "codanā" refers to Vedic speech,
because it specifically indicates the general class;
he then distinguishes its specific application by stating, "that which is the injunction (codanā) of dharma."
Because human intentions such as commands and the like are impossible [in the case of the Veda], there is instruction by means of *codanā* (impulsion) in the authorless Veda.
For this very reason it has been said: "Of that, knowledge... [This is a portion of the fifth sūtra of the first chapter of the Jaiminīya [Mīmāṃsāsūtra]].

The meaning of that [sūtra] is as follows: the knowledge of that dharma is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the instruction (*upadeśa*), and the injunction (*vidhi*). And that [instruction] is... [itself]... the instruction. And that is its own... [nature].
FN: 2. "In its own" means in the subject matter to be established.

[This refers to] the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), which is the human activity directed toward the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and to the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, which are the objects of that [activity].
For that [object] is the domain of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because cultivation— which involves an effort dependent upon its object— is defined in dependence upon it;
this is because the word "domain" (*viṣaya*) is derived from the verbal root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding."

The injunction regarding ritual action (brahma-codanā), by making known through meditation and by means of that [meditation] that sacrifices and the like are the desired means, enjoins the person toward them by way of generating desire; it is only in this manner that it makes known the dharma of sacrifice and so forth, and not otherwise.
The injunction regarding Brahman, however, merely makes the person understand; it does not enjoin him while making him understand.
Why? Because understanding, being devoid of activity, is produced by the injunction itself.

Now, one might argue that since the Vedāntas—through injunctions such as "The Self is to be known"—induce a person toward awakening by forming a single syntactical unity with that [injunction], the injunctions regarding Brahman are equal to the injunctions regarding dharma; to this, he replies: "A person is not enjoined to awakening."
This is the intended meaning: a person cannot be enjoined to the direct realization of Brahman,
because that realization is eternal by virtue of being the very nature of Brahman and is therefore not something to be produced as an effect.
Nor [is it enjoined] with respect to meditative worship (*upāsanā*),

because that too— since its status as a cause for the excellence of knowledge is established through positive and negative concomitance— is already attained and thus not something to be enjoined. Nor [is it enjoined] with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
For that person who has studied the Vedas, who knows the words and their meanings, and who has mastered the principles of verbal logic, [the knowledge] arises without obstruction.
Regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "just as [the cognition of] objects through the senses";
he applies it to the case at hand: "in the same way."
Furthermore, in the Vedānta texts which are intent upon the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, the determination of the reality of the Self would not be verbal (śābda).
For those texts are not primarily concerned with the reality of the Self, but rather with the injunction for the knowledge thereof.
Whatever those [other texts] are primarily concerned with, that indeed is their purpose; and yet,
because cognition does not depend upon being directed toward its object,
the determination of the true nature of the object of cognition can arise even from texts whose primary intent lies elsewhere.

Because that [cognition] is also possible through superimposition (samāropa), as in the case of [the injunction] "One should worship speech as a cow," where even the object of superimposition becomes the object of the cognition of what is to be enjoined.
Therefore, it is established that the Vedāntas do not have the injunction for awakening as their primary purpose.
He concludes the subject at hand with the words, "therefore, something must be stated.
The meaning is: that in the absence of which the inquiry into Brahman does not arise, but in the presence of which it certainly does arise.
Thus he says: "It is said—discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities," and so forth.
The eternal is the inner self (*pratyagātman*); the non-eternal are the body, the senses, objects, and so on.
If the discernment regarding that [object] were a definitive certainty, then there would be no need for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*),
since Brahman would already be known.
Now, if discernment were merely knowledge and not a certainty,
then it would follow that this [discernment] would be a doubt distinct from error.
And thus, one would not cultivate detachment; and if one does not cultivate it, how could it be the cause for the desire to know Brahman?
Therefore, it must be explained in this way.

That which abides in the eternal and the non-eternal is the "eternal-non-eternal entity," and its property is the "discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal entities" (*nityānityavastuviveka*), meaning the discrimination between those two substrates and their respective properties.
What is meant by this is: let it not be that this [world] is real and eternal.
This [statement] "that is false and impermanent" is the distinction between two specific subjects;
it indeed determines the distinction between the mere subjects—namely, the permanent and the impermanent—and their respective properties.
Permanence is truth; that which possesses this [permanence] is permanent and true.
And likewise, it is the domain of non-reliance:
impermanence and unreality—whatever possesses these is impermanent and false;
and thus, it is the domain of non-reliance.

Therefore, while these objects and subjects—the spheres of the notions of "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "I" (*asmad*)—are being experienced, that which is established as real, eternal, and blissful will become the object of one's reliance;
whereas that which is impermanent and unreal, being encompassed by the threefold suffering, will be abandoned.

This discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities arises for one whose internal nature (*sattva*) has been purified by Vedic actions performed either in previous lives or in this life, through both experience and logical reasoning.
Indeed, it should not be said that there is no such thing as truth at all;
for in its absence, even falsehood— which is based upon it— would be impossible,
since even for the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins), emptiness itself is the truth.
Then, as this preeminent among men investigated with great precision through both experience and reasoning— from Satyaloka down to Avīci—

beholding himself and the world of living beings revolving in the cycle of "be born and die," encompassed by moments, muhūrtas, watches, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, years, yugas, the four yugas, manvantaras, pralayas, mahāpralayas, and mahāsargas, as well as intermediate creations, tossed upon the waves of the ocean of saṃsāra, and enveloped by the three-fold afflictions; he attained a profound discernment regarding this sphere of saṃsāra as being impermanent, impure, and essentially suffering.
It turns back;

then, from this discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) characterized by the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, there arises for him dispassion (*virāga*) toward the enjoyment of objects in this world and the next.
That which is sought or desired is called *artha*;
that is to say, the fruit (*phala*).
Detachment (*virāga*) toward that—

FN: 1. This means a state of mind characterized by indifference toward oneself due to a lack of regard [for others]. [This is] a state of mind characterized by equanimity consisting of non-exertion (*anābhoga*).
From that follows the perfection of the means, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).

For the mind, intoxicated by the wine of the impurities such as passion, impels the senses toward various high and low objects; it cultivates diverse activities that bear the fruits of merit and demerit,
and thus casts the person into the most terrible fire of saṃsāra, which is thick with the massed flames of manifold sufferings.

However, the mind—whose intoxication from the wine of the afflictions such as passion has been shattered by the ripening of dispassion attained through the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna*—is conquered and brought under control by the person.
This victory over the mind caused by dispassion is designated as "tranquility" (*śama*) and is also called "the consciousness of mastery" (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*).
And once the mind is conquered, it is led to a state of fitness for application toward the objects of reality (*tattva*).
This very fitness of his is self-control (*dama*).
Just as it is understood that this young bull has been tamed and is thus fit for pulling plows, carts, and so forth;
and by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), endurance toward sense objects, cessation from them, and faith in reality are comprised.

For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Therefore, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and possessed of faith, one should see the Self in the Self alone; he sees everything in the Self.
This refers to the perfection of these means consisting of tranquility, self-control, and so forth.
Excellence is the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).
From that, there arises in him the desire for liberation from the bondage of *saṃsāra*; thus he says: "and the state of being a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣutvam*)."

Having heard that knowledge of Brahman—which is by nature eternally pure, enlightened, and free—is the cause of liberation, there arises a desire to know that [Brahman], both before and after the desire to know Dharma;
therefore, he says "for in those" (*teṣu hi*) to indicate that the immediate succession belongs to those [desires to know] alone, and not to the desire to know Dharma.
It is not merely a desire to know.
But rather, he says that there is also knowledge—“and to know.
He concludes with “therefore.
He explains the word *ataḥ*, which follows in sequence: the word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, he states that very meaning of the word *ataḥ* as having the form of a reason: "Because [it is] in the Veda itself. Regarding this, one might raise the objection: "Since the word *atha* has already established the reason for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), what is the purpose of the word *ataḥ*? Anticipating this, he says: "Regarding this, in this way..."—meaning that by this word (*ataḥ*) there is no restatement of the reason; rather, it serves to dispel the charge of unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) regarding the reason previously stated.
An objection is raised: It is true that the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) occurs immediately after the fulfillment of the aforementioned means;
however, that very [desire] is untenable, because detachment from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next is itself untenable.
For the fruit is to be experienced as favorable, since the characteristic of a fruit is that it is desirable;
and it is not possible for there to be detachment toward that which is the cause of one's passion.

If it is argued that there is detachment even toward pleasure because one perceives its association with suffering, then alas! why does attachment not also arise toward suffering because of its association with pleasure?
Therefore, when pleasure is being pursued, one must strive to avoid suffering.
Having avoided even the suffering that has arrived because it was unavoidable, one will enjoy only pleasure.
It is just as, for example, one who desires fish takes up fish along with their scales and bones; having taken as much as can be taken, he desists.

Or, just as one seeking grain brings in the grain along with the straw, yet returns after taking only what is required, so too it is not right to abandon the happiness— whether pertaining to this life or the next— that is agreeable to experience, out of fear of suffering.
For indeed, rice is not left unsown because deer exist, nor are cooking pots left unheated because beggars exist.

Furthermore, even visible pleasure— born from association with sandalwood, women, and the like— might be abandoned by one who is excessively timid, because it is tainted by the suffering characterized by impermanence.
But it does not refer to the next world, such as heaven and so forth, because that is imperishable;
for it is heard in scripture: "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal."
And thus it is said: "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible.
Nor is an inference of perishability based on the reason of being produced possible here, as would be the case with the inference that a human skull is pure.

Note: The inference that "a human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell" has its object sublated by scripture, such as the statement: "Having touched a human bone while it still contains marrow, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. Likewise, [the claim that] merit is impermanent [is sublated].
The intention is that even the inference "because it is an effect, like a jar" is sublated by the scripture stating "it is imperishable.
This is because its subject matter is contradicted by scripture.
Therefore, since the aforementioned collection of means [for knowledge] is absent, it follows that there should be no inquiry into Brahman. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When this [objection] has been raised, the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra, says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The author of the Bhāṣya explains its meaning: "Because it is the Veda alone" (*yasmād veda eva*).
This is the intended sense (*abhisaṃdhi*): it is true that deer, mendicants, and the like can be avoided by cooks, farmers, and others; however, [the Veda cannot be avoided in the same way].
Suffering, however, arises from the convergence of many diverse causes and is impossible to avoid;
ultimately, this is because there is an invariable concomitance between all conditioned pleasure and two types of suffering characterized by dependence on means and by exhaustion.
For even the most skilled artisan cannot consume food mixed with honey and poison while discarding the poison and keeping the honey.

Furthermore, the scriptural statement beginning with "Just as here, those won by action... which establishes perishability, is reinforced by inference; and statements such as "We have drunk Soma," which would otherwise be taken literally, are relegated to a secondary (metaphorical) sense when a primary one is impossible, as the Paurāṇikas say: "The state [of immortality] until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called 'immortality'. And here, by the word "Brahman," its authority, the Veda, is brought to mind.

And because it is appropriate, that [passage] beginning with "Just as here, those who have accumulated karma... is referred to by the pronoun "from this" (*ataḥ*), and is indicated by the ablative case expressing a cause.
This might be so.

Just as there is an attachment to suffering in the case of produced happiness such as that of heaven, so it would be for Brahman as well; therefore, he says: "Likewise, even from the knowledge of Brahman.

By this, the meaning is as follows: because of the scripture which establishes the perishability of heaven and the like, and because of the scripture which establishes that the knowledge of Brahman is the supreme human goal.
Thus, it is established that there is a desire to know [Brahman] once the aforementioned perfection of means has been attained.
He provides the explanation of the term *brahmajijñāsā* with the words "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*).

By demonstrating that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it should be understood that the dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) proposed by the earlier commentators—namely, that "the desire to know for the sake of Brahman" is *brahmajijñāsā*—is refuted.

Because of the statement of Kātyāyana—"In a *tādarthya* compound, the mention of the relation between material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*) must be made"—there is a restriction that the fourth-case compound applies only to cases such as *yūpadāru* (sacrificial post-wood) where a material cause and its modification exist;
because this is prohibited in cases such as *aprakṛtivikārabhūta* (not being a material cause and its modification);
and because of the provision for sixth-case compounds in cases such as *aśvaghāsa* (horse fodder), stating "in *aśvaghāsa* and so forth, they shall be sixth-case compounds."
And even in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the actual predominance of Brahman is established.
This might be argued: when it is said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇo jijñāsā*), a doubt arises there because the word *brahman* has multiple meanings.
Of what Brahman is there the desire to know?
There is the word "Brahman" used in the sense of the caste of the Brāhmaṇa,
as in the term "brahmahatyā" (the killing of a Brāhmaṇa).
And there is [a statement] in the Veda, such as "the theft of Brahman" (brahmahatyā); and there is [a statement] regarding the Supreme Self, such as "he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed."
He dispels this doubt with the words: "and Brahman is that whose definition will be stated.

Since, having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), he formulates the definition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in order to make it known, we understand from this that this is indeed an inquiry into the Supreme Self, and not an inquiry into the caste of a Brahmin or similar categories; this is the meaning.
Even if one accepts the analysis as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), this is not a genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).
However, it is *śeṣalakṣaṇā* (indication by way of being subordinate),

and since "subordinate" (*śeṣa*) means merely a relationship, when it is said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahma-jijñāsā*), it is effectively said "the desire to know that which is related to Brahman.

Thus, all desires to know the nature of Brahman, its means of valid cognition, its logical proofs, its instruments of realization, and its purpose, are included within the "desire to know Brahman" and are encompassed by it.
This is because [the means of knowledge] are connected to Brahman either directly or through a traditional lineage.
If, however, the genitive case were used in the sense of an object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), then the meaning of the word "Brahman" would be the object;
and since that [object] is merely its own nature (*svarūpa*), its means of knowledge and so forth would not be included [as distinct categories].

To those who think that, in that case, there would be an investigation of matters not proposed [as the subject] regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, he says: "Of Brahman" [is used] in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*).
He states the reason for this: "Because it is to be desired to be known" (*jijñāsya*); for knowledge is the necessary concomitant for the attainment of desire.
And the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is Brahman.

Indeed, knowledge cannot be defined without its object, nor can the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) exist without knowledge; therefore, because it is a prerequisite for comprehension, the desire to know first requires an object (*karman*).
But it is not merely a relation in general; for even in the absence of a specific relatum, an action can still be defined.
Indeed, upon perceiving the moon or the sun, one does not engage in a search for a relatum by asking, "To whom does this belong?"

However, when it is said "there is knowledge," there arises an inquiry into its object, namely, "of what object? Therefore, because it is required first, Brahman is connected [to the verb] specifically as its object (karman),
and not merely by way of being a related entity.
Because that [agent] is subordinate;
thus, the meaning is that the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*).
Now, it is true that without an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) cannot be defined.
"But there will be another object of inquiry for this [text], while Brahman will be connected as a subordinate element"; therefore, he says: "there being another object of inquiry. [Note:
1—The hidden intention is that the status of being well-versed in many scriptures, such as the means of valid knowledge and liberation, is established.]
With a hidden intention, he raises an objection: "But even if the genitive case is taken as a residual one (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*)...

The meaning is that since a general relationship does not contradict a specific relationship, there is no obstacle to [the word *brahma*] being the object (*karman*), and thus the definition of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is established.
With that same hidden intention, he refutes it: "Even so, [it would follow that] Brahman is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*)."

By abandoning the connection with the expressed objecthood— which is first required due to the desire to know it and is most fit for primary relation— and instead connecting with a mere relative that is only somehow required later,
you have well articulated the principle of logic: "the last [to be connected] is the first, and the first is the last."
The mention of "perceptibility" and "imperceptibility" intends [respectively] priority and non-priority, or clarity and lack of clarity.
The opponent reveals his own intention: "It is not useless, because [it concerns] everything dependent upon Brahman."
This has been explained above. The respondent reveals his own underlying intention: "There is no grasping of a primary cause," for the actual primacy belongs to Brahman.

The remainder, including the discussion on "with visibility" (sanidarśana), has its meaning unobscured, and the conformity with scripture (śruti) is likewise unobscured. Having thus established the intended summary, he states the meaning of the term *jijñāsā*: "to know" (*jñātum*).
It might be argued: knowledge is not the object of desire;
rather, it is the attainment or avoidance of pleasure and pain, or the means thereto, that becomes the sphere of desire by way of that [knowledge].
But the knowledge of Brahman is not like this;
for it is certainly not experienced as being "conducive" or as the "cessation of the unfavorable," nor is it a means to those two.

Even when that [pleasure] exists, no distinct pleasure is observed, and the persisting suffering does not cease; therefore, the nature of knowledge as an instrument of action cannot be established merely by the word of the author of the Sūtras. For this reason, he says: "it culminates in comprehension" (*avagatiparyantam*).

It is not merely knowledge that is intended; rather, the object of the desire expressed by the suffix *san* is that which brings about realization—that is, direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*)—extending up to the point of full comprehension.
Why?
Because desire has a result as its object.
The ellipsis is that [the word] "desire" (icchā) refers to that which takes as its object the means to that [end], culminating in the fruit.
Now, let it be granted that knowledge culminates in comprehension; even so, how does this much become the desired goal?

For knowledge that does not have a dependent object is not even desired as culminating in comprehension; therefore, he says: "Brahman is indeed what is intended to be comprehended by means of the instrument of knowledge.
[Objection: Let there be comprehension having Brahman as its object; even so, why is it desired? To this he replies: "For the comprehension of Brahman is the human goal (puruṣārtha)."
Is it worldly prosperity? No;

rather, it is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). The realization of Brahman—which is a mass of supreme bliss from which all connection with suffering has vanished—is the very nature of Brahman; therefore, that alone is the supreme good, the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).
This may be so.
The realization of Brahman is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
for a human goal is that which is reached through human activity.
And in this [realization], which is of the very nature of Brahman, there can be no origination, modification, purification, or attainment.
If that were so, its nature as impermanent would be untenable due to its inherent character;
nor, in the absence of origination and so forth, could there be subsumption under causal operation.

Therefore, since the realization of Brahman would not be a human goal, he says: "Because it eradicates the evils such as ignorance, which are the seeds of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence."
True; although origination and the like are impossible within the nature of Brahman when Brahman is realized,
nevertheless, by the power of beginningless, indefinable ignorance (avidyā), the very nature of Brahman— though its manifestation is independent of anything else and is indeed manifest—
appears as if it were not manifest, as if its manifestation were dependent on another, and though distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, it appears as if non-distinct.

Thus, because it destroys the seeds of saṃsāra— ignorance and the rest— and because, while that [knowledge] is absent, [the goal] is as if unattained, and when it is present, it is as if attained, it is rightly called "the aim of man" (puruṣārtha), since it is what is sought by the person.
By the inclusion of the word "and the rest" in the phrase "ignorance and the rest," its latent impressions (saṃskāra) are also encompassed.

However, it should be understood that the cessation of ignorance and the rest occurs through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), which is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibheda*) resulting from meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
He concludes: "Therefore, Brahman is to be sought after by one who desires liberation and possesses the characteristics already described."
Indeed, without that knowledge, ignorance—which is the cause of various sufferings along with their latent impressions—is not severed.

And without its severance, there can be no manifestation for the individual soul (*jīva*) of the direct realization of the nature of Brahman, which is a mass of bliss from which all connection with suffering has vanished.
Therefore, one who desires the nature of Brahman as a mass of bliss must seek knowledge as the means to that end.
And that [knowledge] does not arise from the Vedāntas alone, but rather from the Vedāntas as aided by the Brahmamīmāṃsā;

for it should be understood here that one who desires the identity of Brahman and the Self must seek knowledge, and since that [knowledge] comes from the Vedāntas through the instrumentality of inquiry, the meaning is that the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken.
If it is asked: "How then is it said that *jijñāsā* (the desire to know) is not the subject of qualification, whereas *vicāra* (inquiry) is?"—[the answer is: *Jijñāsā* is the desire to know.
For that [desire] arises for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion regarding a doubtful matter.
And since that inquiry is to be accomplished through investigation, the necessity of performing the inquiry is understood by implication (*arthāt*).
While this meaning is implied, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "should be performed" (*kartavya*);
however, the literal (*śrauta*) sense is that it is proper for the desire for knowledge of Brahman to arise immediately after the fourfold qualification.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously.
[The inquiry] is set in motion by means of the *Pakaraṇas* through the gateway of desire, but not within the Vedānta texts themselves, nor regarding the intention to express their meaning.

In this regard, since the very sūtra "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) has already set forth the fact that the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) is directed toward the comprehension of its purposeful meaning—
given that the term "Dharma" is used as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the meaning of the Veda in general, and thus indicates Brahman just as it indicates Adharma—
it might be argued that, like the Mīmāṃsā of Dharma, the Mīmāṃsā of Brahman could also be implied by the Mīmāṃsā of the Veda’s meaning. Nevertheless...

Nevertheless, that [qualification] is not established by the earlier Mīmāṃsā, nor is there immediate succession following the mere study of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā; therefore, this sūtra must be commenced both to initiate the Brahma-mīmāṃsā and to demonstrate the immediate succession of the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal and so forth—thus there would be no redundancy.
This might be the case.

It has been stated that by this Sūtra, the status of Mīmāṃsā as a means toward the knowledge of Brahman is established; however, that is incorrect because it cannot withstand critical analysis. Thus, he raises an objection: "But as for that Brahman... and so forth.
It must be either well-known or unknown from the Vedantas, which possess self-evident authority due to their being non-human (apauruṣeya) in origin.
If it is well-known,
it has been made an object of certain knowledge arising from the sentences of the Vedantas.
Therefore, it need not be investigated,
because with respect to an object whose action has already been accomplished,
a means of proof that does not produce any further distinction would overstep the very logic of being a means of proof.
Now, if it were not established by the Vedantas, then the Vedantas would not be propounding it; thus, that which is entirely unestablished cannot be an object of inquiry.
For desire arises toward what has been experienced as dear, but not toward something entirely unexperienced and unprecedented.
Moreover, even if it were desired, it could not be known.
Because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it must be stated that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is its means of valid cognition, as he will state later: "Because [Brahman] has the sacred teaching as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).
If it does not bring about that awakening,
how can it possess authority regarding it?
Nor does any other means of valid cognition apply to Brahman.

Therefore, the objection is that Brahman is not an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), because it is not inquired about even though it is well-known and capable of being known; nor is it an object of desire when it is unknown; and furthermore, because it is impossible to know.
The author provides the following response: It is said that Brahman, whose very nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, does indeed exist.

This is the meaning: even prior to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*), for one who has studied the Vedas and has understood the relationship between words and their meanings through the study of the *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and so forth, there exists—at least at first glance and even without formal investigation—an initial comprehension of the nature of Brahman as endowed with eternity and other such qualities, derived from the textual corpus beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and ending with "That thou art."
FN: 1. The word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is connected with the word "well-known" (*prasiddhi*), not with the reason (*hetu*), because [the latter] would be redundant.
And here, by means of the object of comprehension—namely, "Brahman" and so forth—he indicates the comprehension that has that as its object.

Since there is no certainty regarding its existence prior to investigation, even when such an inquiry occurs, the term "eternal" introduces suffering characterized by perishability. *Note: Eternality (nityatva) should be understood as the state of being neither a counter-positive of destruction nor a counter-positive of antecedent non-existence.* *Note: [The term] "eternal" implies suffering whose defining characteristic is decay.*
Note: "Impurity" (aśuddhi) refers to the stain of agency, enjoyership, passion, and so forth; "pure" (śuddha) means being devoid of that.
By the word "pure," it also removes suffering conditioned by the body and other such adjuncts.
By the word "awakened" (buddha), it shows the Self to be blissful and characterized by independent luminosity.
Because bliss and light are non-different.
This might be so:
these qualities, such as purity and so forth, manifest for him when liberation has been attained.
Now, first, there is a doubt based on the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) regarding the body;
the resolution, however, is that [the soul] is eternally liberated.

Because [the Self] would otherwise be joined with the suffering of birth, old age, death, and so forth, which are properties of those [conditioned things] through their differentiation, it is said: "liberated" (*mukta*).
The meaning is that it is eternally liberated and eternally alone, yet due to beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), it appears as such through delusion (*bhrānti*).
Having thus shown the unconditioned form of Brahman, [the text proceeds to discuss] the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance...
FN: 5. This means "made the object of ignorance.
He describes his [the Lord's] superior form as "omniscient and endowed with all powers.
By this, his status as the cause of the universe is demonstrated.

Since the presence or absence of causality follows the presence or absence of power and knowledge, from what source, then, does such an understanding of the nature of Brahman arise? To this he says: "For of the word *brahman*...

Indeed, the understanding of Brahman as being of such a nature arises not only from a consideration of the preceding and succeeding passages of sentences such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1).
Moreover, the term *brahmapada* itself, by the power of its etymological derivation, confirms this very meaning.
He provides the derivation: because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh*. For the root *bṛh* has the sense of "increasing" (*vṛddhi*) and functions in the sense of "surpassing."
And this [term] "exceeding" (*atiśāyana*)—[the objection being]:

"But even if *bṛhati* has the sense of exceeding, how can there be 'unconditionedness' (*anavacchinnatva*)?"—means that it permits for that [Self] qualities such as being eternally pure and enlightened, which are understood from other words and are unconditioned due to the absence of any limiting factors such as context (*prakaraṇa*). This is the intended meaning.

Having thus stated the well-known nature of the referent of the word *tat* (That), such as its purity and so forth, he also speaks regarding the referent of the word *tvam* (Thou): "And because [Brahman] is the Self of all, the existence of Brahman is well-known.
The phrase "of all" is to be construed with "well-known," and not with the reason.
Because it would be redundant.
[The term *pāṃsula* refers to one whose feet are covered with dust (*pāṃsu*).]
Even for a plowman,
who is one that draws a plough (*hālika*),
there is the established proof of the existence of Brahman.
Why? Because it is the self (ātman).
He clarifies this very point with the words "for everyone" (sarvo hi).
He confirms cognition itself by means of the exclusion of non-cognition with the words "not not" (na na).

The construction is: "It is not that he does not recognize 'I am,' but rather that he certainly does recognize it. Now, one might object: "He will both know 'I am' and yet not know the Self"; to this, he says: "If... (yadīti).
One should not perceive "I am.
For if one does not perceive the individual self (*jīvātman*), which is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
the meaning is that one would not perceive "I."
Now, one might object: "Surely every person recognizes the self as the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
what, then, has this to do with Brahman? To this, he says: "And the self is Brahman," because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between "that" (tat) and "this" (tvam).
Therefore, since the referent of the word *tat*— namely, purity, enlightenment, and so forth— is established through verbal testimony,
and the referent of the word *tvam*— namely, the individual self— is established through direct perception,
and because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words;
The sense is that the realization of the referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) as being Brahman is established through the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi).
The objector states the defect inherent in the first alternative: "If, then, in the world... Here, "the world" refers to the tradition of teachers and students.

In that regard, if [the self] were already well-known as being Brahman through the sentence "That thou art," then—where it ought to have been stated that "the self is Brahman"—the expression "as Brahman-self" (brahmātmatvena) is to be understood as intending to convey non-difference. [The author] refutes this: "No."
Why? Because there is disagreement regarding its specific nature.
By this, it is stated that disagreement—when there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition—is the seed of doubt.
And thus, from that doubt, the desire to know (jijñāsā) arises; such is the intended meaning.
The subject (*dharmin*) of the legal dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) must be accepted as established by the tenets common to all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddha*).
Otherwise, disagreements (*vipratipattayaḥ*) would either lack a basis or have different bases;
for disagreements are indeed contradictory cognitions.
Furthermore, cognitive realizations cannot be without a basis,
for that would entail the consequence of them being without an object;
nor can those with different bases be contradictory.
For there is no contradiction between the cognition that "intellect is impermanent" and the [opposing] cognition that "the self is permanent.
Therefore, the realization of the referent of that [word 'self']— namely, its purity, enlightenment, and so forth— is derived from the Vedāntas.

The existence of the referent of the term *tvam*, namely the individual self (*jīvātman*), is established by common worldly experience and is an accepted tenet of all philosophical systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*). Disagreements (*vipratipatti*) arise here only regarding its specific attributes—namely, whether it is a mere appearance or not an appearance.
Therefore, since the subject (*dharmin*) is generally established while there is disagreement regarding its specific qualities, doubt concerning those specific qualities is appropriate.

In this regard, he first demonstrates the various conflicting views concerning the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you" in "Thou art That"), beginning with the words "the body alone," and ending with "only the enjoyer, not the agent. Here, according to the positions that identify the self with the body, the senses, the mind, momentary consciousness, or pure sentience (*caitanya*), the attributes of the referent of the term *tat* (the "That")— such as its eternity and so forth— are not connected with the referent of the term *tvam*.
Because of the absence of fitness [to be an object of cognition],
even in the case of the position of emptiness (*śūnyapakṣa*), how could that which is devoid of all designations and is not a referent of words (*apadārtha*) be the object of the path to reality?

Furthermore, since even that whose nature is that of an agent and enjoyer is subject to transformation, there is likewise an inconsistency regarding the eternity and other attributes of that referent.
Even on the view that [the Self] is an enjoyer despite being a non-agent, there is an inconsistency with its eternity and other attributes due to its undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitā*).

Even on the view that it is a non-enjoyer, because it would be limited by plurality, there would follow impermanence and so forth, and since this would result in the loss of non-duality (*advaita*), the inconsistency regarding the referent of the word *tat* remains just as it was.
Furthermore, by means of the disagreement concerning the referent of the word *tvam*, disagreement regarding the referent of the word *tat* has also been demonstrated.
For the Lokāyatikas and others who deny the authority of the Vedas consider the cognition of the categories [taught] therein to be false;
whereas the Mīmāṃsakas are those who uphold the authority of the Vedas.

It was shown previously that those who assert that the Veda has action as its purpose consider the Vedāntas to be either figurative or not intended to convey their own literal meaning. Even those who maintain the authority [of the Vedāntas] consider the referent of that term (*tatpada*) to be figurative or unintended.

Thus, having indicated the disagreement regarding the referent of the term *tat* by means of the disagreement regarding the referent of the term *tvam*, he states the disagreement directly concerning the referent of the term *tat*: "There exists a Lord distinct from that, who is omniscient."
Some say it is "all-powerful.
The word "that" refers to the individual soul (jīvātman),
not merely [as distinct] from the body and so forth.
He is also distinct from individual souls (jīvātman).
He rules over the entire world.
For the sake of establishing His sovereignty, two natural attributes of His have been stated: He is omniscient and omnipotent.

Because that [Īśvara] is also distinct from the individual selves (jīvātman), it cannot be in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the referent of the term "thou" (tvam); thus he states his own view: "Others say that he is the self of the enjoyer.
That Īśvara, the referent of the term "that" (tat), is the self of the enjoyer—the individual self characterized by the limiting adjunct of ignorance (avidyopādhika).

Therefore, the individual soul (jīvātman) is non-different from the Lord (Īśvara), just as the space within a jar is non-different from the supreme space; this is the meaning. Concluding the conflicting views, he states the seed of those disagreements: "In this way, many... and so forth.
The construction is: "being based on arguments and fallacious arguments, and on statements and fallacious statements.

Now, one might object: "Granted that there are conflicting views and doubt caused by them, for what purpose is the Brahmamīmāṃsā commenced? To this he says: "In that regard, without having investigated... and so forth.
Furthermore, the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) must result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and cannot arise from the lack of such knowledge.
Moreover, the meaning is that through the lack of knowledge of reality, when nihilism (*nāstikya*) occurs, there is the acquisition of misfortune.
He concludes the purport of the aphorism with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The Vedānta-mīmāṃsā is indeed reasoning (*tarka*);
