and those other reasonings which do not contradict it—those stated in the Adhvara-mīmāṃsā and in Nyāya for the purpose of purifying the validity of the Veda, perception, and so forth—are its instruments (*upakaraṇa*). Thus it is described.
Therefore, it is established that this Brahma-mīmāṃsā must be commenced, as its purpose is the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to the supreme *niḥśreyasa*. //1//
START BsVBh_1,1.2.2:
*janmādyasya yataḥ* (BBs_1,1.2).
Having thus established the commencement of the inquiry by means of the first sūtra, he begins the Brahma-mīmāṃsā: "From which [Brahman] proceed the birth and so forth of this [world]."
The author of the commentary states the introductory lead-in (*pātanikā*) to this sūtra: "It has been stated that Brahman is to be desired to be known.
But what is the characteristic of that Brahman?

Although, by the primary proposition concerning the knowledge of the nature of Brahman, its subordinate elements such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are also implicitly proposed;
Nevertheless, because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is primary, that alone is first established by implication.
In this regard, whatever is experienced is entirely limited, impure, non-intelligent, and perishable;
it is not possible to define the essential nature of Brahman—which is by nature eternal, pure, intelligent, and free—by means of such perceived objects, as they are contrary to it.
For no one ever characterizes anything as eternal on the basis of its being a product;
nor is it characterized by that property, such as eternality,
because that [property] has never been perceived before.
For a definition must be well-known,
not something entirely unknown.
Thus—

FN: 1. If it is argued that even though [Brahman] is not established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it might be established through verbal testimony (*śabda*), to this he replies: "If that were so," etc.
And verbal testimony does not even apply here, because Brahman—being absolutely unestablished—is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*) and therefore cannot be the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*).
Therefore, because of the absence of a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), Brahman is not to be inquired into; such is the intention of the objection.
The venerable author of the Sūtras refutes this very objection with the words: "From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]."

Let it not be that the world, as it is being experienced, is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman either by way of its essential nature (*taddharmatayā*) or through identity (*tādātmyena*). [FN:
2—By virtue of being produced from it, the world makes known its own cause;
the reaching of another location is nothing but the movement of the sun.]
The intended meaning is that, through its arising, [the cause] will [indicate the effect], just as the movement of the sun is inferred from its arrival at another location.
He analyzes the components of the aphorism: "janma-utpatti-ādiḥ asya" (birth, origination, etc., are its beginning).
For the sake of brevity, the author of the aphorism used the neuter form "janmādi"; to justify this, he states the collective compound: "janma-sthiti-bhaṅgam" (birth, subsistence, and dissolution).
The textual passage beginning with "And from birth" and ending with "the indication of the cause" is explained by its own words (*nigadavyākhyāta*).
This might be argued:

while [other causes] such as *pradhāna*, time, the planets, the world-protectors, action, chance, inherent nature, and non-existence are being proposed as alternatives, on what basis is Brahman—omniscient and possessing an omnipotent nature—established as the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe?
To provide a basis for this probability, he says: "of this world.

Here, by the phrase "of that which has been differentiated by name and form," he excludes the possibility of its being produced by an insentient agent such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) or by an agent who is non-existent (*nirupākhya*), through the probability that it has a conscious being as its agent.
For whatever is differentiated by name and form is observed to have a conscious agent.
Just like a jar or similar objects;
and this world, which is the subject of dispute, is differentiated by name and form; therefore, it is inferred to have an intelligent creator.
For an intelligent being, having first delineated name and form in the mind, [designates them] by the name "jar," and so forth.
And by means of its form—such as having a neck shaped like a conch—he produces an external jar.

For this very reason, although the jar is to be produced (*nirvartya*), it possesses the status of an object (*karma-kāraka*) because it is already established within [the agent] in the form of a mental conception (*saṃkalpa*), as in the expression "he makes a jar.
As they have said: "But that which is established by the intellect is not non-existent."
The point is that it is impossible to conceive of an insentient entity acting without having first inscribed [its intention] in the intellect (*buddhi*).
This might be argued:
"The conscious deities (*cetana*), the planets (*graha*), or the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) will produce the world after having inscribed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in their intellects."

To the objection that [the world] could have been created by Brahman, whose nature is that of one who has already acted and ceased acting, he says: "of that which is joined with many agents and enjoyers.
Some are agents, such as weavers, officiating priests, and so forth.
They are not all enjoyers;
however, some are enjoyers,
such as the father, son, and others in rites like the Śrāddha or the Vaiśvānareṣṭi.
They are not the agents.
Therefore, there is the mention of both.
"Place, time, cause, action, and fruit" is a mutual dvandva compound.
The analysis of the compound is: "those [factors] such as place and so forth, which are specifically determined.
The world has that [determination] as its basis.
Indeed, some things arise in specific locations.
For example, black antelopes and the like;
some arise at specific times,
such as the warbling of cuckoos and so forth in the spring.
Some have specific causes,
such as the pregnancy of cranes and the like, which are caused by the sound of new clouds and so forth;
some have specific functions.
Just as for Brahmins there are activities such as officiating at sacrifices which are not for others,
so too are there specific fruits;
for example, some are happy.
Some are suffering;
likewise, those who are happy are at other times suffering.

All of this is incompatible with the view that things are accidental—another name for being arbitrary—or that they are inherent by nature, or that they are produced by a creator who is neither omniscient nor omnipotent.
Because it is impossible for those such as the planetary deities and world-protectors, whose power of knowledge is limited, to know or create it;
this is what is meant by the phrase "whose form is a construction inconceivable even by the mind.
For indeed, the form of even a single bodily configuration can never be conceived by the mind.
The meaning is: "How much more so before the creation of the world, let alone to create it.
He completes the sentence of the Sūtra with the remainder of the phrase: "That is Brahman."

This might be asked: why, then, are only birth, persistence, and destruction included here by the mention of "and so forth" (ādi), and not growth, transformation, and decay as well? To this he says: "The other modifications of being—such as growth and the rest—are also included within these three alone."
Growth (*vṛddhi*) is first of all the accumulation of parts;
therefore, from a composite whole consisting of few parts, such as a two-threaded [fabric], a distinct and large cloth is produced—thus, growth is simply birth (*janma*).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) as well, characterized by the three aspects of quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*), is likewise nothing but origination (*utpatti*).
For the modification of the attributes (*dharma*)—such as bracelets, crowns, and so forth—of a substrate (*dharmin*) such as gold, is its "origination" (*utpatti*).
Likewise, the modification of bracelets and the like characterized by states such as the present is their "origination.
Similarly, the modification of states (*avasthā*), such as newness or antiquity, is "origination."
Diminution (*apakṣaya*), however, is the reduction of parts, which is indeed destruction (*nāśa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that growth and the rest are not mentioned separately because they are included within birth and the others as appropriate.
Now, suppose these—growth and the rest—are not included within birth and the others; [then...]
Nevertheless, only origination, subsistence, and dissolution (utpatti-sthiti-bhaṅga) should be taken as the defining characteristics;

for when that is the case, and the Vedic statement "from which indeed these beings [arise]" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni*)—which establishes those characteristics—is brought to mind, Brahman is defined as the root cause of the world.
Otherwise, if [the states] "is born," "exists," "grows," and so forth were included, the etymological statement (*nairukta-vākya*) establishing them would come to mind.
And that [text] does not have the purpose of propounding a primary cause,

because even during the period of maintenance (sthiti) following the great creation (mahāsarga), the modifications of being (bhāvavikāra)— such as birth and so forth— spoken of in those sentences are possible. To dispel this doubt, he states "yāskaparipaṭhitānāṃ tu" (but regarding those recited by Yāska), thereby including the origination, maintenance, and dissolution mentioned in the Veda.

[Objection: Even so, let only origination be indicated; persistence and destruction will be understood as being inseparable from that. To this, he says: "That which is the origination of Brahman from a cause... [The word] "from a cause" (kāraṇāt) refutes the suspicion that the genitive case ending might be intended.
The word *diti* indicates its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) by means of three [characteristics].
However, mere origination is common to efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) as well.

Note: 2. Here it should be understood that although being a cause of origination (*nimittakāraṇa*) is common to all things, its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established by the statement that it is the substratum of dissolution (*layādhāra*).
For pots and the like do not dissolve within sticks and such [instrumental causes].
Therefore, if it is argued that [the other causes] are redundant, we say no.

It should be understood that this [statement] was not made merely to indicate that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*); rather, it is intended to establish non-duality (*advaita*) by means of the principle of the non-difference between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-abheda*). Thus, the doubt must be dispelled: "Let Brahman be the material cause, but let there be another as the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), just as a potter is for the production of a jar."
One should not indicate an appropriation (*upādāna*).
This is what is meant by the phrase "in that very [context].
He states the purpose of the previously mentioned qualifications of cause and effect with the words "not as previously stated."

Therefore, by this [statement], he dispels the objection: "If Brahman is established through its definition alone, then the two sections concerning 'having scripture as its source' (*śāstrayonitva*) and 'harmonization' (*samanvaya*) would be redundant. He says:
"By this... For a definition makes known the distinction of an already established entity, [showing] that "it is such-and-such."
Through this continuous exposition, the possibility of the subject of the proposition—the nature of Brahman—has been stated by way of its definition. [FN:
4] *Saṃbhāvanā* is a doubt in which one alternative is predominant.
For, by means of the effect, it is inferred that some cause exists.
It is doubted whether that reality is one or many;
when its oneness is established, it then becomes omniscient and omnipotent.

This doubt is said to be "possible" (*saṃbhāvya*) when it is brought to a state where one alternative is predominant by means of the reasoning known as *kalpanālāghava* (the parsimony of postulation).

Since it is observed that palaces and the like have multiple makers, no certainty [regarding a single creator] arises in those cases; therefore, the sense is that the section concerning fire (*agnyadhikaraṇa*) is necessary for the sake of reaching such certainty.

In this regard, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated, as the Naiyāyikas have said: "The subject (*pakṣa*) proposed in the thesis (*pratijñā*) is to be established by means of a reason (*hetu*)."
There is no protection for him from causes, he who is destroyed even as he is arising.
And as in the case of [the statement] "a barren woman is a mother," and so forth;

thus, birth and so on are indeed grounds for probability (*saṃbhāvanāhetu*), since others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others, desire the ascertainment of God (*īśvara*) from this very inference. To strengthen this status as a ground for probability, he says: "This very [inference]," and so on.
He raises an objection with the words, "Is it not so here too?

Having concluded the point of the current section (*adhikaraṇa*) with just this much, he replies out of friendship by restating the point of the section that is about to be discussed, beginning with "Not [by] the Vedāntas.
He demonstrates that the purpose is precisely the stringing together of the flowers of the Vedānta passages with the words, "The Vedāntas..."
The final ascertainment through deliberation (*vicāra*) is the eradication of the two forms of ignorance along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For from that [ascertainment] arises the cessation of [ignorance] and the manifestation of the realization of Brahman.
Therefore, should no other means of knowledge besides the Word (*śabda*) be followed regarding Brahman?

And thus, from where could there be reflection (*manana*), and from where its experience, which is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*)? To this he says: "But when the Vedānta texts exist. It should also be understood that inference is non-contradictory to the Vedānta and dependent upon it.
Reflection (*manana*) is the discernment [of reality] by means of reasoning (*yukti*) that is not in contradiction with scripture and which depends upon it;
and this reasoning is either presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*).
This might be so.

Since one might ask why human intellect does not assist [the understanding] of Brahman in the same way it assists with regard to Dharma, he says: "Not as in the inquiry into Dharma," and "Scripture and so forth."
The Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Direct experience (*anubhava*)—which is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibheda*) consisting of the immediate realization of Brahman—is the result of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*). This result is the manifestation of the true nature of Brahman through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*);
it should be understood as a "result" in the sense that it is like a result.
Although perception and the other means of knowledge do function within the totality [of causes] for the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), they do not do so directly.

In the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), however, direct experience and the like are possible; moreover, the inquiry into Brahman has experience as its goal. Thus it is said: "Because it culminates in experience. The experience of Brahman—the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
"Because it consists of supreme bliss from which all suffering has been wiped away.
Now, one might object: "Granted that the desire to know (jijñāsā) is for the sake of experiencing Brahman, yet that very experience is impossible."
Because Brahman is unfit to be an object [of empirical cognition], he says: "And because the knowledge of Brahman has for its object an existent reality (*bhūtavastu*).
[The term] *vyatireka* refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by the absence of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*).
The point is that the relationship between the direct realization of that [Brahman] and Brahman as subject and object— being of the nature of conceptual construction— does not exist in reality.
[This refers to] the subject-object relationship of direct realization being of the nature of conceptual construction.
But knowledge of Dharma is not thus terminated by experience,
because that experience itself is not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
whereas the human goal is to be accomplished through the performance of that [knowledge].
And since the performance [of an action] is established through verbal knowledge alone even without direct experience, he says, "For in the case of what is to be done," and so forth.
Nor is this [dharma] fit to be an object of direct perception because it is not present;
and it is not present because it is not fixed [in time]. Thus he says, "Dependent on the person."
He states that worldly and Vedic actions depend solely upon a person by saying, "to do or not to do.
He cites an unsettled worldly action as an example: "as in the case of a horse.
Together with this worldly example, he combines a Vedic example: "likewise, the Atirātra [sacrifice]."
This has been stated as an example of [the power] "to do" or "not to do.
He states the example for "to do otherwise" as follows: "when it has risen," and so forth.
This might be the case.

Because human autonomy would render injunctions and prohibitions purposeless—since the engagement and withdrawal of a person are not dependent upon them—it is said: "In this case, injunctions and prohibitions would be meaningful.
"He takes" is an injunction.
"Does not take" is a prohibition;
there are injunctions regarding both the offered and unoffered oblations.
Likewise, the prohibition against touching a human bone and the injunction for a slayer of a Brahmin to avoid it—prohibitions and injunctions of this kind are meaningful.
Why is this so? To this he says: "And there are options, exclusions, and inclusions.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason.

Because there is a contradiction between grasping and not grasping, and between the *uditahoma* and *anudita-homa* offerings, a combination is impossible; and since they are of equal strength, there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhaka-bhāva*). Thus, in the absence of any other recourse (*agatyā*), an option (*vikalpa*) must be accepted.
Since the prohibition against touching human bones and the injunction for wearing them are contradictory and possess unequal force, there can be no option (*vikalpa*) between them.
Rather, the general rule prohibiting touch is set aside by the specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*) concerning the injunction for wearing them.
This is what is meant: by means of injunctions and prohibitions themselves, such a subject matter—one whose form is yet to be produced—is brought forward.
By this, even in the case of a person’s engagement in activity or withdrawal from it—which depend upon injunctions and prohibitions—there exists independence.
However, regarding an existing entity (*bhūta-vastu*), such an injunction does not exist; thus he says: "But an entity is not 'thus' or 'not thus'.
By this, the conceptualization of modes (*prakāra-vikalpa*) is refuted.
He negates the conceptualization of the possessor of attributes—namely, "it exists" or "it does not exist.
This might be argued:
even with respect to an existent entity, conceptualization is observed.
Just as in the case of "Is it a post or a person?", how is it that the object is not conceptualized?
To this, he says: "But there are conceptualizations."
The "human intellect" (puruṣabuddhi) is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
conceptual constructions (vikalpanā)— namely doubt and error— depend upon it,
or else they have as their source the mind alone along with its latent impressions (savāsanamanomātrayoni).
As in a dream; or as the bases of the sense-faculties and the mind together with their latent tendencies; or as the doubt regarding a post, thinking "Is it a post or a person? in relation to a post.
The misconception is that "it is indeed a person," because by the word "other" there is the designation of a person who is actually other than the post;
however, they do not depend upon either the reality of being a person or the reality of being a post.

Because their arising depends solely upon the perception of a common property and its locus, conceptual constructions (vikalpanā) do not represent the object as it truly is; that is to say, they neither conceptualize the real object nor alter it.
However, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is not dependent on the intellect (*buddhi*).
However, [cognition] depends upon the actual object;
therefore, it is logical that the determination of the object arises from that [object], and not from conceptual constructions. Thus he says: "not according to the true nature of the object."

Having thus established that the validity of cognitions whose objects are real entities depends upon those entities themselves, he states that the knowledge of Brahman likewise depends upon the entity itself: "This being so... Here, an objection is raised: "But surely, regarding the word 'real'... For indeed, a sentence whose object is a real thing is observed to be merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), since its meaning falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Just as it is said, "There are fruits on the bank of the river," so too are the Vedāntas;
therefore, by virtue of their having an existent object, they would merely restate an object already perceived through other means of valid cognition.
And it has been stated that there is another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), namely inference, which establishes Brahman as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world.

Thus, that [inference] alone is what must be examined fundamentally, and not the Vedāntic sentences, since their truth is dependent upon it. This is the meaning of the question: how can the aphorisms (sūtras) have the purpose of stringing together the Vedāntic sentences?
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not so, because it is not an object of the senses.
But why is it that the inner self (pratīc) is not an object of the senses? To this he says: "by its very nature."

For this very reason, the Śruti says: "He pierced the openings outward; for the piercing [of the senses] is indeed the looking away from the inward Self. (FN: 1—'vyatṛṇat' means he struck or injured. For the injury of the senses consists precisely in their not looking toward the inward Self.)
"Therefore, the Self-existent looks outward and not at the inner self"—
this is because [the former] exists when the sense organs are present.
However, it has been established that the inward-turning self (pratyagātman) is not an object [of perception].
And just as inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) is also [valid], for example: "The subject under dispute was created by an intelligent agent,
because it is an effect"— this is inference based on general observation.
It does not apply to Brahman; we shall establish this more precisely below. This has also been explained by us in detail in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*.

Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later— in the sūtra "But that [Brahman is known] from the harmony [of the texts]"— that a statement is not merely a restatement by virtue of its referring to an existing fact. Therefore,
everything is clear.

And the Śruti, in the passage "from which indeed," shows birth; in "by which those born live," it shows life, that is, continued existence; and in "into which they pass," it shows dissolution into that very same source.
And its statement of final determination:
regarding the doubt here as to whether [the world] originates from Pradhāna or something else, the statement of final determination is "from bliss alone" (*ānandād dhy eva*).
This is what is meant: just as a stream, which has the rope as its material cause together with the ignorance of the rope, exists only while the rope exists;
And it dissolves back into the rope itself;
likewise, the world, having Brahman together with ignorance as its material cause,
is born from Brahman and exists in Brahman alone.
And it is established that [the mind] dissolves right there. //2//
START BsVBh_1,1.3.3 *śāstrayonitvāt* / BBs_1,1.3 / To introduce another sūtra, he states the connection with the preceding sūtra: "by demonstrating [Brahman's] being the cause of the world."
Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source.
Not only is the omniscience of this Blessed One to be understood from his being the source of the world,
but it must also be understood from his being the source of the scripture (*śāstra*).
He establishes that being the source of the scripture is a means of proving omniscience by referring to "the great scripture, such as the Ṛgveda and so forth."

The *śāstra*— namely the Ṛgveda and the others— is so called because it instructs (*śāsana*) disciples regarding the four castes and the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), concerning the sequence of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites (*nitya-naimittika-kāmya-karma-paddhati*) which begin at the *brāhma-muhūrta* and conclude at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) for each respective stage, as well as regarding the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*).
For this very reason, it is "great" (*mahat*) due to its vast subject matter.

Its greatness is not only due to its vast subject matter, but also because it is supported by numerous primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga) and auxiliary means; thus he says: "of that which is augmented by many branches of knowledge.
The ten branches of knowledge (vidyāsthāna) are the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and so forth; [the treatise] is assisted by these through their respective modes of operation.
By this acceptance by all cultured people (*śiṣṭajana*), even the suspicion of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) has been dispelled.

For the great sages (*maharṣi*) who composed the Purāṇas and other texts are themselves cultured; they have accepted the Veda by explaining it through various means and by respectfully practicing its meaning. Nor is this [Veda] non-informative or of unclear meaning, such that it would be unauthoritative; thus he says: "It illuminates all objects like a lamp."
The meaning is that, by making known every category of objects in every way, he is neither one who lacks understanding nor one whose understanding is unclear;
for this very reason, he is "like the omniscient one" (sarvajñakalpa), that is, similar to the omniscient one.
For the knowledge of an omniscient one has all things as its object.
The treatise (*śāstra*) also has the designation "having all things as its object," which constitutes a similarity.
Having thus stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he also states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "For such [a person]...
The quality of an omniscient being is the state of having all things as its object; the treatise is endowed with that.
Because this [scripture] also has everything as its object, he provides proof for the stated point:
[This is the inference here: Brahman knows objects beyond the scope of the Vedas, because He is their author.

Whoever is the author of a treatise that serves as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is a knower of a subject matter greater than that [treatise], just like Pāṇini. The construction is as follows: whatever extensive treatise originates from a particular person, that particular person possesses knowledge even more extensive than that treatise.
Even today, when a treatise concerning correct matters is composed by people such as ourselves, the knowledge of us, the speakers, has a wider scope than the words [of that treatise].
For those unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*), even when being experienced, cannot be expressed;
indeed, the various distinctions of the sweet taste of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth, cannot be described even by Sarasvatī herself.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "in detail" (*vistara*) is intended to state that even a sentence of extensive meaning does not have a scope equal to the knowledge of the speaker.
He states the conclusion along with its application (upanaya) as follows: "What need is there to say?

Since the Veda originates from that Great Being who is its source, what need is there to mention that Great Being, Brahman, possesses unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence? This is the construction of the sentence.

Regarding the phrase "having many branches" (*anekaśākha*): here, the section beginning with "of the Veda, which is divided into many branch-distinctions" and ending with "is possible" constitutes the application (*upanaya*).
The section beginning with "of that" and ending with "and omnipotence" constitutes the conclusion (*nigamana*).
"Without effort at all" means with very slight effort,
as in the expression "slightly salty gruel."

For that which even the celestial sages (*devarṣi*) are unable to accomplish despite great exertion, he performs with mere slight effort and as if in play; thus his unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence are declared.
Regarding his authorship of the Veda without exertion, the Śruti states: "Of this great Being...
Even those who maintain the eternity of the phonemes (*varṇa*) must nevertheless admit the non-eternity of words, sentences, and so forth.
For a word (*pada*) consists of phonemes (*varṇa*) possessing a specific sequential order,

and a sentence (*vākya*) consists of words possessing a specific sequential order; furthermore, this sequential order is a property of individual instances (*vyakti*), not a property of the phonemes themselves.
Since eternal and all-pervading phonemes (*varṇa*) cannot possess a temporal or spatial sequence,
and since manifestation (*vyakti*) is impermanent, how could the status of being a word (*padatā*)— which is comprised of those phonemes— be eternal even though the phonemes themselves are eternal?
Furthermore, by the impermanence of words, the impermanence of sentences (*vākya*) and so forth is also explained.
Therefore, the imitation of words and so forth is like the imitation of a dance;
for just as a dancing girl, when being instructed, imitates exactly the kind of movement of the limbs and so on that the dancer performs,
rather than manifesting that very [original] itself.
In this way, whatever sequence the teacher establishes for the letters, words, and so forth of the Vedic texts, the student merely imitates that very sequence;
he does not utter those [very same] sounds, because the individual instances of the student are distinct from the individual instances of the teacher.
Therefore, there is no dispute among those who maintain that [the world] is eternal or non-eternal regarding the human origin of worldly or Vedic words and sentences;
the disagreement concerns only whether or not there is human independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to Vedic sentences. As they say: "The independence of persons must be strenuously refuted by us."

In this regard, the followers of Jaimini, who do not accept creation and dissolution, maintain that the lineage of teachers and students for the study of the Veda has been uninterrupted among those like us, and thus they declare the Veda to be beginningless. However, those who follow the doctrine of Vyāsa, in accordance with the creation and dissolution established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and other sources, hold that although the eternal Supreme Self— possessing all powers and knowledge acquired through the adjunct of beginningless ignorance— is the source (*yoni*) of the Vedas, He possesses no independence regarding them.
This is because they are constructed with such and such a specific sequence in accordance with each preceding creation.
For just as causes of benefit and harm, such as sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin, though being transformations of Brahman, do not change even in another creation;
indeed, in no creation whatsoever does the killing of a Brahmin ever become a cause of benefit, nor does the horse-sacrifice become a cause of harm.
Fire indeed moistens,
or water burns;
it is just like that.

Just as in this creation, the study of the Veda in its fixed sequence is the cause of worldly prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*), whereas otherwise that very same study becomes a cause of harm due to being a "thunderbolt of speech" (*vāgvajra*), so it is also in other creations; therefore, even though he is omniscient and omnipotent, the Creator, when composing the Vedas in accordance with the sequence of each preceding creation, is not independent.
Furthermore, even the followers of Jaimini accept that "non-personal authorship" (*apauruṣeyatva*) consists merely in the lack of independence on the part of a person.
And this is the same for us as well, except for our own dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
Nor is it logical to say that there is no confidence in what appears to a single person;
for indeed, there can be no confidence even in the intuition of many people if they are ignorant, unwise, or possessed of defects in their mental disposition.
However, for one who possesses knowledge of reality and has discarded all defects, confidence is indeed appropriate even when [the truth] appears to that single individual alone.

For the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and divine sages (devarṣis) existing at the beginning of creation—who are endowed with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—the determination of its essential nature is possible; and through their testimony, there arises conviction in it even among those of later times. Thus, it is established that Brahman has the scripture as its source.
And [the treatise establishes] the non-human origin of the scripture and its authority.
Thus ends the first section.
He begins another section with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*).
By means of the preceding section, the doubt regarding the impossibility of defining the essential nature of Brahman was dispelled, and the possibility of such a definition was stated.

Now, however, by removing the suspicion that this very definition is merely inferential, he demonstrates that scripture is the authoritative means of knowledge regarding Brahman through the presentation of sacred tradition (*āgama*).
The meaning of the words, however, is not obscure. //3//
It was stated that Brahman is established by the authority of scripture (śāstra) merely by way of a proposition;

it is this that must now be demonstrated by this sūtra. Therefore, the Commentator sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) without a specific sūtra: "But how?"—the word "how" being used in the sense of an objection:
Brahman, whose nature is pure, conscious, and indifferent, is something to be disregarded.
For if the Vedāntas were to denote an already existing entity (*bhūta*), they would result in being purposeless by failing to teach what is conducive to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*);

furthermore, because they would have the same object as perception and other means of knowledge due to their denoting an existing entity, they would face the consequence of lacking authority (*aprāmāṇya*) as mere restatements of that meaning, like worldly sentences.
Indeed, worldly sentences do not possess inherent authority when they communicate an object that is the domain of another means of knowledge.
In the same way, the Vedāntas would also have their authority— characterized by independence from other means of knowledge— undermined; yet it is not proper that they should be non-authoritative,
nor should they be purposeless.
Because there is a rule that the purposefulness [of the Vedas] is established by the injunction for the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*),

therefore their status as being for the sake of action (*kriyārthatva*) consists precisely in their being intent upon explaining the agents, deities, and so forth required by those various enjoined rituals.
However, if you do not find it acceptable that they are intent upon that because of their non-proximity [to the ritual acts], [then consider the following].
Therefore, the Vedāntas are devoted to activities such as the meditation on what is proximate [to the self].

For in this way, their status as authoritative means of knowledge and their possession of a purpose are established by virtue of having a domain not already apprehended through perception and other means, and thus being independent; such is the intended meaning.
The citation of the aphorism of the Great Sage (Bādarāyaṇa), however, is for the sake of strengthening the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
And "uselessness" (ānarthakya) means being devoid of purpose; it also means not producing valid cognition due to dependence [on another source], because it is merely repetitive.
The passage beginning with "ataḥ" and ending with "vāntam" is the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*).
The commentary on its analysis (*vibhāgabhāṣya*) begins with "na hi" and ends with "upapannā vā.
This might be so.
Even if they do not have action as their purpose, the Vedānta texts will be devoted to injunctions regarding the nature of Brahman;
thus, the concluding sūtra—"But [it is so] because of being in syntactical unity with an injunction"—will be supported.
For indeed, an injunction is not merely that which impels one to act who has not yet acted.

Because an injunction for origination has the purpose of making known what was previously unknown, and because the Vedāntas, which make known Brahman—which was previously unknown—possess that same character, [the author] says: "And not in regard to that which is already established.
[Note: 1. "Anāgata" means that because it is yet to come, it is something to be produced.]
Existence (*bhāva*) is the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and its object is the injunction (*vidhi*).
For every injunction is accepted as having for its object an existence that is yet to come and is to be produced;
for the forms of origination (*utpatti*), qualification (*adhikāra*), application (*viniyoga*), and performance (*prayoga*) are mutually dependent.
FN: 2. *Adhikāra* is the communication of the connection with the fruit;
*viniyoga* is the making known of the subordination of an action to the fruit;
*prayoga* is the instigation to performance.
"Origination" refers to the knowledge of the essential nature of the action.
For these [factors] stand in a relationship of mutual inseparability, because the connection of an action with its fruit is not possible without its being subordinate to something else.
Furthermore, being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) does not occur without performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), and that [performance] does not occur without knowledge.
If the result were established independently of human effort, it would follow that it must always be produced; thus, the meaning is that such [results] are impossible.
Because of their inseparable connection, and because they cannot exist [independently] once that [connection] is established; regarding this, he says: "of those sentences" (tadvākyānām).

[Objection: But if there is an inseparable connection between the injunctions concerning qualification and so forth, how can there be a distinction among them? To this, he replies: "of those sentences."
The intended meaning (*tātparya*)—
that is, the ultimate purport— is demonstrated by the textual passage beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) and ending with "are not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣitāḥ*).
However, the purport of these [other types of poetry] differs.
Just as from such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," one obtains the knowledge of qualification (*adhikāra*), application (*viniyoga*), and performance (*prayoga*),
the sentence "He performs the Agnihotra" is concerned solely with the origin (*utpatti*) [of the rite];
yet it is not the case that application and the other factors are absent here.
Even though [the means] exist, they are not intended to be expressed because they have been obtained from another source;
therefore, an injunction can only have a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as its object, and it cannot pertain to an already established entity.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Having stated the reason for dissatisfaction here, he proceeds to another position with the word "atha" (now/if).

And this being so, since the word has no primary purport (*atātparya*) regarding Brahman of the aforementioned nature, [it refers to] that which is of such a kind as established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
namely, that which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*).

The form of this [Self] is established, and it does not contradict that [scriptural] word, because that [word] is intent upon meditation (*upāsana*), and meditation is possible through superimposition (*samāropa*).
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "therefore, not so.
He establishes the final position by means of the aphorism: "This being the case, it is said: because of the inherence of reality."
START BsVBh_1,1.4.4:
"But that [Brahman is the cause] because of the coordination [of all things with it].
(BS 1.1.4) He explains this as follows: "The word 'but'..."
He analyzes the thesis of the opposing side with the word "That": "That is Brahman.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), being of a harsh disposition, asks: "How?"—meaning, in what manner or by what means?
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) states the reason for his own position by way of a specific distinction: "Because of the concordance" (samanvayāt).
Concordance (anvaya) means thorough agreement; the thoroughness of this concordance should be understood as its nature being that of the intended meaning (tātparya).
Therefore, there is concordance (samanvaya). He analyzes this very point with the words: "For in all the Vedāntas," and so forth.
Desiring to declare the unambiguous focus of the Vedāntas upon Brahman, he cites many passages, beginning with "Being alone" (sadeva).

However, the sentence "from which indeed these beings [are born]" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni*), which was cited previously as the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world, is not recited here because it has already been recalled.
For according to the grammarians (*śābdāḥ*), that alone is the meaning of a sentence with which it begins and with which it concludes.

Just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* passage, where there is an injunction for the *upāṃśuyāja* preceded by the mention of the defect of monotony (*jāmitā*) regarding the two *puroḍāśa* cakes, and its resolution is concluded at the end, the *upāṃśuyāja*—which was not previously established—is [the meaning].

FN: 1—"Indeed, a redundancy (*jāmi*) is created in the sacrifice when two *puroḍāśa* cakes are offered consecutively; one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between [with the mantra] 'Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper, for the sake of avoiding redundancy,' and so forth.
Since a state of redundancy would arise from performing the *āgneya* and *āgnīṣomīya* *puroḍāśas* without an interval, the *upāṃśuyāja* is enjoined in the middle.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this an injunction of a previously unknown (*apūrva*) sacrifice, or is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the three sacrifices already mentioned in the text "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper"? Because neither the material nor the deity is explicitly heard [in the injunction], [the former view holds].

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that, because there is no injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) [in the verse], this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the three sacrifices mentioned previously. This being the case, since it would otherwise result in the disruption of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva-bhaṅga*),

and because the Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Agnīṣoma *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses— recited in the Mantra Section in the place of the Upāṃśuyāja— are of equivalent meaning and thus stand in option (*vikalpa*) with one another, the deities such as Viṣṇu and the clarified butter (*ghr̥ta*) substance are obtained from them.

Because the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) contains the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which functions as an injunctive indicator (*vidhipratyaya*), it was deliberated upon in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa* (the section defining difference) that this constitutes an injunction for a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrvayāgavidhi*).
However, passages such as "Viṣṇu [is to be sacrificed] in a low voice" (*viṣṇurupāṃśu*) are merely restatements (*anuvāda*); this is the general direction [of the argument].
The focus on ritual action is based on the force of syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*);

likewise here, because the discourse begins with Brahman in the words "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam*) and concludes with the individual soul being identified as Brahman in the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the sentence has that [Brahman] as its sole purport.
Thus, regarding the sentence—
FN: 1. In the Aitareyaka, beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," it concludes with "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānam brahma*).
In the Vājasaneyaka, beginning with "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), it concludes with "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*).

In the Atharvaṇa, beginning with the inquiry into the universal Self—"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known?"—it concludes with that very same [Self]: "This immortal Brahman is indeed before [us]."
And such sentences as these should be cited as examples.

Furthermore, by examining the preceding and succeeding contexts of other [passages] as well, their focus on Brahman must be understood. And when it is possible for a text to have a perceived meaning directed toward that [Brahman], it is not reasonable to postulate an unperceived meaning directed toward something else.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Not only is their focus on the agent unobserved, it is also logically untenable; thus he says:
And as for the phrase "nor for them":

this refutes the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), which holds that [the Veda] lacks authority because it is dependent [on other means of knowledge]. [The author states: "Nor even when there is the nature of a fully established entity. This...

Here the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The Vedantas depend upon other means of knowledge (*mānāntara-sāpekṣa*), because they have as their primary object an already established entity (*siddha-vastu-paratvāt*), like the statement of a man that "there are jujube fruits on the bank."

In this context, he states—"this is the intended meaning"—to indicate that the reason (*hetu*) favored by the proponent (*pūrvavādin*) is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition) because of its being human in origin (*pauruṣeyatva*).
This is the intended meaning: for, by means of the example of human speech, it is suspected that the Vedāntas possess dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) due to their having a factual referent (*bhūtārthatā*).
In that regard, you should explain when asked as follows:
Is the dependence of human statements due to their having as their object an already existing fact (*bhūtārthatva*), or rather due to their being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*)?
If it were due to their having as their object an already existing fact, then [the same would apply to] perception—

[The objection is: there would follow the consequence of invalidity even for perception and the others, because they too depend upon one another;
for these also have only real objects as their content.
