then in that case, there is no lack of authority even for those Vedānta passages which have as their object an already existing reality (*bhūtārtha*) and are not preceded by such [human] agency, just like perception and the other means of knowledge which arise from fixed sense organs, logical marks, and so forth.
If it should be argued—
as in the passage beginning "yadyucyeta"—
that once the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedāntas is established, their authority would be established by virtue of being independent (*anapekṣatayā*);
However, that very [Veda] cannot be established as having a real (bhūta) object,

because a person who possesses a real object can know it through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) independently of words, and thus its composition could be explained as being preceded by intelligence (*buddhipūrva*).
Furthermore, there exists an inference for the human authorship of the Veda based on such logical marks (*liṅga*) as its being a collection of sentences (*vākyatva*).
FN: The Vedāntic statement is of human origin,
because it is a statement,
like the statement "Bring the jar"— this is the inference.
There would be no obstacle to its arising [from human effort].
Therefore, dependence due to being of human origin is unavoidable, but not so dependence due to having a real object as its referent.
If the collection of Vedānta statements were intent upon an action (*kārya*), then dependence could not be inferred on the basis of being a "sentence" (*vākya*),
because "being of human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*) would serve as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

However, since the effect—the *apūrva*—is not within the scope of any other means of knowledge and has never before been experienced, it cannot enter the human intellect either in its own nature or through superimposition; consequently, because the Vedāntas concerning that [effect] could not have been composed by anyone, they lack human authorship, and their status as an independent authority (*anapekṣa-pramāṇatva*) is established. Thus, for the sake of their validity, we maintain that the Vedāntas are intent upon an action (*kārya*).
In this regard:

since the fact that [the subject] is unfit for other means of knowledge (*mānāntarāyogyatva*) with respect to what is not an effect (*akārya*) is unestablished, it is possible for the Vedāntas to be of human origin even if they are intended to convey that [Brahman]; thus, there is a "pervasion by the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpti*).
Consequently, human authorship cannot be denied by the inference based on marks such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*); thus he says: "To this we reply."
We reply: What, then, is this "effect" (kārya) intended by your venerable self, which is impossible for a person to know?
If you say it is the "unprecedented" (apūrva), then alas, from where does its status as the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth derive?
Because that [injunction] is non-worldly (*alaukika*), it lacks the experience of connection [with worldly objects];
for, in accordance with worldly convention, it is understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth that only a worldly action is the object to be accomplished (*kārya*).
Thus, in the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is one characterized by a heaven that is yet to be achieved.
[Note: This means "possessing an intention toward the eight fruits. It is understood [that the agent acts for a result], and he understands that very action to be one conducive to heaven (*svarga*).

Since an action, which perishes in a moment, cannot lead to a heavenly realm in the afterlife, it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the connection of the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. with the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished is grasped from the Veda itself—if this is your argument, [we reply:]...

Furthermore, in sentences such as those for the worship of a *caitya*, there would follow the consequence that they must have the *apūrva* (the unseen transcendental result) as their purpose, due to the connection with terms such as "one desiring heaven.
Consequently, since such sentences would also be impossible for a human being to compose, they would fall into the status of being non-human (*apauruṣeya*).

Alternatively, if their status as having the *apūrva* as their purpose is denied because their human origin is clearly perceived, then by the same mark of being a sentence and so forth, the Vedāntas would also be inferred to be of human origin; thus, they too would not have the *apūrva* as their purpose.

FN: If it is argued that the reason "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) is fallacious due to the presence of an extraneous condition (*upādhi*), namely "having an author who is being remembered," [we reply: since that same condition applies equally even to the Vedāntas which have established facts as their subject matter, the fact of having a purpose consisting of an action to be performed (*kāryārthatva*) cannot be the determinant of their independence. Thus he says: "But from another [source]...

"But from another source"—namely, by establishing through inference that [the Vedas] possess the nature of being sentences and so forth—it is rendered unnecessary here to establish that [independence] by means of the fact of having an unprecedented object (*apūrvārthatva*). And the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) has already been established by us in the *Nyāya* [section].
FN: Since perception produced by the ten types of sense-object contact cannot have *dharma*—which exists in the form of an effect—as its object, *dharma* is not perceptible.

Furthermore, it should be understood that what was stated there—that the Veda is not of human origin because the composition of sentences by persons is impossible without [prior] knowledge—is also applicable here;
however, it has not been discussed in this *Kaṇikā* for fear of prolixity.

Therefore, once it is established that [the Vedas] are not of human origin, there is no impairment of the authority of the Vedāntas—even those whose subject matter concerns existing realities—due to their being dependent [on other means of knowledge].
Nor is it the case that they lack the quality of making known what was previously unknown (*anadhigata-jñāpakatva*). This is the meaning.
There is no going by which its validity [as a means of knowledge] would be negated, because the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman cannot be apprehended through any other means.
This is what was stated: "And even though it is the nature of an already established reality..."
Having recalled the second seed of the prima facie argument, he refutes it with the words: "But as for [the claim] that [the Upanishads] are devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted...
Indeed, the attainment of the human goal occurs through the understanding of the meaning of an injunction, albeit by way of a traditional succession.

Here, however, from the knowledge of the sentence-meaning culminating in realization—namely, "That thou art"—which does not depend on the exertion of external performance, [the goal is attained] directly.

The attainment of human goals is not like the knowledge that "this is a rope, not a snake"; rather, this is the excellence [of the Vedic injunction] arising from the knowledge of its specific meaning.
What is meant is this: for a person, there are two kinds of desired objects;
one is that which has not yet been attained.
A village and so forth;
furthermore, something that has actually been reached may, due to delusion, be perceived as not reached,
such as a necklace fastened around one's own neck.
In this way, that which is to be abandoned is also twofold:
one desires to abandon some things that have not yet been diminished,
such as a snake coiled around one's foot.
Furthermore, one wishes to abandon even that which is slightly inferior,
such as a serpent that has been placed upon an anklet worn as a foot-ornament.

In that regard, since the attainment of what has not yet been attained and the non-abandonment of what has not yet been abandoned are to be accomplished through the performance of external means, there remains a dependence on subsequent practices based on the knowledge of the reality of those means.
Knowledge alone never removes an object;
for even a thousand instances of the cognition of a rope are not capable of altering a snake that exists as a real entity.

However, in the case of what is superimposed—whether it be something desired or something to be abandoned—it is possible to either attain or abandon them through the mere direct realization of reality, without depending on external practice.
For in your view, since life consists merely of superimposition,

and that which is superimposed is destroyed by the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra) along with its very root; so too here, in the case of Brahman— which is bliss and in reality devoid of sorrow, suffering, and the like— this state of being a living soul, which is superimposed and based upon such superimposition, ceases through the knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), culminating in direct realization.
Upon its cessation, even that which is of the nature of bliss, though already attained, becomes as if unattained;
and even sorrow, suffering, and the like, though abandoned, become as if unabandoned.
Thus it has been said: "From the realization of Brahman as the Self alone, all the afflictions of the individual soul, along with their latent impressions and misconceptions..."
For it afflicts living beings; therefore, it is called *kleśa* (affliction).
Because through its complete abandonment, the human goal—characterized by the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness—is accomplished.
As for the statement, "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'":

It was stated that the Vedāntas are devoted to meditation (*upāsanā*) by means of teaching deities and so forth contained within meditative injunctions such as, "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world.
He refutes that: even if the teaching of deities and so forth—limited merely to the word "Self"—is for the sake of the meditation found in its own sentence, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
If there is no contradiction, [then...]

"Let it be then that the Vedāntas are solely intent upon injunctions for meditation by means of propounding deities. To this he says: "But not so with regard to Brahman. Meditation depends upon the establishment of distinctions such as the object of meditation, the meditator, and the act of meditation; therefore, it is not possible in the case of Brahman—the object known through the Vedāntas—in whom the entire manifold of difference has been eliminated. Thus, the meaning is that the Vedāntas cannot be subordinate to injunctions for meditation, because they are in contradiction with such injunctions.
This might be argued:

if the Vedāntas possess authority even in the absence of an injunction, then alas, let there likewise be authority for independent passages such as "He wept," which have objects that are to be disregarded.
For the cognitions of rejection and acquisition are not the only fruits of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*),
since authoritative persons accept that the cognition of indifference (*upekṣābuddhi*) is also a fruit thereof; thus, [the objection] is refuted.
To the objection that these [Vedic passages] are intended as prohibitive injunctions—such as "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*)—he says: "Even though...

Since the entire mass of the Veda is understood to be subservient to human purpose because its acquisition is governed by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), it is not logical that even a single syllable therein should fail to serve a human purpose.
How much less, then, could this purpose be found through such a sequence of words as "He wept" (so 'rodīt) and so forth?
Nor is any human goal obtained merely from the comprehension of that meaning, as is the case with the Vedāntas.
Therefore, this collection of words remains expectant, awaiting a human goal.
The prohibitive injunction, "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass," also requires a censure of that which it prohibits;
for otherwise, a conscious being could not be turned away from it.

If it had not obtained even a remote censure, then the prohibitive injunction itself would have had to postulate a twofold capacity—both for the prohibition of silver and for its censure—just as in the case of the *darvihoma*.

Thus, in the case of these two refined textual compositions—namely, "He wept" and "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass"—they are mutually dependent like the man who lost his horse and the one whose chariot was burned, by means of the implied censure perceived in each.

However, it has been stated that such mutual dependence does not exist in the Vedāntas; for once the meaning of those [Vedāntas] is understood, there is no further dependence, as the supreme human goal is attained from that very understanding.

[Objection: But surely, since no authority is observed for any other part of the Veda that does not touch upon injunction (*vidhi*), how can the Vedāntas—which do not touch upon it—possess such authority? To this, he says: "And [the self] is not to be known through inference.

For the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) consists in producing a cognition that is uncontradicted, previously unknown, and free from doubt; and it has been established that this [status] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

Even though the capacity of these [Vedāntas] to produce such a cognition is to be understood through the presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on the [otherwise inexplicable] fact of their being [authoritative], [it remains intrinsic].

Nevertheless, for the production of that cognition, it does not depend on another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*), nor does it depend on this very presumption (*arthāpatti*); for [if it did], there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). This is why it is said to be "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*). [Note: The meaning of the footnote is as follows: When a valid cognition has arisen, one might infer that the means of valid cognition produced that valid cognition; from that, the production of the valid cognition [would follow]. Thus, the meaning is that there would be mutual dependence.

And since the capacity to generate such an understanding exists in the Vedāntas regarding Brahman, just as it does in the case of injunctions regarding their respective effects, their authority with respect to Brahman is established without the need for an external example;
otherwise, just because other sense organs are not seen to reveal color, the eye too would not reveal color.
He concludes the subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He introduces the view of certain teachers who hold a partial position with the words "In this regard, others object" (*atrāpare pratyavatiṣṭhante*).
For it is said: "Because its connection [with the goal] is unknown, because it is a treatise (*śāstra*), and because it possesses purposefulness..."
And through the cognition of reflection and so forth, there is the ascertainment of Brahman by means of its effects.
"Indeed, the Vedantas cannot have as their ultimate purport the nature of Brahman as an already established entity,
because the relationship [of those words] with that [meaning] is not known.
For where words are not employed by people in common usage, there the apprehension of their relationship [to a meaning] does not occur."

No discerning person intends to speak of mere form (*rūpamātra*) that is neither to be abandoned nor to be adopted, because such a thing is not desired to be known; and if one were to bring about the understanding of what is not desired to be known, their status as a discerning person would be undermined.

Therefore, this world, desiring to communicate what it wishes to understand, would communicate only that object which serves as the cause for engagement or withdrawal; and since it is understood that the effect is the cause [of such activity], it would teach only that.
And thus, from the usage in the linguistic practice of elders, one understands that words have the effect as their primary purport.

In that regard, some [words] directly denote the action to be performed (kārya), while others denote their own meaning for the sake of the action; however, words do not have as their ultimate purport an already established fact (bhūtārtha).
Moreover, there is the cognition of meaning in another person who is proficient [in language];
[this is the form of inference here]: this activity directed toward the bringing of a cow is preceded by the cognition of the object, because it is an activity.
It is like my own activity.
And that cognition of the meaning is produced by the sentence "Bring the cow," because it conforms to the presence and absence of such a word.
Having inferred that [the child's] behavior conforms to the presence or absence of the word, one must determine that the word denotes that object.

Furthermore, there is no mark (liṅga) whatsoever for a cognition of the mere form of an existing thing as it exists in another person; however, in the case of a cognition of an effect existing in another person, activity and cessation serve as the causes. Thus, because their connection [with an object] is not known through such means, the Vedāntas do not have the nature of Brahman as their ultimate purport.
Moreover, the Vedāntas possess the established status of being a *śāstra* because they are the Veda;
for a collection of texts (*saṃdarbha*) that is intent upon engagement (*pravṛtti*) or desistance (*nivṛtti*) is a *śāstra*.
As they have said: "Whether it be engagement or desistance, [effected] by that which is eternal or by that which is produced..."
That by which men are instructed is called a śāstra.
Thus,
because they are established as being scriptures (*śāstra*), their status as having the nature of Brahman as their primary purport is contradicted.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any purposefulness in these [texts] if they were intended solely to propound the nature of Brahman.
Note: This negative particle (*na*) should be construed as meaning that there is no cessation of the phenomena belonging to saṃsāra.

Just as the cessation of fear, trembling, and so forth occurs when the true nature of the sentence-meaning is determined—either through some figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) or by some other means—such as "This is a rope, it is not a snake," in the same way, the cessation of the phenomena of saṃsāra occurs from the comprehension of the sentence-meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).
Because those [worldly attributes] remain in their original state even for a person who has heard the meaning of the words [of the Vedanta].
Moreover, if the cessation of transmigratory attributes occurred for one who has heard [the teachings on] Brahman, why then are reflection and the other [stages] prescribed after hearing?

Therefore, because it would otherwise follow that they are purposeless, the Vedāntas do not have the nature of Brahman as their ultimate purport; rather, they have as their purport an action (kārya) directed toward the realization of the Self.

And that action, which enjoins the person to be impelled (niyojya) upon itself, is called "enjoinment" (niyoga); and because it is not known through any other means of knowledge, it is termed the "unprecedented" (apūrva).

And since that [knowledge] cannot be established without the performance of its object, for the sake of its own establishment, it implies the very performance of that instrument which has itself as its object— namely, the knowledge of the Self. Just as an action, whose determination depends upon its object, is determined by the object of knowledge, so too knowledge, being impossible to determine without the Self which is its own object, implies such a Self for the sake of its own determination.
That very thing is the effect (*kārya*). [Objection:

Now, if the effect, while being known for the purpose of defining the cognition of its own object, implies the existence of the self, then the self would not be something established by direct scriptural authority (*śrauta*); having raised this doubt, he cites the consensus of the Guru regarding the scriptural authority of that which is implied by an injunction:
"As they say"—namely, "Whatever is employed or implied for the sake of establishing that [injunction] is also to be regarded as enjoined; such is the convention in the *Tantra*."
And "subservience" (vidheyatā) refers to the fact that the knowledge which is the object of the injunction must be performed because it is an action (bhāvārtha);
whereas for the Self, which is its object, it is the ascertainment of the existence of its own nature.

[Note: Now, one might ask: "Why could the superimposed [Self] not be the object of the enjoined knowledge, as in the case of 'one should meditate on speech as a cow'? To this he says: "The superimposed..."]
The state of that [identity] is the state of oneness (*aikyabhāva*).
This being so, cognition could not be defined by means of a superimposed state of oneness;
the underlying point is that superimposition is not tenable when a real basis exists.
However, if something else were made the defining correlate (*nirūpaka*) of that [self] by superimposing its nature upon it, then the self would not be defined by that [other thing].
Therefore, the ascertainment of such a self arises from the Vedāntas, which are intent on the injunction for the realization of that very self.
He states all of this with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*).

Regarding the point that the ascertainment of the true nature of reality occurs even for those intent upon ritual injunctions, an illustration has been stated: "As in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

When it is enjoined for the purpose of binding, "One binds the animal to the sacrificial post," and since the sacrificial post is something not known from worldly experience, the question arises, "What is this sacrificial post? [In response, it is said: "The sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood."

From such sentences as "he fashions the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ takṣati*) and "he makes the sacrificial post eight-cornered" (*yūpamaṣṭāśrīkaroti*), which are intended to enjoin the fashioning and other such acts, it is understood that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a piece of wood characterized by specific marks and a particular shape, consecrated through those preparatory rites.
Thus...
FN: 1—It is heard in scripture: "When one offers in the Āhavanīya fire.

In that regard, when there arises the inquiry, "What is the Āhavanīya?", it is understood from injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in the spring" that the fire characterized by the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) is the Āhavanīya.
Thus, it is demonstrated that the determination of the true nature of things proceeds from the scripture.
The Āhavanīya fire and others are also to be understood in this way:
the status of being a scripture belongs to that which is intent upon engagement or cessation, not to that which is intent upon the essential nature [of things];
and the relationship exists only with respect to what is to be done (kārya), not with respect to the essential nature.

Thus, these two reasons have been established by the words of the Bhāṣya, beginning with "because they have as their purpose engagement and disengagement" and ending with "by virtue of that similarity, the Vedāntas also would likewise possess purposefulness.

Nor can an independent action exist without a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), an eligible person (*adhikārin*), and an agent (*anuṣṭhātṛ*); thus, he states the distinction of the person to be enjoined with the words "and when there is subservience to an injunction.

Even though becoming Brahman—understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" as if it were already established—requires a specific person to be enjoined, [the text identifies] the specific person to be enjoined as one who desires to become Brahman.
FN: 1—Regarding the statement, "Those who perform these *rātris* (night-sacrifices) indeed attain a firm foundation," the word *rātri* prescribes specific Soma sacrifices.

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the fruit mentioned in this sentence is "attaining a firm foundation" or "heaven. Since no desire for a specific result (*evamkāma*) is heard [in the text], and because [the result] can be obtained through the force of the injunction itself, [it is concluded that heaven is the fruit].

Since heaven has a fixed result, and because the attainment of stability is understood from the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the text, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that heaven alone is the fruit.
However, since the fruit of stability is directly indicated, it is improper to postulate an inferential heaven; therefore, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that stability itself is the fruit.
Thus, it should be understood that one who intends that [stability] is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) therein.

Its acquisition is according to the principle of the *sattra* sacrifice; it is prescribed in the general injunction recited outside of a specific context: "On the afternoon of the new moon day, they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the New Moon sacrifice; this is because, in order to avoid the necessity of postulating a separate result, the word *amāvāsyā* must be understood as referring to the ritual act itself. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *amāvāsyā* refers to time, because it is used in grammatical coordination with the word *aparāhṇa* (the afternoon) and because it is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for that specific time.
And thus, by postulating a person enjoined who desires heaven (*svargakāma-niyojya*), the Piṇḍapitṛyajña has heaven as its fruit.

Similarly, in this [present] postulation, the meaning "heaven" would not be integrated with the word *brahmabhavana*; and the implication is that this would result in an indirect mode of operation (*parokṣavṛttitā*).

According to the logic of the sacrifice (*yajñanyāya*), however, if one were to postulate a person enjoined who desires heaven, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would have a meaning not integrated [with the injunction], and its operation would be entirely indirect.
It has been stated that "the state of Brahman is immortality" for one who desires immortality;
and since immortality is indeed immortality itself,
it cannot be inferred as something impermanent on the grounds of being produced.
The sense is that [this would result] in contradiction with scripture (*āgama*).

He raises an objection regarding the fact that, due to the aforementioned difference between the knowledge of *dharma* and the knowledge of *brahman*, the latter is not the object of an injunction, by saying "Now, [is it not so?
He refutes this, saying "It cannot be thus."

And here, the vision of a self (ātmadarśana) is not something to be enjoined; for that [vision] is a synonym for apprehension (upalabdhi), and it must be either auditory or perceptual. Even if it is perceptual, it must be either the worldly notion of "I" or that which arises at the culmination of the intensification of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
In that case, the act of reciting should not be enjoined,
because it has already been established by the injunction for Vedic study itself, just like the recitation of ritual texts.
Nor is it worldly perception, because that is innate;
nor is the excellence produced by cultivation regarding the Upanishadic Self something to be enjoined.

Precisely because of the injunction for the meditation upon that [Self], the "vigour" (vājina) arises as a byproduct— just as, for example, curd is brought for the sake of alms and the whey (*vājina*) is produced incidentally; likewise, since direct realization arises from the meditation enjoined for the sake of immortality, its production is not itself something to be enjoined, because it is accomplished as a secondary result.
Therefore, the meditation on the Self taught in the Upaniṣads is enjoined for one who is to be directed toward the desire for immortality.
As for passages such as "He is to be seen," these have the form of injunctions but are not injunctions themselves.
This is what was stated: "And because of the meditation upon that."
The remainder of the elaboration—namely, [the arguments] regarding "possessing purpose" and the perception of "reflection" (manana) and so forth—is explained by the words themselves.
He refutes the view of that partial proponent: "To this it is replied: the view of the partial proponent is not [correct].
Why? Because of the difference between the fruits of ritual action and the knowledge of Brahman."
The fruits of meritorious and non-meritorious karma are happiness and suffering.

In this regard, beginning from the human world up to the Brahma-world, there is a gradation of happiness characterized by increasingly higher excellence. Likewise, beginning from the human world down to the Avīci hell, there is a gradation of suffering.
And all that is an effect and subject to destruction;
however, absolute bodilessness— being unsurpassed, eternally established by its own nature, uncreated, and the fruit of self-knowledge—
is indeed a fruit, though it is like a fruit [in name only].
Because [the Self] manifests merely through the removal of ignorance.

This is what is meant: even by you, who accept that the Vedāntas are intent upon the injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), it is maintained that the identity of the individual soul with Brahman—characterized by being eternally pure and enlightened—is innate and is what is understood from the Vedāntas;
and yet, that [identity] is not the fruit of the injunction whose object is meditation.
Because it is eternal and not an effect;
nor is there the removal of the veil of beginningless ignorance,
since that occurs only through the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), which is its direct opposite.

Nor is there the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), because that too occurs only when the mind is assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by meditation (*upāsanā*) preceded by hearing and reflection.

If it is argued that, like the impressions of meditation, the mind itself must be a cooperative factor even prior to the meditation, [we reply: indeed, it is observed that a result produced by a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*) can be experienced even in this life, as for example—

FN: 1—The fruit of the *citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ* injunction, which prescribes the *citrayāga*, occurs either in this life or in another birth. FN: 2—When the crops are withering, the fruit of the *kārīryāga* prescribed for the sake of rain must necessarily manifest in this very life.
If it is argued that ritual injunctions (*niyoga*), which have both uncertain and certain fruits, result in results pertaining to this life, we say no;

for just as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the practice of the meaning of the *Gāndharva-śāstra* is sufficient for the direct perception of the notes *ṣaḍja* and so on without depending on a new unseen potency (*apūrva*), so too the latent impression from the practice of the meaning of the Vedāntas is sufficient for the direct perception of the identity of the individual self and Brahman without depending on an *apūrva*.
Thus, the *apūrva* resulting from meditation is not a cause for the state of immortality.
One who desires immortality ought not to understand that [the ritual] as the thing to be accomplished;
for it is a contradiction to desire one thing while performing another.
Nor is it tenable to claim that one desiring that [immortality] will understand the ritual action itself as the thing to be accomplished, rather than the *apūrva*.
Since the fact that it is a means to that [end] is understood from another means of knowledge, the injunction would be redundant;
nor is it comparable to injunctions such as threshing (*avaghāta*), because even in those cases, the "unprecedented force of restriction" (*niyamāpūrva*) is not known from any other source.
Furthermore, there is no other form of immortality (amṛtatva) apart from becoming Brahman that is mentioned even as a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda),
by virtue of which one desiring it might be qualified for the meditation;
[this is illustrated by the example of the injunction] "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," where no specific qualification is explicitly heard.

In that context, by the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the qualification was postulated as "he who desires heaven"—that is, one possessing the desire for heaven, which is desired by all—on the grounds that "heaven would be [the result], because it is common to all.

The point here is that if one were to postulate heaven in this manner, it would follow that the fruit is non-eternal (anitya). However, even if one assumes heaven according to the Viśvajit-nyāya, since that [heaven] is characterized by gradation and perishability, meditation does not have an eternal fruit.
Therefore, since the manifestation of the state of Brahman occurs merely through the removal of the veil of ignorance,

and since the removal of ignorance is possible only through the realization that culminates in direct comprehension (*avagati*) of the meaning of the Vedānta, and since it is established by other means of knowledge that meditation serves as a cause for purification and that such purification acts as an auxiliary to the mind in producing immediate intuition;
The statement "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" is not an injunction;
rather, it is similar in form to an injunction.

The intended meaning is that, just as in the sentence concerning the Upāṃśu sacrifice—"Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper"—and so forth, these are similar in form to injunctions but are not actual injunctions.
It has been stated that [this] is well-established by means of Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning (nyāya).
In this regard, he shows the Śruti with the words "And so the Śruti says," and he states the reasoning with the words "For this very reason."
That which is indeed intrinsic is eternal,
such as consciousness;
and this [nature] is intrinsic.
Therefore, it is eternal.
For others indeed speak of two kinds of eternity: immutable eternity and transformative eternity.
In that context, when "eternal" is stated, let there be no [confusion] regarding this—
FN: 1. Transformation (*pariṇāma*) means the attainment of another form through the relinquishing of a previous form.
Regarding this, he says "in that case, some... [to explain] transformational permanence (*pariṇāminityatā*);
for transformational permanence is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
For instance: would that [entity] transform in its entirety or in part?
If it transforms in its entirety, how is there not a contradiction of its own nature?
Or, if it transforms in part, is that part distinct from it or non-distinct?
If it were distinct, how could there be its transformation?
For when one thing is undergoing transformation, another is not transformed, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Or, if there is non-difference, why would there not be transformation in its entirety?
If it is argued that "it is both different and non-different," for instance:
it is indeed non-different from the perspective of its causal nature, yet...
And it is distinct in its nature as an effect,
being non-distinct in its nature as gold— just as bracelets and the like are non-distinct in their nature as gold yet distinct in their nature as bracelets— and so forth.
Nor is it correct to argue that distinction and non-distinction cannot coexist in a single locus due to their mutual contradiction.

FN: The construction is as follows: "In what respect do we have the conviction that something is 'contradictory' (viruddha), [given that] it exists in opposition to, or in contradiction with, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-viparyayeṇa)? That which is understood by a means of valid cognition exactly as it is, exists precisely in that manner.
Furthermore, in the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), "This earring is gold," both difference and non-difference clearly manifest.
For instance, if there were absolute non-difference, it would follow that one of the two would appear twice;
and if there were absolute difference, there could be no coreferentiality, as in the case of a cow and a horse.
There is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the case of the relationship between the locus and the located, or when there is a single substratum;
for it does not occur that "the bowl is the jujube fruit," nor that "Caitra is Maitra" in the case of Caitra and Maitra sitting on the same seat.

Thus, this very cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which is uncontradicted, free from doubt, and universal, establishes both the difference and non-difference between cause and effect.
And so, because effects have the nature of their cause,
and because the cause— which is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*)— is pervasive throughout everything, [the two are established].
There is non-difference of the world, which is an effect, in its form as the Real (sat-rūpa); there is difference in its form as effects such as cows, jars, and so forth.
As they have said: "There is multiplicity in the form of effects, but non-difference in the nature of the cause."
Just as there is non-difference in its nature as gold, yet difference in its nature as earrings and so forth.
Thus it is said: What, moreover, is this so-called "difference" (bheda) which could exist in the same locus as "non-difference" (abheda)?
If it is argued that they are mutual non-existence,
does this exist between the effect and the cause, such as a bracelet and gold, or not?
If it does not, then there is simply oneness.
And yet there is no difference;
if there were a difference, there would be only difference and not non-difference.
Furthermore, there is no lack of contradiction between existence and non-existence.
Because coexistence is impossible; or,
if it were possible, it would follow that even a bracelet and a golden ornament are non-different in their true nature,
since difference is not incompatible with non-difference.

Moreover, if the bracelet were non-different from the gold, then just as bracelets, crowns, earrings, and so forth do not differ from the perspective of being gold, they likewise would not differ from the perspective of being the bracelet, because the bracelet is non-different from the gold.
And thus, only the gold would be the real entity, not the bracelet and the rest.
Because difference does not appear [in that way].
Now, if non-difference exists only by virtue of being gold (*hāṭakatva*) and not by virtue of being a bracelet (*kaṭakatva*),
then there is indeed difference from the earring (*kuṇḍala*) and so forth by virtue of that [bracelet-ness].
If the bracelet is non-different from gold, why does it not persist in earrings and other ornaments? If it does not persist, how can the bracelet be non-different from gold?
For those things which, while something else persists, undergo change (vyāvartante), are indeed different from that thing.
Just as various flowers do not follow from a single thread,
and earrings and other ornaments do not persist even when the nature of gold persists,
therefore they too are indeed distinct from the gold.
Furthermore, if all things were followed by the persistence of existence (*sattā*), there would be no distinction such as "this is here, not that" or "this is thus,
not so," because there would be no cause for the differentiation of anything from anything else at any time or in any manner.
Furthermore, when gold is cognized from a distance, its particular features such as earrings and the like would not be objects of inquiry,
because they are non-different from the gold and that [gold] has already been known.
Now, if it is argued that there is also a difference between gold and its ornaments such as earrings, and therefore they remain unknown even when the gold is cognized—
well then, since there is also non-difference, why are they not cognized? On the contrary, their cognition alone is logical.
For it is a general rule that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect, and that [absence] is set aside by the existence of the cause.

Since the existence of the cause is present in the case of non-difference, when gold is known, earrings and the like are indeed already known; thus, the desire to know them and the cognitions thereof would be purposeless.
Therefore, when one thing is being apprehended, that which is not apprehended is distinct from it;
for example, when a camel is being apprehended, a donkey—which is not apprehended—is distinct from the camel.
And when gold is apprehended from a distance, its particular forms such as earrings and the like are not apprehended [as separate].
Therefore, they are distinct from gold.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression 'a golden earring'?"—

it has already been stated that grammatical coreferentiality does not occur in the relation of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), nor in the state of having a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*).
Furthermore, how could there be the determination of persistence and exclusion, as well as the desire to know earrings and so forth once gold is known?
Indeed, it has been stated that neither of these two is possible if there is either absolute non-difference or absolute difference.
Therefore, since one of the two—difference or non-difference—must be accepted, the conceptualization of difference is based solely upon non-difference.
It is not logical to suppose that non-difference is derived from difference;
for difference is dependent upon that which is differentiated, and each of those things being differentiated is individually one.
Furthermore, since difference cannot exist without a substratum in the absence of a single entity,
and since a single entity does not depend upon difference,
and because the apprehension of difference— expressed as "this is not that"— is dependent upon the apprehension of its counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
Furthermore, since the apprehension of oneness is independent of anything else, it is logical that the conceptualization of an indeterminable difference is based solely upon non-difference;
and thus says the Śruti: "Only 'clay' is real."
Therefore, it is established that only immutable eternity (*kūṭasthanityatā*) is ultimate, not transformative eternity (*pariṇāminityatā*).
Furthermore, the illustration "like space" is one accepted by the opponent;
for in our own view, even that [space] is impermanent because it is an effect.
In this context, the term "unchangingly eternal" (*akūṭasthanitya*) excludes the status of being an object to be produced (*nirvartyakarma*);
"all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpin*) excludes the status of being an object to be reached (*prāpyakarma*);
and "devoid of all modification" (*sarvavikriyārahita*) excludes the status of being an object to be transformed (*vikāryakarma*).

By the term "partless" (niravayava), the status of being an object of action through refinement (saṃskāryakarmatā) is excluded; for while a specific quality called "refinement" is produced in rice grains by sprinkling water, no such part of Brahman exists that could be produced by an action.
Because it is partless;
that is to say, because it is without components.
He states its being for the sake of the person as "eternally satisfied."
Through satisfaction (*tṛpti*), one discerns a happiness free from suffering;
for satisfaction is indeed happiness accompanied by the cessation of the suffering of hunger.
And since happiness that is not being experienced is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), he says: "self-luminous" (*svayañjyoti*).

Thus, having established by means of scripture and other authorities that the fruit called liberation is eternal according to his own view, he demonstrates the contingency of impermanence for a liberation produced by ritual action with the words "If, however... Nor is there any contradiction with scripture,
because scripture is shown to be consistent through the manner already explained.

Moreover, he states that there are many scriptural passages that preclude the view that liberation is produced by a transcendental result (*apūrva*) generated by knowledge and is thus the result of a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*). He says: "And furthermore, [he who] knows Brahman...

Liberation is the means to be achieved through knowledge merely by the removal of the obstruction consisting of the two kinds of ignorance, and not by itself through the production of a transcendental result; regarding this point as well, he cites scriptural passages: "For you are our father...
Not only are the Vedas and other authorities in favor of this meaning, but...
Furthermore, he states that even the aphorisms of the teacher Akṣapāda have *nyāya* as their foundation: "And likewise, it was composed by the Teacher.

The Teacher is described in the *Purāṇa* with the following definition: "Because he gathers (*ācinoti*) the meaning of the scriptures, establishes others in right conduct (*ācāra*), and practices it himself, he is therefore called an *ācārya* (Teacher)."
Thus it is said.

Therefore, the refined Sūtra states: "Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each preceding one, resulting in liberation (apavarga).
In terms of the sequence of the text, the cause is mentioned later.
Furthermore, the effect precedes [the cause];
when the cause ceases, the effect ceases,
just as a fever arising from phlegm ceases when the phlegm ceases.
With the removal of birth comes the removal of suffering;
with the removal of activity comes the removal of birth; with the removal of defects comes the removal of activity.
Upon the disappearance of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), there is the disappearance of defects (*doṣa*).

False knowledge is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*), which, through the process of generating passion and other afflictions, is the ultimate cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) as perceived by us.

And that [ignorance] is removed by its opposite—namely, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), specifically the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikatva-vijñāna*), culminating in direct apprehension (*avagati*).
Therefore, liberation is the manifestation of the nature of Brahman through the removal of ignorance;
it is not, however, an effect of knowledge, nor is it the effect of the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by that knowledge—such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
The Sūtra is cited merely to show that the cessation of false knowledge occurs through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
However, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) accepted by Akṣapāda is not what is intended here;
thus, this point has been strengthened by agreement with another teacher.
This might be so.
The cognition of unity does not have as its object a thing as it exists [in itself], such that—
by negating the false cognition which appears as difference— it would not become an object of positive injunction; rather, [it functions] as follows:

FN: 1. An excellence (*saṃpat*) in which the superimposed [quality] is primary. Thus, that which is not previously established by the injunction (*vidhi*) will become the object of the injunction once it has become something to be performed according to human desire.

Just as, by way of another mode of meditation (*vṛttyantara*), one identifies the Viśvedevas with the mind due to their similarity, and having made the mind—the object of focus—equivalent to something non-existent, one meditates primarily on the Viśvedevas themselves who are being identified;
and through that, one attains infinite worlds;

even so, by identifying the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman due to their similarity in nature as consciousness, one makes the soul—the object of focus—equivalent to something non-existent, and meditates primarily on Brahman.
And by that [knowledge], the attainment of the fruit of immortality occurs;

whereas in superimposition (adhyāsa), there is primarily the contemplation of the object itself as having been superposed with the nature of that [other], as in: "One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman."
"The instruction is: 'The sun is Brahman.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the individual soul (jīva), which is not Brahman, as "Brahman.
Or [it may be so] through connection with specific ritual actions.
Just as in the passages, "Air, indeed, is the absorber" and "Breath, indeed,
is the absorber," [it is shown that] the external deity of air indeed absorbs fire and the other elements.
For at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the wind (*vāyu*)—having gathered together and withdrawn fire (*vahni*) and the other elements—establishes them within itself.
As the Draviḍācārya said: "The wind is the absorber (*saṃvarga*) because of its withdrawing, its enveloping, or its making [them] its own. And internally, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the absorber.
For he indeed withdraws all things, beginning with speech;
for at the time of departure, he alone departs after having gathered together all the sense organs.
This very perception of the "absorber" (saṃvarga) shows the world, which has gone to the ten directions, in both the wind and the vital breath (prāṇa), just as follows:
Thus, by means of the act of expansion (*bṛṃhaṇa*), the view of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) upon the individual self (*jīvātman*) conduces to the fruit of being remembered.

Therefore, in all three of these positions, the vision of the Self, meditation (*upāsana*), and so forth, are primary ritual acts (*pradhānakarma*), because they have the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as their object. [This is] like the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns.
"They praise with *ājya* verses; they recite the *prauga*. Thus, the *stotra* and *śastra* are traditionally handed down together.
A *stotra* is the description of a connection between a deity and its attributes, accomplished by means of chanted (*pragīta*) mantras.
A *śastra* is accomplished by means of non-chanted (*apragīta*) mantras.

Regarding the doubt as to whether, based on the restrictive rule that "the purpose [of the mantra] must be remembered by means of the mantras themselves," it is a subsidiary action (guṇakarma) for the sake of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting in the manifestation of the deity, or a primary action (pradhānakarma) for the sake of the *apūrva*—since the remembrance of the deity useful for the sacrifice is a visible result, and thus it would initially appear to be a subsidiary action—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

here, praise (*stuti*) in the form of manifesting its own nature through the mention of qualities is enjoined; this is heard in the scriptural statements "they praise" (*stuvate*) and "they recite" (*śaṃsati*).
Since praise is impossible when there is an intention to express a literal meaning,
the verbs *stauti* (he praises) and *śaṃsati* (he recites) must enjoin the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns with a view toward the production of a transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Thus, the underlying intention here is that the vision of the self (*ātmopāsana*) is a primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*).
It is like the case of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns.
However, since the self (*ātman*) is the substance and [the act] is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) within the ritual action, the seeing of the self is prescribed as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
This is just as it is recorded in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakaraṇa*): "The clarified butter (*ājya*) is to be inspected by the wife."

And just as the act of looking (*avekṣaṇa*), which is grasped by the context (*prakaraṇin*) as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) substance that serves as a constituent of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice, is enjoined as a subsidiary action (*guṇakarman*);

so too, with respect to the Self (*ātman*) who is a constituent of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*) by virtue of being its agent, the act of seeing (*darśana*)—as in "The Self, indeed, is to be seen"—is enjoined as a subsidiary action. [Note: The meaning of Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.8 is:
"In those cases where threshing and the like are intended for a substance—that is, desired to refine it—a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is understood there."]
The meaning is that action is understood as being subordinate to the substance.

[This follows] from the principle: "But where a substance is intended to be produced, there a quality is understood. Therefore, he says: "And this is not the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self. Why? Because the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self consists of forms such as *saṃpad* (meditative identification) and so forth.

etc. For indeed, the "inspection of the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) mentioned in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is appropriately understood as a purificatory rite for the clarified butter that constitutes a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of those sacrifices.
FN: Regarding the second [point], he replies with "And not..."—
and it is neither recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of any [specific ritual] as in "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," nor is it studied as an independent statement (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Just as the word "juhu" (ladle), by means of the *juhū* which has an invariable connection with the sacrifice, recalls the sacrifice through the sentence "He whose *juhū* is made of *parṇa-wood," and thereby establishes that the *parṇa*-nature is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of the sacrifice;
in the same way, the Self does not have an invariable connection with the sacrifice,
such that the contemplation of it— being an auxiliary of the sacrifice— would purify the Self for the sake of the sacrifice.

Therefore, even if this is an injunction, [the following applies]: Regarding the passage recited as an *anārabhyādhīta* (unattached instruction), "Therefore, gold should be worn; one's rival becomes ill-favored," there arises a doubt:

is the wearing of beautiful gold an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, or is it a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*)? Since the desire for being "ill-favored" is not heard in the text, and because postulating an independent fruit would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), [it is concluded that it is an auxiliary].

When it is argued that [the wearing of gold] is an auxiliary of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), we reply: because that which is not recited within a specific context (*aprakaraṇapaṭhita*) lacks the distinction from the duties belonging to that context;
because the wearing [of gold] exists even in the world (*loka*), and thus, unlike the case of being made of *parṇa*-wood, there is no necessary deviation from the sacrifice (*kratvavyabhicāra*);
therefore, the wearing with gold as its instrument is enjoined for the sake of a fruit mentioned in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), and is thus a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

Likewise here too, because of the injunction that one should cultivate immortality through the vision of the Self (*ātmadarśana*), it is indeed a primary action (*pradhānakarman*). [The opponent argues: "Just as in the case of the rule 'Gold should be worn,' by breaking the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*), it is a primary action because its object is the *apūrva* (unseen potency), and not a subsidiary action (*guṇakarman*). Without stating this refutation—which is so obvious that it need not be mentioned—the author has stated a refutation common to all positions.

It has not been commented upon because its meaning is not obscure. Furthermore, he states "nor is it an object of the act of knowing" (*na ca vidikriyā*), because the injunction that this [Self] is an object of the activity of knowledge contradicts many scriptural passages.
He raises an objection: "If it is not an object... (*aviṣayatve*).
And thus, the implication is that there would be the emergence of a *vetāla* during a rite for pacification (*śāntikarman*).
He refutes this, saying: "No. Why?"
This is because [the Upanishads] have as their primary purpose the cessation of the distinctions imagined through ignorance.
For no sentence whatsoever is capable of making known a difference between real entities by way of "this-ness" (idantā);
indeed, it is impossible to describe the specific differences in the sweet taste of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth.

Thus it should be understood everywhere else as well. Since such is the course of verbal testimony even regarding worldly objects established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what need is there to mention its status with respect to the inner self, which is non-worldly?
However,
the manner of conveying [the meaning] through some degree of remoteness is the same here as well.

For it is the play of ignorance that the referent of the word *tvam*—the knower (*pramātṛ*)—pervades the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such as a jar, by means of a cognition dependent upon the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Since this [knower] lacks the status of being a knower through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is the indifferent referent of the word *tat* and has become its object, when that [ignorance] ceases, the three categories beginning with the instrument of knowledge cease.
For indeed, if the cook were non-existent, the thing to be cooked, the cooking, and the act of cooking could not possibly exist as real entities.

For it is said: "When the *tvaṃ*-pad has its meaning—consisting of external orientations—dissolved, then, through oneness of meaning with the word *tat*, that very word *tvaṃ* also attains oneness with *tat* and abandons all its own innate impurities of objective referents, such as agency, [revealing] the nature of the pure consciousness-self."
This is an intermediate verse.
On this very point, he cites scriptural authority: "And so the scripture says, 'He by whom it is not thought...
He concludes the subject under discussion: "Therefore, it is imagined through ignorance."
Regarding the opponent's position, he demonstrates the impermanence of liberation with the words "But for one who...
Liberation depends upon an effect, namely the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by the activity of sacrifices and the like, for its own origination.
[This applies] to those two positions.
The Buddhists maintain that the self is momentary cognition (*jñāna*) which is to be produced (*nirvartya*) or modified (*vikārya*);
thus, liberation is the production of pure consciousness, and so liberation is something to be produced.

For others, however, liberation is the attainment by the self of a state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) after abandoning its state of being composed of formative impressions (*saṃskāra*); thus, for them, liberation is something to be modified.
Just as curd is a modification (*vikāra*) of milk because it attains another state through the abandonment of its prior state, so too,
according to these two positions, liberation is impermanent because it is an effect.
[This is] like a jar of curd and so forth. [Objection:

Since the scripture states, "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven," there is understood a distinction between modified and unmodified locations for Brahman; therefore, [the meditation on Brahman] will have as its result an injunction for meditation consisting in the attainment of Brahman in its unmodified location, and thus Brahman would be an object to be attained (*prāpyakarma*). To this, [the author] says: "Nor even as something to be attained."
One thing is reached by another through the avoidance of a corrupted region and the attainment of an uncorrupted region.
For example, the ocean near the shore is corrupted by clusters of foam-masses that surge as they strike one another in a series of exceedingly thick and restless waves;
however, in its center, it is free from the affliction of all waves, transparent, and uncorrupted due to its stability. A merchant reaches that uncorrupted center by means of his ship.
But since the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed Brahman itself, what could be attained by whom?
The meaning is that attainment presupposes duality.
Even if the soul were different from Brahman, nevertheless Brahman would not be attained by it.
He says—"even though it is distinct from its own nature"—because Brahman is eternally attained through its omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
He refutes the status of being an object of refinement (*saṃskāra-karmatā*) by stating—"nor is it something to be refined. For the state of being refined is of two kinds:
Or by the infusion of qualities (guṇādhāna), as for example the sprinkling of lac juice upon the flower of the citron tree;
for by that, the flower is refined and produces a fruit of the same color as the lac juice.
Or, by the removal of defects, just as the surface of a mirror, when rubbed with brick powder, becomes refined and possesses a manifest brilliance;
in that regard, the addition of qualities to Brahman is first of all not possible,
for a quality must be either identical to the nature of Brahman or distinct from it.

If it were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could it be something to be produced, since that is eternal? But if it were distinct, then because it would be an effect, it would follow that liberation is impermanent.
Furthermore, there can be no relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between things that are distinct,
as in the case of a cow and a horse;
and the coexistence of difference and non-difference is also excluded, because they are contradictory.
With this intention, it was said: "Because liberation is the very nature of Brahman, to which no excellence can be added.
He rejects the second position with the words: "Nor by the removal of defects.
Impurity, being real, is removed from a mirror; [but it cannot be removed from Brahman].
But [ignorance] does not exist in Brahman as something to be removed, because it is eternally absent; this is the meaning.
[The opponent] objects: "It is indeed a property of its own self."

Liberation is indeed the very nature of Brahman; though veiled by the impurity of beginningless ignorance, it is manifested when the Self is refined through such activities as meditation, but it is not produced.
What is meant by this is that the eternally pure nature of the Self is not unestablished.
"It is because of the impurity of ignorance during the state of saṃsāra.
He refutes this doubt: "No.
Why?"
Because it is impossible for [ignorance] to have action as its locus,
ignorance does not reside in Brahman, but rather in the individual soul (jīva).
But it has been stated that she (avidyā) is indefinable;
therefore, Brahman is indeed eternally pure. Even granting the existence of impurity for the sake of argument, its susceptibility to purification through ritual action is refuted.

For an action would either sanctify Brahman by being inherent in it— just as the continuous accumulation of rubbing, consisting of the conjunctions and disjunctions of brick-dust, is inherent in the surface of a mirror—
or else by being inherent in something else.
Action is not, first of all, a property (*dharma*) of Brahman, because, as the cause of a modification in its own substratum, it would contradict the eternality of Brahman. [FN:
