And those two do not belong to the self; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, how could that which has one substratum benefit another?
For that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
For it is not observed that a gem becomes purified by being rubbed against a mirror;
and that [consequence] is undesirable. Thus, there is a sublation [of the opponent's position].
Note: [The opponent objects] because there is no immediate proximity;
the sense is that it was stated that impermanence would follow for the self, yet impermanence is not proximate. [The author] refers back [to this point].
Here, he raises an objection regarding inconstancy: "But [if it is said] 'having the body as its locus'... He replies: "No;
[it refers to that which is] comprised within the body."
They declare that the individual soul (jīva) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) are Brahman itself as conditioned by beginningless and indefinable ignorance (avidyā).

And this [jīva], being joined with the aggregate of the gross and subtle bodies, the senses, and so forth, and having fallen into the midst of that aggregate, becomes the object of the notion "I" through non-difference from it;
therefore, even the refinement of the body and so forth, though a property of the body and such, becomes a property of the self.
This is because of the determination of non-difference [between the substratum and the action].
Just as the quality of fragrance, which is a property of the cosmetic ointment, is attributed to the women who possess it;

so too here, when an action is performed upon a substratum that has been made an object of conventional means of valid cognition (*saṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs to that very [substratum] and not to anything else—thus there is no deviation [in the rule].
In reality, however, there is neither action nor purification.
As for the remaining [points], they have been explained with illustrative examples in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* itself, and thus are not explained here.
"Of these two, one eats the fruit... [and so forth].
The living self is one;
the fruit of action is the *pippala*;
"the other does not eat" refers to this.
The Supreme Self.
A Vedic mantra states that the capacity to be an enjoyer belongs only to the composite aggregate: "The self, the senses...
He recites two mantras intended to reveal Brahman, whose pure nature is unconditioned: "The one God..."
Pure means radiant;
unblemished means free from suffering;
without exudation means not leaking.
"Indestructible" means up to that point.
He concludes with "therefore.
Now, one might object: let there not be the fourfold nature of the object, such as that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth.
But there might be some fifth mode by which liberation could be established as the object [of action]; therefore he says, "other than these.
There is no other mode distinct from these aforementioned modes.
Because there will be the entry of action into liberation.
This is what is meant: among the four types [of things], being the fruit of action is pervaded by being one or another of them;
and that [property of being a fruit of action], being excluded from liberation, excludes liberation's being a fruit of action through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Is it then the case that there is no action whatsoever in liberation, and consequently that the scriptures intended for that purpose and the activities directed toward it are useless? To address this, the author states by way of conclusion: "Therefore, knowledge alone [is the means]. Now, one might ask: why is mental action (jñāna) not within the scope of an injunction?

And why is it that its fruit is not liberation, which is one among [the categories] such as the produced (*nirvartya*)? He raises this objection: "Is it not knowledge? He refutes it: "No. Why? Because of the difference in nature (*vailakṣaṇya*)."
The meaning is this: it is true that knowledge is a mental activity, yet this [knowledge] is capable of producing a result in Brahman.

It has been stated that because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), it is impossible for it to be the object of the act of knowing (*vidikriyā*). This being the case, while this distinction remains established, he states another distinction: "For that which is called action (*kriyā*) is that which is enjoined with respect to an object regardless of the nature of the thing itself."

The construction is as follows: "Just as, in the taking up of the oblation intended for a deity, there is the act of meditating upon the deity without regard for the actual nature of the deity's substance;
or just as, in the case of a woman, there is the cognition of fire without regard for the substance of fire—that indeed is what is called an action.

For meditation on the deity is not already established prior to this injunction: "He should meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken up, when he is about to utter the vaṣaṭ-call."

But for one who has studied the Vedānta, who knows the relationship between words and their meanings, and who has mastered the principles of verbal testimony, the [knowledge of Brahman] is attained through the power of the word from the textual context beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and ending with "That thou art"—
just as, for one whose mind is concentrated, there occurs the experience of a jar situated in bright light through the power of the contact between the sense organ and its object.
For that [cognition], having arisen by the power of its own causal complex, cannot be made otherwise, or not made at all, by human will— unlike the meditation on a deity—
such that an injunction here would have any purpose.
Furthermore, neither meditation (*upāsanā*) nor its culmination in direct experience (*anubhava*) falls within the scope of this injunction;

for since these two possess a potency established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they are already attained—either in the case of direct realization or in the removal of beginningless ignorance—even without an injunction. Consequently, because they cannot be otherwise performed or not performed at will by a person, the knowledge of Brahman, even though it is a mental act (*mānasī kriyā*), is not within the scope of an injunction.
However, for an action dependent upon the mental activity of a person, independence from the actual nature of the object is not in some cases contradictory,
as in the case of the act of meditating on a deity;
for here there is no contradiction whatsoever with the actual nature of the object.

In some cases, it is opposed to the very nature of the object, as in the case of the notion of fire regarding a woman or a man; by this much distinction, the presentation of the two pairs of illustrations is made.
By the particle *eva* ("only") in the word "activity alone" (*kriyaiva*), he excludes dependence on the actual nature of the object.
But surely, injunctions such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" are heard in the scriptures;
and these are not the mere idle chatter of the negligent, for they are equal [in authority].
(FN: 1—The meaning is that study and so forth from the mouth of a teacher are common to both.)
This is the established tradition;
therefore, one must act accordingly here. To this he says: "The optative suffixes (*liṅga*) and so forth have that as their object.
It is true that the optative suffixes and so forth are heard [in the scriptures].

These [objects] are not the domain of injunctions, for if they were its domain, it would follow that [the scripture] lacks authority; for an injunction has as its object that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted.
And that alone is to be abandoned or adopted which a person is able to do, not to do, or to do otherwise;
and only with respect to that is one capable, an agent, authorized, and enjoined.

And such hearing of the Self (ātma-śravaṇa)— which consists of an activity in the form of reasoning conducive to determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the collection of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) regarding Brahman as the Self— is not [possible] in this way.
For if there is no comprehension of the subject matter (*viṣaya*), how can there be a cognition of its necessity?
Furthermore, regarding realization (*avagama*), there is the impossibility of performing it, not performing it, or performing it otherwise.
This should be understood to apply equally to reflection (*manana*) and the other stages as well.

Thus, because of the absence of both the object and its performer—which are the pervaders of an injunction—with respect to hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), meditation (*upāsana*), and vision (*darśana*), there is an absence of any injunction.
Thus, even when employed, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are incapable of instigating action; like a razor’s edge upon a stone, they become blunted and cease to be authoritative.
This is because their object is not one who can be enjoined (*aniyojya-viṣayatvāt*).
For it is only a capable agent who is entitled to act and is thus fit to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
But since there is no capacity [for action], there is no agency; therefore, one is not qualified [for the rite] and thus not a person to be enjoined—this is the meaning.

[The opponent asks: "If these injunctive statements do not exist because of the absence of contradiction, then for what purpose are these statements that have the appearance of injunctions? Thus he asks: "For what purpose?"

Nor are they logically useless, because it would be impossible for their acquisition to be dependent on the injunction for the study and recitation of one's own Veda (svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi); this is the sense. The answer is: "intrinsic" (svābhāvikā).
For hearing and the other [means of knowledge] are indeed already obtained from other sources and are merely restated by means of sentences that have the form of injunctions;
nor is this restatement purposeless,
because it serves to produce a specific mode of activity.

For instance, because one's heart is carried away by the desire to obtain or the wish to avoid various desired or undesired objects, one is oriented toward the external world and is unable to concentrate upon the inner Self (pratyagātman).

However, through statements that take the form of injunctions for hearing the Self and so forth, the stream of the mind toward sense-objects is blocked and the stream toward the inner Self is opened. Thus, since these restatements (anuvādas) possess a specific mode of operation, they have a purpose; and because they serve a purpose, it is logically established that their study is governed by the injunction for Vedic study (svādhyāya-vidhi).
As for the objection that the knowledge of the Self is not a human goal because it is not an auxiliary to ritual performance—that is incorrect.
Since its status as a human goal is established in itself, the fact that it is not an auxiliary to performance is an ornament, not a defect; thus he says, "Even that which...
One would "be tormented" (anusaṃjvaret), meaning one would feel regret while the body is being consumed by suffering.
The rest is easy to understand.
He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, it is not a [means of] practice.
[This is] for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Vedānta with respect to an already established reality.
The meaning is that [the author] states "because the connection is unknown," etc., in order to refute [this].
He restates the view of a partial proponent (ekadeśin) for the sake of establishing the fundamental nature [of the argument], saying, "As for what some say...
and then refutes it, saying, "That is not so."

The intention here is as follows: "Just as purposeful activity is the inferential mark for the cognition of something to be accomplished, so too are joy and other such states the mark for the cognition of what is already established; thus, the status of being a scripture (śāstra) arises from the teaching of what is beneficial."

For if the capacity of words— whether in denoting an action or in denoting their own meanings as connected with that action— were established by necessity through the usage of elders, then the Upaniṣads could not have as their purport the nature of Brahman, which is neither to be rejected nor to be acquired.
In this regard, because the capacity of words is unknown in common worldly usage, and because the comprehension of Vedic meaning is preceded by that [worldly usage],

if it were possible to grasp the relationship between words and even an already-existent (bhūta) object in the world, then— by examining the sequence of preceding and following passages— the fact that the Upaniṣads have that [existent reality] as their purport would be understood, and one could not set aside that purport to claim they are directed toward action (kārya).
It is possible to imagine [this],
because it would entail the abandonment of what has been heard and the postulation of what has not been heard.
In that regard, first of all, there is no grasping of the relationship [of word and meaning] with respect to an object that is not to be performed.

If that usage directed toward [the primary meaning] were not observed in the world, or if the cognition thereof could not be inferred by one who is linguistically proficient, then indeed such usage directed toward it would not be seen in the world;
however, it is not the case that such usage is not observed in the world.
For in common worldly usage, we frequently encounter compositions of words intended for the cessation of curiosity, fear, and so forth, which are not directed toward any practical action;

for example: "The abode of the circle of world-protectors beginning with Khaṇḍala, surrounded by a retinue of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases, its stone slabs made of gold washed by the falling streams of the Mandākinī as it descends from the realm of Brahmā."
"Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is enchanting with the lovely warbling of jewel-like birds that roam the pleasure groves such as Nandana";
"this is not a snake, this is a rope," and so forth—
nor can it be inferred that the cognition of an object as it truly is, which occurs in a learned person, is impossible to discern.
Because there is the possibility of [inference] from signs such as joy that lead to the ascertainment [of a fact];

for instance, a Dravidian who did not understand the meaning of the local dialect of the region and was preparing to go to the city, while staying in the house of Devadatta near the royal highway, was informed by a messenger of the birth of a son, which was the cause of his father's joy.

Having arrived near Devadatta who was staying in the city, and after first presenting him with a gift of cloth and perfume, he observes Devadatta—whose body is covered in a coat of horripilation immediately upon hearing the words of the messenger announcing, "Congratulations, Devadatta! A son has been born to you!"—his lotus-eyes blossoming and his great lotus-face beaming with a smile; and from this, he infers that joy has arisen within Devadatta.
And one understands that the previously non-existent joy, which arises immediately upon hearing those words, has them as its cause.
Furthermore, since these words do not lead to joy unless they communicate a matter that is a cause for joy, one concludes that the matter which is the cause of joy has been stated by them.
And because no other cause for joy is perceived, and because the birth of a son is understood to be such a cause, one determines that this very thing was what the messenger announced.

In this way, fear, sorrow, and so forth may also be cited as examples. Thus, because it possesses a purpose, the employment of the statement of the true nature of reality by a discerning person is justified. And since the knowledge of the nature of Brahman is the cause of the supreme human goal, the status of the Vedāntas as a scripture (śāstra) is established; for even though they do not enjoin activity or cessation, they instruct men regarding their welfare.
It follows;
thus it is established that these words under dispute have as their object an existent reality.
Because it generates valid cognition (pramā) regarding its object as it truly is.
Whatever generates valid cognition regarding a particular object has that very object;
just as the eye and other sense faculties have form and so forth as their objects.
And since these are so, therefore it is so; thus,
what was said is well-stated— that it is not [the case].
Because the person of the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣada-puruṣa) is not subordinate to anything else.
The word *upaniṣad* is derived from the root *sad*, preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*, in the sense of "dissolving" (*viśaraṇa*), with the suffix *kvip*.
It denotes the knowledge of Brahman, for it brings one near to non-dual Brahman (*upanīya*) and destroys ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-avidyā*).
Because they are the cause of that [knowledge], the Vedāntas are also called *upaniṣads*; therefore, the person known from them is "the one known through the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣada*).
He analyzes this very point with the words: "He who is found in the Upaniṣads alone."
He distinguishes [the Self] from the object of the notion of "I" by stating it is "not subject to saṃsāra.

Precisely for this reason, because it is devoid of activity, it is distinct in character from the four kinds of substances; and thus, being endowed with these qualities that distinguish it from the four kinds of substances, it is not subordinate to anything else.
For a substance that is subordinate to another can only exist as something intended to be produced, and thus remains dependent on origination and the like.
For example, "he fashions the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ takṣati*), and so forth;
whereas that which has no other remainder and lacks utility for either the past or the future,
such as "gold is to be worn" (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*).
[In passages] such as "He offers groats," there is no attainment [of a result] through its origination and so forth.
Why, then, is this not subordinate to anything else? To this he says: because it stands within its own context (prakaraṇa).

The meaning is this: since the Upaniṣads, which are studied as unattached (anārabhyādhīta) texts, are—upon a thorough examination of their internal consistency—devoted to the exposition of the Person (puruṣa), this section has the Person alone as its primary subject.
Furthermore, it has been established that the Person does not have an invariable connection with ritual action (kratu), unlike the *juhū* ladle and other such implements.
Therefore, the point is that this very Person, being situated within his own context and thus perceived from the Upaniṣads in such a manner, cannot be said to be non-existent.
It might be argued:

since Brahman is not an object of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its relationship [with words] cannot be grasped; therefore, as it is not the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*), it is impossible for it to be the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). How, then, can it be the subject matter of the Upaniṣads? To this he says: "This very Self is 'not this, not this' (*sa eṣa neti netyātmā*).
Because of the word "Self" (*ātman*), although the Self does not fall within the range of other means of knowledge like a cow or similar objects, [it is nevertheless denoted by the word].
Nevertheless, even though it exists as the very nature of luminosity, it is possible to define it as the meaning of a sentence through the removal of this or that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
just as gold is defined by the removal of its forms such as bracelets or earrings.
For luminosity, being self-cognizing, does not fail to manifest.
Nor is that aggregate of causes and effects its delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*).

Therefore, by the exclusion of each such limitation through the teaching "This Self is 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*)," and because of its resulting vastness and self-luminosity, it is possible to define it from the Upanishadic statement as both "Brahman" and "the Self. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: why is the nature of the Self, even as qualified (*upahita*) by adjuncts, not likewise discarded, just as the adjuncts themselves are? To this he says: "And because the Self cannot be denied."
For light is the self of all, because the delusion of the phenomenal world has that as its substratum;
and a delusion cannot exist in the absence of a substratum. Indeed, never before has a delusion such as "this is a snake" or "this is a staff" been observed in the absence of a rope.
Moreover, the light of the Self is the radiance of the phenomenal world (prapañca);
thus says the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
And it is not logical that the manifestation of the phenomenal world should occur if the light of the Self is denied.

Therefore, since it is impossible to deny the self, the meaning is that the realization of the nature of Brahman—which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and is not the object of any other means of knowledge—is established through the Vedāntas.
One who cannot tolerate the restriction that [Brahman] is known only from the Upaniṣads raises an objection: "But surely, the Self...
For the Self is the object of the universal notion of "I," and it is the transmigrating being who is both agent and enjoyer.
Furthermore, because the word "self" (ātman) is employed by worldly investigators in that very sense,
the principle that "whatever words are worldly, those same are Vedic, and their meanings are the same," implies that the Vedic term *ātman* must also function in that very sense,
and not in some other contrary meaning. This is the intended meaning.
He replies: The person taught in the Upaniṣads is not the object of the notion of "I.
Why? Because he is its witness.

That which is the object of the notion of "I" is the individual self (jīvātman), the agent conditioned by the aggregate of the body and the senses; [the Upaniṣadic person is not that, but] the witness of that.
Because it has been refuted that the Supreme Self is the object of the notion of "I," the following is meant:

although there is an ultimate identity between the individual soul and the Supreme Self in the sense of "by this living self," nevertheless, the individual soul is its conditioned form (upahita-rūpa).

But its pure form is that which is the witness-consciousness and is not apprehended by other means of knowledge; it is the province of the Upaniṣads. He elaborates on this very point: "For it cannot be led [into the realm of ritual] as a subordinate element of an injunction, because it is not the object of the notion of 'I'."
Why? Precisely because it is the Self (ātman).

For the Self is not for the sake of another, whereas everything else is for the sake of the Self. And thus says the Śruti: "Verily, O Maitreyī, it is not for the sake of all that all is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that all is dear."
Moreover, because it is the very self (*ātman*) of all things, it is neither to be rejected nor to be accepted.
For Brahman alone is the reality and the self of the entire manifold (*prapañca*);
and one's own nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be rejected.
Because it cannot be abandoned,
and because it has already been appropriated, it is not something to be taken up.

Therefore, injunctions and prohibitions have as their objects that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted; they do not take as their object the reality of the Self, which is the opposite of those two. Thus, the Self alone is the reality of the entire phenomenal world. He establishes this: "For every collection of perishable modifications perishes up to the limit of the Puruṣa.
The meaning is this: the Puruṣa is ultimately real because it is established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and by reasoning not inconsistent with them.
Proliferation (*prapañca*), however, is shown by beginningless ignorance and is not ultimately real.
That which is not ultimately real is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), just as the essence of the rope is [the ground] for the transformation that is the delusion of a snake.
For this very reason, because its nature is unstable due to its being inexpressible (*anirvācya*), it undergoes destruction.
The Puruṣa, however, exists as the ultimate reality; he cannot be rendered non-existent even by a thousand causes.
For it has been said that even a thousand artisans are not able to turn a jar into a cloth.
Therefore, the destruction of modifications ends with the indestructible Puruṣa, just as the destruction of the silver and the snake ends with the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and the rope.
For the *puruṣa* alone is the reality (*tattva*) of the entire collection of transformations belonging to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

And there is no destruction of the *puruṣa*, from which [otherwise] destruction would be endless; therefore, he says: "For the *puruṣa* [is indestructible], because of the absence of a cause for destruction.
Indeed, it has been stated that not even a thousand causes are capable of transforming one thing into another.

Now, it might be argued that while the Puruṣa himself may not be something to be abandoned or accepted in his own nature, some of his attributes could nevertheless be abandoned and others accepted; to this, he says: "And because of the absence of any cause for modification, he is immutably eternal."
It has been stated that there is no transformation characterized by the three types—namely, of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), state (*avasthā*), or condition (*pariṇāma*).

Furthermore, since the *dharma* of a self that exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*) must itself exist in the ultimate sense, it is impossible for causes to effect a change in its nature, just as they cannot affect the self itself.
And there is no transformation other than the alteration of the *dharma*.
This has been stated: "Because of the absence of the nature of modification.
The rest is easy to understand.

Furthermore, he explains otherwise that which was cited by the partisan of a partial view as an authoritative statement from those who know the purport of the scriptures: "That which is the enumeration of those who know the purport of the scriptures... and so forth.

For while it should have been stated that "its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of a meaningful object," because the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) is the subject at hand and Dharma consists of ritual action (*karman*), it was said "the comprehension of [ritual] action. This, however, does not preclude the Veda's function of bringing about the comprehension of Brahman, which exists as an established reality (*siddharūpa*).
For when Somaśarman is the subject under discussion, the description of his qualities does not preclude Viṣṇuśarman’s possession of qualities.

Both the scriptural injunction, which concerns the action being enjoined, and the scriptural prohibition, which concerns the action being prohibited, are intended solely for the purpose of making known the action.
Moreover, there is the statement of the author of the treatise: "Because the Veda has action as its purpose.

In that context, if the term "purpose" (artha) were taken to mean "denotable object," then it would follow that entities already existing—namely substances, qualities, and actions—would be purposeless, since they would not be denotable objects; for these are not themselves actions. Therefore, he says: "And because the Veda... [and so forth].
If it should be argued that "having action as their purpose" does not mean having action as their denotation, but rather having action as their motive,
and that words for substances and qualities denote existing substances and qualities precisely because they have action as their purpose;
It is not by virtue of residing in itself.
As those learned in the Śāstra have said: "For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known what has been, what is being, [and what will be]," and so forth. (Note 1:
In the *Śābarabhāṣya*, it is understood that an injunctive sentence possesses the capacity to convey a fact regarding the past.)
How, then, is action understood from [words such as] *dravya* and so forth? To this he says: "This is what is meant.
This is what is being stated:
An injunction (*codanā*), while making known a task (*kārya*), also makes known its object, such as a past event (*bhūta*) and so forth.
To this, he replies: "If [it were] a past [event], apart from engagement and withdrawal.

This is the underlying intention: it has already been established by those who demonstrate that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) exists even regarding past objects, that the apprehension of the relationship between words and their meanings does not pertain solely to tasks, nor to other types of objects.

Objection (FN): If there is no rule that words must have as their primary referent objects already connected to an action (*kāryānvita*), then for the sake of extreme parsimony, even the requirement that they refer to objects already connected [to an action] (*anvitaparatva*) should be abandoned. To this, he says: "Nor...
Nor do words have as their sole purpose their own individual meanings (*svārthamātrapara*).
For if that were the case, there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
For syntactic unity is never observed among words that are individually independent, lacking the relationship of primary and subordinate elements.
Therefore, while words express their own individual meanings, they [form a single sentence]—[the meaning being:
the fact that word-meanings are subservient to the accomplishment of a single purpose is impossible without their mutual qualification.]

Since that [literal sense] is not tenable, and for the sake of establishing that [intended meaning] and achieving syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), it is postulated that words have as their primary referent the related meaning (*anvitaparatva*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, in the absence of such a purpose, words denote only their own individual meanings (*svārthamātra*).
Thus, there is syntactic unity by virtue of the words having as their primary referent the word-meanings that possess a purpose.
And thus, the cognition of a single sentence-meaning qualified by those respective individual word-meanings becomes logically established.

As the experts in the scriptures have said: "Although the phonemes directly perform the presentation of the individual word-meanings, they do not terminate in that alone, for it would otherwise be fruitless."
In their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the presentation of word-meanings is an indispensable factor,
just as fire is for wood in the process of cooking.
Thus,

since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is established merely by the fact that words have as their primary purport the connection with other meanings, there is no restrictive rule that words must have as their purport a connection with an action (*kārya*).
This being the case, there is no fault even if [the Veda] has as its purport the nature of Brahman, which is immutable and eternal.
"Future" (*bhavya*) means that which is to be accomplished.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that when a past thing (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of a future purpose, it is no longer past? For by virtue of its connection with the future, it too would possess the nature of being future. To this, he says: "For a past thing, when being taught... [and so forth].

[Note: Regarding the statement that "even what has come into being (bhūta) is called 'to-be' (bhavya) by virtue of its connection with what is to-be," does "what is to-be" refer to the effect (*kārya*) or to the action (*kriyā*)?
He says, "not through identity" (*na tādātmya*), because the entity that has already come into being cannot be identical with either of those two.

The connection is not characterized by identity; rather, it is a relation (*anvaya*) with the effect characterized as that of the purpose (*prayojana*) and the thing possessing the purpose (*prayojin*).

The meaning is that because the verbal root (bhāvārtha) has as its object those things whose nature is already established (bhūtārtha), characterized by action and its factors (kriyākāraka), established things do not have action as their purpose.
He raises an objection: "Even if they are not actions.
The implication is that, in this case, the teaching of Brahman—which is non-actional, immutably constant, and eternal—would be untenable.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault, even if it has action as its purpose.
For an existent thing (*bhūta*) being taught for the sake of action does not thereby become non-existent; rather, it is precisely that existent thing which is suitable for bringing about action.
And likewise, words whose capacities have been determined to refer to an existent entity (*bhūta*)— meaning, in some cases, they have as their object an existent that is not connected to an action—
are observed to be restricted to that existent; having died or become cold, they can by no means be made to signify a state of being centered on an action.
Note: For the connection with an action (*kāryānvaya*) is not the meaning of the word, but rather an adventitious property (*upādhi*).
To explain: engagement and withdrawal depend upon the comprehension of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) and its absence;
and the purpose (*prayojana*) depends upon those two.
The desire to speak and the actual employment [of words] depend upon that [intention]; and the comprehension of the sentence-meaning depends upon the employment.
Therefore, just like the desire to speak and so forth, the connection with the action [as the meaning of the suffix] is understood to be a means for the apprehension of the word-meaning.
Therefore, even apart from its connection with an action, an existing entity (*bhūta-vastu*) can be the denotation of a word when there is a difference in usage.
This is what was stated: "For that which is qualified (*upahita*), even if seen hundreds of times, does not become unseen simply because it is not seen somewhere unqualified (*anupahita*).
For that which is qualified, even if seen hundreds of times, does not become unseen simply because it is not seen somewhere unqualified.

And likewise, there are many instances in common usage where statements in the present tense, though associated with the verb "to exist" (asti), do not have an action as their meaning, such as descriptions of a forest and the like.
Similarly, even those [statements] terminating in a verbal action may result in a mere relationship, as for example, when the question "Whose man is this? is answered with "The king's."
Likewise, there are those that rest upon the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*),
such as the answer "fruit-bearing" (*phalinaḥ*) to the question "What kind of trees are these?"?
For it is not the case that the person asking intends to ascertain the existence or non-existence of either the man or the trees.
Rather, while explaining the difference in owners for a person and the difference in types for trees—
according to what was required by the questioner— one specifies the difference in owners and the difference in types for each individual instance,
but not their mere existence.

Because that [past object] is not what he intends to understand. Furthermore, it has been established that words possess a productive capacity (*vyutpatti*) even with respect to an existent (*bhūta*) object when that object serves a purpose.
He objects: "Even if an existent object is taught, what purpose would there be for you—the teacher—or for the listener?"
Therefore, even that which is real must be taught only if it possesses a purpose, not if it is purposeless.
And Brahman is purposeless; the meaning is that, being indifferent and devoid of all activity, it cannot be of service [to anything].
He addresses this [objection]: "And likewise, the teaching of the reality of the Self that has not yet been understood must indeed be purposeful.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "also" (api).
This is what is meant: even though Brahman is indifferent (*udāsīna*), [the teaching remains purposeful].

Nevertheless, verbal knowledge concerning that [Brahman], culminating in direct realization (*avagati*), is true knowledge (*vidyā*); its purpose is to eradicate ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and its own opposite.
Furthermore, even those who maintained that all words have action as their ultimate purport must admit this in the case of such injunctions as "A Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed."

It is impossible to maintain that statements such as "liquor must not be drunk" have the efficient force (kārya) as their primary purport; for the efficient force, whose limits are defined by the verbal suffix (kṛti), is pervaded by that suffix, and thus ceases upon the cessation of the latter— just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* ceases when the property of being a tree ceases.

For *kṛti* (human effort) is indeed human exertion, and it is defined in dependence upon its object (*viṣaya*). And this object of [effort], by virtue of having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), must necessarily be the meaning of a verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) itself, consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages whose essence is conducive to the production of another;
it cannot be a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*).
For the object of an action (*kṛti*) is that which is to be pervaded by the realization [of the action].
Now, established substances and qualities do not possess the property of being pervaded by an action.
For this very reason, the author of the treatise says:

In this regard, there arises a doubt: do the words *soma* and *yāga* respectively restate the Soma-juices and the sacrifices enjoined in the sentences concerning Indra-Vāyu and the others, or do they enjoin a ritual act associated with a specific material?

On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the nature of a sacrifice—consisting of a material and a deity—is perceived in the sentences concerning Indra-Vāyu and the others through the inference of a sacrifice, whereas such a nature is not perceived elsewhere, these [latter] terms must be restatements of a collective whole. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), established in the second book, is as follows: they are not restatements because there is no recognition [of what has been previously enjoined].

Therefore, in the Soma-sentence there is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga*), whereas in the other [sentences], the extractions (*grahaṇa*) and preparations of juices for deities such as Indra are enjoined.

For in this way, just as the sentence "with Soma" (*somena*) is indeed an injunction of a qualified [action], so too the sentences concerning curd and continuity (*dadhisāṃtatya*)—if they were injunctions of oblations (*homa*) and pouring (*āghāra*) qualified by substance and quality—would then merely refer to the two collections of those previously enjoined oblations and pourings in the Agnihotra and Āghāra sentences; that being the case, [the sentences would not be original injunctions].
There is a doubt that the distinction between their respective bases would not be consistent;

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is: these two must be injunctions, because the objects to be performed are understood from the words *āghārayati* and *juhoti*.

In the proximity of that [injunction], the sentence concerning curds and so forth (*dadhyādi-vākya*), which prescribes continuity (*sāṃtatyam*), cannot be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) because that would entail the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*).
Rather, its purpose is to enjoin a subsidiary element (*guṇa*) by way of restating the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) already enjoined by that [primary injunction].

Therefore, in all cases, by way of the channel of human effort (*kṛti*), the rule (*vidhi*) has as its object exclusively that which consists in the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). This is the settled conclusion. (Note 9: The meaning is that [the rule] has as its object the meaning of the verbal root.)

And likewise, in cases such as "one should not kill" and "one should not drink," if a task (kārya) were admitted, then its pervader— namely, volitional effort (kṛti)— would have to be admitted, and its pervader— the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) as the object— would also have to be admitted.

And thus, by the principle of Prajāpati’s vow (*prajāpativrata*), through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) characterized by the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) not to kill or drink, there would be an injunction (*vidhi*) directed toward that [resolve].

In this way, having explained the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpaka*) between the commission (*niyoga*), the action (*kṛti*), and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), he states the cessation of the pervaded through the cessation of the pervader:
"And thus, it would follow that the absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) would be rendered as good as dead."
And when a primary meaning is possible, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not logical.
[This is stated] to exclude that [figurative indication] in the case of prohibitions such as "one should not look," following the principle of the Prajāpati-vratas (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.3–6).

The point is this: because the passage begins with the word *vrata* in the phrase "the vow of that student" (*tasya brahmacāriṇo vratam*), and because within a single sentence the conclusion depends upon the introduction, the negation (*nañ*)—even though it is connected with a verb—is understood as a prohibition that must be disregarded since it cannot be performed as a positive act; consequently, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) not to look.
However, such a construction should not be assumed for the sentence "one should not kill" (*na hanyāt*).

In passages such as "One should not look at [the rising sun]," however, because of the governing context "His vow," a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is impossible; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret it through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to refrain from looking.

Consequently, in cases of simple negation such as "One should not kill" or "One should not drink," since there is no verbal root meaning (*bhāvārtha*), there is an absence of the volitional effort (*kṛti*) that is pervaded by it.

And since that [prohibition] is absent, there is an absence of the effect pervaded by it; thus, he says that there is no rule that every sentence must have an action as its primary purport: "such as 'A Brahmin is not to be killed,' and so forth. Now, one might ask: why can cessation itself not be the action, or the means to that [action]? To this he replies: "And that is not an action."
The word "action" (*kriyā*) refers to that which denotes an effect (*kārya*).
This is because the *Bhāṣya* states that words whose meaning is not action are purposeless; therefore, here the term "action" signifies an effect.
It is a word denoting an effect.
He analyzes this very point with the words, "of those [words] whose meaning is not action.
This might be the case:
since an injunctive suffix is heard, a task (kārya) is indeed understood here, and that cannot exist without an act of being (bhāvārtha).

Furthermore, for one who has set out toward passion, a state of indifference regarding killing, drinking, and so forth does not arise spontaneously without an effort that restrains them; therefore, that very effort which restrains the mind, speech, and body as they are oriented toward activity is the object of prohibitory injunctions and constitutes action (*kriyā*).

Thus, there is no statement whatsoever that has non-action as its ultimate meaning. To this he says: "And [there is no such thing] apart from the indifference consisting in the cessation of the act of killing..."
It is not possible to conceive of the negative particle (*nañ*) as having the meaning of an action that has not been attained.

To the question "For what reason is it not possible?", he says: because the negative particle is colored by the meaning of the verb *han* (to kill), which is [already] established by its own nature (*svabhāva*).
[Question: What is to be enjoined here?

Having raised the alternatives—whether the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is "killing" and so forth, or whether it is the "effort of restraint"—the author begins to expose their flaws with the words "This is the meaning," and so on.
This is the point: the general rule (*utsarga*) is that when an injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) is perceived as being directed toward killing or drinking, it enjoins those very acts.
And these cannot be enjoined,
because they are already obtained through passion;
nor can a non-preservative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) of the negative particle be what is to be enjoined.
Furthermore, because that [state] which consists of indifference is already established and thus attained,
it is not a restraining effort; for such an effort is not explicitly stated in scripture and would therefore have to be inferred.
Furthermore, since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is improper when a primary sense is possible,
and because the injunctive suffix cannot have the injunction as its object— since it merely restates an activity already prompted by natural inclination—
it follows that the phrase "what one might drink or eat" is restated and then negated by "that [one] shall not."

Its absence is made known, but the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not being enjoined. [Note 3: One might object: "If the meaning of the negative particle is not being enjoined, then it would be perceived as an established fact, like in the case of 'there is no killing' (*hananaṃ nāsti*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And its absence... (*abhāvaśca*).

The meaning is that the property of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*), which resides in the counter-correlative characterized by the destruction [of the object] through the attainment of passion (*rāga*), is superimposed upon the absence (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, since an absence follows the "shadow" of a presence because it is defined by the presence of its own opposite, it appears as established when the presence is established, and as a probandum when the presence is a probandum; thus, there arises the delusion that the referent of the negative particle (*nañ*)—which has the probandum as its object—appears as if it were the probandum itself, and that this referent of the negative particle is the effect (*kārya*).

This is what [the author] says: "And this is the very nature of the negative particle (*nañ*). Now, one might ask: "Granted that the negative particle makes known the absence of the related object, how can there be a sudden cessation of the mind, speech, and body—which were previously intent on activity—without any apparent cause? To this, he replies: "And the cognition of absence leads to indifference (*audāsīnya*). [Note 1: Since it is a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it does not depend upon any cause; therefore, [the author] supplies the word "protection" (*pālana*).
The reason for [the injunction] is protection.

[The author] demonstrates, by means of the section beginning with "This is the intention" and ending with the passage prior to "in sentences that incite action," that through the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), positive and negative injunctions convey the fact that something is a means to what is desired or undesired.
This is the intended meaning: regarding the statement, "One who has a fever should eat wholesome food," [it is understood that eating wholesome food is a means to the desired state of health].

Immediately upon hearing such statements as "One should not offer one's finger to a snake," the child seeking to acquire knowledge observes that the elder being prompted acts toward eating wholesome food and desists from offering his finger to the snake; he thereby infers that desire and aversion are the causes of the prompted elder's engagement and withdrawal.

For instance: the engagement and desistance of an elder are caused by desire and aversion, because they are independent engagements and desistances, just like my own independent engagements and desistances.
[The state of being] "that which ought to be done" (kartavyatā) [is established].

NOTE 3: The distinction is that, within a single verbal root-meaning, the states of being a means to the desired and the undesired are inherent along with the "ought-to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*), and these are preceded by the knowledge thereof.

Furthermore, one's desire and aversion are preceded by the comprehension of the states of being a means to the desired and the undesired inherent in the same object, because desire and aversion are the causes of engagement and withdrawal.

Like desire and aversion, which serve as the causes for my engagement and withdrawal, desire and aversion have never at any time arisen in me without being preceded by cognitions— whether past or present— of words, their functions, the intentions of persons, or the uninterrupted cultivation of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*). Rather, when one repeatedly reflects upon one's own internal state, they appear only as being preceded by the aforementioned causes.

Therefore, the causal relationship is established by the following sequence: the independent activity and cessation of the elder, as well as the distinctions of desire and aversion, are preceded by the cognition of the state of being a means to what is desired or undesired, which inheres in the same object as the sense of "what ought to be done. Thus, it is proven that the activity and cessation of the elder who is prompted result from the cognition of the state of being a means to what is desired or undesired. Furthermore, since that cognition—which did not previously exist—arises immediately after hearing the word, it has the hearing of the word as its cause.

In injunctive statements such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta), it is the word itself that, by making known the activity which is to be performed as a means to a desired end, makes known both its status as a means to a desired end and its status as something to be performed; for both of these are not obtainable through any other source,
and that which cannot be obtained through any other source is the meaning of the word.
But where the necessity of action is obtained from another source,
as in cases such as "one should not kill" or "one should not drink," [the negative particle indicates a prohibition].

Because the engagement in killing and drinking arises from passion, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and other such forms, when used in conjunction with a negative particle (*nañ*) in reference to those acts, convey merely that these two are causes of undesirable results— something not otherwise established. For their status as means to achieve what is desired is indeed perceived through direct perception.
Otherwise, it would be impossible for them to be objects of passion;

therefore, sentences such as "one should not kill" and "one should not drink" are primarily intended to make known that [certain acts] are means to undesirable ends, by way of restating the duty already established by passion and so forth.

But it is well said that prohibitions do not have "what ought to be done" as their primary purport; rather, they result in the understanding that the prohibited acts are means to undesirable ends (*anartha-sādhana*).
This very cognition of the prohibited act as an undesirable end is what constitutes the cognition of the absence of the prohibited act.

For by means of this, even while perceiving an immediate attractiveness, the conscious agent—having reflected upon the future consequence and having understood non-engagement as cessation (*nivṛtti*)—desists from action.
That is to say, it establishes indifference in the self.
This might be the case:
if the cognition of non-existence is the cause for establishing indifference, [then...]
It would have to persist as long as indifference persists;
yet it does not so persist.
For even one who is indifferent, if his mind is distracted by another object, does not possess the cognition of that [object's] absence.
Moreover, the persistence of an effect is never observed in the absence of a cause that sustains it;
for indeed, when the pillar collapses, the palace does not remain standing.
Therefore, he says: "And that [flame] subsides by itself, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed."
Indeed, this [desire] remains intent upon activity only so long as it does not realize its status as a cause of harm.
Once it realizes its status as a cause of harm, its activity is uprooted along with its root, and it subsides of its own accord like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
Note: For the cognition of non-existence is not the cause for establishing indifference.
Because indifference (*audāsīnya*) is beginningless.
Furthermore, he says "this is what has been stated" to show that it serves to dispel objections:
this is what is meant—just as a pillar is the cause for the stability of a palace, the cognition of non-existence (*abhāvabuddhi*) is not the cause for the stability of indifference.
Rather, it is a cause for remaining by way of protection from an adventitious cause of destruction;

just as armor, as hard as the back of a tortoise, is the cause for the survival of a warrior through protection from the blows of weapons. And yet, when the armor is removed and there is no blow of a weapon, [the life does not persist].
"In the case of a king, there would be the destruction of his livelihood.
He concludes: "Therefore, it is simply indifference characterized by the cessation of an activity that has been undertaken.

He qualifies this by specifying "characterized by the cessation of an activity that has been undertaken," because indifference exists even for one who does not know [the object], [and thus it must be distinguished from mere absence].

Therefore, under the guise of a conclusion, he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating, "Therefore, for the sake of the human goal," etc., thus showing that Jaimini’s attempt to avoid the charge of meaninglessness by describing [the Upanishads] as being for the sake of action is indeed inconsistent.

For the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and final (uttara-pakṣa) positions regarding whether they are for the sake of action or not concern subjects such as narratives which are useless for the human goal; they do not concern the Upanishads.
The meaning is that the realization of Brahman, which is itself the supreme human goal, is not yet fully concluded by the Upaniṣads alone.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated by one who considers the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads to be not a human goal—namely, that it cannot exist "without entering into an injunction of duty"—the author, whose intention remains hidden, recalls the previously mentioned refutation: "That has already been answered."

Here, the objector recalls his own stated point: "But even for one who has heard [the teachings on] Brahman... The author of the commentary reveals the hidden intention behind the response: "To this it is said: not for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self. NOTE 1:
Regarding the word *avagata* in the phrase *avagatabrahmātmabhāvasya* from the commentary, he states its intended meaning: "True," and so forth.
True; it is not merely the knowledge of Brahman that is the cause for the cessation of worldly phenomena, but rather that which culminates in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

And this direct realization of Brahman is a specific modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), born of the mind aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by hearing, reflection, and so forth.

Just as the direct perception of the distinctions between the musical notes, such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth, has its origin in a mind refined by the study and practice of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*), this [knowledge] likewise uproots the entire illusory net of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mahendrajāla*) along with its very roots; and it has been demonstrated below that it thereby uproots even the Self, since the Self is not distinct from the nature of the phenomenal world.
Therefore, it is established that the situation here is exactly like the description of the true nature of a rope.
And here, because it is rooted in the authority of the Veda, it is said to be "generated by the authority of the Veda.
In this very context, he provides two illustrations based on the distinction between the non-arising of pleasure and pain, beginning with the words, "For [the case] of the wealthy...
He cites a scriptural passage as an example, saying, "That has been stated..."
The opponent objects: "When the body has fallen [the cognition ceases].
The author replies: "Not because of being embodied.
For if being embodied were a real property, it would not cease for one who is living.
But that [bondage] has its cause in false knowledge;
and since it can be removed by one who has arisen to the knowledge of reality, even while still living,
that which is his true nature— namely, bodilessness— cannot be removed.
He says that "bodilessness is eternal" because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of existence through the loss of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This might be argued:
"Bodily existence is not caused by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), but rather by merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*)."
And that [state] does not cease without the cessation of its own causes, namely merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).

Furthermore, since death itself occurs upon their cessation, one might raise the objection—expressed by the words "tatkṛta" (produced by that)—that there can be no bodiless state for one who is living.
Here, the word "tat" refers back to the self (ātman).
He refutes this, saying "no, because of the connection with the body.
To begin with, the self is not able to directly perform dharma and adharma.
For those two [bondage and liberation] are produced by the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body; they do not occur when there is no connection with a body.
However, one who seeks to establish a connection with a body through those two clearly incurs the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
This is what he says: "of the connection with a body."

If it should be argued: "True, there is indeed mutual dependence, but this is not a fault because it is beginningless, like the case of the seed and the sprout," to this he says: "This conception of beginninglessness is merely a succession of the blind."

NOTE 1: The proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādī*) avoids the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) by means of a distinction between individual instances; thus he says: "But as for him who thinks... He who considers that this beginninglessness is not equivalent to a blind succession [of causes]—for it is not from the very same difference in merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) that the difference in the connection between the self and the body arises, such that that difference in merit and demerit would depend on itself—but rather, this [present difference] arises from a prior connection between the self and the body, which was produced by a previous difference in merit and demerit.
Regarding the claim that "this connection between the self and the body arises from this distinction between dharma and adharma," he replies: "Because there is no inherence of action [in the self].
He raises an objection: "[It occurs] by mere proximity."
He avoids [the objection] by saying "no.
"Acquisition" (upārjana) means taking possession;
however, he states "but not of the self" to show that this [acquisition] does not pertain to the self.

However, those who maintain that the conceit of self with respect to the body and so forth is not false, but rather figurative— just as there is a conceit of "lion" with respect to a young boy— are mistaken.
Having set forth that view, he refutes it with the words "here they say" (*atrāhuḥ*).
A person for whom the distinction between entities is well-established is described as such. And since this has already been demonstrated by us in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*, it is not demonstrated here.

Just as in dim darkness, regarding an object whose specific features are not apprehended, the word and the cognition "this is a person" are both doubtful and have a post as their actual object; for in that case, even though "personhood" is indeterminate, it is merely superimposed.

Having thus cited an example of what is superimposed and uncertain in the case of doubt, he now cites an example of what is certain in the case of erroneous cognition: "Or, as in the case of mother-of-pearl.

When a white and lustrous object stands before one, and because it possesses qualities common to both mother-of-pearl and silver, a determination of it as silver occurs—why, until that point, does a determination of it as mother-of-pearl not occur, or why is doubt not appropriate?
Both would indeed be logical.

Because of the perception of the subject possessing common properties (*samāna-dharma-dharmin*), because of the lack of a fixed rule regarding apprehension and non-apprehension, and because of the recollection of two specific features (*viśeṣa*); since similarity—which is the cause for the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—resides in both [objects], this [recollection] would be equal in both cases. Therefore, it is said: "accidentally" (*akasmāt*).
By this, although the perceived cause is the same, the unperceived cause is stated.

The meaning is that this [doubt] is uncommon (asādhāraṇa) because it is to be inferred from the observation of the effect. "Of those who discriminate between the Self and the non-Self" means of those who are learned merely by virtue of their proficiency in hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana).
This refers, in short, to those who have not realized the reality of non-arising (*anutpanna-tattva*).
As it has been said: "Because there is no distinction [between them] and cattle and the like.
The remainder of the text has its meaning self-evident.
He cites both Śruti and Smṛti regarding the bodiless state of the wise one while living, with the words "And likewise. This is easy to understand.
He concludes the present topic with the words: "Therefore, for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self..."

Now, it might be argued: "If the realization of the selfhood of the individual soul as Brahman alone is the cause for the cessation of transmigratory attributes, then alas, the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and so forth are rendered purposeless;
therefore, the Vedāntas must be intended solely for the injunction of such a realization."

Having restated that, he refutes it: "As for what was further stated regarding those [means] subsequent to hearing (*śravaṇa*)—namely, reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—there is no injunction (*vidhi*) for them either;

for these two have as their fruit the direct realization established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and are thus merely restated by means of statements that have the form of injunctions."

This is what was stated: "because it has comprehension as its purpose. The meaning is that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is "comprehension," and that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) have that as their purpose is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, why is it not simply an injunction (*vidhi*) for reflection and so forth? To this he says: "For if [Brahman] were already comprehended... and so on.

It has already been stated above that reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) are not primary rites (*pradhānakarman*) directed toward a transcendental result (*apūrva*) with immortality as their fruit.
Therefore, [they must be subordinate rites].
Note 1: For a subordinate rite (*guṇakarman*) is, in some cases, of the nature of a remnant intended for future use.

For example, the threshing of rice grains intended for use in the *havir-yajña* is performed according to the injunction, "One threshes the rice grains. In other cases, however, it takes the form of a remnant of what has already been used,

such as the sprinkling of the oblations (*havis*) with the residue of the clarified butter (*ājya*) used in the *prayāja* offerings, according to the injunction, "One should sprinkle the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*."

It should be understood that neither of these two forms is possible for the Supreme Self, because it lacks the status of being something already used or yet to be used as a subordinate element (pradhāna).
What remains for these two is the state of being auxiliary actions (guṇakarma), like threshing or sprinkling (avaghāta-prokṣaṇa) and so forth.
That too is incorrect;
for the self lacks the state of having been used or being about to be used elsewhere,
and especially because, for one who follows the Upaniṣads, there is a contradiction with the performance of ritual action— this is the meaning.
He concludes the subject at hand with the words "therefore":
thus, since the Upaniṣads have as their purport Brahman in its established nature,
and since Brahman, the meaning of the scripture, is distinct from dharma.

Because the scriptures are distinct due to their having different subject matters, the status of "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) as the commencement of a separate scripture is justified; thus he says, "And this being so.

Otherwise, however, since it would be merely an inquiry into Dharma, it would not be a different scripture, and consequently, it would not constitute the commencement of a new scripture; thus he says, "If it were intent upon an injunction for realization (*pratipattividhiparatve*)."

The identity of Brahman and the Self is not only distinct from dharma because it is an established reality (*siddharūpa*), but also because it is in opposition to it; thus, by way of a conclusion, he says: "Therefore, 'I am Brahman'.
By the use of the particle *iti*, he refers to knowledge.
For injunctions (*vidhi*) are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma.

The meaning is that these [means of knowledge], which have as their basis the distinctions between the goal (sādhya), the means (sādhana), and the procedure (itikartavyatā), and which produce dharma based on those distinctions, do not prevail when there is the identity of Brahman and the Self, because of the contradiction.
Not only does this apply to the scripture, which is the authority for dharma; [it applies to all means of knowledge].
Rather, he says that it applies to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), stating: "And all other means of valid cognition.
Why? Because [he says] "for not," since in non-duality (*advaita*) there is no relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).
Nor is there agency, because of the absence of an effect;
nor is there causality, for the very same reason.
This is what is meant by the phrase "and [they are] without a knower," where the word "and" (ca) is used.
In this very context, he cites the verses of those who know Brahman, introducing them with the words "Moreover, they say."
The identification of the self with one's sons, wife, and so forth is secondary (gauṇa);
it is just as one becomes sorrowful through one's own sorrow,
and joyful through one's own joy.
Likewise, this same quality applies even when [the self] is identified with sons and so forth;
however, there is no conceit of identity,
because difference is established by experience.

Therefore, [the identification of the self with the body] is figurative (gauṇa), like the expression "The Vāhīka is an ox. However, because there is an experience of non-difference regarding the body, senses, and so forth, the conceit of self (ātmābhimāna) is not figurative;
rather, it is false (mithyā), like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Thus, this twofold conceit of a self sustains the course of worldly life;
however, in its absence, there would be neither the course of worldly life nor the experience of the identity of Brahman and the self.
This is because there is an absence of the means for that [liberation], such as hearing and reflection.
This very point is stated: "Because of the sublation of son, body, and so forth;
when the secondary self (gauṇātman) does not exist, there is the sublation of son, wife, and the rest."
This means the absence of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*).
When the false self (*mithyātman*) does not exist, there is the sublation of the body, the senses, and so forth, as well as the sublation of hearing and other such functions.
Consequently, it is not merely that worldly activity (*lokayātrā*) is cut off; rather, there is the duty whose nature is the realization: "I am the True Brahman."
That is to say, the direct realization of non-duality (advaitasākṣātkāra).

How could that even come to be? Why is its impossibility [claimed]? To this he says: "Prior to the knowledge of the Self that is to be sought, the Self possesses the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva)."

And this is merely an illustration; one should also understand that the distinction between valid cognition (*pramā*), the object of cognition (*prameya*), and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intended.
What is meant is this: for this very distinction is the cause of the direct realization of non-duality (*advaita-sākṣātkāra*).
Therefore, because [the cause] necessarily precedes [the effect], the effect does not arise in its absence.
Furthermore, he states that the Self of the knower is not something else to be sought: "When sought, it is the knower himself who is found, free from evil, defects, and the like."
The illustration of the necklace fastened to the neck has been stated.

This might be asked: how can the experience of ultimate non-duality arise from that which is not a valid means of knowledge? To this he says: "Just as the notion of the body being the self is imagined to be a valid means of knowledge..."
This worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is exactly like that.
He states its limit: "until certainty regarding the self" (*ātmāniścayāt*).
This means until the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the nature of Brahman.

This is what is meant: even by those who maintain that ultimate conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) exists, it must be admitted that the conceit of a self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth is false, because it is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it must be accepted that this [conceit] is the cause of all means of valid cognition and that it sustains the worldly course of affairs (*lokayātrā*) as something real.
This very [means] will also serve as the instrument for our direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of non-duality.
Moreover, this direct realization of non-duality, being a particular modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is not ultimately real in an absolute sense.
As for that realization which is ontologically real (*bhāvika*), [it is the ultimate reality itself].
That [Brahman] is not an effect,
because its nature is that of Brahman;
as for ignorance (avidyā), however, it might either destroy ignorance or produce it.
There is no inconsistency whatsoever in this;
and thus says the Śruti: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge."
Thus,
therefore, everything is completely clear.
Thus ends the *Catussūtrī*.
In this way, [the Upanishads] possess authority regarding Brahman, which is established as an accomplished reality, even without a connection to an action (*kāryānvaya*).
Thus, it has been established that the Vedāntas themselves have human purpose as their goal.

Having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to that which is omniscient, omnipotent, and the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world has been established by the collection of sūtras beginning with "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this" and ending with "But that [is so] because of the harmony [of the texts]. And that [validity] belongs to Brahman in the ultimate sense.
However, it has not yet been established that [the cause] is Brahman alone.
Therefore, a doubt arises here: is that material cause of the world conscious or unconscious?
And in this matter, since there is a disagreement among disputants and no specific distinction can be perceived, doubt occurs.
Regarding this, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the Upaniṣads merely restate what is established by inference—that the primary cause (pradhāna), which is insentient, is the material cause of the world.

The followers of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that the Upaniṣads restate what is inferred—that the four kinds of atoms, presided over by a sentient Lord who is distinct from the individual soul and the atom, are the material cause of the world.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should understand [theories such as] that non-existence (abhāva) is the material cause, and so forth.

The knowers of Brahman maintain that the world, as established by scripture, has as its material cause a conscious entity endowed with the power of beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyānādyavidyāśakti*).
And the seeds of these conflicting views are inference, scriptural statements, and fallacious inferences and statements.
Thus, since there is doubt due to this conflict of opinions, what is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

In that regard: "Because the unchanging Brahman lacks the powers of knowledge and action, the possibility of possessing all powers and consciousness does not exist in it; however, such a possibility does exist in the Pradhāna."
Indeed, the powers of knowledge and action have their existence inferred from the observation of the effects of knowledge and action;
yet knowledge and action do not exist in the conscious self (cidātman),
because it is unchanging and unitary.
However, these two are possible within the *pradhāna*, which consists of the three *guṇas* and is subject to transformation.
Even though, in its state of equilibrium, activity and cognition do not exist as manifest functions within the *pradhāna*, they nonetheless exist in an unmanifest form as potencies.
And thus, it is Pradhāna alone that is omniscient and omnipotent,
and not Brahman;
for its intrinsic consciousness, being veiled, is of no use to us, just as it is to the individual souls (jīvātman).
Moreover, agency does not belong to the consciousness that is one's own essential nature, because that is unproduced;
or, if it were produced, there would be no omniscience at all times.

However, creation is the transformation of the insentient *pradhāna*— which, though not presided over by a conscious being, proceeds through the sequence of *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth— caused by the primordial conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* impelled by the two aims of human life characterized as enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
And it is observed that even an insentient thing, without being presided over by a conscious being, acts toward the aim of a person.

Just as insentient milk flows forth for the sake of the growth of the calf, and scriptural passages such as "It thought: May I be many, may I procreate" show— even regarding that which is insentient— a tendency toward its own effects by means of figurative treatment as if it were sentient, just as one says, "The bank wishes to fall."
Whatever is heard in a context that is predominantly [of a certain type] is understood to be of that same nature;
since this [text] is heard in a context that is predominantly figurative, it is therefore understood to be figurative.

Moreover, the elders say: "Just as when one sees something written about a preeminent person, they say, 'This must be that preeminent person,' so too in this case— where there is a predominance of figurative usage in such passages as 'Those waters thought' and 'That fire thought'— the statement 'That [breath] thought' should be understood as purely figurative."

And by the statement, "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms," [the scripture] declares that the primary cause (pradhāna) possesses the nature of the living self because it acts for the sake of the living self.

For just as King Bhadrasena, acting for the king's interest, is figuratively addressed by the king as "Bhadrasena is my very self," so too scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) should be understood as being figurative or intended for the purpose of meditative identification (saṃpatti).

And the etymological explanation (nirukta) stating "he becomes merged in his own" (svam apīto bhavati) declares that the merging of the individual soul (jīva) into its own primary cause (pradhāna) occurs during the state of deep sleep. For while asleep, the soul is submerged as if in darkness within the vessel of the tamas-portion of the primary cause. As they say: "Sleep is a mental modification (vṛtti) supported by the notion of non-existence."

The meaning is that sleep (*nidrā*) is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the living being (*jīva*), having as its cause the darkness (*tamas*) which is the absence of other modifications such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, and taking that [darkness] as its object.
Likewise, with reference to the Omniscient One, the Śvetāśvatara mantra—"the cause of causes, the lord of the lords of the organs"—is intended to refer to *Pradhāna*.
For it has been established above that omniscience belongs to *Pradhāna* alone.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the Śrutis merely restate that the insentient Pradhāna is the material cause of the world.
In this way, even in the systems of Kaṇāda and others, the Śrutis may somehow be interpreted;
however, as for the literal meaning, it applies to the position of Pradhāna as the cause as well—meaning "of the Pradhāna too."
The particle *api* has the sense of *eva*.
This might be argued:

"If his omniscience results from the perfection of existence (*sattva*), then why does he not also possess non-omniscience through the perfection of darkness (*tamas*)? To this, he says: "And by that quality of existence, which is knowledge."
For *sattva* is by nature luminous, possesses unsurpassed excellence, and is the seed of omniscience.
Thus they have said: "The seed of omniscience is unsurpassed.
Indeed, whatever is surpassable is seen to reach a point where it is unsurpassed somewhere.
