Just as magnitude is comparative in the case of the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, but reaches its ultimate limit (is non-comparative) in the infinitely great space (*vyoman*),
so too knowledge is comparative by virtue of having one, two, or many objects; therefore, by this very fact, there must exist somewhere a knowledge that is non-comparative.
And this very state constitutes its unsurpassed nature: that it has known all that is to be known.
This omniscience is possible for *sattva* when it reaches a state of unsurpassed excellence.

What is meant is this: although *rajas* and *tamas* also exist, nevertheless, due to the preeminence of the differentiation among the qualities (*guṇa*) impelled by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, [this occurs] in *sattva*.

Since omniscience arises as an effect when there is unsurpassed excellence, even in the state of Pradhāna, by intending or not intending that [excellence] alone, Pradhāna is metaphorically designated as "omniscient" with respect to the effect of Tamas.
By means of the two particles *api*, he states what is excluded by the restriction: "not of the solitary [Pradhāna]."
For a single entity cannot produce even one effect, much less many;
and since the conscious self (cidātman) is one while primordial matter (pradhāna) consists of the three guṇas, it is from the latter alone that an effect can arise.
The meaning is that [agency] does not belong to the conscious self (cidātman).
Furthermore, you too admit that the conscious self possesses agency merely by virtue of its inherent capacity, and not through connection with an effect; this he states with the words "by you too.
He elaborates on the point that it does not belong to the solitary [self] which is neither cause nor effect, using the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita) method, with the words "prior to origination."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of the pradhāna," the word "ca" has the sense of "but. When this [objection] has been raised, it is said in reply:
"Because of the act of seeing, [the cause] is not one that is not based on scripture (aśabda).
"If it is argued that [the term 'Self'] is figurative, we say no, because of the use of the word 'Self'.

There is a means of valid cognition for the general conceptualization that this [cause] possesses only a causal nature, based on the observation of the effect characterized by the manifold expansion of names and forms.
However, there is no inference to support the conceptual distinction that this [cause] is either insentient or sentient; this will be explained further below.
Therefore, regarding the authoritative knowledge of the distinction between the cause and its effects—the manifold world of name and form—the Blessed One, the Scripture itself, is to be relied upon.

Thus, since the cause of the world is to be understood solely through the Scripture, whatever the Scripture directly declares—upon a thorough examination of its preceding and succeeding passages—is to be accepted as the truth.
That alone is accepted as the seed of the world, and it resides directly within consciousness.
Indeed, in various sections of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the birth of the world from a conscious cause is declared by such statements as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*).

Furthermore, it is not logical for an insentient entity such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or atoms (*paramāṇu*) to possess the quality of being a thinker; [if one argues] that primordial matter is a thinker by virtue of its *sattva* component, [we reply:]...
If it is argued that this is because [sattva] is illuminating, we say no;
for since it is insentient (jāḍya), its being such [an illuminator] is untenable.
What, then, is the distinction of sattva from rajas and tamas?
Transparency; for sattva is transparent,
whereas rajas and tamas are non-transparent.
And because it receives the reflection of consciousness due to its transparency, it alone is designated as "illuminating," not the other two, since they lack that capacity due to their opacity.
Even though they are equally composed of earth, the jewel possesses the capacity to receive reflections while clods of earth and the like do not.
But the status of being a seer belongs directly to Brahman, because it is determined from scripture that its nature is eternal knowledge.
[Objection: But for this very reason, it cannot be a seer.
Because the eternal vision, which constitutes the very nature of knowledge, is non-active, Brahman lacks the status of being its efficient cause (*nimitta*);
and since the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) ceases when there is no efficient cause for an action, the specific quality of agency—which is pervaded by that [status]—also ceases.
True; consciousness, which is the intrinsic nature of Brahman, is not an action because of its eternity.

However, for that [Brahman], which is in itself undivided, its impermanence and its status as an effect are established through the divisions conceptually constructed by the distinctions of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of those respective objects.
And thus, in such a perception regarding all objects, Brahman’s agency—characterized by sovereignty—is logically established.

Even though its actual nature is one of indifference, as it is immutable, eternal, and non-transforming, nevertheless, because it appears to possess activity when delimited by beginningless and indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*), its agency is justified.

Moreover, even by others, such agency of the eternally immutable consciousness (*cit-śakti*) with respect to its modifications must be admitted; for the state of being a knower is perceived through its co-occurrence with consciousness in general.
Indeed, the thirteen internal and external organs, though composed primarily of the quality of *sattva*, are themselves insentient.
And those who possess the functioning of that [vision] are capable of knowing either the void or the supreme;
for indeed, even a thousand blind travelers do not find the path,
whereas if it is known by a single person endowed with sight, [it is known].

In that case, he alone is the seer of the path, the independent agent, and their leader. Likewise, although the intellect (*buddhisattva*) is itself insentient, if the state of being a knower is attributed to consciousness (*caitanya*) through the transfer of the reflection of consciousness [into it],
then consciousness alone is the knower and is independent.
The internal and external organs, which resemble a thousand blind men and are not independent, [cannot perceive].
Nor is there any connection with activity for this consciousness, which is immutable and eternal;
yet, even in the absence of such a connection, it is not a non-knower.
Because even those things possessing activity are insentient and thus lack consciousness,
the conceit of agency is attributed to the power of consciousness (citiśakti) by superimposing upon it the activity residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
or else, by superimposing consciousness upon the internal organ, the conceit of being a knower is attributed to it.
In every respect, even in your own view, this knowership is not inherent anywhere; rather, the ultimate truth is that it is merely conventional.
Furthermore, the claim that knowledge is a transformation (pariṇāma) of the eternal self has been rejected by those who refute the position of both difference and non-difference.
Furthermore, it will be refuted later on that knowledge is an attribute distinct from the immutable and eternal Self which is devoid of activity.

Therefore, it is established that consciousness, which is in reality undivided, becomes the effect known as "knowledge" when delimited by the objects of name and form—which are themselves indeterminable as either identical to or different from [consciousness], unmanifest, and intended to be manifested;
and its agent is the Lord, the knower, who is omniscient and omnipotent.
And so says the Śruti: "By austerity Brahman is built up; from that food is born;
from food arise vital breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in ritual acts."
He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving—his austerity consists of knowledge;
from him this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food, are born.
Thus,
through austerity and knowledge concerning the unmanifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it accumulates and becomes desirous of manifesting that [unmanifest],
just as a weaver or similar artisan, having first sketched an unmanifest cloth or the like in his mind, desires to produce it.
One who possesses a single attribute is said to be "accumulated" through the production of a second attribute.

And when there is accumulation due to the desire to manifest (*vyācikīrṣā*), from that arises the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—the food to be consumed, common to all transmigrating beings—which is intended to be manifested.

From that undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) food intended for manifestation, Prāṇa is born: Hiraṇyagarbha, the Brahma who is the substratum of the powers of knowledge and action, the Sūtrātman of the world, and the common [principle] of all.
Just as from an unmanifested cloth that is intended to be manifested there arises an intermediate effect consisting of two threads and so forth,

from that [intermediate effect] there is born what is called the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), whose nature consists of the manifestation of volition, doubt, and so on. From that mind, which is of the nature of manifestation, there are born space and the other elements, which are denoted by the word "truth" (*satya*).

From those [truths] known as the *satyas*, the worlds beginning with Bhūr arise in succession; within them, living beings such as humans give rise to actions in the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) according to the sequence of castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).
And from these actions arises the immortal fruit, such as heaven, hell, and so forth.
Because it does not perish as long as its causes—merit and demerit—exist, it is called "immortal" (*amṛta*).
"Up to the point of being the agent of dharma and adharma" means:
he who is omniscient in a general sense and all-knowing in a specific sense.
The austerity and dharma of that Blessed One consist of knowledge, not of physical exertion; therefore, this subsequent Brahman is the effect of that prior Brahman.
Furthermore, name-and-form and food—such as rice, barley, and so forth—are born from it.
Therefore, because the Pradhāna lacks the capacity for seeing while in its state of equilibrium,
and because the Kṣetrajñas, despite possessing consciousness, do not perceive objects at the beginning of creation, and because metaphorical attribution is improper when a primary sense is possible;

Furthermore, for one desiring liberation, an instruction that is not in accordance with reality is untenable because it would contradict liberation; and since fire and the other elements cannot exist in their primary sense [in the liberated state], it is logically established that they must be understood through metaphorical usage.
Furthermore, in cases of doubt, the context of similar enumeration (*tatprāyapāṭha*) serves as a determinative factor;
however, in this instance, since the primary sense is established by its inherent naturalness (*autsargikatva*), there is no room for doubt.
Otherwise, even a Brāhmaṇa born of a lineage who dwells in a region crowded with hundreds of Kirātas would incur the status of being a Kirāta himself.
Brahman alone, accompanied by beginningless and inexpressible ignorance (avidyā), is the material cause of the world,
just as mother-of-pearl is the cause of the superimposed silver, or as a mirage is the cause of water.
Thus it is like one moon [reflected] in a second moon;
however, it is not the insentient *pradhāna*, atoms, or the like,
for those are not mentioned in the scripture (*aśabda*).

Nor is it tenable that either primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or atoms, when presided over by an omniscient Lord distinct from them, constitute the material cause of the world; for [the world] is an effect.

Since there is no difference between a cause and its effects, the thorough knowledge of all effects through the knowledge of the cause has been established by scripture using the illustration of clay and so forth, and because such knowledge would be impossible if there were a difference.

Furthermore, because of the direct negation of the world as something distinct from Brahman through such passages as "One only, without a second," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "He goes from death to death," the established conclusion is that the world has consciousness alone as its material cause,
just as a superimposed serpent has a rope as its material cause.
For once it is established that the world has Being (Sat) as its material cause, one may then investigate— after raising the doubt whether that conscious material cause is sentient or insentient.

But even now, the fact that [the world] has a real material cause (sadupādānatva) remains unestablished; therefore, he says—from "In this regard, that which is denoted by the word 'this'" up to "he shows"—that [the cause] is so. Nevertheless, there might be an Ishvara who is distinct from the ultimate Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña, as the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha say; hence the Śruti declares: "One only, without a second."
And by the phrase "May I be many," the non-intelligent cause itself declares its own state of becoming manifold;
by this also, it is accepted that the effect is non-different from the intelligent cause.

Although the creation of the elements begins with ether and so forth, nevertheless, because the threefold compounding (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) specifically concerns fire, water, and earth, fire is mentioned first there due to its priority.
Regarding the point that the one without a second is the material cause of the world, he cites another scriptural passage: "And so elsewhere.
"Brahman has four quarters, eight hooves, and sixteen parts.
For example: the east, the west, the south, and the north—these four parts constitute the first quarter of Brahman, named 'The Radiant' (prakāśavat)."
Half of that is a *śapha*.
Likewise, earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the ocean are four other parts; this second foot is named "the infinite" (*anantavat*).
Similarly, fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning are four parts.
That which is named "The Radiant" is the third foot.
Breath, sight, hearing, and speech are the four times;
that is the fourth foot of Brahman, named "Possessing Abodes."
Thus, it is established that Brahman, consisting of sixteen parts—that is, having sixteen constituent elements—is the object of meditation.
This may be so;
however, in the [sūtra] "because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*), the verbal root itself is expressed by the suffix *tip*.

And since it is impossible for the mere form of a verbal root—whose meaning is not intended to be expressed—to serve as the instrument for the acquisition of consciousness, he says: "Because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*) is intended as a designation of the meaning of the verbal root, because that which possesses the object (the subject) indicates the object itself.
And he says "as in the case of *yajateḥ*" to show that this indication is well-known.
"He who is all-knowing" refers to it in a general sense; "all-seeing" refers to it in a specific sense.
Having presented the Sāṃkhya's own resolution of their position, he refutes it with the words: "As for what was said regarding the quality of *sattva*."
Again, he raises the Sāṃkhya objection with the words, "But has it not been said? He refutes this with, "That too...
[The argument is: first of all, *sattva* does not possess an active mode of operation (*sāmudācaradvṛtti*).
The meaning is that because of the consequence of an inequality among the qualities (guṇas), their state of equilibrium is untenable;
furthermore, knowledge is not rendered useful by an unmanifest form,
since even rajas and tamas exist in a subtle form as obstacles to that knowledge.

Furthermore, the verb *jānāti* denotes a function whose primary locus is consciousness (*caitanya*), and its usage has never been observed in reference to mere unconscious activity; thus he says, "Moreover, it is not without a witness.
If that is so, how then is the omniscience of yogins caused by the excellence of the *sattva* component? To this he replies, "But in the case of yogins...
For the excellence of the *sattva* component assists those yogins who possess the eye of consciousness.
This means "not of the insentient Pradhāna.

However, if one were to set aside the doctrine of Kapila and adopt that of Hiraṇyagarbha, he says regarding that as well: "Or rather, it is caused by a witness. For even according to them, omniscience belongs only to a specific Puruṣa who has taken up preeminent Sattva and is untouched by afflictions, karma, its fruition, or latent dispositions.
But it does not belong to the non-conscious Pradhāna;
moreover, that [Pradhāna] has been refuted by the scriptural texts on non-duality (advaita)—this is the intended meaning.
He restates the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "As for what was further stated regarding Brahman also..."

Even though pure consciousness is eternal, that which is conditioned (upahita) is non-eternal and an effect, just as space is [non-eternal] when delimited by a jar; intending this, he offers the rebuttal: "First of all, you [must consider] this... The statement "in the sun, whose heat and light are pervasive" also intends that the illumination delimited by an object is an effect.
He raises an objection regarding inequality: "Is it not the case that [you say] 'of the sun'?
Do you state the inequality with the intention of referring to the actual absence of action, or rather to the absence of the desire to speak of it?
In that regard, if it is the absence of the desire to speak of it...
By the phrase "it illuminates," let there be no equality [with the object];
however, by the phrase "it shines," there is [equality]. For here, the object (karman) is not intended to be expressed.
And yet, he offers a rebuttal, stating that the sun possesses independence with respect to its nature of luminosity:
"No; even in the absence of an action.
The phrase "even in the absence" means even when it is not intended [to be present].
Alternatively, if it were argued that this inequality is stated with the intention of referring to the non-existence of action in a real sense,
that is not so,
because the non-existence of action is unestablished.
And because the object [of the action] is intended to be expressed here, he offers the rebuttal: "But when there is a requirement for an object...

This means that for those scriptural passages which are logically consistent when an object is not intended to be expressed, they are all the more so consistent when an object is indeed intended to be expressed.
[This refers to the phrase] "by whose grace."
The construction of the sentence is as follows: "What need is there to say that eternal knowledge belongs eternally to that eternally perfected Lord (Īśvara) by the grace of that Blessed Lord?
As the authors of the Yogaśāstra state: "From that [practice], there arises the realization of the inward Self and the disappearance of obstacles.
And the commentators on that [work] state: "The Lord, won over by a particular kind of devotion, favors him with knowledge, dispassion, and so forth."
"Like the light of the sun.

Having stated that, in reality, that which is eternal is independent of causes by way of its own nature, he also states it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Moreover, for one possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth," and so on.
By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), desire (*kāma*), action (*karman*), and the rest are subsumed.
"Not for one who lacks the causes that obstruct knowledge.
The meaning is this: although transmigrating beings possess eternal knowledge in reality, ignorance (avidyā) and other factors exist as obstructing causes;
however, for the Lord, who is devoid of ignorance, it is impossible for any cause that obstructs knowledge to exist.
The sense is that for him there is no need for the removal of obscurations and so forth, because he is unobscured;
[this] activity is performed by the power of knowledge.
The meaning is that because the *pradhāna* is insentient and lacks the power of knowledge, it does not perform the act of creating the world.
It is handless yet grasps;
it is footless yet swift and vigorous in its movement.
The rest is clear in meaning.
This might be the case:
let there be, in the case of space—which is not a self—the delusion of limitation caused by adjuncts such as jars and the like.
But that [superimposition] is not possible in the case of the Self, whose luminosity is established by its own nature; therefore, he says: "And it is seen to belong to the Self alone which exists.
"Adherence" (abhiniveśa) means false conceit (mithyābhimāna).
"By the preceding mere false cognition" means by the prior state consisting of nothing but erroneous understanding.
By this, beginninglessness is shown.

By the use of the term "mere" (*mātra*), the indeterminability [of the world]—on the grounds that it could withstand critical analysis—is refuted. The remainder is explained by its own words (*nigadavyākhyāta*). //5 // //6//
START BsVBh_1,1.5.7:
Because liberation is taught for one who is established in that. BBs_1,1.7:
"Because liberation is taught for one who is established in that."
This sūtra is intended for the refutation of Pradhāna, either as a response to an objection or independently;
and the objection has been stated in the Bhāṣya. //7//
It might be argued as follows:
Brahman alone is what is intended to be known.

And since that [Self] cannot be made to be grasped by Śvetaketu at the outset due to its subtlety, it is the *pradhāna* (the primary principle) associated with it that is grasped as the Self in its grossness; just as one who wishes to show the extremely subtle star Arundhatī first points out a nearby gross star, saying, "This is that Arundhatī."
The answer to this doubt is the sūtra: "And because there is no statement that it is to be abandoned" (1.1.8).
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of including what has not been mentioned;
and that which was not mentioned [is] stated in the Bhāṣya. //8//

Furthermore, with reference to the cause of the world, the Śruti provides an etymological explanation (nirukta) for the word "svapiti" (he sleeps), stating "he covers himself" (saṃvṛṇoti); thus, the Śruti declares that the conscious [Brahman] alone is the cause of the world.
Even if the word "sva" signifies the self (ātman), it is nonetheless impossible for a conscious Puruṣa to have the non-conscious Pradhāna as its nature.
Furthermore, even if it were the case that [the world] belongs to the Self, since it is insentient, its dissolution would be impossible for the sentient being, even though it belongs to him.
For a pot, whose nature is clay, does not dissolve into water—even though the water belongs to it—but rather only into the clay which constitutes its own self.
Nor does silver dissolve into an elephant, which is not its own self.
But [the Self] exists in the nacre itself, which has become its own body; thus he says:
"Because of its merging in sleep" (BBs 1.1.9) and "Because of the uniformity of the way of going" (BBs 1.1.10).
"Going" means comprehension. "As in the systems of the logicians" means that,
just as there is a mutual contradiction among the various tenets of the logicians, [so it is here].
In the Vedāntas, however, there is no such mutual contradiction; rather, throughout them all, there is a uniform understanding of the consciousness that is the cause of the world,
just as the eyes and other senses have a common apprehension of form and other objects.

For just as the eye of everyone perceives only form and does not show taste or other objects to anyone, nor does it show form to some while showing something else to others; so too, the commonality of function should be observed regarding the tongue and the other sense organs. //10//
START BsVBh_1,1.5.11:
And because it is so stated in scripture (śrutatvāt).
In the passage, "It thought (tadaikṣata)," only the act of thinking (īkṣaṇamātra) is heard as belonging to the cause of the world, but not [thinking] regarding all objects.
However, because it is connected with the cause of the world, it is understood from that very source to have all things as its object;
the distinction is that in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, it is stated directly that the omniscient Lord is the cause of the world. 11.
He introduces the context of the subsequent sutras with the words: "beginning with 'janmādy asya yataḥ'.
For it was indeed promised that Brahman is to be investigated, and that [Brahman] is to be understood solely through the scripture (śāstra).

Furthermore, it has been established through reasoning that the scripture (*śāstra*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to Brahman—the omniscient and omnipotent cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world—and not with respect to the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or other such entities.

Nor is there any portion of the Vedānta that could teach anything contrary to this; thus it was said, "because of the uniformity of the purport" (*gatisāmānyāt*). What, then, remains [to be explained]?

"What is the purpose for which there would be the introduction of this composition of sūtras concerning another matter?"—this means "What is the motive? or "What is the objection? (kim-utthānam = kim-ākṣepaḥ).
He provides the resolution: "It is said—'for it is of two forms'.
Although Brahman is in reality devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nevertheless, it cannot be taught in that [pure] form; therefore, it must be taught by means of its conditioned form.
And in that regard, in some instances, the limiting adjunct is intended to be expressed.
Among those meditations, some are for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and are included here because they have the mind alone as their means;
some are for the sake of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*); and some are for the sake of the successful accomplishment of ritual acts (*karmasamṛddhi*).
In some cases, however, even a repeated limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not intended to be significant,

as for example here with the five sheaths (*kośa*), beginning with *annamaya* and ending with *ānandamaya*. Therefore, it has not yet been determined which [sheath] here intends a limiting adjunct and which does not.

Likewise, the commonality of destination (*gatisāmānya*) has been stated as if already established, yet it has not actually been proven even now; therefore, the meaning is that the subsequent textual context is commenced for the purpose of proving that.
This might be so.

Since the Supreme Self remains non-different even when qualified by various distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), how can there be a difference in meditation (*upāsanā*) and how can there be a difference in the fruit? To this, he says: "But [the Self] is indeed one.

The meaning is that although there is no difference in the essential form (*rūpa*), there is a difference in meditation due to the difference in limiting adjuncts and the resulting difference in the conditioned [Self], and thus there is a difference in the fruit as well.
*Kratu* means volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Now, if the Self is one, immutable, eternal, unsurpassed, and hidden in all beings, how can there be these scriptural declarations regarding gradations within this very basis of beings? To this he says: "Even though the Self is one," and so forth.
Although the nature of the Self— its sovereignty, knowledge, and bliss— is indeed one and without superior, nevertheless,
being shrouded by the darkness of beginningless ignorance, it appears as if non-existent in some among the various classes of living beings, and as if existent in others.
In some places it was as if extremely diminished, in some places as if slightly diminished,
and in some places it possessed excellence.
In some places it appears as if possessing extreme excellence;
for what reason?
Because of the gradations of intensity and deficiency in the darkness of ignorance.

Just as the sun, though it fills the entire circle of the quarters with light of a single nature, appears as if its light were inferior during the rainy season but as if its light were superior in autumn,
so too is this [meditation].
It is [the meditation] upon that which is connected with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) as the object of worship.
As being the object of knowledge, it is free from any connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi). //11//
START BsVBh_1,1.6.12-14:
"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition" (BBs_1,1.12).
"If it be argued that it is not so because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance" (BBs_1,1.13).

"And because of the designation of its cause. (BBs 1.1.14) First, he formulates the discussion according to the view of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*): "In the *Taittirīyaka*, [it says] 'consisting of food' (*annamaya*) and so forth.
Even though it falls within a series of secondary [meanings], the primary sense of 'seeing' (*īkṣaṇa*) is appropriate."
But when both are equally primary, the observation of the majority serves as the differentiator.

Since the suffix *mayaṭ* has an equal primary meaning in both the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) and in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), it is logical that the term *ānandamaya* also signifies a modification, given its placement within a series of terms such as *annamaya* which denote modifications. Nor is it correct to argue that in the case of *prāṇamaya* and the others, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own (inherential) sense because it is impossible for them to signify a modification.

For the Self, when delimited by limiting adjuncts such as the vital breath (prāṇa), becomes subject to the modifications of those [adjuncts], just as the space within a jar is subject to the modifications of the jar.
And it is not appropriate for a word to have a derivative meaning (svārthika) when its primary meaning is already established.
"But if there were a separation of four sheaths, it would not be called the innermost of all;
moreover, it would be illogical for the living soul (jīva), which possesses a body and partakes in states such as being dear, to be Brahman."
Nor is it correct to claim that Brahman alone is the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) because it is the innermost of all, rather than the individual soul (jīva).

For this scripture does not state that the one consisting of bliss is the innermost of everything; rather, it states that the sheath consisting of bliss is the innermost of the four preceding sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of food.
Nor is it logical to conclude that "this alone is the innermost" simply because no other thing more inner than it has been heard of;
for whatever is heard to be the innermost in relation to something else is innermost only in relation to that very thing.
Indeed, when it is said that Devadatta is strong, he is not understood to be strong in relation to all things such as lions and tigers, but rather in relation to another person of the same kind.
Thus, even the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is internal only relative to those beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), but not relative to everything.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the partless Brahman to possess limbs such as "dear" (priya) and so forth, nor is it possible for it to have a body; therefore, the one consisting of bliss must be a transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) alone.

Therefore, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that it is only Brahman as conditioned (upahita) that is intended here as the object of meditation, and not Brahman in its true nature as the object of knowledge.
Furthermore, even if the suffix -maya denotes abundance (prācurya), [the objection remains].
Nevertheless, it is the transmigrating being alone who consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*),
and not Brahman.
For an abundance of bliss occurs when there is the presence of even a slight trace of suffering, which is its opposite, and not when such [suffering] is absolutely non-existent.
Furthermore, not even the slightest trace of suffering can possibly arise for the Supreme Self, because its sole essence is bliss; thus he says, "nor for one who possesses a body.

On the other hand, for that which is bodiless, there is not even the slightest connection with anything unpleasant; therefore, the sense of abundance expressed by the suffix *-maya* is also not applicable here. This is the meaning.
It is said:
first of all, Brahman as the tail—the limb consisting of bliss—is not primary by virtue of being a subordinate part; rather, Brahman as the whole consisting of bliss is indeed primary.
And so, it is rightly said that the repetition of the word "bliss" (ānanda), which is recited within that context, produces the cognition of that very self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).

Just as in the section on the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the phrase "one should sacrifice with the Jyotis in every spring"—where the word "Jyotis" is a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma intended to enjoin a specific time—so too is this the case here.
Moreover, the repetition of the Self consisting of bliss is heard directly in scripture: "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss."
Having restated the seed of the prima facie argument—that [the self] is "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth—he refutes it:
For the vision of the primary Arundhatī does not become a vision of the secondary Arundhatī simply because it is recited in proximity to those various visions of the secondary Arundhatī.
If it is argued that, because they serve that same purpose, the preceding visions must conform to the final vision and cannot be in contradiction with it—[we reply: no.

Here too, since no other entity is heard of as being more internal than the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), and since that [bliss] is declared in scripture to be the innermost of all, beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), it follows that the conclusion [of the text] rests upon it; thus, its status as the ultimate goal is equal [to that of Brahman].
Furthermore, the objection regarding its connection with limbs such as "pleasure" and its nature as a body has been resolved by the commentary already explained.

Furthermore, it has been established that even when there is a slight connection with suffering due to association with limbs such as those of a beloved, it is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) for the Supreme Self.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *ānandamaya* signifies abundance (*prācurya*). // 12 // // 13 // // 14 //

Furthermore, because there is agreement between the mantra and the brāhmaṇa— which stand in the relationship of the goal and the means— the very Brahman is the referent of the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
For in the mantra, the quality of being "innermost" is repeatedly heard with respect to the supreme Brahman in the phrase, "There is another inner Self."
And because that very same [Self] is recognized in the Brāhmaṇa passage, "Another inner Self consists of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5),

the author of the Sūtras declares that the one consisting of bliss is indeed the supreme Brahman: "And it is proclaimed as being exactly that which is described in the words of the mantra" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.15).
The supreme Brahman, which is indeed described by the words of the mantra, is likewise celebrated in the Brāhmaṇa as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). //15//
Furthermore, with reference to that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), there is the scriptural hearing of its being the creator prior to the origination of the body and so forth;
and because of the hearing of the non-difference of those things being created from their creator, who consists of bliss, in the passage "May I be many."
He states that the one consisting of bliss is indeed the Supreme:
"Not the other, because of impossibility" (Sūtra 1.1.16).
The other, the individual soul (jīva), is not the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), because that [interpretation] is untenable. //16//
And because there is a designation of difference:
"For this Self consisting of bliss is the essence, the sap; for having obtained that very sap, he becomes blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).

Thus, this state of being the attainer belongs to the individual self (jīvātman), while the state of being the object attained belongs to that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya); therefore, non-difference is not logically tenable.
Therefore, the status of the Supreme Brahman is established for the individual self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) through its difference [from it].
He raises an objection: "How then? If, having attained [it], there is nothing further to be attained, [how can there be a distinction?].

How, then, is the supreme self attained by means of the individual self, which is in reality non-different from the supreme self? This is the meaning. He provides the answer: "Certainly; nevertheless... [tathāpi].

True; although there is non-difference from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the relationship between the attainer and the object to be attained is established by relying on the difference superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
For the individual soul (*jīva*) is shown to be distinct from the Supreme Brahman due to ignorance, but not distinct from itself.

And likewise, if the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) were the individual soul (*jīva*), then no distinction of the soul from itself even through ignorance would have been shown; thus, the relationship of the attainer and the object attained would not exist.
Furthermore, it has already been stated above that neither difference nor non-difference exists between the individual soul and the supreme Brahman.
It might be argued as follows:

just as the individual soul (*jīvātman*), being non-different from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), does not exist as a distinct seer, so too the Supreme Lord is non-different from the individual soul who is the seer; thus, if the individual soul were indefinable (*anirvācya*), the Supreme Lord would also be indefinable.
And so, because [the world] exists as a reality, he says: "But the Supreme Lord [is different] from that which is imagined through ignorance.
For silver, when superimposed, does not differ from the mother-of-pearl;
indeed, it cannot be defined either as distinct from it or as non-distinct.
The mother-of-pearl, being ultimately real and definable, is indeed distinct from the indefinable silver.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration based on mere similarity: "just as [the illusion] of a magician.
Out of dissatisfaction with that, he provides an illustration of extreme similarity: "or just as [the space] within a jar from [the space] outside."
The remainder has its meaning not hidden [and is thus self-evident]. // 17 // // 18 //
START BsVBh_1,1.7.19 In order to uphold his own position, [the author] refutes the view of the partialist (ekadeśin), stating: "But this must be said here.
First of all, this is the general rule: that from the word "Brahman" in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," [Brahman] is understood.
The pure Brahman, however, is modified [into the form of the self] by virtue of the term "consisting of bliss."

In that case, since the word "tail" (puccha) is used here in coordination with the word "tail," and since it is used in the passages concerning the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth in the sense of a limb,

one might argue that because the word "tail" here also refers to a limb, the word "Brahman" (brahmapada), which is in grammatical apposition with it, must also somehow be explained as referring to a limb by abandoning its primary meaning;

and furthermore, the word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is either a term denoting a modification, as it is read in a series primarily consisting of terms denoting modifications such as "consisting of food."
Alternatively, even if the term "abounding bliss" (ānandavācin) is not commonly used for Brahman,
it may be explained as referring to Brahman through some secondary figurative application;
and by the repetition of the word "bliss," the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) may be indicated, just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is indicated by the word "light" (jyotis).
Furthermore, let the term *ānandamaya* have the sense of a modification (*vikāra*),
and let the term *brahman* remain in its own primary sense as "Brahman," and let the repetition of the word *ānanda* also be in its own primary sense.

Let those of refined intellect understand that this text—which consists primarily of a written enumeration of constituent parts—should be explained as being directed toward the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the mere words of the questions alone.
In this regard: "There would be an abandonment of the context of the majority of readings and a transgression of the three primary [criteria];
in the former position, there is a sublation of the context of the majority of readings."

For the word "tail" (*puccha*) is primary when referring to the tail itself, whereas it is only secondary when referring to a limb consisting of bliss; thus, the transgression of the primary meaning of the word is equal whether one takes it as referring to a limb or as referring to a locus.
Furthermore, the subversion of the impression that it refers to a limb is equal to the subversion of the impression that it refers to a modification (*vikāra*).
Moreover, there is the additional [burden] of transgressing three terms: the word "Brahman," the word "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), and the word "bliss" (*ānanda*).
Therefore, because it violates the three primary [criteria], the former position is less sound;
rather, the latter position alone is appropriate, as it accords with the three primary [criteria].
Furthermore, if the term *ānandamaya* were to have Brahman as its referent, [it would entail the following]:
The statement "Brahman is the tail" is not tenable;
for it is not logical that the same thing should be both the whole and its part.
Furthermore, if the word "tail" were intended to mean a substratum, [it would be inconsistent].
This [interpretation] as "establishment" (pratiṣṭhā) is also more appropriate;
for while the inner nature of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is [explicitly stated] in relation to the sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya),
the inner nature of Brahman is understood by implication from the one consisting of bliss, and thus it was not explicitly stated by the scripture.
Thus, it is appropriate for the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) to possess limbs such as "dear" (*priya*), just like the *annamaya* and the others;

however, regarding the Supreme Brahman— which is beyond the reach of speech and mind— the possession of limbs such as "dear" and the state of abundance [of bliss] are possible only by including limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
They should be explained by means of the affliction (*kleśa*).
And thus, because it is the Brahman mentioned in the Vedic mantra itself that is designated as "Brahman is the tail, the support"— being the primary subject—
its reference is to that [Brahman] alone, not to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
The summary of the meaning is that even such scriptural passages as "He desired" and so forth refer to Brahman and do not refer to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya);
the rest is easy to understand.
As for the aphorisms (sūtras), they should be explained as follows.

In the event of a conflict between the Vedas and the Sūtras, the principle "but when there is no [inferior] quality, the assumption of the improper [is not to be made]" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.34) dictates that the Sūtras must be interpreted otherwise.
By the term *ānandamaya*, the word *brahman* found in the sentence "Brahman is the tail, the support" is indicated.
What is meant is this: in the passage beginning with "consisting of bliss," the word *brahman* in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support" is indeed primary (referring to Brahman itself).
As for the fact that the Śruti says "Brahman is the tail" when it ought to have said "the locus of Brahman," for what reason?

Because of the proximity in the intellect of that very usage following the previous usage where the member was the primary sense; and because even by that [usage], the definition of a locus is established.
And it is proclaimed as being based precisely on the wording of the mantra. //15//
That which was described as Brahman by the Vedic verse beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," etc., is itself proclaimed as the primary subject in the Brāhmaṇa passage, "Brahman is the tail, the support.

For if this [word "Brahman"] were taken in its sense of a mere limb, then there would be a contradiction between the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa— the means and the end— since it would be primary in the mantra but secondary in the Brāhmaṇa.
Not the other, because it is not possible. //16//
In this context, instead of the commentary reading "And for this reason, [the Self] consisting of bliss," one should read "And for this reason, Brahman is the tail, the support.
And because of the designation of difference. //17//

In this context as well, the commentary on the passage "And for this reason, [the Self] consists of bliss" and the commentary on the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) should be read instead as the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support" and the section concerning the tail that is Brahman (*brahmapuccha*).
Furthermore, because of desire, there is no dependence upon inference. (Sūtra 1.1.18)
And in this [state], he teaches his union with that. // 19 //

Thus, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on these two sūtras as well, the reading "Brahman is the tail, the support" (*brahma pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*) should be understood in place of "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

If Brahman were merely a limb—the tail—of the modification consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-vikāra*), how could Brahman be declared to be the cause—the tail—of this entire collection of modifications, including that which consists of bliss, according to the scriptural text: "It created all this, whatever there is"?
For it is not logical that Brahman, being a modification and a part of the *ānandamaya*, should be the cause of everything.

Therefore, it is established that Brahman—as a part of the *ānandamaya* modification—is not intended here as an object of meditation; rather, Brahman itself, as the primary subject, is intended here as the "tail" (*puccha*) to be known. // 19 //
[The Self] is within [the body], because there is instruction regarding its attributes;
and it is distinct [from the body], because of the designation of difference. (BS 1.1.20–21)

In the preceding section, it was determined that the five sheaths exist merely as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) serving as means for the realization of Brahman, in which all distinctions have been discarded; they were not intended [as the primary objects],
whereas Brahman alone— designated as "the tail, the support"— was presented as the principal object to be known.

At present, however, Brahman is introduced as the object of meditation with its intended limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), but it is not determined here that the individual self (*jīvātman*)—which is designated by the term "sun" due to its excellence attained through the preeminence of knowledge and action—is [Brahman]. In this regard, [the text states]: "The boundaries, supports, and forms belong to the transmigrating soul, but not to the Supreme."
Therefore, that sun, which is not subject to worldly action, is to be worshipped.
Because of the hearing of descriptions such as "having a golden beard," and because of the hearing of different loci in the passages, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye."

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement regarding the limits of his sovereignty— namely, "He rules over those worlds that are beyond this one, and over the desires of the gods"— it is the transmigrating self alone, consisting of the aggregate of cause and effect and endowed with form and other qualities, who is to be meditated upon here; and not the Supreme Self, who is devoid of all form according to such scriptural texts as "Soundless, touchless," and who has had any substratum rejected by such texts as "In His own glory."
Furthermore, he whose boundless sovereignty has been understood through such scriptural passages as "He is the Lord of all" is capable of being apprehended here as an object of meditation.
Moreover, the absence of all evil is possible in the Person within the Sun,
because the scripture has human beings as its primary authority, and deities lack the capacity for merit and demerit.

Furthermore, since it is otherwise impossible for [the Self] to possess form and so forth, when the individual soul (jīva), consisting of cause and effect, is intended as the object of meditation, the fact that its being the Self of all is heard in scripture— by virtue of its nature as the Seer (Ṛg) and so on— is somehow merely a praise of the person in the sun; thus, the conclusion reached is that the person in the sun alone is the object of meditation, not the Supreme Self.
And in the case of having no substratum, the reasons are eternality and omnipresence.
For an impermanent effect has a cause as its substratum and thus does not lack a substratum;

likewise, even that which is eternal but not omnipresent stands in a lower position relative to something else, such that it serves as the substratum for that which is above it, and thus does not lack a substratum.
Therefore, both have been stated.
This being the case, it is replied: "Because of the teaching of his attributes within.
Here, [the Lord] is spoken of by virtue of His universal selfhood and His freedom from all evil.
Brahman alone, like any other cause of transformation, is the cause of all things through its two non-deviating [powers].
For by the etymological derivation of the name, its arising is said to be due to the removal of all evil (*sarvapāpman*).

And even though the deity Āditya is not entitled to perform ritual acts, it is not possible for him to be free from all evil, given the possibility of the existence of evil in the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) from previous births. Nor is it correct to say that these [deities] possess only merit from previous births and no evil at all.
Even when there is the manifestation of excellence in knowledge and action, it is possible for evils acquired through the beginningless succession of births to remain dormant;
nor is it correct to claim that the one who identifies with the body of the sun is free from all evil on the basis of the authority of scripture,
since the authority of that scripture is equally established by its having Brahman as its subject matter.
Nor is there an absence of a reason for determination (*vinigamanāhetu*), because the freedom from all evil is repeatedly heard in various places in reference to Brahman alone;
and because that very [Brahman] is recognized here as the existing reason for determination.

Moreover, the state of being the self of all (sārvātmya) is possible only for Brahman, the cause of the world, because the entire collection of effects is non-different from its cause, and Brahman is the cause of the world.
However, the individual self (jīvātman), which identifies with the body of the sun, cannot be the cause of the world;
nor is it appropriate for a passage to be intended as praise through the figurative indication of excellence when the primary meaning is possible.
Furthermore, its possession of form may be due to the manifestation of a body for the sake of bestowing grace upon others.
Or, because the entire collection of effects is a modification of that [Brahman],
and because a modification is not different from that which possesses the modification, it is taught through such a distinction of form, as in: "He is the one who possesses all fragrances."

Furthermore, a scripture that describes a form created by Brahman as an illusion (*māyā*) does not thereby cease to be a scripture; rather, it is precisely by creating that [illusion] that it remains a scripture—thus there is no risk of it being non-scriptural.
However, in cases where Brahman, with all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) eliminated, is presented as the object of knowledge, [it is treated differently].
In this regard, the scripture proceeds: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying.
Therefore, even the possession of form is logically consistent with the Supreme Self.
By this very [argument], the distinctions of spatial limits (*maryādā*) and support (*ādhāra*) are also explained.

Moreover, the transmigrating soul who identifies with the body of the sun is mentioned as distinct from the Inner Controller; yet that very same soul must be recognized here through the similarity of the scriptural term "within" (antar) in the phrase "the one within the sun" (antarāditya).
Therefore, [the verse says]: "Therefore, they are the winners of wealth."

"Those who possess wealth" means those who possess power (*vibhūti*). Why, then, is the possession of power possible only through being accepted by the Supreme Lord? To this he says: "Whatever possesses power...
Even though He is the Self of all, the manifestation of the Supreme Lord's own nature occurs specifically in those things that possess power.
But this does not apply to those whose nature as the Supreme Lord is veiled by the darkness of ignorance, for they lack such manifestation; this is the meaning.
"Even the lordship over the worlds and desires" means that, according to the principle of absolute self-interest, their sovereignty is unrestrained. // 20 // // 21 //
START BsVBh_1,1.8.22:
"The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark" (BBs_1,1.22).

In the preceding section, because of the observation of attributes unique to Brahman, it was established that the meditation intended here belongs to this very [Brahman] as qualified by a particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
However, it has been established that [the reference] is not to the individual self (jīvātman) which identifies with the body of the sun;

rather, it is now being determined that, because of the perception of unique attributes, that very [self] is taught as the object of meditation by being superimposed upon the *udgītha*, and not the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
In this regard, should the passage "He said, 'Space,'" be interpreted in some way in accordance with the primary meaning of space— so that the questions "What is the goal of this world?

and the statements "All these beings," "Greater than the great," and "The ultimate resort" are somehow explained— or rather, should the word "space" be explained as referring figuratively to the Supreme Self in accordance with those [other] passages?
Because it is the ground for all leaves and because it is primary, space alone is indeed our principal [element];
the certainty is that the others are to be explained in accordance with it.
In response to the question, "What is the goal of this world? it is stated, "He said, 'Space (ākāśa),'"; since space is presented as the goal, it possesses primacy.
However, because the passages beginning with "All these indeed... serve as its qualifiers, they are subordinate.
According to the principle that "when there is a subordinate element, there is an assumption of something else," even many subordinate elements must be interpreted in accordance with the primary one.
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage, "He said, 'Ether,'" ether is first understood and is not yet subject to contradiction;

therefore, when that [notion of ether] has colored the intellect, whatever else subsequently occurs within that same single sentence—being of secondary importance and already subject to contradiction—must be established in accordance with that [primary notion].
Nor, because the word "ether" is used figuratively for Brahman in some instances, must it necessarily refer to that [Brahman] everywhere.

In the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" refers to the bank because of semantic inconsistency; however, by this same logic, the word "Gaṅgā" in the expression "the waters are in the Gaṅgā" would also have to refer to the bank.
Yet the possibility [of both meanings] is equal in both cases.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) is not primary even when applied to Brahman.
Because it is improper for a word to have multiple primary meanings,
and because its usage with respect to Brahman can be justified as being figurative;
furthermore, because this term is established in common worldly usage to denote the sky (*nabhas*).
Furthermore, since the comprehension of Vedic meaning is preceded by that [ordinary usage], its reversal is untenable;
and the Commentator himself has interpreted passages such as "All indeed... in accordance with that principle.
Therefore, it is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) alone that is taught here as the object of meditation.
It follows, therefore, that it is not the Supreme Self.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the term "ether" (ākāśa) refers to Brahman.
Why? Because of its characteristic marks (liṅga).

For it is said: "Because of the consideration of the sequence between the question and its answer expressed in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), there is a state of being secondary (gauṇatā) even when [the subject] is primary."
"Even though the word *ākāśa* primarily refers to the Pradhāna, nevertheless, one must answer exactly what was asked.
Indeed, no sane person, when asked about mangoes, would describe jackfruit trees.

Therefore, in this context, since the question, 'What is the goal (*gati*) of this world? concerns the goal of the entire manifest expansion of names and forms as it is perceived, it is in accordance with that [question] that he who is the goal of the entire world is designated by the word *ākāśa*."
One should reply:
"Furthermore, the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) is not the refuge of the entire world,
because it too is included within the world."
For it is untenable that its destination could be that very [elemental ether], because such a thing is logically impossible.
Nor is it correct to say that because the elemental ether is heard of in the subsequent reply, the question itself must have been about the effect of the elemental ether;

for it is illogical to restrict a primary understanding—which concerns the common worldly ether and has not yet encountered any contradiction—by a subsequent reply that does encounter contradiction. Rather, the reply must be explained in conformity with that primary understanding.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that an answer of established meaning cannot be restricted by a question whose subject matter is unstable in the form of a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa); for even though the ignorance, doubt, and error caused by that [question] may be unstable, the answer itself remains established with respect to its own object. Otherwise, the answer would either lack a basis or result in a mismatch of referents (vaiyadhikaraṇya).
Moreover, there are many further inconsistencies in the subsequent passage as well.
For instance, in the statement, "All these beings, indeed, arise from space alone," the word "all" (sarva) would have to be interpreted in some way as having a limited scope.
Likewise, the restrictive particle "eva" (alone) is also inconsistent.
Indeed, water does not have space alone as its cause, but fire as well;
likewise, for food too, space alone is not the cause, but fire and water as well.
However, when there is the intention to speak of the ultimate cause, the restriction [to Brahman alone] is entirely appropriate.
But this is inconsistent with the elemental ether;
thus, the dissolution of all elements occurs in Brahman alone,
and thus Brahman alone is greater than all.
Thus, Brahman alone is the supreme goal.

This is because the inquiry begins with the question, "Of all the worlds," and because in the subsequent portion there is a reference to the unique attributes of Brahman, and because the movement that was asked about is concluded by summarizing the unique attributes of Brahman as "the supreme goal."

For the sake of favoring the majority of the scriptural texts, it would be better for the single term "ether" (ākāśa) to be inconsistent— just as in the maxim "one should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family"—
for by this much, a great deal would be consistent. Moreover, the ether does not hold primacy in what follows.

However, because the answer pertains to what was asked, because the common understanding of the world is what was inquired about, and because the conclusion "the supreme goal" refers back to that very same thing, Brahman alone is the primary subject.
And thus, for that purpose, the word "ether" (ākāśa) has the primary meaning of Brahman, and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the primary subject denoted by the word "ether" here as the object of meditation, and not the elemental ether.
Moreover, at the very beginning of this [section], Śālāvatya is criticized for the fault of finitude with the words, "Your Sāman is indeed finite.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (ākāśa), even if used in a secondary sense, does not entail a delayed comprehension.

In various instances, because the word "ether" (ākāśa) and its synonyms are frequently employed to denote Brahman, even this [word] is understood as primary without delay due to extreme habituation; it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the Commentator has cited Vedic usage to show the frequency of its application to Brahman.
And in that very case, the subsequent [word] is interpreted in accordance with what was first understood, provided it can be so interpreted;
however, where that is not possible, the first [word] is interpreted in accordance with the subsequent [words]. Thus he says: "Even at the beginning of the sentence" (vākyopakrame 'pi). //22//

For this very reason, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). In the *Udgītha* [section], beginning with "The deity that is connected with the *Prastāva*," it is heard: "Which is that deity? "It is the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," said Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa.
In connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, the Commentator has stated that the meditation on the *prastāva* is also [included] under the term *udgītha*.
The *prastāva* is a specific division (*bhakti*) of the Sāman; the deity associated with and following it is Prāṇa.

Here, because the word "Prāṇa" is seen to refer both to Brahman and to the modification of air (the vital breath), a doubt arises: does this word denote Brahman, or does it denote the modification of air?
In this regard, for this very reason—namely, because of the characteristic marks of Brahman—it is logical that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed Brahman itself and not a modification of air.
If this is so, then since the matter has already been settled by that [previous discussion], what is the purpose of commencing a new section?
To this it is replied: "When the meaning is to be known through scripture alone, we must indeed rely upon scripture."
But when [an object] is cognizable through another means of knowledge, its determination occurs by virtue of that [other means].

Regarding either Brahman’s status as the cause of all beings or ether’s status as the cause of the elements such as air, no means of knowledge other than scripture (*āgama*) is capable [of providing proof].
In that regard, by examining the preceding and following passages, only that meaning for which the scripture is consistent is accepted as its intended sense.

If the other [the individual soul] were being abandoned [as the subject], then here, regarding the statement that "at the time of the entry and exit of beings, they enter into breath," there arises a doubt as to whether Brahman is being referred to or a modification of air (vāyu-vikāra). In this context, there is the passage beginning: "When a person sleeps, then speech enters into breath."

By the force of the Śruti— which, by means of demonstrating the entering and emerging of the senses that are the essence of all beings, demonstrates the entering and emerging of all beings, and has obtained its capacity through the support of other means of knowledge— it follows that the entering and emerging belong to the vital breath (prāṇa) which is a modification of air alone,
and not to Brahman.

Moreover, in this context, regarding the two Sāman-chants, the *udgītha* and the *pratihāra*, other deities than Brahman—namely Āditya and food—are mentioned as being of the nature of an aggregate of cause and effect;

by virtue of their association with these, Prāṇa also must be a deity of the very same nature, consisting of an aggregate of cause and effect. Although this point was already refuted in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, [it is raised here again].
This has been restated again to reinforce the reasons for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) mentioned previously.
Therefore, it follows that the meaning of the word "prāṇa" here is simply a modification of air.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "The greater authority of a human statement [is established] through its convergence with other means of knowledge."
In a sentence that is not of human origin, what will its connection with that [human author] accomplish?

Indeed, an impersonal (apauruṣeya) word, whose status as a means of valid cognition is established intrinsically, does not depend on another means of knowledge for the production of the cognition of its own object or for its practical application; for that impersonal word, from which all suspicion of defect has been dispelled, is by itself determinative. It is determinative by itself.
Since the engagement in worldly activity is preceded by certainty,

there can be neither lack of firmness nor firmness regarding that very [object], whether it be with respect to color— as in the case of the eye which does not correspond— or with respect to the substance itself— as in the case of the tactile faculty which does correspond. Therefore, let there be the subsiding and arising of the mere sensory faculties within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of wind.
However, the fact that all beings enter into and emerge from [it] is not understood from that sentence.
Or, if it were so understood, then even there the "prāṇa" would be Brahman itself and not a modification of air—
just as in the sentence, "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone," the word "prāṇa" denotes Brahman.
Furthermore, the dissolution and emergence of all beings within this modification of air are not observed by means of any other instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor can the statement regarding the dissolution and emergence of all beings be explained in any way as referring to the sense organs, on the grounds that the statement about the dissolution and emergence of the senses is strengthened by corroboration established through other instruments of knowledge;
for a statement whose status as a means of valid knowledge is self-evident and inherently firm has no need for other instruments of knowledge.
Nor does this [passage] form a single syntactical unit with that [preceding one];
for it has been stated that if there were a single syntactical unit, even that would have Brahman as its sole subject.
Furthermore, the entering and emerging of the senses can be construed even as a partial restatement (avayutyānuvāda).
It is like saying "he chooses one" or "he chooses two";
however, the meaning of the word *sarva* (all) does not admit of such restriction.
Therefore, one should meditate upon the *prastāva* division as Brahman, which is denoted by the word *prāṇa*.
It is established that this is not seen as a transformation of air; likewise, for the lay practitioner (upāsaka), the attainment of vital breath or the success of ritual action constitutes the fruit,
by virtue of the power of the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa).
The meaning is that proximity is weaker than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
As for another example, it has been refuted by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which explains itself through its own words (*nigada-vyākhyāta*). //23//
