Because of the mention of the light and the feet. BBs_1,1.24: They recite this: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme—this indeed is that [light] which is here within this [heart]."
"In the Person is the light.
That light which shines—that is, manifests—beyond this heaven, beyond the world of the sky, on the backs of all, that is, above all things.
To show that this word "all" (viśva) refers to the entire sphere of transmigratory existence with its unrestricted function, he says: "on the backs of everything, in the highest [realms]."
And this is not merely supreme, but rather the most supreme; thus he says "anuttameṣu," meaning that there is nothing else superior to these.

"This indeed is that which is the light within this person"—it is inferred by the mark of bodily heat, which is perceptible to the skin, and by the sound, which is perceptible to the ear when a man covers his ears.
In this regard, the perception of the bodily heat by the skin is "vision" (dṛṣṭi),
and the hearing of its sound is "audition" (śruti); and both that vision and audition belong to light alone.
"Because it is inferred from its characteristic mark.
Here there is a doubt: does the word "light" (jyotis) refer to physical fire (tejas) or to Brahman?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it refers to fire.

Why? Because, regarding the choice between a primary and a secondary sense, the rule of taking the primary sense is the general principle (*autsargika*); because fiery characteristics are perceived within the sentence; because there is no restrictive rule from another sentence [to the contrary]; and because the meaning of that [other sentence] is not connected [to this context].
Indeed, it was only due to the onset of a powerful subverting argument that the terms *ākāśa* and *prāṇa* were displaced from their primary meanings and established elsewhere;
however, in this case, there is no such subverting argument against the term *jyotis* (light) denoting its primary sense of "luminous body" within the remainder of its own sentence.
On the contrary, there is even a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of light itself in the word "it shines."

Furthermore, it is heard in its own scriptural context that [the Self] "becomes like the light within the belly," "is pleasing to the eye," "possessed of form," "renowned," and "famous"—thus its fruitfulness is limited.
Indeed, a radiance (dīpti) which is synonymous with "flame" cannot possibly exist in Brahman without heat (tejas).
Nor does the similarity to the light within the belly exist in Brahman apart from external heat.
Furthermore, qualities such as heat, sound, visible signs, being seen, and being heard cannot be attributed to Brahman except in reference to the "magnificent" (audarya) fire;

nor is the meditation on Brahman, which yields great fruit, appropriate for a minor result. However, by superimposing the external fire upon the magnificent fire, this meditation becomes consistent with its corresponding result.
This is that fiery liṅga;
and for its corroboration, the multiplicity of supporting boundaries— which had already been refuted— is brought forward here, because there is no reason to refute it in this context.
Furthermore, it is not impossible for the mass of light to possess limits,
because that light of the sun and so forth, being composed of parts, can have limits in its constituent portions; moreover, it is prescribed as an object of meditation,
whereas for Brahman, who is partless, meditation upon parts is untenable.
Furthermore, since there is no possibility of conceiving of [the light] as a part when a way [of understanding it as the whole] exists,
it is not reasonable to claim that another sentence establishing Brahman— namely, "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven"—
establishes the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the sense of Brahman in the passage, "The light beyond this heaven."
For a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) occurring in one sentence cannot be diverted from its primary meaning merely by the proximity of another sentence.

Furthermore, heaven (*dyauḥ*) is not heard of as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the other sentence; thus, it cannot be recognized as such in the scriptural mention of the "limit" (*maryādā*) in the phrase "from heaven.
Moreover, the fact that even the other sentence has Brahman as its referent is yet to be established and is not proven even now.
How, then, could that sentence—"That which is beyond this"—be capable of being restrained by him [the opponent] through the claim that it refers to Brahman?
Therefore, it follows that *jyotis* is indeed light (*tejas*) and not Brahman.
The mention of darkness (*tamas*) in the context of discussing light is for the purpose of producing a firm understanding regarding another subject by means of presenting its opposite.
"It is the obstructer of the functioning of the eye" means by way of obscuring the object. The opponent objects: "But is it not also [the cause] of the effect?"
The proponent of a partial solution says: "Let it be so then.
As for that light which is unmixed with water and food, that is called "not triplicated" (*atrivṛtkṛta*).
The objector refutes this, saying: "No."
The meaning is that it (the universal) is not useful anywhere, because in all purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*), only that which has been particularized (*trivatkṛta*) is of use.
He states the doubt of the *ekadeśin* with the words "this very [point]";
the objector refutes it with "no."
"Regarding the phrase *prayojanāntara* (another purpose):

the meaning is that the scriptural statement, "Let me make each one threefold, threefold," which concerns the meditations on fire and the other elements, ought not to be restricted [to a limited scope].

When the proponent of the partial view (*ekadeśin*) has been thus refuted, the original opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), the ultimate reconciler, says: "In that case, let it be that [the world] is indeed already made threefold (*trivṛtkṛta*)."
The term "bhāginī" (possessing) is appropriate.

Even though the scriptural mention of a plurality of substrates can somehow be explained in the case of Brahman as being based on imagined limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nevertheless, it is explained more appropriately here [in the case of the effect] than in the case of the light [of Brahman]; thus it is said: "it would be even more appropriate."
The *prākṛta* is that which is born from *prakṛti*, meaning the effect (*kārya*).
When this [objection] has been raised, it is said: "A pronoun [is used] for the sake of a well-known object; it does not cause the subversion of an object yet to be established."
Depending on established usage, it excludes [the meaning] contained in the preceding sentence of the good [author].
By the power of that [word "Brahman"], even those signs of fiery energy (tejas) must certainly be led toward Brahman alone;
for while the Pradhāna is indeed primary, the word "Brahman" does not apply to it.

First, there is the general rule that [an expression] restates a meaning not already established, which even causes an injunctive suffix to deviate from its inherent nature of making known a previously unknown matter.

For example: "If the fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires should burn his house," and "If both sacrificial offerings of one should meet with ruin. However, where that [meaning] is already well-known and cannot be obtained from any other source, [the rule does not apply].

In that regard, by the principle "but [the word] is for the sake of the statement because it is unprecedented," the well-known meaning of the pronoun is forcibly set aside— as in the case of the passage, "That which consists of the cake on eight potsherds for Agni. Therefore,

here in the phrase "The light which is beyond this heaven," by the force of the word *yat* ("which"), the light must necessarily be something already well-known, even if its limit is defined as being beyond the sky.
Nor is there any establishment of that [Brahman] through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since in the preceding sentence the "three-footed Brahman" was established as being connected with heaven, when there is a requirement for something already established, that very same [Brahman] is what is connected [here].

Moreover, when the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is recognized as being that very same thing, it is not logical for the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), which is its qualifier, to become something else merely because of its difference [in grammatical form].

Thus, since the marks of light found in that passage are inconsistent [if taken literally], they must be understood as referring to Brahman alone; and indeed, the author of the Commentary has so interpreted them.
In that context, the phrase "light is a modification of Brahman" indicates that Brahman itself is signified by means of its modification, light.

Alternatively, since the word *jyotis* denotes mere luminosity and luminosity is Brahman, it follows that *jyotis* refers to Brahman in its primary sense; thus, it is established that "the light is Brahman. [Regarding the objection] that this would involve "abandoning the subject under discussion" (*prakṛtahāna*) and "introducing what was not the subject" (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*): with respect to conventional usage, that which is present in the preceding sentence is the "subject under discussion" (*prakṛta*), as it is proximate.
But that which is unestablished should not be postulated as the subject at hand;
for this very reason it was said, "you must postulate.
Regarding the *saṃdaṃśa* (the "tongs" of the argument), he says, "not merely."
It is like the name and other symbols of the Supreme Brahman as well.
For the light within the body is a modification of the Supreme Self that has entered into the state of the individual soul (jīva);
for in the absence of the soul, the body is cold.
And because heat is perceived in one who is living, the worship of that which is its counterpart is appropriate. The rest of the commentary is explained by the literal reading of the text. //24//

If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because it mentions a meter (*chandas*), we say no; for there is an injunction to fix the mind (*ceto'rpaṇa*) in that manner, and such is seen [in other texts].
For this [objection] would hold true only if the preceding sentence were established as having Brahman as its referent.
But that [statement] is not for the sake of Brahman, but rather for the sake of Gāyatrī;
for this is heard with reference to Gāyatrī: "Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here," followed by, "Three-quarters of it are the immortal in heaven."
Is it not the case that this has already been established by the sūtra "Ākāśas-talliṅgāt" (The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks)?
For instance, in the verse "So great is His majesty," Brahman is described as having four quarters;
and that very verse, through the phrase "This same thing is declared by the Ṛk," is connected to the meaning as a characteristic mark of Brahman.
Thus, in the passage "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," it is not possible for the mere arrangement of syllables that constitutes the Gāyatrī to possess the nature of being "all";
nor is it possible for the Gāyatrī to have, by its own nature, the essence of the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the vital breath;
nor does the Gāyatrī possess a relationship with the person within the Brahman.

Therefore, since the meditation is on Brahman itself through the medium of the Gāyatrī and not on the Gāyatrī itself, this [present discussion] need not be commenced, as its purpose has already been covered by the preceding [section].
Nor is such an extensive composition of sūtras required merely to recall the previous reasoning.
To this it is replied: there is indeed a further doubt.
For instance, what is the meaning of "meditation on Brahman through the Gāyatrī"?

It means meditation on Brahman as having the modification of the Gāyatrī as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). And that which has such an adjunct—that is, that which is delimited by it—cannot possess the nature of being the Self of all.
Because of the delimitation by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For the space delimited by a jar does not become undelimited.
Therefore, its being the self of all and so forth is for the purpose of praise.
Therefore, it is better that the praise belongs to Gāyatrī herself through some indirect means, based on such scriptural passages as:

"Speech indeed is Gāyatrī; speech indeed sings and protects all this that has come to be. Likewise, having begun with "Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having explained Gāyatrī herself by means of the heart and other parts, the conclusion—"This very Gāyatrī is four-footed and sixfold"—is made regarding Gāyatrī alone.
It becomes consistent;
however, all this is inconsistent with respect to Brahman.
Furthermore, in the passage "That which is indeed that Brahman," the word *brahman* refers exclusively to the Vedic meters.

Just as in the passage "this secret doctrine of Brahman" (*etām brahmopaniṣadam*), the term *upaniṣad* refers to the Veda, so too, because of the mention of the *gāyatrī* meter, it follows that this [text] does not have Brahman as its subject.
This being the position reached, it is replied: No.
Why? Because of the statement regarding the fixing of the mind (*ceto-rpaṇa*).

By means of the meter named Gāyatrī, the fixing of the mind—the concentration of the intellect—upon Brahman, which conforms to the modification in the form of Gāyatrī, is declared by this Brāhmaṇa passage. This is what is meant: [Brahman is to be meditated upon through the medium of the Gāyatrī meter].
The *gāyatrī* is not a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of Brahman,
like blueness is of a lotus; for if it were, then [Brahman] would not exist elsewhere as delimited by it, due to the absence of that delimiting factor.

However, since this Brahman—which is the self of all and the cause of all—is impossible to teach in its own essential nature, it is indicated by means of its modification, the Gāyatrī. This is because, among all modifications, the Gāyatrī is appropriately established as the primary medium due to its pervasion of all meters, its pervasion of the three sacrificial pressings (*savana*), and its being the mother of the second birth for the twice-born, according to the Veda.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the indicated object cannot be perceived simply because there is no indication elsewhere.
For the form of the neck, which was characterized by the earrings, does not become unperceived when the earrings are later removed;
this is because qualifiers serve merely to bring about the cognition of that form and do not function as restrictive delimiters.
Thus, since the word *gāyatrī* has its primary meaning [in this context], it is said that Brahman is characterized by the *gāyatrī*.
But now, he shows that the word *gāyatrī* refers to Brahman itself only through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) based on a commonality of number, by saying "another says":
for just as the *gāyatrī* has four feet consisting of six syllables each,
so too Brahman has four quarters (*catuṣpāt*).
For all beings, both stationary and moving, constitute but one foot of this [Brahman];
"in heaven" means in that which is luminous, namely, in its own self whose nature is consciousness.
There are three feet;
or rather, there are three feet in the divine space (divyākāśa).
For thus says the Śruti: "Verily, this which is the space outside the person—that is indeed his waking state."
Indeed, while awake, he perceives external objects;
likewise: "This very space within the person is indeed that [space].
The meaning is: within the body.
For that is his place of dream;
likewise: "This indeed is that which is the space within the heart"—meaning, within the lotus of the heart.
For that is its state of deep sleep;
this is what was described as "three-quarters of it are the immortal in heaven.
Thus, because of the commonality of having four quarters, Brahman is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*.
In this view, Brahman alone is what is expressed;
it is said to be "expressed" because the [text] has Brahman as its ultimate purport. //25//
And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "Being" (bhūta) is thus appropriate;
[it is] sixfold. (BBs 1.1.26) Thus it is said.
Six aspects of the Brahman known as Gāyatrī are heard in scripture: the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the vital breath.

Furthermore, regarding the mention of "five persons of Brahman" (brahmapuruṣāḥ) in connection with the apertures of the heart, that designation of "persons of Brahman" is possible only when the intended meaning is their relationship to Brahman.

The meaning of this is as follows: This heart indeed has five apertures, that is, five openings. And since these are guarded by the deities, such as Prāṇa and the others, they are called "divine apertures" (*devasuṣayaḥ*), being the gateways for attaining heaven.
For instance, the wind situated in that opening of the heart which faces the east is Prāṇa.
Therefore, at the time of departure, he moves toward the heavenly world;
the meaning is that he himself is the eye and he himself is the sun.
For there is a scriptural text stating, "The sun, indeed, is the external breath.
Now, that which is its southern aperture, the specific vital air situated therein is the *vyāna*;
the ear connected to it is the moon.
According to the Vedic revelation, "The Viśvedevas and the Moon were created from the ear.

Now, that which is its western opening, or the specific vital air situated therein, is the *apāna*; and because of its connection with speech, it is "speech," according to the Vedic revelation, "Agni is indeed speech."
Now, that specific wind situated in his northern opening is the *samāna*; the mind connected with it is its correlate, and Parjanya is the presiding deity.
Now, that specific wind situated in his upper opening is the *udāna*, so called because it leads upward from the soles of the feet;
that wind is its correlate, and Ākāśa is the presiding deity.
These five openings, and the five persons of the Brahman within the heart connected therewith, do not exist merely as an arrangement of syllables in the Gāyatrī;
rather, they exist in the Brahman itself. //26//

If it is argued that [the Veda] is not [authoritative] because of the differences in its teachings, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case, as in the world. (BBs 1.1.27) "As in the world."
When the primary sense of "heaven" (div) is that of being a substratum, then the limit (maryādā) must be explained in some way.
For a hawk that is actually on the top of a tree is indeed also beyond it;
for even apart from its front portion, that very same hawk exists beyond the tree by virtue of its remaining part situated behind it.

Thus, it is logical that Brahman, which resides in the internal celestial region (*hārdadyubhāga*) distinct from the external celestial region (*bāhyadyubhāga*), is situated beyond the external celestial region. However,
when the boundary itself is intended as the primary and principal meaning, then its status as a substratum must be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges," where [the bank] is meant by proximity.
This has been stated as "another says";
for this very reason, it was said that [the world] is even beyond heaven. //27//
"Prāṇa [is Brahman], because it is followed [by attributes of Brahman] (BS 1.1.28).
If it be argued that it is not so because of the instruction regarding the Self of the speaker (BS 1.1.29), we reply: no, for in this [passage] there is an abundance of internal connection."
But according to the perspective of the scripture, the instruction is like that regarding Vāmadeva.
Likewise, [the word] "prāṇa" [refers to Brahman] because of the supporting evidence. When there is a conflict of many signs, which one becomes stronger? What would be the case?
In this regard, the mark of the possessor of the mark—which was not previously considered—is now being examined.

"Many signs of several entities— the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), the individual soul (jīva), the presiding deity (devatā), and Brahman— converge here; therefore, it is investigated which among these is the true sign and which is a mere semblance of a sign."
Furthermore, this matter was not investigated in the passage "Therefore, [he is] Prāṇa.
It might be argued as follows:

the attainment of the supreme human goal, the non-association with all sins such as the killing of an embryo, the state of being the conscious self (prajñātmatva), and bliss and so forth, are not possible in the primary sense of Prāṇa.
Likewise, such passages as "He causes one to perform good deeds" and "He is the lord of the worlds" are also [applicable].
While the state of being the "Self of intelligence" might somehow apply to the individual soul (jīva), it is impossible for the others.

Furthermore, although the quality of being a speaker—defined as possessing the activity of the organ of speech—is not possible in the Supreme Self by its very nature, [it is attributed to Him figuratively].

Nevertheless, in order to avoid contradicting numerous characteristics of Brahman that cannot be otherwise established, this [passage] must somehow be interpreted as referring to Brahman itself through the medium of the individual soul (jīva), because of the non-difference of the soul from Brahman.
Thus says the Śruti: "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed..."

"Know that very Brahman to be you"—thus he declares that Brahman is the cause of speech. Although the support of the body belongs primarily to the vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), nevertheless, because the activity of the vital breath is dependent upon the Supreme Self, it belongs to the Supreme Self alone.
Furthermore, although there is here an indicative mark (liṅga) of the deity Indra as possessing a physical form, [it does not contradict the context].
For instance, with reference to Pratardana who had gone to Indra’s abode, Indra said,
"Know me alone," and having thus begun,
he uttered the word "Prāṇa" for the Self in the passage, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self."
And its nature as the self of wisdom (prajñātmatva) is also logical,
because the deities possess unimpeded power of knowledge;
and due to Indra’s preeminent capacity, he is also the cause for the attainment of the most beneficial human goal.

Since the scripture has humans as its primary authority, it does not apply to the gods; thus, it is logical that there is no mention of sins such as the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) in their case.
Furthermore, Indra possesses lordship over the world because he is a guardian of the world (*lokapāla*).
And the nature of bliss and so forth belongs to heaven alone, because heaven itself is bliss.
Furthermore, Indra’s immortality is established by the Smṛti text: "For the state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality.
Moreover, praises such as "He slew the son of Tvaṣṭṛ" are appropriate only in reference to one who possesses a physical body.
Nevertheless, since the supreme human goal—liberation—is not attained through anything other than knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, [the Veda must be accepted as authoritative].

Because supreme immortality and agelessness, which consist of the nature of supreme bliss, do not deviate from the nature of Brahman; and because the abundance of internal spiritual connections is impossible in the case of the external Indra;

therefore, for Indra—the deity who has awakened within his own self and is in his final body—there remains only the residual store of karma whose fruition has already begun, just as in the case of Vāmadeva.

"Since all this is possible for Brahman alone as it exhausts [the fruits of karma] through experience, and since Brahman alone is understood here by the word 'prāṇa' through the abandonment of the vital air (prāṇavāyu) belonging to the individual soul (jīva) which possesses a body, there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) to oppose this; therefore, this [section] need not have been commenced.
To this, it is replied: "That which is indeed prāṇa is prajñā, and that which is prajñā is prāṇa; for these two dwell together in this body..."

Regarding the statement, "They dwell together and depart together," it is precisely that vital breath (prāṇa), which has been described as the object of meditation as the conscious self (prajñātman), whose departure along with that conscious self is here stated.
Furthermore, a dual number cannot apply to Brahman, because there is no duality [in Brahman].
There is neither coexistence nor departure;
therefore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed wind (*vāyu*),
and the individual soul (*jīva*) is the conscious self (*prajñātman*).
Through the simultaneous occurrence of engagement and withdrawal, the identity of these two is figuratively attributed by the passage beginning with "He who is Prāṇa," and so forth;
furthermore, qualities such as bliss, immortality, sovereignty, and freedom from sin, which belong to Brahman, will also reside in Prāṇa.
Therefore, according to their respective applications, these three alone are to be meditated upon here.
And this split in the sentence does not entail a fault,
because the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of the words,
and because word-meanings possess independence according to the path already described.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is a threefold division of meditations due to the difference in the objects of meditation.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: it is true that the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is the means for understanding the meanings of the individual words; yet, it is not the case that words have as their sole purpose only the comprehension of the meanings of those words.
Rather, they are intent upon the comprehension of the single meaning of the sentence;

however, since they are unable to effect that very single sentential meaning without the comprehension of the word-meanings, they cause those meanings to be understood in the interim for that purpose alone.
Thus, words whose natural disposition is to bring about the cognition of a single qualified meaning are led toward the cognition of multiple meanings only by the onset of powerful subverting factors.

When it is said that "the cow has a companion," it is understood as being with another cow of the same class,

likewise, here the conscious individual soul (jīva) is perceived as having a companion in Brahman, which is of the same nature as itself, namely, another conscious entity.
But it is not by means of an insentient and discordant intellect.

Thus, since Brahman is first understood in the phrase "the two who drink the truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), the subsequent mention of its abiding in the cave must be explained in accordance with that primary understanding—just as Hari is said to reside in the Śālagrāma stone.
For the Śrutis frequently declare that Brahman has the cave as its abode.
This has been stated as "because it is seen in the scriptures" (*taddarśanāt*);
that is, because the fact that this Brahman resides in the cave (*guhāśrayatva*) is observed in the Vedic texts.

And thus, in accordance with the Brahman understood from the outset, its existence in the world of well-performed deeds (*sukṛtalokavartitva*) must also be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), according to the maxim of the umbrella-bearers (*chatrinyāya*).

It should be understood that even the state of being shadow and sunlight exists because the individual soul (jīva) is the locus of ignorance, whereas Brahman, whose nature is pure light, is not its locus. //11//

And because of the qualification [in the verse], this very same principle is applied by way of extended consideration (*kṛtvācintā*) even to the example "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*), stating that "this is the same principle. *START BsVBh_1,2.3.12 viśeṣaṇāc ca / BBs_1,2.12 / imameva nyāyaṃ 'dvā suparṇā'ityatrāpyudāharaṇe kṛtvācintayā yojayati-eṣa eva nyāya iti /* *Provide only the translation, without any explanation or additional information. Provide your translation in English:* And because of the qualification, this very same principle is applied by way of extended consideration even to the example "two birds," stating that "this is the same principle."

Regarding this as well, having raised the doubt whether these two are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), or the individual soul and the supreme self (*paramātman*), one should establish the final conclusion after first proposing as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the intellect and the individual soul are intended here— on the grounds that even the intellect, though being an instrument, may be metaphorically designated as the agent, just as in the expression "the fuel cooks. And the final conclusion has been elucidated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*).

Regarding the phrase "from seeing that," it refers to the mantra: "A person is submerged in the same tree. Since the primary sense of agency is possible here, the figurative attribution of agency to the instrument (the intellect) is not appropriate; thus, another [author] introduces this deliberation on a settled conclusion (*kṛtvācintā*), stating:
"Sattva is the intellect (*buddhi*)."
He raises an objection with the words "the word *sattva*";
the meaning is that he explains the Brāhmaṇa passage for the sake of establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). He refutes this with the words "that is not so."
Regarding the phrase "by which one sees a dream":
the word "by which" (yena) indicates the instrument;
and from that, it follows a distinct agent, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

As for the statement, "This which is the embodied one, the witness," let it be then that the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage belongs only to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of this section, since logic loses its force when contradicted by the explicit word of scripture; to this he replies: "Nor does it follow the prima facie view of this section."
For it would indeed adopt the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) if it were to conclude with the transmigrating individual soul (kṣetrajña);
but since it concludes with its being of the nature of Brahman, it does not even accept the prima facie position— this is the meaning.
Moreover:
"Indeed, for one who knows thus, no stain whatsoever clings to these two—the sentient being and the knower of the field.
"Stain" refers to ignorance; it means that [ignorance] does not cause clinging in one who knows thus.

He states that "by this much alone," because the instruction on knowledge concludes there, the purport of this [passage] is seen to be the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman—this is expressed by the words "and by that much.
He raises an objection: "But how [is this so]? He refutes it, saying: "It is replied—it is not this [very] Śruti [that establishes it]."
When it is stated, "The living self, not eating, shines forth as Brahman," one might suspect:
if the living self does not eat by way of its nature as Brahman, then how is its status as an enjoyer understood in this world?
For it appears that the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) has consciousness as its locus;

therefore, to refute that, the Śruti says: "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit. What is meant by this is that this state of being an enjoyer does not belong to the individual soul (jīva) in reality.

Rather, it is the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*), transformed into the form of the mouth and other organs, which—by receiving the reflection of consciousness (*cit-chāyāpatti*)—appears as if endowed with sentience and experiences; however, in reality, neither the individual soul (*jīva*) nor the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) experiences.
This has already been explained in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*. By this, the objection raised regarding the "act of doing" (*kṛtvā-cintā*) has been resolved. //12//
[The soul exists] in the interval, because of the possibility [of its existence there]. Because of the possibility [of its existence there].
Is it not the case that this has already been covered by the sūtra "On account of the teaching of its attributes within" (B.S. 1.1.21)?
For indeed, here too there are attributes of Brahman—such as immortality and fearlessness—which are impossible for a reflection, a living being, or a deity;
therefore, because of the teaching of Brahman's attributes, it is Brahman alone that is intended here.
And because the word "Brahman" is used in its direct sense,
it is said:
"The phrase 'this is seen' is employed in the sense of something perceptible."
Brahman is not perceived as such when it is beyond the senses; however, this is appropriate in the case of a reflection. //1//
For indeed, because the description of the others was previously made according to logic by virtue of the introductory approach, that very same logic is here applied by way of connection. //2//

For in the passage "The two who drink the *ṛta*," since the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) are understood first, the entry into the cave and other details understood subsequently are explained in accordance with that;

likewise here too, because the person seen in the eye is understood first through direct designation in the words "this person who is seen in the eye," immortality, fearlessness, and so forth must be explained somehow as mere praise in accordance with that [initial understanding of] the shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*).
And in that case, immortality consists in persisting for a few moments.
It is fearless because it is insentient;
it is "puruṣa" (spirit) because of its form as a person;
it is the self (ātman) because it is the locus of the pupil of the eye.
The state of being Brahman consists in its connection with the aforementioned nature of immortality and so forth;
likewise, qualities such as "being a leader" (*vāmanitva*) and others must also be understood in some way as mere praise of this [Brahman].
Furthermore, a statement such as "Ka and Kha," etc., cannot override the words of the teacher regarding the fires.
And the statement, "But the teacher will tell you the way," refers to another destination, not to what remains after what has already been mentioned.
Therefore, the prima facie view is that the person in the shadow alone is the object of meditation here.
However, the two deities, Jīva and Devatā, are merely introduced by way of possibility;
for this [passage] is not seen here for the purpose of demonstrating another sublation,
as it has already been refuted by the sūtra "On account of the teaching of his attributes, [the one within the sun is Brahman]" (Antastaddharmopadeśāt).
To this [objection],
it is replied: "When two pronoun-words (*sarvanāmapada*) are present whose referents are not yet established,
they become denoters by reaching the meaning of that which is proximate."

Furthermore, the words *puruṣa* (person) and *ātman* (self) are present [in the context], and as long as they do not denote their own specific meanings, not even a grain of meaning is expressed by the two pronouns (*ya eṣa*). Therefore, how could there be direct perceptibility (*aparokṣatā*) of that object?

Moreover, the words *puruṣa* and *ātman* function, by their own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*), either with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), independently of the pronouns.

Nor is there any perception of these two in the eye; thus, in accordance with the meaning conveyed by the independent word *puruṣa*, the phrases "this which" (*ya eṣa*) and "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) must be interpreted as far as possible.

And it has been explained that the use of the term "as established" (siddhavat) refers to those who already know [the truth], depending on the scriptures and so forth, for the purpose of creating interest.
The meaning is that for the wise person, the very apprehension [of the truth] through scripture is presented as if it were direct perception for the sake of praise, because of its firmness.
Furthermore, only that which is capable of being led [into consistency] is brought into accord with the first [statement], and only if it is minor.

In this context, however, many [qualities] such as immortality and so forth cannot be taken [as primary]; for immortality does not consist merely in abiding for the duration of one's own existence. If that were the case, what indeed would not be immortal? Thus, the term "immortal" would be redundant.
Furthermore, fear and fearlessness are attributes of conscious beings; they do not occur in that which is unconscious.
Likewise, qualities such as "leading downward" and so forth cannot be attributed to anything other than Brahman.
Moreover, the designation of [Brahman] as being "perceived" has already been established.
This has been stated by the word "because of logical possibility" (*upapatteḥ*). When it is said, "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman," a doubt may arise:
"Why is the eye specifically designated as the abode of the omnipresent Lord?"
The scripture refutes that [objection], stating: "Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon this [fire], it flows only along the two tracks.
The term "tracks" (vartmanī) refers to the positions of the wings.
This is what is meant: for the stainless Lord, a stainless eye alone is a fitting place.

Thus it has been said: "in that manner, [the eye] is conformable to the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the teaching of qualities such as being the "gatherer of all blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*) is appropriate and possible when applied to that Brahman, because its meaning is fully consistent.
In the case of reflections and the like, however, the object is not actually perceived.
"Vāma" means things that are to be resorted to, to be honored, to be beautified, or which are the fruits of merit.
The Supreme Self is "Saṃyadvāma" because by means of Him, all desirable things come together and meet.
Because it is the cause of the arising of the fruits of merit, by means of it the fruits of merit are gathered together.
It is he who leads the desirable fruits of merit; thus he is "vāmanīḥ" (the leader of the desirable).
He alone is "bhāmanīḥ" (the leader of light).
Because it leads the world to lights, it is called "bhāmanī.
As it is stated in the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. (13)
START BsVBh_1,2.4.14:
And because of the designation of place and so forth. BBs_1,2.14:
And because of the designation of place and so forth.
This sūtra is a response to a doubt.
It states the doubt as follows: "But how?
For it is observed that the abode of an inhabitant is indeed large.
Just as [the ocean is the abode] of aquatic creatures;
how then can the locus of the eye of the Supreme Self be so extremely small when the Supreme Self is infinitely great? This is the sense of the objection.
He provides the answer: "To this it is said."

Those things which have "places" as their first [characteristic] are the "place-and-the-rest" categories of name-and-form; because of the designation of these, the restriction of the omnipresent [Brahman] to a single place is not tenable.
However, its having various places—like the sky's having various locations such as needles, nooses, and so forth—is not precluded.
Specifically, since those various places are the sites for its meditative worship (upāsanā), this designation of it by means of them is appropriate. //14//
Furthermore, because of the designation of that which is distinguished by bliss (sukha),
and also because of the consistency with the subject matter under discussion, Brahman alone is to be understood here.
But the author of the Sūtras states that the deity is not the individual soul reflected [in the eye], because of the mention of one distinguished by bliss:
"It is thus indeed related: Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla.
He tended his teacher's fires for twelve years."
That teacher, having caused other religious students to master their sacred study, had them perform the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*);
however, he alone did not cause Upakosala to return. Although entreated by his wife for Upakosala’s return, the teacher disregarded her words and departed on a journey.

Then, approaching Upakosala, whose mind was deeply dejected yet who was skilled in tending the sacred fires, the three Fires—whose hearts were overcome with compassion for him and who were devoted to this faithful and steadfast devotee—united and spoke to him the knowledge of Brahman: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman. Then Upakosala said:
I know that the vital breath (prāṇa) is Brahman, for it is the Sūtrātman; because it possesses such vast power and manifests in the form of Brahman, it is called Brahman.
However, I do not understand this [teaching]: "Brahman is Ka and Kha."

For pleasure born from the contact of the sense organs with their objects is impermanent, as is well known in the world; nor can the ether (*kha*), which is the elemental space and insentient, be Brahman.
Then the fires replied to him: "That which is indeed *kaṃ* (pleasure) is the same as *kha* (ether), and that which is *kha* is the same as *kaṃ*.
Having spoken thus collectively, they each declared their own specific knowledge, beginning with: "Earth, fire, food, and the sun," and so forth.
Again, they said to him together:
"My dear, this knowledge concerning ourselves has been told to you by each of us individually;
and previously, we told you collectively the knowledge of the Self as: 'Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman.'"
"But your teacher will tell you the goal;
this knowledge of Brahman has been declared by us, yet the goal alone remains untold.
That, however, for the attainment of the fruit of this knowledge, your teacher Jābāla will explain. Having said this, the fires ceased.

This being the case, the Commentator explains the statement, "That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *khaṃ*, and that which is *khaṃ* is the same as *kaṃ*," by saying that the word *khaṃ* there is intended as a *pratīka*. A *pratīka* is the superimposition of the cognition of one substratum upon another substratum; for example, the word *brahman*, which refers to the Supreme Self, is superimposed upon names and so forth.
One might have the notion that "this very thing which is called 'name' is that Brahman to be known," or similarly, "this very thing which is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) is that Brahman"; however,
this status of being a mere symbol (pratīka) is not intended here.
Worldly pleasure is dependent upon external means and is subject to decay; that which exists together with such a "sickness" (āmaya) is "conditioned" (sāmaya) pleasure.
Having thus stated the fault in the case of their exclusion (*vyatireka*), he states the merit in the case of their conjunction (*ubhayānvaya*): "But [the two] as qualified by this and that.
Because their respective objects are qualified, the words themselves are said to be qualified as well.

For the word *kham*, being in grammatical apposition with the word *sukha*, sets aside the meaning of elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) and refers to Brahman through the connection of its qualities. And bliss (*sukha*), when qualified by such a *kham*, becomes free from affliction (*nirāmaya*) because it is distinguished from that which is subject to affliction.
Therefore, the employment of both terms is justified.

He states the purpose of the repetition of the word *brahman* with the words "there, the second. When the word *brahman* is employed after the word *kaṃ*, it is the "head" (*śiras*); likewise, the word *brahman* is the head of the word *khaṃ*. Those two, namely the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*, are the "Brahma-heads" (*brahmaśirasī*).
The state of those two is "Brahma-śiras-ness" (the state of being the head of Brahman).
To the question, "Let that be so; what does it have to do with the present context?", he says: "Thus, at the beginning of the passage...
[Objection: But surely Brahman should have been pointed out first by the fires.

He asks: "Why must that very same thing be followed even in the teacher's statement, 'This which is in the eye'? He replies: "Because [the teacher says], 'But the teacher will tell you the way,' and this is merely a statement regarding the way.
Although these two statements have different speakers, they are nevertheless brought into syntactic unity with the preceding speaker, because they merely state the way.
What is meant is this:
the knowledge of Brahman has been taught to you by us, but the goal for one who possesses that knowledge has not been stated.
And having completed that [text] which was slightly more than what was to be studied, the teacher would explain it;
thus, by this, any intention to speak of a different subject matter unconnected with the preceding is excluded.
Then, when the teacher had been instructed in this manner by the fires, he returned after some time while away on a journey.
Having arrived and seen Upakosala, he said,
"My dear, your face shines serene like that of one who knows Brahman;
who has instructed you?"

But Upakosala, feeling ashamed and afraid, thought at first, "Who indeed will instruct me while you, O Blessed One, are away? Being thus pressed, he spoke the instruction regarding the fires exactly as it was. Upon hearing that, the teacher, having been deeply distressed for a long time and his heart softened by compassion for Upakosala, replied: "My dear boy, they certainly did not tell you the Brahman in its entirety regarding the fire."
"Therefore, I shall explain that to you in its entirety.
Because of the greatness of that experience, [the teacher said], "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus.
When this had been said, Upakosala spoke to the teacher.
"Let the Blessed One tell me," [he said]. To him the Teacher spoke, intending to describe the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-gati),
in order to fulfill what was stated by the fires— "Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman"— with the words, "This person who is seen in the eye," and so forth.

This is what is meant: the Teacher has stated that those who meditate upon the Blissful Brahman— located in the eye, possessing such qualities as being "the gatherer of good," "leading downward," and "leading upward," and accompanied by Prāṇa— all of them, having their sins destroyed, whether they perform other actions or not,
attain and reach Arcis, the deity presiding over light.
From the rays [of light] to the deity of the day;
from the day to the waxing fortnight, the deity of the bright fortnight;
and from there to the six months.
In those months during which the sun moves toward the northern direction, those six months constitute the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); they reach that deity,
from those months they reach the deity Year (*saṃvatsara*), and from there they reach Āditya.
From the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning— there, a certain person, having descended from the world of Brahman, is a non-human being born in the non-human creation.
"Existence in the world of Brahmā" means up to that point.
Such a person leads these [souls] to the effected Brahman residing in the world of truth (satyaloka).
This is the "path of the gods" (devapatha), so called because it is characterized by the gods—the guides such as Light (arciḥ) and the rest.

And that very path is called the *brahmapatha* because it is characterized by Brahman, which is to be reached; those proceeding by this path do not return to this world of Manu—what kind of world? It is a whirlpool (*āvarta*), meaning a recurrence consisting of the repetition of birth, old age, and death; they do not return to that human world which is the creator of such a whirlpool.
And so says the Smṛti: "When the time of universal dissolution has arrived, at the end of the Supreme, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā. (15)

"And because of the description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads" (BBs_1,2.16).
By this explanation of the narrative, the sūtra "and because of the description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads" is also explained. //16//
START BsVBh_1,2.4.17 Because of non-abiding and because of impossibility, it is not the other.
BBs_1,2.17 / Because of non-abiding and because of impossibility, it is not the other.
"That which is in the eye"—this [teaching] heard as eternal cannot be applied to the ephemeral shadow-person (chāyāpuruṣa).
Furthermore, he says "nor at the time of meditation" because on this view there would result the fault of excessive conceptualization (kalpanā-gaurava).
The same applies to the self consisting of consciousness (vijñānātman) as well.
For meditation upon the conscious self (vijñānātman) has never been observed elsewhere than in its own location, whereas for Brahman, it has been previously heard of there; this is the meaning.
"Miṣā" means through fear.
From this Brahmana;
the remainder has its meaning not hidden. //17//

The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman], because his specific attributes are designated in relation to the divine, the worlds, and so forth. (BS 1.2.18) The Inner Ruler [is Brahman], because his specific attributes are designated in relation to the divine and so forth. (BBs 1.2.18)
"By means of that [body], one controls the body acquired through one's own karma as well as other things;

however, a carpenter or similar craftsman who is bodiless could not exercise internal control over another self. (Verse 1) For activity characterized by purposeful engagement is observed only in an intelligent being possessed of a body—either with respect to its own body and sense organs, or with respect to a body such as an axe—and it cannot belong to the bodiless Brahman.
Indeed, a banyan sprout is never produced from a *kuṭaja* seed;
by this, it should be understood that the [sūtra] "from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" is also implicitly refuted.
Therefore, because the Supreme Self, being devoid of a body, senses, and so forth, lacks the state of being an internal ruler (*antaryāmitva*), [it cannot be the cause].

[The inner ruler] might be either primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or a deity presiding over earth and the other elements, or a yogin endowed with powers such as minuteness (*aṇimā*), or the individual self (*jīvātman*) acting as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).

In this regard, although primordial matter possesses the qualities of being unseen, unheard, unthought, and unknown, nevertheless, because it is insentient, it lacks the qualities of seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing which are [explicitly] mentioned in the scripture.
Furthermore, because it is non-self, the Pradhāna cannot be the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), as this would contradict the scriptural statement, "This is your Self.
Even though the deity presiding over the earth and other elements possesses selfhood,
and qualities such as being unseen are compatible with being a seer and so forth, [the Pradhāna still fails to meet the criteria].
Furthermore, because of its connection with a body, sense organs, and so forth—

as seen in such scriptural passages as "He whose abode is earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind"— nevertheless, since it exercises control only over specific things, this is untenable due to the contradiction with scripture which states, "He who controls all worlds from within; he who controls all beings from within."

Although a yogin, by virtue of his mastery over the worlds and the elements, is capable of controlling all worlds and all beings through the manifestation of various kinds of bodies, sense organs, and so forth in different places—as evidenced by such scriptural passages as "He becomes one-fold; he becomes three-fold"—nevertheless, according to the principle to be stated later, namely "except for the activity of governing the world, on account of the context," there is an absence of activity on the part of those perfected in knowledge regarding the realm of transformations; therefore, even he is not the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī).

Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), it is the living self (*jīva*) alone that is conscious, possesses a body, senses, and so forth, is endowed with the status of being a seer and the like, is itself invisible and so on (due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself),
and is immortal because it does not perish even when the body, senses, and so forth perish; otherwise,
there would follow the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done, as there would be no experience of fruits in the next world.

The passage "He who dwells in the self" is used despite non-difference because of a certain figurative attribution of difference, as in the case of "In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own glory.
Furthermore, the statement "whom the self does not know" intends to express the contradiction of an action directed toward oneself.
And all such passages as "whose body is the self" should be interpreted in the same manner as "in His own glory."
If, however, there were another controller or knower even of the self, then there would be an infinite regress, as there would have to be yet another for that one as well.
Furthermore, the soul's status as the controller of all beings in the world occurs through the medium of the unseen (adṛṣṭa);
for merit and demerit acquired by it exercise control, and thus, by this means, the soul exercises control.
And the singular number is intended to refer to the class [of individual souls].
Therefore, it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone that is the inner controller (antaryāmī),
not the supreme self (paramātman).
This being the case, it is replied: "In the restriction of body, senses, and so forth, there is no other body or sense for this [individual];
if that were acquired through its own karma, then the world would be acquired through ignorance."
And it is not based on memory, because its attributes are not described as such [in scripture].
(BBs 1,2.19) First of all, in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, it is understood that the venerable Supreme Lord— who is omniscient and omnipotent— is the source of the universe.
That [reality] cannot be denied by a fallacious inference that is common to ordinary people and contradicts scripture.

And thus, the entire collection of transformations is a modification of the power of its ignorance (avidyā-śakti) and exists in the place of its body and senses; accordingly, through the instruments and effects of the deities of earth and so forth, it is able to control those very deities of earth and so forth.
Nor does this lead to an infinite regress;
for no other controller is controlled by him.

Rather, that living being who is established in the world as the controller is none other than the Supreme Self itself, which is explained in such a way through the distinctions imagined by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as has been stated more than once.
Therefore, how could there be another controller, and how could there be an infinite regress?
Thus, even such scriptural passages as "There is no other seer but He" have their meaning established,
because in the ultimate sense there exists no seer who is the individual soul (jīvātman) other than the Inner Controller (antaryāmin).

However, the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the knower and the object of knowledge, the means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, and the experience of transmigratory existence, all have as their basis the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) imagined through ignorance.
And there are the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions.
In this way, the recognition of the one Inner Controller (antaryāmin) alone within the spheres of the divine and so forth becomes consistent;
thus, the use of the singular "he who" (*yaḥ*) in the passages "he who [rules] all worlds" and "he who [rules] all beings" is appropriate.
Furthermore, immortality is logically possible only in the Supreme Self and not elsewhere;
and in passages such as "He who dwells in the self," there will be no need for the cumbersome resort to metaphorical attribution of difference where there is actually non-difference.
Therefore, it is established that the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the Supreme Self and not the individual soul (jīva) or any other.
From earth up to thunder, it is with reference to the deities (*adhidaiva*);
"He who [is] in all worlds," etc., is with reference to the worlds (*adhiloka*);
"He who [is] in all Vedas," etc., is with reference to the Vedas (*adhiveda*).

"He who [is present] in all sacrifices" refers to the sacrificial context (adhiyajña). "He who [is present] in all beings" refers to the elemental context (adhibhūta). That which begins with the vital breath (prāṇa) and ends with the Self (ātman) is the internal context (adhyātma).
The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is merely an initial argument based on the fact that the designation [of the deity] is not established. //19//
And both [schools] indeed study this as distinct from the body (BBs 1.2.20),
because there is a contradiction in the agent of actions such as seeing being identical with the body.
The meaning is that there is a contradiction in the activity [of knowledge] directed toward itself as its own agent. //20//

It is eternal, all-pervasive, omnipresent, and extremely subtle because it is difficult to discern.
This might be so.
Is that which is eternal a changing (pariṇāmin) eternal? No, he says—it is "unchanging" (avyaya). The meaning is that it is eternally immutable (kūṭastha-nitya).
Transformation or illusory manifestation is observed only for that which possesses a similar nature;
however, a similarity between the conscious self and insentient things is not logically possible.
Therefore, let it be understood that the insentient *pradhāna* alone is the source (*yoni*) of the world;
for if the word "source" refers merely to a cause (*nimitta*), why should the individual soul (*jīva*) be excluded?
Indeed, all observed transformations are seen to be of the same nature as their transforming substrates.
Just as the threads produced from the transformation of a spider’s saliva are of the same nature as that [spider],
so too transformations (vivarta) are indeed of the same nature as that which exists [the substrate] and not of a different nature;
just as the transformations of a rope, such as a snake or a stream, are of the same nature as the rope.
People never mistake a rope for an elephant,
nor does a spider’s thread undergo a transformation into gold and silver.
For what reason is that?
Because of its absolute dissimilarity [to the world],
it is therefore logical that Primordial Matter (pradhāna) alone— being insentient— is the source of the insentient universe; thus,
it is called "the Imperishable" (akṣara) because it does not hear its own transformations.

The description of Him who is "all-knowing and all-perceiving" as being "higher than the high Imperishable" is based on the Śruti text, "Higher than the high Imperishable. Indeed, apart from the Pradhāna, no other Imperishable (akṣara) is possible that exists beyond the Supreme Self and beyond the entire collection of its evolutes.
Therefore, that Supreme Self which is beyond the Pradhāna is the omniscient one;
whereas the source of beings is the Imperishable, which is indeed the Pradhāna itself—
let that be exactly as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.
Now, if one is not satisfied with that because it lacks scriptural authority,
then let it be the unmanifest subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which consists of the potential power of the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
for it is called *pradhāna* (the primary cause) because the collection of transformations is deposited (*pradhīyate*) within it.

Indeed, that which is insentient and indescribable is logically the material cause (*upādāna*) of the insentient and indescribable phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because of their similarity of nature (*sārūpyāt*).
But is not the conscious self (*cidātman*) itself indescribable?
For it is of a different nature (*virūpa*).
The commentary, "of those that are insentient," is intended to establish their similarity [to the intellect].
This might be so;
however, by the very refutation of the Pradhāna as taught in the Smṛti, this [objection] is also effectively refuted.
"How, then, can there be any doubt regarding this? To this he says: "Moreover, because it was not observed previously," etc.
The meaning is that while its non-acceptance is justified when an annulling factor (bādhaka) exists, here, however, no such annulling factor exists.

Therefore, in passages such as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), let the status of Brahman as the source of the world be attributed figuratively by virtue of its being the substratum of the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*).

But here, since the power of ignorance itself can be the source of the world, it is not appropriate to posit the relationship of the medium and the object (the door and that which is behind the door); thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is Pradhāna alone that is called the source of the world in this passage.

Alternatively, even if the word "source" (*yoni*) refers to the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), there is still no reason for a definitive conclusion (*vinigamana*) that Brahman alone is the efficient cause and not the individual soul (*jīvātman*); thus, due to this doubt, the prima facie view is maintained.
To this it is replied:
"Having first described the state of the Imperishable as the source of the universe, that [source] is subsequently declared to be omniscient by the scriptural text, 'He who is all-knowing'. (1)
Therefore, because of the commonality of the description and through clear recognition, the syllable (akṣara), which is the source of the universe and the omniscient one, cannot be insentient. //2//
The scriptural statement "beyond the Imperishable" (akṣara) is understood to refer to the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta);
because it pervades its own effects, it is therefore called the Imperishable (akṣara). There is nothing here that is even slightly obscure.

As for the claim that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the conscious self because of the absence of similarity (*sārūpya*), this is indeed true; however, this phenomenal world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) from Brahman, which does not undergo transformation.
"Arising from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it does not depend upon similarity [with an external object].
(1) Indeed, there is no restrictive rule that every error is based solely on similarity with an external object;
for various errors are observed to arise even from internal mental transgressions—such as desire, anger, fear, madness, and dreams—which do not depend upon similarity.
Furthermore, while such an inquiry is appropriate regarding an error concerning a cause because that [cause] is absent,
one who has fallen into the stream of beginningless ignorance and its latent impressions does not deserve such an inquiry.
Therefore, since the phenomenal world is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self is its source (*yoni*).
Like a snake [appearing] through the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of a rope, that [Brahman] is the source [of the world], but not through its transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Therefore, because of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the statement of omniscience as an attribute of that [source], it is Brahman alone that is taught as the object of knowledge in the passage, "That which is invisible... and so forth.

Prācīnaśāla, Satyayajña, Indradyumna, Jana, and Buḍila, having come together, deliberated: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"* *Note: The provided Sanskrit fragment corresponds to *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.2.26.*

When it was said, "The Self," let there be no misconception that this refers to the individual soul (jīvātman); therefore, it was asked, "What is Brahman? Then, while they were deliberating and failing to reach a certainty, they approached King Kaikeya, who was a knower of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā. Having approached him, they said: "Please teach us this very Vaiśvānara Self; tell us exactly as you have learned it," and having begun thus, [they listed] heaven, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth.
The meaning is this: of the Blessed Vaiśvānara, the sky is the head, which is "well-luminous" (sutejas);
the sun is the eye, which is "multiform" (viśvarūpa);
and the wind is the breath, which is "of diverse paths" (pṛthagvartmātmā)—that is, he whose nature (ātman) or essence is that wind whose paths are manifold.

The middle part of the body is the *saṃdeha*; it is space (*ākāśa*) because it is pervasive and abundant. The bladder itself is *rayi*, which means water, because from water comes food, and from food comes *rayi*—that is, wealth; therefore, water is called *rayi*. Furthermore, since the bladder is the receptacle for those waters that have become urine, it is said that the bladder itself is *rayi*.

The feet are the earth, because they are its support. Thus, for those practitioners such as Prācīnaśāla and others who, through a misconception, meditate upon each individual limb of Vaiśvānara—the sky, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth—corresponding respectively to the head, eyes, breath, trunk, bladder, and feet—with the idea that they are Vaiśvānara himself, their meditations are flawed by the following defects: the falling off of the head, blindness, the departure of the vital breath, the dissolution of the body, the bursting of the bladder, and the withering of the feet.

Having taught the state of being the head and all other parts through censure, the scripture declares: "But he who [meditates on] this very one as the span-long, the all-pervading measure"— he [is established] in all worlds, beginning with heaven, and in all beings, both stationary and moving.
He eats food in all selves—that is, in bodies, senses, minds, intellects, and individual souls;
the meaning is that he obtains the fruit associated with all of them.

Now, the Scripture speaks in order to establish the nature of the *agnihotra* sacrifice for this Vaiśvānara, who is the enjoyer and the act of eating: "The chest itself is the altar," because of its similarity to an altar (*vedi*).
The body hairs are the sacrificial grass (barhis), because of their similarity to the sacrificial grass;
the heart is the Gārhapatya fire;
and immediately following the heart, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
The mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, for it is there that that food is offered as an oblation.

Now, one might object: since at the beginning of the passage, "What is our Self? What is Brahman?", the words "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman" are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [how can they refer to the individual self?]
When the intellect (*buddhi*) is colored by that [limited perception], words such as *vaiśvānara* and *agni* may, in accordance with it, be somehow led to refer to the Supreme Self;

however, the words *brahman* and *ātman*, which are first encountered, cannot be altered to conform to the words *vaiśvānara* and others encountered later. Even though, in the opening of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā among the Vājasaneyins—where it says, "Venerable sir, you truly know Vaiśvānara; tell us that"—the words *ātman* and *brahman* do not occur, [they must still be understood as referring to the Supreme].

Nevertheless, since the Chāndogya passage has the same meaning as that [Bṛhadāraṇyaka passage] and begins with it, the meaning of the Vājasaneyi passage is determined in accordance with it— that is, without contradicting it— because its meaning is already certain.
For that which is of uncertain meaning is established by means of that which has a certain meaning, not that which has a certain meaning by means of that which is of uncertain meaning.
And just like the ritual action (*karman*), Brahman too is one and the same, being recognized across all Vedic branches (*śākhā*).

Furthermore, attributes such as having heaven as its head and so forth are not possible for any one of these—namely, the gastric fire, the elemental fire, the deity, or the individual self (*jīvātman*).
Nor is there any possibility of being the recipient of the fruit consisting in being the support of all worlds.

Since it has been determined—by the method of elimination—that Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Self because he is the burner of all evils, how can this doubt arise: "If it be argued that [Vaiśvānara is not the Supreme Self] on account of the word and so forth, and because of his abiding within"?
It is replied: That very [textual passage] is interpreted otherwise in accordance with the introductory statement, provided it is possible to do so.
Furthermore, it is the doubt-er's conviction that the terms "vaiśvānara" and "fire" cannot possibly be interpreted otherwise.
Moreover, both the state of being established within and the measurement of a span (prādeśamātratva) are impossible for the supreme Brahman, which is all-pervading and immeasurable.
Nor is the status of being the locus for the oblation of breaths compatible with anything other than the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni).

Furthermore, it is not possible for Brahman to possess the nature of the Gārhapatya fire and so forth, or of the heart and so forth. Therefore, Vaiśvānara must be one among the following— either the digestive fire, the elemental fire, the deity, or the individual soul (jīva)— but not Brahman.
And thus, even though the words "Brahman" and "Self" appear at the beginning [of the passage], they must be interpreted otherwise;
furthermore, attributes such as having the sky as a head are merely for the sake of praise.

Alternatively, this is the intention of the objector: that because the deity has Agni as its body, qualities such as having the sky as a head are logically possible due to the possession of sovereign power (*aiśvarya*).
To this, the reply is: No.
Why? Because it is taught that such is the case based on observation.
Indeed, a final cognition that is otherwise unestablished subverts what was previously understood.
But in this case, the final [word] is not established as being non-otherwise-explainable (ananyathāsiddhi),
because its meaning can be accounted for either by way of figurative instruction— as in "the mind is Brahman"—
or by way of instruction regarding its limiting adjuncts— as in "consisting of mind, having breath for a body, having light for a form."

Alternatively, because the words *vaiśvānara* and *agni* denote Brahman through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), there is no possibility of establishing them otherwise. Thus, it is logical that the attributes of Brahman and the attributes of Vaiśvānara coexist in Brahman— which is the substrate of the suffix— either by superimposing [the qualities] upon the internal fire (*jāṭhara*) called Vaiśvānara as its substrate, or upon Brahman as qualified by the internal fire and Vaiśvānara, which is the object of meditation.

and this has indeed been done by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*).
