But as for the phrase, "However, he indeed speaks beyond [the ordinary]," by means of the word "however" (tu), the text distinguishes the speaker who speaks beyond from the one who merely perceives the vital breath (prāṇa) while describing his state of speaking beyond through Truth; how then could it intend to denote the plenitude (bhūman) of the vital breath?
To this, it says:
"But [he speaks beyond] the vital breath alone," and thus the state of speaking beyond belongs to the perceiver of the vital breath.
The meaning is that it refers to the state of being one whose speech transcends [the levels] beginning with name and ending with hope.

This is what is intended: this word "but" (*tu*) does not exclude the status of being a "speaker of the vital breath" (*prāṇātivādin*); rather, on the contrary, by drawing that very status along with it, it serves for the sake of realizing that very same True Breath through hearing, reflection, faith, steadfastness, and practice.
"One speaks beyond [the truth] by means of the Truth for the sake of certainty"—this "speaking beyond" is said to be the very vow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the "speaking beyond" that pertains to Name and the rest; one who speaks up to Name and so forth is not a "speaker beyond."
Moreover, it means being one who speaks with truth as his life-breath and who is free from excessive speech.

In this context, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the truth occurs through scripture (*āgama*) and the instruction of the teacher (*ācāryopadeśa*). Then, reflection (*manana*) consists in the application of reasoning that is not in contradiction with scripture.
Having understood this, and having deliberated with his teacher, disciples, and fellow students—all of whom are free from malice—he places his faith in the truth.
Immediately following that faith, perceiving other objects [of worldly experience] and becoming dispassionate, he turns away from them and practices the cultivation of the knowledge of reality;
this is his action, his effort (*prayatna*).
Now, when there is steadfastness in the practice of the knowledge of reality, immediately thereafter the direct experience of the realization of reality manifests;
this is the external [means].

Some have said: "The knowledge of the yogi arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the meditation on the real object (*bhūtārtha*). This means that the culmination—the final stage—of the intensification of meditation gives rise to the direct experience of reality (*tattva*). Thus, when it is argued that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the "Full" (*bhūman*), the following is stated: after saying, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth (*satya*)," the "Full" is then described. In this context, the word *satya* has a conventional usage established in the sense of the supreme reality (*paramārtha*); thus, through the scripture (*śruti*), it denotes the supreme reality.
And the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For everything else, being a product of transformation (*vikāra*), is unreal; it is called "true" only in some respect and in a certain sense.
Thus, the Śruti declares the status of Brahman as the "supreme speaker" (*ativādī*) independently of anything else: "But he indeed speaks supremely who speaks supremely by means of Truth."

How can that which has been understood as being stronger than the indicative mark (liṅga) and the rest be explained in any way as referring to the vital breath (prāṇa) merely on the basis of proximity— a factor far weaker than direct statement (śruti) and the others?
And thus, since the "Fullness" (bhūman) is understood to be Brahman, which is superior to the vital breath, it cannot possibly have the vital breath as its object.
But [it refers] only to the True Supreme Self.

Thus, Sanatkumāra— possessing the intention, "In response to the question of Nārada, who does not know the Self and desires to know the Self, I shall explain to him the Supreme Self alone"— proceeded by the method of ascending a staircase, beginning from the gross and teaching each successive stage, because the Infinite (bhūman) is exceedingly difficult to comprehend.
He explained this most subtle point:

that there is no rule requiring every answer—even one occurring in the flow of a discussion—to be preceded by a question; this has been demonstrated by the easily understood commentary beginning with those words.
The succession of means for [attaining] consciousness and so forth consists of reflection, faith, and the like.
Furthermore, since the section concludes with the instruction regarding the end of life by that much alone, the dependence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on anything else would not be stated.
For if that were mentioned, the section would not conclude due to the resulting state of expectancy.
Therefore, this is not a section concerning the vital breath itself, but rather concerning that upon which the vital breath depends.

And since "that Self" refers to the Self itself, it is the very context [of the Self]. He raises an objection: "at the end of the context," meaning at the conclusion of the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
He refutes this, saying: "No, that is the Blessed One.
For, according to the logic of the tongs, this entire section concerns the *bhūman*.
If that plenitude were breath, this would be a section concerning breath;
and that has been declared to be incorrect. //8//
The author of the Sūtras states that the identity of the Supreme Self with the Ground is established not only by scripture, but also by an inferential mark (liṅga): "Na kevalam... and so forth.
And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine (dharmopapatti).
Having restated that which was somehow interpreted by the opponent, the author of the Bhāṣya refutes it with the words: "As for that [self] in the state of deep sleep...
In the state of deep sleep, there is indeed the self alone, as it is no longer in contact with the sense organs and so forth.
It is not the vital breath (prāṇa),
because the context concerns the Supreme Self;
everything else is subject to suffering.
The meaning is "perishable. The rest is clear in its sense. //9//
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether. (BS 1.3.10) The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether. (BBs 1.3.10)
The word *akṣara* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "phonemes" (*varṇa*) by virtue of its conventional usage as a whole;

however, it is etymologically derived (*yaugika*) in the sense of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by virtue of its constituent parts. Since conventional usage as a whole is stronger than etymological derivation from its parts, the phonemes alone are the *akṣara*.
Nor is it untenable for space to be woven across and through the phonemes,
because everything that has a form consists essentially of name;
for every object possessing form is experienced as permeated by name.
"‘This is a cow,’ ‘This is a tree’— and because [the word] is a means [to cognition], there is no possibility of its being mixed with that [object].
For the cognition of fire which has smoke as its means does not apprehend fire as mixed with smoke, such that one thinks, ‘This smoke is fire.’"
However, there is a cognition of the form [of an object] distinct from its name, such as "fire from smoke" through a difference of substratum (vaiyadhikaraṇya), or "this is Ḍittha. Furthermore,
even in the case of a cognition of form produced by a mark (liṅga) or a sense organ, which does not depend on words, a confusion with a name is observed.

Therefore, the elements beginning with earth and ending with space are not distinct from name; they are measured by name and pierced by it, and names themselves consist of the syllable *oṃ*, because they are pervaded by it.
As the Śruti declares: "Just as all leaves are perforated by a stalk, so all speech is pervaded by the syllable *oṃ*."

Therefore, since the elements beginning with earth and ending with space consist of the syllable *oṃ*, it follows that the syllables themselves are the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*), and not the Supreme Self.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the Imperishable is indeed the Supreme Self alone, and not the syllables.
Why?
Because of the support of everything up to the ends of space (*ambarāntadhṛti*).
Indeed, the elements such as earth and so forth are not capable of supporting even the ends of space.
But it is the Supreme Self alone [that is the cause],
because they are modifications of the Supreme Self;
nor is it logical that the form (rūpadheya) should consist of mere names (nāmadheya).
Due to the difference in intrinsic nature, the difference in means, and the difference in purposeful action.

For instance, names—which consist of the universal *śabdatva* (soundness), are perceivable by the auditory organ, and perform the causal functions of denotation and cognition—are experienced [as distinct].

However, physical objects (*rūpadheya*) such as jars and cloths—which consist of the universals *ghaṭatva* (jarhood) and *paṭatva* (clothhood), are not perceivable by the visual organ and other senses, and perform causal functions such as holding honey or providing clothing—are experienced as distinct [from names].
Thus, how could there be a confusion of name and object?
Nor is there a cognition of verbal co-referentiality such as "this is Ḍittha";

for indeed, there is no experience that "this physical body is of the nature of the word," but rather the meaning is: "that body which was encountered across various places and times is this very one present here and now."

However, a name (*saṃjñā*) is remembered as something directed toward the individual object (*piṇḍa*) due to extreme habituation once the relationship has been grasped; it arises through the occurrence of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
As they have said: "In that case, the remembrance of the name does not have any other cause;
for it is the individual object itself, when perceived, that is capable of causing the name to be remembered. (Verse 1)
"For even when a name is being recollected, it does not subvert the perceptual nature [of the object];
for that name stands apart from the named thing and is incapable of obscuring its form.

Furthermore, there is no worldly recognition of the term "syllable" (akṣara) or "word" (pada) as referring to a non-worldly entity called *sphoṭa* that is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*). Nor will it be demonstrated later that this [theory] is authoritative; indeed, we have already explained this in our *Tattvabindu*.

Therefore, since it is impossible for letters— which are perceivable by the ear— to support everything up to the sky, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is the Imperishable (akṣara), by means of the etymological derivation of its parts (avayava-prasiddhi) which overrides the conventional meaning of the whole (samudāya-prasiddhi).

As for those who, having proposed *pradhāna* as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), establish with this Sūtra that the Supreme Self alone is the Imperishable, they must explain how *pradhāna* is refuted by the phrase "because of supporting everything up to the sky."
Now, if it is argued that "support" (dhṛti) does not consist merely in being a locus, but rather in being the locus of governance (*praśāsanādhikaraṇatā*),
as the scripture states: "O Gārgī, by the governance of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon stand held apart"— even so,
the phrase "because of the support of everything up to the sky" would be redundant.
This much must be stated: "The syllable (akṣara) because of its imperishability. For by this much alone, the refutation of Pradhāna is established.
Therefore, the meaning of this [sūtra] is precisely the refutation of the status of the letters as being the syllable.

Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of doubt regarding the letters (varṇas) because prohibitions such as "not gross" (*asthūlam*) would be untenable if grossness and so forth were never applicable to them;

for prohibitions do not necessarily presuppose prior application, since we observe that even in cases where something is not applicable, there exist restatements of what is eternally established (*nityānuvāda*).
Just as the statement "neither in the intermediate space nor in heaven" is a restatement (anuvāda) of the prohibition against piling the fire-altar, so too is this [objection] trivial. //10//
And that [direction] is from the command;
and that is from the command.
The meaning is that governance (*praśāsana*) is a command, which is a property of a conscious being; it cannot possibly belong to the unconscious *pradhāna* or to the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, when the primary sense of a word is possible, it is not appropriate to resort to a figurative sense—as in the expression "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*). This is the intended point. //11//
And because of the exclusion of other states.
And because of the exclusion of other states.

The scripture—beginning with "That, indeed, O Gārgī, is this Imperishable"—completely excludes the state of being anything else (anyabhāva) from that Imperishable Lord who supports the ends of heaven; that is to say, it excludes any other entity such as the phonemes, the Pradhāna, or the Unmanifest.
By this very Sūtra, the status of being the Imperishable is also denied to the individual soul (jīva); therefore, he says "likewise" (tathā).
For by the scripture beginning with "not other" (nānyat), the difference of the Self is prohibited;

thus, the meaning is that the individual souls (jīvas), though appearing distinct due to the difference of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), are shown to be prohibited [as such] because of the declaration of non-difference.
For this reason as well, he says "without eyes" (acakṣuṣkam) to show that the term "Imperishable" (akṣara) does not refer to the embodied soul (śārīra).
The meaning is that the Śruti, by negating the adjuncts such as the eye for the Imperishable (akṣara), denies the imperishability of the individual soul (jīva) which is conditioned by those adjuncts.

Therefore, since it is impossible for the syllables, the primary unmanifest (avyākṛta), or the individual soul to be [the subject], and because it is possible for the Supreme Self (paramātman), [it is the Supreme Self].
It is thus established that the Supreme Self alone is the Imperishable. //12//

Because of the designation of [Him] as the object of the act of seeing, He [is the Self]. BBs_1,3.13:
Because of the designation of [Him] as the object of the act of seeing, He [is the Self].

Because the fruit of vision and meditation consists in attaining the world of the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahma*), it is understood that the lower Brahman is the object of meditation due to this difference in purpose.

Because of the Vedic scripture, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," when there is knowledge of the all-pervading Supreme Brahman and the attainment of its state, the attainment of a specific location—as in the text, "He is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman"—is not logically tenable;
therefore, it is only the lower Brahman that is enjoined here as the object of meditation.
Nor can it be argued that because the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) is well-known in the world as having reality for its object, it must refer to the Supreme Brahman alone.
And because meditation (*dhyāyati*) has the same object as that [knowledge],
it is correct to say that meditation has the Supreme Brahman as its object;
however, this is not so, because the identity of their objects is unestablished.
For the Supreme Person is the object of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while that which is even higher than the Supreme is the object of direct vision (*darśana*).
Furthermore, not every form of vision has reality (*tattva*) as its sole object.
For that [seeing] is observed even with respect to an unreal object;
nor is it correct to say that "seeing" is merely "reflection," since that [reflection] has only reality as its object.

Because reflection (*manana*) is taught as distinct from that [hearing] in various places; and because reflection, which is synonymous with reasoning (*tarka*), does not necessarily have reality (*tattva*) as its object, as they say: "Reasoning is unstable" (*tarko 'pratiṣṭhaḥ*).
Therefore, it follows that here the non-supreme Brahman alone is to be meditated upon, and its supremacy is relative to the body.
This being the position reached, it is said: "Between the two acts of seeing and meditating, which stand in the relation of cause and effect," [there is a single agent].
The object [of inference] generally has reality as its domain, just as is seen in the case of perception.
For the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
And direct realization generally has reality as its object;
however, when an obstructing factor intervenes, it may have a superimposed object as its domain.
Furthermore, when there is no denial of the general rule, it is not possible to abandon that general rule.
Thus, because this [knowledge] has reality as its object, its cause—meditation—likewise has reality as its object.
Moreover, since it is possible for the sentence to form a single syntactical unit with the supplementary portion, a split in the sentence is not appropriate.

Furthermore, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is established through the recognition of the same referent as having the Supreme Person (*parapuruṣa*) as its object, as well as through the co-occurrence of the terms.

In accordance with this, in the phrase "higher than the high" (*parātpara*), the word "than the high" (*parāt*) should be understood as referring to the "mass of individual souls" (*jīvaghana*). Therefore, the Supreme Person is both the object of meditation and the object of vision.
This has been stated: "And here, by the term *jīvaghana*, the Supreme Person who is the subject of meditation is not being referred to;

rather, it is said that the *jīvaghana*—the individual soul (*jīva*) which, under the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), has fallen into a state of fragmentation (*khilyabhāva*)—is mentioned in order to speak of that which is beyond the *jīvaghana*, that which is to be meditated upon and seen."
The "mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*) mentioned in the immediately following passage, "He is led by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman," refers to the world of Brahman itself.

For that world is the "mass of living beings" in the sense that it is the abode of the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha—the *sūtrātman*, who is the self of all the organs—and thus it constitutes a collection of individual souls (*jīvas*) surrounded by their instruments.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman alone, which has the three-measured *Oṃ* as its locus, is to be meditated upon.
For this very reason, the attainment of a specific location is its fruit because it possesses limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
and liberation occurs through the gradual arising of right vision (samyagdarśana).
As for the scriptural statement, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," that refers to the knowledge of Brahman devoid of limiting adjuncts.
Furthermore, it should be understood that Brahman alone is to be meditated upon as the abode of each individual syllable. //13//
The small one [is Brahman] because of the subsequent [passages]. The small one [is Brahman] because of the subsequent [passages].

Now, as for this small, subtle, cave-like dwelling in the form of a lotus within this city of Brahman— the small space (ākāśa) that is inside it, that which is within that is what must be sought; [this seeking consists of] hearing (śravaṇa) through scripture and the instruction of the teacher,
and reflection (manana) by means of reasoning not inconsistent with them.
The investigation of that [object] is the process;

and through the ripening of the practice of meditation—cultivated with respect, continuity, and over a long period of time preceded by that investigation—there arises direct realization, which is "knowledge.
For that knowledge is indeed superior to the previous ones.
The desire for that is the wish to know it.
Regarding this, he states a doubt with the word "therein.
Therein, first of all, the doubt is as follows: is there something other than the small ether (daharākāśa) that is to be sought and desired to be known, or is it the small ether itself?

Even when the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is to be sought, one asks "Why? to inquire about the cause of doubt: whether it is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), or the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), or the supreme self (*paramātman*). He states the reason for that [doubt]: "On account of the two words *ākāśa* and *brahmapura*."

In this regard, first of all, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) proposes that the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) itself is the "small" one, on the grounds that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether. However, because this position contradicts the majority of the subsequent context, the opponent—dissatisfied with such a trivial prima facie argument—adopts another alternative: "Or rather, it follows that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the small one";
the meaning is that this is the logical conclusion.

In this regard, it is appropriate that the body is the city of the individual soul (jīva) because of its being a locus of inherence and because of its particularity; however, it is not appropriate for Brahman, due to the absence of these two reasons.
For designations are made by way of what is unique [to a thing].

For example, although a sprout is produced from the convergence of a collection of conditions such as earth, water, wind, and seed, it is designated by means of the rice seed as a "rice sprout," but not by means of the earth and so forth.
Because those [causes] are common even to other effects;
therefore, here, although this body is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, it should not be designated as Brahman,
because Brahman, as the cause of all modifications, is too common [to such a designation].
It is logical that this [body] is designated by the term "living being" (jīva) because it is acquired through the merit and demerit of the living being, as it is its specific cause.
Furthermore, in the expression "the city of Brahman" (brahmapura), the locative case is used to denote a locus; therefore, it must be connected with this [living being] which is contained within it.

Furthermore, for Brahman, which is established in its own majesty and is incapable of having anything added to it, a connection with a substratum is not conceivable. The individual soul (jīva), however, being the size of the tip of an awl, is something that can be supported.

Therefore, the word "Brahman" must be explained—either etymologically (*yaugika*) as that which nourishes (*bṛṃhaṇa*) the body and so forth, or figuratively (*bhākta*)—with reference to the individual soul, rather than by abandoning its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
And consciousness is devotion;
the distinction lies in the presence or absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Expressibility is [the state of being] what is directly denoted, while suggestibility is [the state of being] what is implied.
This might be so: let the body be the city of the individual soul (jīva),
but the state of being within the small lotus (puṇḍarīka) will belong to something else.
Because it is as if in the city of Ujjayinī belonging to Vatsarāja, [the term] "friend" (mitra) is understood; therefore, he says: "there, of the lord of the city.

This is the meaning: a house is indeed a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for which no substratum (*ādheya*) has been specified. When there is a requirement for a specific substratum, since the "lord of the city" is the subject under discussion, the [house], being connected with that very substratum, does not require another and does not imply a connection with any other substratum.

[Objection: Even so, the body itself is its locus of experience; what then is the distinction of the heart-lotus such that it alone is its seat of consciousness? To this he says: "And the individual soul (jīva) has the mind as its limiting adjunct. [Objection: But since the mind, due to its mobility, dwells throughout the entire body in succession, how can it be restricted? To this he says: "And the mind [is in the heart] for the most part. Furthermore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) is applied figuratively to the individual soul based on common characteristics such as formlessness and so forth.
Or, let this word "ether" (ākāśa) refer to the elemental ether itself, as in the passage, "This small ether within it";
even so, there is no fault, for he says: "And here, it is not the small ether that is to be sought.
This being the position reached, it is replied: First of all, the elemental ether cannot possess smallness.
"‘As far as this space extends, so far is this space within the heart’—this contradicts the intended analogy.

For indeed: ‘The status of one thing as the object of comparison to another [is seen] like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa; it is only through necessity that a distinction is superimposed, for when a [direct] correspondence exists, such [superimposition] is not appropriate.’"
However, there is a way to understand the comparison of the small ether (*daharākāśa*) with the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) by virtue of its being Brahman;
for that which is of unlimited dimension cannot become limited,
since if it were so, limitation would be logically impossible.
In this context, it is not being enjoined that Brahman has the same measure as the elemental ether,

which would contradict the scriptural statement, "Greater than the ether. Rather, by means of the comparison with the elemental ether, the smallness [of the heart] resulting from the limiting adjunct of the lotus is set aside.
Moreover, all the subsequent reasons serve to exclude the possibility that the small ether is the elemental ether; thus he says: "And not a distinction imagined [by the intellect].
Nor is the small ether the individual soul (jīva); thus he says: "Even though the word 'Self' [is used].
"The body is accepted as the locus of perception for Brahman."
Therefore, by virtue of its uniqueness, the body becomes the city of Brahman.

For since Brahman is perceived within the body, the body is designated as the "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*) by virtue of this unique relationship, and not because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman;
thus, the meaning of the word "Brahman" remains primary (*mukhya*).

Or, let the city of Brahman be the city of the individual soul; nevertheless, just as Maitra’s residence is in the city of Ujjayinī, the king of the Vatsas, so too will the lotus of the heart be the abode of Brahman within the city of the soul.
Because Brahman is determined by the subsequent marks of Brahman;

for it is only when there exists a stronger subverting authority regarding Brahman and a supporting authority regarding the individual soul (jīva) that the marks of Brahman are somehow explained as applying to the jīva with the intention of expressing non-difference.
But here, there is no subverting authority regarding Brahman.
There is no evidence for the existence of a living soul [in that context].
Furthermore, the designation "city of Brahman" has been justified as being the place for the perception of Brahman,
and its having a small abode has also been stated.

Therefore, since it is possible [to interpret them] as referring to Brahman, it is not appropriate to explain its characteristics as belonging to that which is not Brahman; thus, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is indeed Brahman, and not the individual soul (jīva) or the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
Having understood through hearing and reflection, and having realized Brahman, their "wandering" (caraṇa) consists in wandering among their desires—this is the meaning.
It might be argued: "If it were established that the small ether is to be sought after, then an inquiry into it would be appropriate; however, it is not something to be sought after."
Furthermore, he restates what was said—that there must be something else entirely which serves as the substratum for that—by saying, "As for this [which you say]...
He refutes this restatement by saying, "To this we reply...
If some other thing distinct from space were to be accepted as its substratum, then that very thing should have been explained above.
The meaning is: "But what is the use of explaining space? He raises an objection: "Is this not also [the case]?
Even the mention of space is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the existence of the objects contained within it.
Now, [the opponent asks]: "Why does it not simply have space as its ultimate? To this, he says: "And if they should say...

For when the Teacher had taught, "The space within this is small; that which is within it is what must be sought, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand," the student objected: "What is there in this that must be sought?"
The lotus is already extremely subtle; the space enclosed within it is even more subtle. Within that most subtle space, what else could there be?
The meaning is that it does not exist at all.
Therefore, what is there to be sought?
When this objection has been concluded, the Teacher’s speech—beginning with the analogy of space—provides the opportunity for a resolution: "Both heaven and earth are contained within this."
Therefore, the meaning is that heaven and earth alone, which rest upon the space enclosed by the lotus, are taught as the objects to be sought, not the space itself.
He refutes this: "It is not so."
"Indeed it is so.
This might be the case; it is exactly so.
Indeed, it is not merely the admissions [of the opponent] that are urged as defects; therefore, he says: "In that regard, there is a remainder of the sentence" (*tatra vākyaśeṣaḥ*).
For the remainder of the sentence declares that the knowledge of the Self as the small ether (*daharākāśa*) possesses a fruit;
and whatever possesses a fruit is enjoined as something to be performed.
And because it is said, "Whatever is to be done, that he desires," and "That is to be sought after, that indeed is to be desired to be known," this refers to the small ether (daharākāśa).
This might be argued:
"The heaven and earth themselves will be the two selves."
The Self will be indicated by those two alone, just as in the case of the word "ether" (ākāśa).
Therefore, since those two themselves are referred to as having ether as their substratum, he says: "In this, desires are contained—that is, established."
"This Self is free from evil"—
by this [phrase], having drawn back the ether (ākāśa) which is the subject under discussion and the substratum for the support of heaven, earth, and so forth,
[the text implies] that it is so even though separated by the designation of "heaven and earth"; this is the remainder [of the sense].

One might object: "Is this not the fruit of the knowledge of the one whose desires are true (satyakāma), because it is mentioned immediately after that, and not the fruit of the realization of the small ether (daharākāśa)? To this he says: "By the word 'and' (ca), which has the sense of conjunction."

The collective sense is that because the words "in this" (*asmin*) and "this" (*eṣaḥ*) are in the singular number, they cannot refer to the two, heaven and earth; therefore, it is the small ether (*daharākāśa*) alone that must be referred to.

By this sequence, it is stated that in the phrase "that which is within it" (*tasminyadantaḥ*), the word "that" (*tat*) bypasses even the immediately preceding ether and refers to the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*). The meaning is: "That which is the ether within that lotus of the heart—that is what is to be sought. //14//
[The self exists] because of movement and because of the word [denoting it]; for thus is the mark observed. Because of movement and because of the word; for thus is the mark observed.

This is an elaboration on the phrase "from those who are superior. Having introduced this very same small ether (*daharākāśa*), [the text says]: "Alas! What a tragedy this is for living beings who lack the realization of reality—that although Brahman is within their own grasp, it is not attained by them.
This is just as when pieces of gold, long since buried under thick, firmly settled impurities, have fallen upon the road, yet remain [unrecognized] right above them.

Even though travelers passing by, seeking wealth, do not pick up these [pebbles] because they mistake them for a heap of stones, that [river], as if possessing the intention [to express this], proceeds with a sense of wonder and sorrow, having heard: "All these creatures go to this world of Brahman day after day, yet they do not find it."

For at the time of sleep, this entire world of living beings— both the wise and the ignorant— having reached the world of Brahman known as the small ether (daharākāśa) which resides within the lotus of the heart, does not know, "I have become Brahman," because their vision is veiled by the cataract of beginningless ignorance.
Thus, both the term "world of Brahman" and the description of reaching it refer daily to the very fact that the small ether of the individual soul attains the state of being the world of Brahman.

The author of the Bhāṣya states this: "For this reason also, the Supreme Lord alone is the one within the small [space], because [the qualities described] belong to the remainder of the passage concerning the small [space].
By this, the two terms "movement" (gati) and "word" (śabda) have been explained.
He explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "for it is seen thus" (tathā hi dṛṣṭam) as follows: "For it is seen thus, that day after day [the movement] of living beings..."
This is seen both in the Veda and in the world;
although there is no other worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the state of being Brahman in deep sleep,
nevertheless, this is stated in order to establish the very well-known Vedic tradition.
"This is indeed such a well-known Vedic usage that it is even sung in the world.
The construction is as follows: "Just as in another Śruti passage and just as in the world, so too here the word *brahmaloka* [is used].

He introduces the explanation of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "And because of the indicative mark" (*liṅgaṃ ca*) by way of an objection: "But [does it not also refer to] the world of the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā)?"
He refutes [the objection] by saying, "if [it means] 'to the world of Brahman'.
In this regard, it is already established that, according to the principle of the *niṣādasthapati*, a *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound;
nevertheless, here the author of the Sūtras has also stated an additional indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the purpose of establishing the *karmadhāraya* compound by rejecting the genitive compound.

For instance, the very mention of attaining the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) every day—which is well-known in both worldly usage and the Vedas—is the *liṅga* (indicative mark). Since this [attainment] is impossible for any other than the world of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), it excludes the suspicion of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) and remains fixed upon the attainment of the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) itself.
Now, the small ether is not the world of Brahman; rather, that [ether] is Brahman itself. Thus, the *karmadhāraya* compound—"that which is Brahman and is the world"—is established.
It is called "loka" because it is seen (*lokyate*). Indeed, this [Self] is seen when situated within the heart-lotus (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*).

When that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) residing in the lotus is purified—by which means the other organs have been withdrawn by the yogis—the consciousness, whose nature is the light of pure intelligence, becomes exceedingly clear, like the reflection of the moon in stainless water.
Brahmā is beheld. //15//
And because this greatness of its support is perceived in this [earth].
And because this greatness of its support is perceived in this [earth].
The word *dhṛti* in the Sūtra expresses a state of being;
and the one who possesses this support (*dhṛti*) is none other than the Supreme Lord, the small ether (*daharākāśa*).
Why? Because this greatness characterized by supporting is found in this very Lord in other scriptural passages.
The commentary on this is an explanation by means of synonyms. //16//
And because of common renown. And because of common renown.

Furthermore, this application of the word "ether" (ākāśa) to Brahman—based on its association with qualities such as all-pervasiveness that are indicated—is not a contemporary or occasional one, like the metaphorical usage where the name "chariot-part" refers to the ruddy goose;
rather, it is a thoroughly established (atyantanirūḍha) one. This is the meaning of the Sūtra.
However, those who assert that the word "space" (ākāśa) is indeed primary even for Brahman, just as it is for the physical sky,

have broken the seal of the Mīmāṃsakas— namely, the principles that "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings" and that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained through any other means. How so?
For Brahman can indeed be understood from the word "space" (*ākāśa*) through its association with qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

Nor should it be argued that while the word is primary in reference to Brahman, it may nevertheless function in reference to the physical ether (*nabhas*) by virtue of that same association of qualities;
for the determination of the relationship between a word and its meaning depends upon common worldly usage, and the comprehension of Vedic terminology is preceded by that [worldly usage].

But surely, because of the indication of distinction in the passage, "As far as this space [outside] extends, so far extends this space within the heart," figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate;

for when one intends to say "the bank of the Gaṅgā," the expression "the Gaṅgā of the Gaṅgā" is never used. Is it then the case that the Vedic usage in "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the Paurṇamāsī day" and "With the Amāvāsyā on the Amāvāsyā day" is incorrect?
Furthermore, the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are not primary (*mukhya*) with respect to the Āgneya and other sacrifices.

As for the claim that "where there is comprehension of the word's meaning, there is secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); but where a word is not employed when its meaning has been determined elsewhere, there it possesses direct denotative power (*vācakatva*) alone"—that is incorrect.
Because both [alternatives] are subject to deviation:
from the word "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), the meaning is understood;
and herein, there is no figurative usage (*lākṣaṇikatva*) for anything except for the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Furthermore, in the passage "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day; he who, knowing thus, [sacrifices] on the new moon day," the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are not figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence. //17//

If it is argued that "it is that [self] because of the reference to the other," we say no, because of impossibility. (BBs 1,3.18) If it is argued that "it is that [self] because of the reference to the other," we say no, because of impossibility. (BsVBh 1,3.5.18)

Because the individual soul (jīva) becomes perfectly serene in this state, casting off the turbidity born from the contact between the sense objects and the senses, it is called "deep sleep" (suṣupti) or "perfect serenity" (saṃprasāda); this is a specific state of the jīva, not of Brahman.
Likewise, the "rising out from the body" also refers to the jīva which has the body as its support, and not to Brahman, which is without any support.

Therefore, just as the small ether (daharākāśa) is understood to be Brahman by means of the indicative marks found in the supplementary passages as previously stated, why is it not likewise understood that the small ether is the individual soul (jīva) on account of the very two [marks] found in the supplementary passages— namely, its state of serene repose (saṃprasāda) and its emergence therefrom? Thus, the meaning of the objection is that there is no decisive factor for determination.
"Not so, because of impossibility.

For the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) made through the contexts of "serenity" (*saṃprasāda*) and "arising" (*samutthāna*) does not concern the individual soul as such; rather, it concerns its true nature as being Brahman.

Thus, this reflection belongs to Brahman alone; therefore, it is not a characteristic of the individual soul (jīva) arising from the state of serene clarity, but rather it pertains to Brahman because it has that as its purpose, as will be explained later.
Furthermore, attributes such as the comparison to space are non-deviating characteristics of Brahman and are intended for Brahman; this is the meaning of the decisive criterion. //18//

The small ether itself is introduced by way of a narrative: "Having sought that Self, one obtains all worlds and all desires.
Desiring to know that Self, Indra and Virocana, the kings of the gods and the asuras, approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands to serve him.
Having arrived, they dwelt there in celibacy for thirty-two years, devoted to his service.
Then Prajāpati said to them two, "What desire do you have that you both stand here? They replied, "We wish to know that Self which is free from evil."

"This is the immortal, the fearless. Now, having heard this, because their veil of impurity was not yet exhausted, they both grasped at the shadow-person and questioned Prajāpati.

"Now, O Blessed One, as for this one who is seen in water, and in a mirror, and in the limbs of one's own body and so forth— which among these is he? Or is it that he is one and the same in all of them?"
Having heard this question of theirs, Prajāpati thought: "Alas! These two have wandered very far astray;
we pointed out the Self as being situated in the eye, yet these two have identified it with the person in the reflection."

Thinking, "If we were to say that you two are mistaken, then, having been insulted by the pride of learning you have projected upon yourselves, you would become dejected and fail to grasp the instruction as it truly is," he replied with the intention of making them understand the truth in accordance with their own dispositions: "Look at yourselves in this bowl of water; tell me what you see there."
Seeing them, their hearts were filled with satisfaction, yet they said nothing.
Then Prajāpati, intending that these two should not hold a perverted view, asked:
"What did you see there?"

The two of them said, "Just as we ourselves possess nails, hair, and so forth, which have arisen due to our long practice of the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), we saw in the water-jar something resembling us that likewise possessed nails, hair, and so forth.

Desiring to remove their delusion regarding the reflection-self (*chāyātman*), [the teacher explained]: "For just as the person in the reflection, being perceived through the properties of arising and passing away, is not the Self itself because it lacks the characteristics of the Self, even so is this body."

However, intending that they should understand these two as distinct from that [reflection] through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), Prajāpati said: "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look again at yourselves in a vessel of water, and tell me what you see there."
Having become well-adorned, dressed in fine garments, and with their nails and hair clipped, the two of them acted exactly as before.
When questioned again by Prajāpati, they identified that very shadow as themselves.
Hearing this, Prajāpati thought, "Alas! Even now, their delusion has not subsided."
I shall now explain the true nature of the Self exactly as it is intended.
Thinking that when their impurities have been exhausted over time, they will realize the truth of the Self by themselves through an examination of the sequence of my discourse, he said:
"This is the Self; this is the immortal; this is the fearless; this is Brahman."

Of the two, Virocana, because the reflection is dependent upon the body, concluded that the body alone was the true essence of the Self; having returned to his own abode, he taught the Asuras exactly as he had understood it.

Indra, however, before reaching his own abode, while still on the way, perceived certain defects in the reflected self—which conforms to the qualities and defects of the body—and reflecting upon each of those defects, thought, "I see nothing enjoyable in this perception of the reflected self," and [returned] to the presence of Prajāpati.
Then, with sacrificial fuel in hand, he returned once more; and when questioned by Prajāpati regarding the reason for his return, he spoke of what he had contemplated on the path.
Prajāpati said, "Although you have been well-instructed in the reality of the Self, you did not grasp it because the veil of your impurities was not yet exhausted;
therefore, practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*) again for another thirty-two years in order to destroy those [impurities]."
Then he said, "I shall explain this very Self to you again, once your impurities have been destroyed.
And Surendra, having thus practiced the life of a religious student, approached Prajāpati.
To him who had arrived, Prajāpati spoke:

That Self, characterized by freedom from evil and other such qualities, which was shown in the eye—that very same one is this one who, being honored in the dream state by women and others, moves about experiencing various dream-enjoyments.
Even with regard to this [state], Devendra perceived fear;
for although this [Self] does not follow the attributes of the body like the shadow-person, [it is still subject to change].

When Madhavi replied, "Nevertheless, because one experiences various afflictions such as grief and fear, there is no attainment of well-being even there," Prajapati spoke again: "Practice pure celibacy for another thirty-two years; even now, you have not exhausted your impurities."
Then, when Madhava had approached him in this manner, Prajapati said:

"That very Self which was shown as possessing qualities such as being free from evil, and which exists in the eye and in the dream state—that same Self is the one who becomes serene in the state of deep sleep due to the absence of contact with objects and senses.
Even regarding this, Indra did not find peace.

For just as one who is awake or one who has entered a dream cognizes "I am this" and "these beings exist," so it is not at all that one who is in deep sleep perceives anything whatsoever; then indeed, being without cognition, he becomes as if he has reached non-existence.
Therefore, what is the state of cessation in this case?
When Madhavī had spoken thus, Prajāpati said, "Alas! Even now your stain has not been destroyed;
therefore, practice the life of celibacy for another five years.
In this manner, ninety-six years passed for this Madhu through three such cycles.
And in the fourth section, for Madhava— who had practiced the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) for five years, thus completing one hundred and one years— the thousand-eyed Prajāpati,

seeing that his impurities had been wiped away by the perfection of his studentship, revealed to him this very Self— endowed with qualities such as being free from evil— which is woven through the eye, through the dream state, and through deep sleep;
he explained it clearly with the words, "O Madhava, the body is indeed mortal," and so forth.
This is his intended meaning: whatever pleasure or pain arises and passes away, all of that pertains to the body, the senses, and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), but not to the Self (*ātman*).

However, due to the power of the beginningless impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), he perceives these very things—the body and so forth—as the Self. Consequently, imagining himself to possess the pleasure and pain residing in them, he suffers.

But when he experiences the Self—which is indifferent and characterized by freedom from evil and so forth—as distinct from the body and other such things, then, although possessing a body, he is effectively bodiless; thus, there is no possibility of experiencing the bodily attributes of pleasure and pain, and he does not grieve.
Established solely in that form which is dense with eternal consciousness and bliss, he attains all the desires of the world.
For all desires are but mere fragments of this very supreme bliss;
since suffering, however, is a creation of ignorance, the man of knowledge does not experience it.
"Confusion arises here among those who have not practiced the Upanishads."
For their benefit, I have related this narrative.

Thus, from the context of the subsequent passage beginning with "from the one belonging to Prajāpati," it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone— characterized by qualities such as being free from evil— that is spoken of by the Śruti in the third and fourth sections concerning the eye, the dream state, deep sleep, and the state of "emerging" with the words, "this serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen up from this body. Indeed, the abode of the eye is not possible for the Supreme Self.
Nor is there any connection with states such as dreaming,

Since all this belongs to the individual soul (jīva), it is that very soul which is described by the Śruti as possessing qualities such as being "free from evil" (apahatapāpman); therefore, the supreme Brahman is not indicated by these qualities like being free from evil.
But was it not stated that freedom from evil and the other qualities cannot belong to the individual soul?
They will exist [in the soul] on the basis of scriptural statement.
What kind of statement would it not carry out? There is no burden too great for a statement,
nor is there any contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

The meaning of the objection is this: the individual soul (*jīva*) does not have sin and the like as its inherent nature; rather, its sin and so forth arise from the activity of speech, intellect, and body. Therefore, in the absence of the body and other such instruments, sin and the like do not exist for it, just as smoke does not exist in the absence of fire.
To refute this, he says in response: "But [the soul] whose true nature has become manifest..."

This is the intended meaning: through a consideration of the preceding and following passages, it is understood that the purport of the Upaniṣads is that Brahman alone is pure, awakened, liberated, one, and devoid of phenomenal expansion (aprapañca), while everything other than that is its illusory transformation (vivarta), like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope;

and thus the individual soul (jīva) is also not the essential nature of Brahman, but rather the form of Brahman as conditioned by the body, senses, and so forth, which are imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
Thus, qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) are not possible in that [self] when it has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
however, when the nature of Brahman has become manifest and it is devoid of adjuncts, these qualities are possible, and they belong to Brahman alone, not to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, since Brahman alone possesses the qualities of being free from evil and so forth as stated in the Śruti, that very Brahman is the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*), and not the individual soul.

This might be so: if, upon the manifestation of its true nature, it is Brahman itself and not the individual soul (jīva), then this statement— that "the individual soul has manifested its true nature"— is a contradiction.
Therefore, he says: "by way of what occurred in the past," referring to the *Udaśarāva-brāhmaṇa*.

For just as the reflections of Madhu in a bowl of water possess the nature of arising and passing away, yet are not the self because they lack the characteristics of a self; [so too is the case here].

The meaning is that the dissolution of its state [of being an individual soul] is intended to demonstrate its ultimate nature as Brahman. //20//

Since the non-appearance of light is observed when another light is present, another element of light is therefore inferred from that and from its resemblance.
For it is observed that a weak light, such as that of the moon or the stars, is overwhelmed by a more powerful solar radiance,
but never by something other than light;
likewise, those things that obscure a lamp, such as houses or jars, are not capable of illuminating the lamp by means of their own luster.
And it is heard in scripture: "By its light all this shines.
The word "all" refers here to the previously mentioned sun and other luminaries.
Furthermore, imitation in the form of "shining after" (anubhāna) is not possible between things that are not of a similar nature.
For it is not the case that cows run after black birds; rather, it is the running after such boars that is appropriate for cows.

Therefore, although Brahman was the subject under discussion in the passage, "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven," [the subsequent reference to the "two birds" does not contradict this].

Nevertheless, by means of the inferential mark (liṅga) characterized by the capacity for overpowering and imitation, the element of fire (tejodhātu) is understood through the sublation of the general context (prakaraṇa),
and not Brahman, because no such inferential mark is applicable to Brahman.
In that context, the pronouns *tam* and *tasya* will merely obscure what is actually intended to be shown.
Furthermore, there is no fixed rule that the word *tat* must refer back to something previously mentioned;
for instance, in expressions such as *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* ("colored by that dye") or *tasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of him"), there is nothing whatsoever previously mentioned.

Therefore, although it is not known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), another extraordinary light is understood from the word as an object of meditation; this being the position reached, it is said in reply: "For that mark (*liṅga*) belongs to Brahman alone, and not to an extraordinary light; therefore, Brahman is to be known, and not that [light], as the object of meditation."
Regarding the doubt as to whether, in the passage "tameva bhāntam," one should postulate some extraordinary light (*alaukika-tejas*) to account for the shining of the sun and other luminaries,
or whether the shining of the sun and others should be explained by the shining of Brahman— well-known from another scriptural text as "consisting of light and possessing true resolve"—
the conclusion is that when what is already heard [in scripture] is possible, the postulation of what is not heard is not appropriate; thus, [an extraordinary light] is not established.
It is not logical that a supramundane radiance should be the object of worship;
rather, it is Brahman, as established by scripture, that must be known.
This is what he says: "The Self must necessarily be the Prājña."
He states the contradiction with the words "and because of equality.
Now, one might object: in their own manifestation, the sun and so forth depend upon ocular light;
for these are not seen by the blind.

Likewise, that very same ocular light, when nourished by external light such as solar light, illuminates form and so forth, but not when it is not so nourished; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving forms even in darkness. Therefore, he says: "following him who shines.
For we do not deny that one light may depend upon another light.
But the manifestation of that [object] is what constitutes its being manifested;
and the sun and other luminaries do not manifest the manifestation of the eye.
This is what was stated: "For it is not the lamp... and so forth.
Having restated the prima facie argument, he states the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words, "As for what was also said.
This is what is meant: if the imitation is rejected on the grounds that there is no identity of essential nature (*svarūpa*), then there is a fallacy of deviation.
Now, as for the claim that there is an absence of similarity in action, that is unproven;
for even between air and dust, which differ in their intrinsic natures, there is a similarity in their action of moving in a fixed direction and location.
As for fire and an iron ball, although their action of burning does not differ, one must explain the similarity of action by postulating a difference in action based on the difference in substance.
Thus, having analyzed the [sūtra] portion "anukṛteḥ" (because of imitation), he analyzes the part of the sūtra beginning with "tasya ca" (and of that): "And of that, the fourth.
The meaning is that Brahman is the light that illuminates the luminaries, such as the sun and so forth.
It is not well-known that the light of the sun and other luminaries shines by means of another light that has attained the state of a sense organ.
For the natural function (*vṛtti*) of the word "all" (*sarva*) is to denote everything without exception.
This function would be restricted in the case of the non-worldly element *tejo-dhātu*, which illuminates only form;
however, with respect to Brahman, which illumines the entire universe, the function of the word "all" is not restricted. Thus, [the author] employs the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Indeed, this word *tatra* everywhere refers back to what has been previously mentioned.

Even in rules such as "that which is colored by it [is called *rakta*] because of passion" (*tena raktaṃ rāgāt*), when a suffix is prescribed after a base (*prakṛti*) with a different meaning, the referent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has occurred previously; thus, because of that reference by the word *tena*, there is no inconsistency.
And thus, the hearing of the pronoun itself brings Brahman to mind.
Therefore, even if it were granted that an indicative mark (liṅga) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa),
since direct statement (śruti) is stronger than an indicative mark, it follows that here Brahman alone is understood through direct statement.

Moreover, between the mention of what is required and what is not required, the mention of what is required is more appropriate because it serves a visible purpose; thus he says: "And immediately thereafter, in the golden supreme sheath.
In this sentence, it is said, "the light of lights."
In this regard, when the question arises as to how it is "the light of lights," the following verse presents itself: "There, the sun does not shine.
If this were stated independently, it would be irrelevant and its purpose would be unperceived;
however, even with respect to Brahman, the negation of their manifestation is logically consistent.

The intended meaning is this: in the statement "the sun does not shine there," this is not a locative absolute (satisaptamī), for if it were, one would perceive the suppression of the sun and other luminaries by that [Brahman] while it exists; rather, it is a locative of object (viṣayasaptamī).
Therefore, when that Brahman is to be illumined, the sun and other luminaries do not shine as its illuminators;
rather, it is Brahman alone that shines as the illuminator within the sun and others which are to be illumined.
And that [Brahman] is self-luminous.
"Because of such scriptural passages as 'It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped,'" and so forth. //22//

"There is no direct distinction in measure with respect to the Supreme, who is devoid of all measurement; since lordship over the past and the future does not apply directly to the individual soul (jīva), there is therefore doubt."

"Should this passage be taken as being concerned with the meditation on the individual soul (jīva) in order to conform to the scriptural mention of [the soul] as 'thumb-sized,' and the term 'Lord' (īśāna) be interpreted somehow in accordance with that; or rather,
should it be taken as being concerned with Brahman in order to conform to the scriptural mention of 'Lord'?"

In accordance with that [latter], the scriptural mention of "the size of a thumb" should be interpreted in some way. Regarding the question of which of the two should conform to the other, it is logical that the first should conform; thus, the mention of the "Lord" (Īśāna) must be interpreted in conformity with the mention of the "thumb.
Furthermore, it is appropriate for the Supreme Self to have its abode within the small lotus of the heart.
Because it is specified as a distinct location;
for that is the place of his perception,
just as Śālagrāma is for the Blessed One Kamalanābha.
And in this case, a difference of location is not indicated by the scriptural mention of "the size of a thumb," because only the measure is specified.
Furthermore, in the phrase "in the middle of the self" (*madhya ātmani*), no difference of location is understood;
for this word "self" (*ātman*) may denote either one's own nature, the individual soul (*jīva*), or Brahman.

In that regard, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) depends upon that which possesses it for its determination, and because that which possesses it—the self—is not specified, it is not known of what the "middle" is.
Furthermore, there is no clear middle between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*); thus, this indication of location is not explicit.
However, the indication of magnitude (*parimāṇa*) is clear.
Furthermore, since a difference in magnitude is not possible in the Supreme [Self], it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone that is "the size of a thumb.
Indeed, that is a portion of the Supreme Self, conceptualized through limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
And the internal organ generally has its locus in the cavity of the heart-lotus.

The lotus-bud of the heart of human beings is the size of a thumb; therefore, the individual self (jīvātman), being delimited by it, is also thumb-sized, just as the ether is one cubit in length when delimited by the joint of a bamboo.
Furthermore, the thumb-sized nature of the individual self is clearly recorded in traditional scripture (smṛti): "Yama forcibly dragged forth the person the size of a thumb."
For it is not possible for the extraction of the Lord of All, Brahman, by Yama to be accomplished by force;
indeed, Yama himself declared: "I am subject to Hari and my Guru; Viṣṇu is not subject to my restraint even in the case of myself.

Therefore, since the state of being the size of a thumb is certain to belong to the individual soul (jīva), the soul's lordship over some past and future beings must be explained as being merely relative.
And by the words "This indeed is that," [the text] refers back to the form of the individual soul (jīva) perceived through direct perception.
Therefore, it follows that the individual self alone is the object of meditation here.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "Because of its being the answer to a question, and because the hearing of the term 'Lord' (īśāna) is without distinction."
This statement is intended to convey that the individual soul has the nature of Brahman.
For here, absolute sovereignty (*īśānatvam*) with respect to all that has been and all that is to be is perceived;
and Brahman was previously asked about in the passage beginning, "Other than dharma, other than adharma," and so forth.
Since it is appropriate for the subsequent textual context to provide an answer to that question, it is logical that the designation "This indeed is That" refers to Brahman.

And thus, although the individual soul (jīva) is understood through its thumb-sized dimension, nevertheless this statement does not have that as its primary purport; rather, it is intended to establish that the thumb-sized soul is of the nature of Brahman.
In this way, the unrestricted sovereignty [of the Lord] must not be restricted.
Nor should the fact that this is an answer to the question concerning Brahman be abandoned.

Therefore, just as in the statement "That thou art," the identity of the individual self—the referent of the term *tvam*—with the Supreme Self—the referent of the term *tat*—is established through knowledge, so too here it is logical that the state of being Brahman is established for the individual self, which is measured by a thumb, by means of the scriptural declaration of its being the Lord (*īśāna*). //24//

Well then, do you intend to prove that even the bodies of gods and others are produced from the union of a mother and father on the grounds of their being "bodies"?
If so, the reason is fallacious due to inconclusiveness (anaikāntika),
because the bodies of those born from sweat (svedaja) or those born from sprouts (udbhijja) do not have that as their cause.
If it is argued that the creation of bodies and so forth by mere will is something never before observed, we say no;
for their being created by mere will is unestablished, since they are derived from the primary elements (*bhūta*).

For when gods and others who have mastery over the elements produce the activity of the elements by virtue of their desire to create various bodies, various bodies arise through the mutual conjunction of those elements.

And it is observed that the action of those who possess mastery occurs over their object by the power of their will, just as one skilled in the science of poisons causes a fragment of poison to move by mere wish.

Nor should it be argued: "Since the skill in the science of poisons is seen through its manifestation [in the practitioner], and since beings that are obstructed or distant are not seen, how can there be a manifestation [of power] over gods and other such beings?"
Because there is no deviation [in the rule] due to the observation of terrestrial objects such as Saturn (Śanaiścara) and others that are obscured by glass or clouds, or are at a great distance;
and because the unimpeded visions of gods and others are not obstructed by the earth, mountains, and so forth, in the same way that glass or clouds obstruct vision;
nor should it be argued that, like those of us [ordinary beings], their inability to perceive what is obstructed or distant is inferred on the grounds of their possessing a physical body.
Because it is impossible for an inference that contradicts scripture to arise;

furthermore, invisibility— such as that of humans through the use of ointments and the like— is possible even for those who possess such powers, and therefore, despite being present, they will not be seen at the site of the sacrifice.
