From that [come] the Vasus.
"Who are the Rudras? [The answer is: these ten vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person—the ten organs of cognition and action—and the mind as the eleventh.
Therefore, these are the Prāṇas because they function as such;
for they are called Rudras because, when departing at the time of death, they cause the person to weep (rodayanti).

Who are the Ādityas? They are the twelve months, the constituent parts of the year, which revolve again and again, causing living beings to take up their lifespans and the enjoyment of the fruits of their actions; thus they are called Ādityas.
Indra is the thunderbolt, for that is his strength.
For that is Indra’s supreme lordship;
by means of it, he causes all living beings to perish; therefore, the thunderclap and the lightning bolt are Indra.
The sacrifice is Prajāpati;
and the sacrificial animals, being both the means of the sacrifice and the form of the sacrifice, are Prajāpati.
These very thirty-three gods are the manifestations (mahimānaḥ) of the six—namely Agni, Earth, Vāyu, Antarikṣa, Āditya, and Div—their greatness being such that they do not differ from them.
There are indeed only six deities.
However, by combining fire and earth into one, the intermediate space and wind into one, and the sky and the sun into one, they become three worlds and thus only three deities.
Furthermore, since these same three are included within food and vital breath, they become two deities: food and vital breath.
Those two together are one and a half gods. Which one is the "one and a half"?
It is this wind that blows.
How is it that this one alone is "one and a half" (adhyardha)? Because when this exists, all of this attains increase by one and a half, therefore it is called "one and a half. Which one is it?
That very same single Prāṇa, being one and a half-fold, is Brahman.
Because it is "great" (bṛhat) by virtue of being the self of all the gods, they call it "Brahman" using a term that expresses it indirectly.
Therefore, the Śruti declares that by the power of its own majesty, a single deity simultaneously assumes the forms of many deities.
And *smṛti* has already been explained [by the word "nigama"].
Furthermore, it is heard that even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), by virtue of practicing the means [of yoga], having attained powers such as *aṇimā*, can simultaneously manifest various bodies;
what then need be said regarding the gods, who possess these powers by their very nature? Thus he says: "of the yogins who have attained the powers such as *aṇimā*."

The supernatural powers (*aiśvaryāṇi*) are: atomization (*aṇimā*), levitation (*laghimā*), magnification (*mahimā*), extension (*prāpti*), irresistible will (*prākāmyam*), sovereignty (*īśitvam*), mastery (*vaśitvam*), and the power of determining things according to one's desire (*yatrakāmāvasāyitā*). This is one explanation; there is another interpretation: it is the simultaneous attainment of the state of being a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) in many actions at once, that is, the process of becoming a subordinate factor.
From the observation of that [fact], in order to demonstrate it clearly, he first states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "In some cases, one [person].
Indeed, among many faithful [donors], a single Brahmin cannot simultaneously become a constituent part (*aṅga*) for all of them.
He explains how a single entity can simultaneously function as a subordinate factor (aṅga) in multiple places with the words "and sometimes one.

Just as a single Brahmin is saluted simultaneously by many people, so too, when a single deity situated in her own abode is addressed by many sacrificers located in various places, the oblation is offered simultaneously;
and although she is not physically present there, she functions as a subordinate factor in that rite.
For it has been established that she possesses the capacity to perceive multiple distant objects simultaneously. //27//

If it is argued that [the world] is [produced] from sound, no; because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by perception and inference. (BBs 1,3.28) If it is argued that [the world] is [produced] from sound, no; because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by perception and inference. (BsVBh 1,3.8.28)

Like the word "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, because there is no prior recollection [of a universal] and because not even a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is perceived, words such as "Vasu" and the like are denotative of individuals (*vyaktivacana*), just like words such as "cook" or "space. And since that individual is eternal, its relation with it would be eternal.

However, if there were a connection with a physical body (*vigraha*) and so forth, then because Vasu and the others would possess parts and thus be non-eternal, the word "Vasu" and the like would not have been previously connected with its own referent.
Because there is no such thing as a self-referential object [prior to cognition],

the connection with words such as "Vasu" that arises once Vasu and so forth have been produced must— like the connection with words such as "Devadatta"— originate from human intellect; consequently, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence preceded by that [connection] would also be dependent upon human intellect.
The meaning of the objection is that since human cognition arises dependent upon other means of knowledge, the authority of the Veda would be undermined by its dependence on those other means.
The answer is: "No, because [the Veda] originates from Him."

From a word denoting a genus such as "Vasu" (*vasutva*), there arises the manifestation of an individual belonging to that genus which is intended to be produced, existing as it were within the intellect;
this is what is meant by "origination from that" (*tatprabhavatva*).

What is being said is this: although the word is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the Vasus and others—since Brahman is their material cause—[the word is still the source of their manifestation].
Nevertheless, according to the sequence explained by those who maintain that [the relationship] has a causal basis (*nimittakāraṇa*),

the relationship between word and meaning is not rendered non-eternal by this much; for the genus (*jāti*) such as "wealth" (*vasu*) and so forth, or its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as delimited by some form or other, is eternal.
He analyzes this very point through objection and resolution: "But [it was said], 'That from which there is the origin, etc., of this [world]'" (BS 1.1.2).
These two [sūtras] are explained by their very recitation.
Now, has this been composed by the Self-born [Brahmā] himself, like the *Kumārasambhava* and other works by Kālidāsa and others?

And thus, since that very [Veda] would result in being non-authoritative because it is a sentence dependent on other means of knowledge, he says: "This general rule regarding speech consists in the transmission of the tradition.
Tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the study [of the Veda] through the succession of teacher and pupil.

This is what is meant: even though the Self-existent One (*svayaṃbhū*) is the author of the Veda, he does not possess independence like Kālidāsa and others; rather, [he acts] in accordance with a previous creation.
This has been established by us, and the author of the Commentary will establish it further below;
moreover, this is seen even today.
He says, "Moreover, [it is] what is intended to be done," because from seeing that, the same state of even the ancient creators is inferred.
He objects: "But of what nature is it?
The underlying intention is this: indeed, it must be accepted that the gods originate from expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*).
Because they are not denotative, as they do not leave an impression upon the intellect;
for among those [phonemes], the letters such as *va* and so forth are not denotative of objects and the like,
because since they are different with each utterance, it is impossible to grasp their relationship [to a meaning].
Furthermore, if they were denotative despite the absence of a grasped connection (*saṃgati*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Moreover, do these [words] denote the sentence-meaning individually or collectively? First of all, not individually.
Because no comprehension of meaning is observed immediately after the utterance of a single phoneme,
and because it would follow that the utterance of subsequent phonemes would be purposeless;
nor are they [the phonemes] combined.
Because there is no possibility of mutual concomitance among those [phonemes] which are uttered by a single speaker, since they perish moment by moment either in their form or their manifestation;
nor is any other mode possible besides the individual or the collective.

Nor is it tenable to claim that even in the absence of concomitance in their own nature, phonemes possess concomitance by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), as is the case with the *Āgneya* and other [sacrifices].
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis:
what indeed is this "formative force" (saṃskāra) intended to be?
Is it something previously non-existent, produced [by ritual acts] such as the Āgneya sacrifice, like [the apūrva]?
Or is it the seed for the production of memory, which is another name for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
It cannot be the first alternative;

for a word, whether its own form or its constituent parts are unknown, cannot—provided its connection [to the meaning] is also unknown—be the cause of the cognition of the object, unlike the sense organs.
Because a word that has been uttered is not communicative if it is not grasped by a deaf person, or even if it is grasped, provided there is no connection with what was previously understood;

therefore, one must accept that a word—being known, having its conventional connection known, and having all the factors for making something known known—is communicative, just like smoke and other such signs.
Consequently, its *saṃskāra* (mental impression), which denotes the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*), must be understood as a factor in communication prior to the cognition of the object.
And at that time, there is no means for its comprehension;
yet, one who attempts to justify the comprehension of it through the cognition of the object falls into an inescapable circularity:
the cognition of the object arises from the determination of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), [while the determination of the impression arises from that very cognition].
And therefore, it is the determination of that [object]. However, the mental formation (saṃskāra) denoted by "cultivation" (bhāvanā) is the soul's capacity to produce recollection;
and that very [capacity] cannot also be the capacity to produce the cognition of an object.

Nor is there another capacity belonging to that very capacity; for the burning power of fire is not the same as its illuminating power, nor is the illuminating power the same as the burning power. Furthermore, if the seeds of memory—the latent impressions (vāsanā)—were identical [to the sounds], then the cognition of meaning would result even from phonemes uttered in a reversed order.
And yet it does not exist;
therefore, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are in no way the causes of the cognition of meaning,
nor is there a *sphoṭa* essence distinct from them.
Because that [eternal word] does not enter into experience;
for it has already been stated that if its existence were known through the effect, which is the cognition of the object, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
Furthermore, if that eternal entity were the cause of the cognition of the object by its mere existence, there would be the consequence that the cognition of the object would arise at all times.

Because a cause that is independent [of anything else] would be eternal, it is therefore untenable to claim that the production of the signified arises from the word which is the signifier. Regarding this, a teacher-like authority says: "He spoke of the *sphoṭa*."
We do not tolerate the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are the conveyors [of meaning],
but we do not tolerate the view that it is the *sphoṭa*.
This is because, immediately after the experience of those [phonemes], the cognition of the object arises for one who has known the conventional relation [between word and meaning].
Nor is it the case that there is no experience of that [word] as something distinct from the phonemes;

for everyone’s common experience consists in the cognition of a single word— such as "gauh" (cow)— or a single sentence— such as "gām ānaya śuklām" (bring the white cow)— as something distinct from the various phonemes and words.
Moreover, this experience of a single word or sentence cannot be declared false in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*),
nor can it be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).
For an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) would indeed have to be either the state of being grasped by a single cognition, or...
Or [it might be] the state of being the cause for a single cognition of an object.
First of all, there is no cognition in which objects such as a *dhava*, a *khadira*, and a *palāśa* tree—which are the domain of a single cognition—appear as a single manifestation.
If that were the case, the expression "the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*" would never occur.
Nor can they be the cause of a single cognition of meaning, because the causality of that [cognition] has been refuted in the case of the phonemes. Furthermore,
if their simultaneity were postulated on the basis of being the cause of that [cognition], it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence.
"Concomitance [sāhitya] exists because of its being the cause of that [the cognition], and its being the cause of that exists because of concomitance.
Therefore, this uncontradicted and unconditioned experience of a single manifestation, which pertains to words and sentences, relies upon a single denoter distinct from the phonemes;
that is the *sphoṭa*. And although the sounds (*dhvani*s) manifest it individually, they do not make it clear all at once.
By what means could the cognition of the meaning arise immediately?

Rather, just like the knowledge of the reality of the jewels, the reality of words and sentences shines forth clearly in the final moment of consciousness—born from a perception produced by two, three, four, five, or six [moments of] seeing, and accompanied by the ripening of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the cognition of the meaning arises immediately after that [final consciousness], which had not arisen previously.
Thus, the term "arising" (udaya) does not render the subsequent sounds meaningless,
nor does it render the preceding ones so;
for in their absence, there would be no assistance due to the lack of the mental impressions (saṃskāra) produced by them and the resulting maturation of those impressions.
Because the final consciousness alone lacks the capacity to produce [the cognition],
nor can the preceding phonemes, like the cognitions of individual words, produce an indistinct cognition of the meaning for each one individually.
But it is logical that its assistant, the *carama* [the final cognition], should manifest it even more clearly;
for there is a restriction regarding perceptual knowledge such that it manifests both the manifest and the unmanifest,
and because the cognition of the *sphoṭa* is indeed perceptual.

However, in the case of the cognition of meaning—which is not itself perceptual but arises from another means of knowledge—the manifestation is clearly either present or absent; it cannot be indistinct. Thus, the parallel argument is not equal. Therefore, the eternal *sphoṭa* alone is the expressive agent, not the phonemes (*varṇas*).
While presenting his own view, he refutes this opinion of the quasi-teacher (the Mīmāṃsaka) by stating: "But the phonemes themselves are the word."
For in this way, the sphoṭa would have to be accepted as something distinct from the phonemes (varṇas) only if the capacity of the phonemes to denote meaning were impossible,
and that [sphoṭa] were to enter the path of empirical experience.
Furthermore, the capacity of letters to denote meaning is twofold:
either because they cannot be grasped as having a connection due to their momentariness, or because the two modes—individual and collective—are absent.
First of all, it is not the first alternative.
There is no evidence for the momentariness of phonemes (*varṇa*).
[Objection: Is it not well-known to all people that phonemes are different with each utterance? [Response: No, because they are recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor is it correct to say that this recognition is based on similarity— like that of a flame— even in the absence of identity;
for its being based on similarity would have to be accepted only if there were the onset of some powerful subverting evidence.

Or [it is because] a deviation is observed in some cases, such as with flames and the like. Regarding that, since those who maintain the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of cognition speak thus when a deviation is observed in some instances and one suspects it [might occur elsewhere]: "For he who, out of delusion, suspects an unperceived sublation (*bādhana*), being characterized by doubt in all practical transactions (*vyavahāra*), shall come to ruin."
Thus it has been explained by us at length in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*. Furthermore,
this recognition does not have the universals (*jāti*) such as "g-ness" as its object, nor does it have the individual instances (*vyakti*) such as the letter *ga* as its object.

Because a distinction is perceived among those [individual sounds] for each person, and precisely because a difference in the sounds is perceived, it is logical that a difference in the speakers is inferred, as in the case of "Somaśarman is reciting, not Viṣṇuśarman.
Therefore, let experience be carefully examined when many people are pronouncing the sound *ga*:

just as for one observing both Kālākṣī and Svastimatī, while the manifestation of the difference between the individuals is indeed present, a single universal (*sāmānya*) that conforms to them manifests.
Likewise, when the individual sounds such as *ga* and so forth manifest with distinction, does a single universal *gatva* shine forth as that which persists through them?

Or rather, is it like the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), which is inherently one, yet—due to the differences in the limiting adjuncts of the individuals in terms of location, size, and configuration—appears as if it were in different locations, as if small, as if large, as if long, or as if short; similarly, is the individual manifestation of the sound *ga*, though inherently one, as if it followed those properties due to the difference in its manifestors (*vyañjaka*)?
Let your honors yourselves understand that it is "extended" (*prathata*).

In that regard, even if one accepts a distinction between individual instances of the letter *ga*, the effort required to postulate a difference based on external adjuncts for a single universal *gatva* (the property of being *ga*) would be better applied to the individual instance of *ga* itself. What is the use of accepting an internal, superfluous (*antargaḍu*) *gatva*, as they have said:
"Therefore, whatever is sought from a universal (*jāti*), that will be obtained from the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself."
But since the individual [phoneme] is obtained from the sounds (nāda), the cognition of [abstract properties] such as *gata* is futile.
Furthermore, unlike [the case of] "Svastimati" and so forth, there is no clear cognition of a difference between individual *g* sounds with each utterance.
If that were the case, the cognition would be "Caitra uttered ten *g* sounds," rather than "He uttered the sound *g* ten times."

Nor is this repetition intended to refer to the universal (jāti), as in the case of the expression, "Devadatta ate partridges a hundred times. For even when people cry out with their hands beating their chests, the cognition of the practice of pronunciation regarding the manifestation of the phonemes *ga* and so forth still arises. The opponent raises an objection against recognition: "How can there be [simultaneous pronunciation] by many people at one time?"
Whatever possesses a simultaneous conjunction of contradictory properties is manifold,
such as a cow, a horse, and so forth, which possess [respectively] two hooves, one hoof, a mane, and a dewlap;
and this phoneme possesses a simultaneous conjunction of contradictory properties such as acute and grave accents.
Therefore, it must be diverse;
nor is it correct to say that the acute accent and so forth are properties of the manifesters rather than properties of the phonemes.
For the manifesters of this [sound] are the winds;
if they are not audible, how could their properties be audible?
This, first of all, must be addressed here.

For a sense faculty that has a quality as its object does not also have the possessor of that quality as its object; otherwise, it would follow that for the nose, tongue, and ear, which have smell, taste, and sound as their objects, the possessors of those qualities—earth, water, and space—would also be their objects. And thus, let it be that the ear does not have wind as its object.
It will perceive those qualities, such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others;
and because they are grasped as being associated with the word, they are determined to be properties of the word.

However, for a word whose unity is established through recognition, it is impossible for mutually contradictory properties like the acute accent and others to exist simultaneously in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) without succession.

Therefore, just as a single face undergoes the illusion of appearing with various differences in location, size, and shape due to the influence of adjuncts such as a gem, a sword, or a mirror, so too this illusion of a single phoneme being associated with various contradictory properties is caused by the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*);

it is not a real association with various properties. Having established this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states the following rebuttal while conceding the point: "Or rather, [the difference] is caused by the sounds."
The word "or rather" (athavā) sets aside the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Even if it were granted that the quality and the possessor of the quality are both perceivable by a single sense organ,
there would still be no fault.
Since sounds (*dhvani*) are also audible, just like words (*śabda*), he extracts the nature of sound by means of a question: "But what is this?

Nor is it correct to claim that this is merely a cognition of the general property of phonemes whose specific differences have not been determined, and not a cognition of a manifesting sound (*dhvani*) distinct from the phonemes.
Because there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that [sound] which is differentiated by distinctions such as nasality— just as there is none for individual instances of the letter *ga*—
and because it is impossible for a universal to exist when there is no unity in what is not being recognized;
therefore, this sound is not of the nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Whether sound (*dhvani*) is admitted as distinct from the word (*śabda*), or as the audible manifester of the word— in either case, qualities such as nasality (*ānunāsikatva*) and so forth, which are perceived through the mediation of various specific sounds (*dhvani*) in the manifesters of the word, are understood as properties belonging to those very sounds; they are not properties of the word itself by its own nature.
And thus, while those sounds (dhvanis) in which properties such as nasality appear to be mutually contradictory may indeed be impermanent—
for there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of them as identical—
those phonemes (varṇas), however, of which there is recognition do not possess properties such as nasality; therefore, they are not impermanent.
And this being the case, regarding the statement "they have an object":
if the opponent's position is that when the substratum (dharmin) is not apprehended, its attributes (dharmas) cannot be apprehended, then let it be so; let the opponent be satisfied with that.
The meaning is that even so, there is no fault.

Thus, by this preceding argument, the objection that letters are non-expressive because their connection [to a meaning] cannot be grasped due to their momentariness has been refuted. Now, wishing to refute the objection raised on the grounds that neither the individual nor the collective form of letters is possible, he says: "And because the cognition of meaning arises from the letters."
Unable to tolerate the notion of conceptual construction, the partisan (ekadeśin) says: "I do not construct.
[The author] refutes this: "No;
for even of this cognition..."

Let the venerable one first examine this cognition: "The word 'cow' is a single unit. Does this cognition apprehend in its entirety just the previously experienced phonemes, such as the letter *ga* and the rest, or does it apprehend something distinct from the letter *ga* and the others—just as a *gavaya* is distinct from animals such as the boar?
If it were to manifest as something distinct from the letter *ga* and so forth, the cognition would not be colored by the form of the letter *ga* and so forth;
for the cognition of a boar does not apprehend a boar that is colored by the form of a buffalo.

The sounds (*dhvani*), produced by distinct efforts and differentiated by their respective places and articulators (*sthāna-karaṇa*), each manifesting the single reality of a word (*padatattva*); through their similarity to the various sounds that manifest other mutually dissimilar words, they bring about a resemblance to many mutually dissimilar words for the one reality of the word they themselves manifest.
Due to this differentiation caused by the superimposition of similarity, they cause even that which is unitary and partless to appear as if it were manifold and possessed of parts.

Just as a single primary [color], though possessing fixed distinctions of color, dimension, location, and shape, appears as many distinct colors, dimensions, and shapes in jewels, swords, mirrors, and so forth; and if you argue that its parts— the letters— are thus merely imagined, then why do you now resolve to declare these distinctions of letters to be false even in the absence of any subverting evidence?
If it is argued that the single cognition itself sublates plurality,

then why does the appearance of plurality— not seen in the form "alas, various colors are manifested here"— not sublate oneness? Alternatively, like the cognitions of a forest or an army, oneness and plurality are not contradictory.

Indeed, the cognitions "army" and "forest" do not arise by subverting the distinctions between elephants, foot-soldiers, horses, and so forth, or between *campaka*, *aśoka*, *kiṃśuka*, and other trees; rather, they bring about a sense of unity for things that are already distinct but delimited by a single common attribute (*upādhi*).
Nor is inherent plurality contradicted by a unity derived from an external attribute.
For the metaphorical nature of fire in the case of a young boy does not contradict his actual human nature.

Therefore, it should be understood that the letters appearing in a single recollective cognition— which arises from the accumulation of mental impressions produced by the experience of each individual letter and which encompasses all the letters— possess a metaphorical unity, either by virtue of being objects of that single cognition or by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition of meaning.

Nor is there a circularity such that their being the cause of a single cognition of an object depends on their unity, and their unity depends on their being the cause of a single cognition of an object;
for it is not the case that prior to the cognition of the object, these many phonemes do not manifest as ascending into a single recollection,
nor is it the case that the cognition of the object by an elder person is not inferred immediately after their manifestation.

And because they arise together, one understands that they possess a single causal efficiency (*kārakatva*) toward the cognition of a single meaning; thus, there is the determination of their being a "single word" (*ekapada*), and so there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor should it be argued that since the phonemes (*varṇa*)—which reside in a single memory and are employed either sequentially, non-sequentially, or in a reversed order—are not distinct, it would follow that a cognition of meaning could arise from them regardless of how they were uttered.
For it has been said: "However many [phonemes], of whatever nature, and whichsoever [they may be] in the communication of a word-meaning..."
The phonemes, whose capacities are well-known, are likewise the means of comprehension.

[Objection: "But surely, even though there is no sequence in the single cognition of a row, it is logical that there is a manifestation [of the row] exactly as it is, because the row of houses and so forth exists in reality;
however, such a real sequence does not exist here for the letters, which are eternal and all-pervading."
If it is argued that there may be an adventitious condition (*pratyayopādhi*),
and since that too is one, from where could this sequence of these [cognitions] arise?

This is because, even in a single act of recollection, there is a reflection upon the fact that [the letters] were previously experienced in a specific sequence, just as there is with the forms of the letters themselves.

For instance, when the two words *jāra* and *rāja* are being presented, although the letters are identical, a difference between the words is clearly manifested due to the difference in their sequence.
Thus, there is no lack of distinction in a single cognitive act of recollection regarding letters employed in a sequence versus those employed in a non-sequential or reversed order.
As they have said: "The wise desire many means for determining the words [of the Veda]:
order, deficiency, excess, accent, sentence, scripture, and tradition."
Thus;
the remainder has its meaning not obscured.
Only a mere indication of the direction has been shown here.
The detailed account, however, is to be understood from the *Tattvabindu*.
Or rather, enough with this dispute with the Naiyāyikas;

even if phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed non-eternal, nevertheless, the acquisition of linguistic convention (*saṃgatigraha*) will be established through the delimitation of universals such as *gata* (the "g-ness" of the letter g), and thus beginningless worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) will be maintained. Thus he says: "Even if that were so... (verse 28).
And for this very reason, it is eternal. And for this very reason, it is eternal.

[Objection: But surely the eternity of the Veda has already been established in the earlier Mīmāṃsā; why then is it being proven again? To this he says: "For the eternity of the Veda stands precisely because no independent author is remembered.
Indeed, the world cannot possibly arise from that which is non-eternal.
Since that [Veda] also possesses the quality of being produced, it is dependent [on causes];
therefore, the eternality of the Veda is already established by the fact that it is the cause of the origin of the world,
just like Īśvara, and this [argument] merely confirms that eternality.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //29//
And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, on account of both scripture and tradition.
(BS 1.3.30) And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, on account of both scripture and tradition.
Since the sūtra is intended as a response to an objection, he recites the words of that objection: "But it might be argued...
For the eternity of the relationship would exist only if there were no interruption between the signifier and the signified;
likewise, the eternity of the Veda would exist if there were no interruption in the succession of teachers and students.

If the world were to undergo dissolution without any continuity (*niranvaya*), and if something entirely non-existent and unprecedented were to arise, then both the signifier and the signified would be utterly severed; what, then, would the relationship be based upon?
Furthermore, if the succession of teachers and students were interrupted, on what basis would the Veda exist?
Nor can it be said that living beings remain permeated by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For those [impressions] are indeed imagined through limiting adjuncts such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); they cannot persist when those [adjuncts] are severed.
Nor can that impression belong to Brahman, because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of pure knowledge and possesses a pure essence to be associated with it.

For example, in the passage "One should not offer *ājya* in the *darśa* sacrifice," the statement is intended to provide knowledge of the exception to the general rule. Thus, the status of *arthavāda* is proven. Furthermore, the status of *arthavāda* is established by the fact that they are intended to provide knowledge of the purposes (*prayojana*) of the ritual act. For example, in the passage "The *barhis* grass is the earth," the statement is intended to provide knowledge of the purpose of the *barhis* grass. Thus, the status of *arthavāda* is proven. Furthermore, the status of *arthavāda* is established by the fact that they are intended to provide knowledge of the results of the accessories (*guṇaphala*). For example, in the passage "One who desires cattle should offer *payas* in the morning libation," the statement is intended to provide knowledge of the result of the accessory *payas*. Thus, the status of *arthavāda* is proven. Furthermore, the status of *arthavāda* is established by the fact that they are intended to provide knowledge of the results of the sequence (*kramaphala*). For example, in the passage "By performing the *pūrṇamāsa* first, one attains longevity," the statement is intended to provide knowledge of the result of the sequence. Thus, the status of *arthavāda* is proven. Furthermore, the status of *arthavāda* is established by the fact that they are intended to provide knowledge of the results of the restrictions (*niyamaphala*). For example, in the passage "By sacrificing with *samidhs*, one overcomes hunger," the statement is intended to provide knowledge of the result of the restriction. Thus, the status of *arthavāda* is proven. Furthermore, the status of *arthavāda* is established by the fact that they are intended to provide knowledge of the results of the alternatives (*vikalpaphala*). For example, in the passage "By sacrificing with *ghee*, one attains brilliance; by sacrificing with *milk*, one attains strength

For in this case, if the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyāyana-vidhi*) had not brought the collection of Vedas denoted by the word *svādhyāya* to the status of being a human goal, then the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), which terminate in merely describing existing facts, would not have attained syntactic unity with the injunctive statements.

Therefore, by virtue of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda, when there arises an expectancy as to its purpose (*kaimarthyākāṅkṣā*), these passages—having as their domain historical events and the like—indicate the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the enjoined act by means of making those facts known; they do not, however, possess the power to indicate that [excellence] while their own literal meanings remain unintended.
If that were the case, there would be no indication at all,

because the seed of indication— the inseparable relation with the expressed meaning— would be absent. For this very reason, in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the word "Ganges" indicates the bank as something connected to its own primary meaning, but not the ocean shore.
For what reason?
Because there is an absence of proximity to one's own purpose;
and none of this is possible when there is no intention to express one's own purpose.
Therefore, in cases where explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are seen to contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
such as "The sacrificial post is indeed the sun" or "The grass-bundle is the sacrificer," there [the interpretation] must be such that there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

And as for how these serve the purpose of praise, Jaimini, in order to establish both of these points, composed the two sūtras: "But it is figurative speech" (*guṇavādastu*) and "the establishment of that" (*tatsiddhiḥ*).

Therefore, where the meaning of the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) is contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the definition [of their function] is that they indicate excellence (*prāśastya*) through figurative speech (*guṇavāda*), which is a case of a "defined-indirect indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

However, where there is corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that object is established through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) just as it is through that other means of valid cognition; for both function with mutual independence regarding a single object, like perception and inference.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of the cognizer, [the arthavāda] is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*).
For an unlearned cognizer does not understand an object from the Veda in the same way that he understands it through perception and other means of knowledge,
because in the latter case there is a dependence on linguistic proficiency and so forth;
however, this is not due to a dependence on the means of knowledge themselves.
It has been stated that "because two [means of knowledge] are independent with respect to their own objects.
Now, one might ask: even when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), why does it become a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*)?
For, when there is a contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabda*), why is it not the other means of knowledge itself that is sublated?

Just as perception and the other means of knowledge have the phenomenal world as their domain, while the Vedāntas have non-duality as their object, why then are the Vedāntas not interpreted according to figurative description (*guṇavāda*), like explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)?
To this it is replied: in accordance with worldly usage, the objects of words are indeed twofold.
Both by way of the door (*dvārataḥ*) and by way of the purport (*tātparyataḥ*).

Just as in a single sentence the meanings of the words are the object by way of the door and the meaning of the sentence is the object by way of the purport, so it is also in the case of two sentences forming a single syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
For example, "This cow belonging to Devadatta is to be purchased" is one sentence.
"This cow has much milk"—this is another [instance], where the demonstration of its having much milk serves as the means (*dvāra*).

However, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in the sense of another sentence, namely, "it should be purchased. In that case, what is presented by way of the means is interpreted otherwise when it contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Just as the statement "Eat poison" is intended to convey the meaning of another sentence, such as "Do not eat in his house," so it is that where the primary intention (*tātparya*) lies, human testimony (*pauruṣeya-pramāṇa*) remains valid even when contradicted by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). However, the Vedantas, upon thorough examination of their preceding and succeeding parts, are devoted solely to establishing the Brahman in which the entire manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*) has been eliminated.

Those [scriptural statements] which possess the status of ultimate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being non-human in origin and self-established, displace perception and the other [means of knowledge] from their status as ultimate means of valid cognition and establish them within that conventional [realm].
Furthermore, the sentence "The sacrificial post is indeed the sun" does not aim at establishing the sun's identity as the sacrificial post, but rather aims at the praise of the sacrificial post.
Therefore, when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the subject matter, acting as a medium, is interpreted through figurative speech (*guṇavāda*).
However, where no contradicting *pramāṇa* exists—
as in the case of the physical form of a deity and so forth— [the literal sense is accepted].
In that case, an object being perceived even through the door [of the senses] cannot be abandoned;
nor can it be interpreted as figurative speech (*guṇavāda*), for who would resort to a figurative sense when a primary one is possible, given the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
If it is argued that, such being the case, a sentence that sets forth unestablished things like the body and so forth would be subject to division, this is certainly true;
this sentence is indeed divided.
If it is further argued that, such being the case, there would also be a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), we say: no.
Furthermore, since it is impossible to assume another intended meaning when that [meaning] is already understood from the door [of the context],
and it is not the case that something lacks authority regarding that which it does not intend;
thus, [it is established].

If it were the case that a sentence whose primary purport is the qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*) is not an authority regarding the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), then even a sentence purporting to convey the qualified object would not exist,

because its qualifiers would not be its objects. On the other hand, if it implies them by virtue of having the qualified object as its domain, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*).
When the qualification is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*), there is a qualified object; and from that qualified object, its implication follows.

Therefore, even when the words are primarily intended to convey the qualified [entity], the qualifications being perceived must be accepted—even by one who does not wish it—as objects of that very sentence.

Just so, even though they appear in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which have other purposes, the forms and other attributes of the deities being perceived cannot be rejected as long as there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For figurative description (guṇavāda) is not tenable when the primary meaning is possible;

nor is it said that even a non-human (apauruṣeya) statement, though expressing a real fact, depends on other means of knowledge regarding its own object, such that it would become non-authoritative in the absence of those other means of knowledge.
It might be argued:

"If there is a split in the sentence even when the intended meaning (tātparya) is one, then how can it be said that 'a single sentence consists of a single meaning'? No; [this objection does not hold].
This is because, in each respective case, it is possible for the cognition to culminate in a single object qualified by various other objects according to their specific natures.
However, the distinction is merely this: in some cases that single object qualified by other objects serves as a means (*dvārabhūta*), while in others it is the end (*dvārī*).
[Objection: If this were so, would it not follow that there would also be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) in such cases as "Having eaten rice, he goes to the village"?
For the connection in "having eaten rice" is one thing, whereas the connection in "he goes to the village" is another; this is not so,
because the cognition in each case does not terminate within itself.
For by the suffix -ktvā in *bhuktvā*, both the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) and the priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*) are perceived.
And this perception does not reach its completion without the cognition of another action occurring at a subsequent time.
Therefore, a single sentence consists of as many word-groups as are required for the recollections of word-meanings produced by those words to reach their culmination.
And these [words] culminate in an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), since a specific meaning is understood even without an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*).

Nor does it follow that there would be a multiplicity of sentences in a single sentence containing five or six words, because the understanding of a specific meaning is completed by each pair of words;
for even though the qualifiers are multiple, the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is one.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for that which is heard only once—the primary element—to be repeated merely to conform to its subordinate qualifiers;

and since a difference in the primary element necessarily entails a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), it is established that the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is a distinct sentence from the injunctive passage (*vidhivākya*). Thus, two sentences—each having completed its function by producing the cognition of its own respective sentence-meaning—subsequently enter into mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) when some requirement arises.
Moreover, it is precisely by means of injunctions that [the sacrifices] have Indra and others as their deities.
The body of a sacrifice consists in the relinquishment of one's own ownership over an object, directed toward a deity after having taken hold of the oblation.
And a deity cannot be designated unless it has been inscribed in the mind.

And since that which is devoid of form cannot be depicted in the mind, the very injunction for sacrifice— which requires such a form— accepts whatever form is understood from even those Mantras and Arthavādas whose primary intent lies elsewhere;
for there is no evidence for postulating any other form,
and because it would otherwise result in the Mantras and Arthavādas functioning in an entirely indirect or figurative manner.

For just as in the case of the injunction, "A *vrātya* performs the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice," when there is a requirement to understand the nature of the *vrātya*, the definition of a *vrātya*— namely, "he whose father or grandfather does not drink *soma* is a *vrātya*"— is understood; and being required by the injunction for the *vrātyastoma*, it becomes authoritative on the basis of that very injunction.

Or, just as the extraordinary nature of heaven— which is required by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and is understood from the explanatory passage (arthavāda)— is validated by that very injunction as its source of authority,
so too is the form of the deity.
Now, it may be argued that the mention [of a deity] requires the cognition of its form, but not the actual existence of that form;

and since the cognition of a form is possible even through superimposition, it follows that the form of the deity mentioned in the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) is merely superimposed.
True, it does require the cognition of a form.
And since that [form] cannot be established from any other source, it must come from the mantras and arthavādas alone.
Now, when there is no sublation, it is improper to abandon the existence of that form as it has ascended into experience and instead imagine another state that is not experienced.

Therefore, it is logical that the form of the deity—though presented to the mind by mantras and arthavādas intended for other purposes (such as praise)—is indeed based on the authority of the injunction (*vidhi*).
This might be so:
even from a sentence whose primary purpose is something else, a meaning understood through the requirement of an injunction is accepted; however, in this case, there is no such requirement at all.
Because the deity consists of the form of sound, and because that [sound] is cognizable through other means of knowledge, he says: "Nor is it mere sound.
The establishment of the corporeal form and so forth is not derived from mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) alone.

Rather, [the author] states "itihāsa... [etc. to show whether [the knowledge of dharma] derives from Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the traditional recollections of the world—which are rooted in the explanatory passages (arthavāda) of the Mantras—or from direct perception, which is rootless.
[The word] "śliṣyate" means "is joined" or "is applicable.
The rest is explained merely by the literal reading (nigada).

Thus, since the embodied form and other attributes of the deity are established through mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, a sacrifice consisting of the worship of the deity—just like the worship of a guru and others—is logically possible as being fruitful by means of the deity’s grace and the like.
However, for that which is insentient, such as fire, which does not comprehend worship, this [fruitfulness] is untenable.

Nor is it the case that, because the sacrificial act is subordinate to the deity, the fruit arises from the deity; for if that were so, the scripturally stated fruitfulness of the sacrificial *bhāvanā* and the sacrifice itself with respect to that [deity] or its portion of the fruit would be contradicted.
The status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) must be abandoned [in favor of the object].

For it is the very *bhāvanā* of the sacrifice—which possesses the fruit—that has the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) characterized by the sacrifice as its own instrument; thus, the feeding of the deity, its gratification, and so forth, function as the means for attaining the result, just as the various intermediate operations of the act of farming are the means for obtaining the harvest.

In your own view, the means of attaining heaven (*svarga-sādhanatva*) belongs to the Agni-oblation and the rest, which possess as their intermediate operations the *utpatti-apūrva* (origination-merit) and the *parama-apūrva* (final merit), just as it does for the sacrifice.

Therefore, since the fruitfulness resides either in the action (*karman*) with its intermediate operation of *apūrva*, or in the deity with its intermediate operation of divine grace (*devatā-prasāda*), the status of being the primary factor (*pradhānatva*) is equal in both positions; however, there is no primacy for a deity possessing a physical form (*vigraha*) and so forth. Thus, the aphorism of the *Dharma-mīmāṃsā*—"Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act is primary, while the mention of the deity is subordinate"—is not contradicted.
Therefore, it is established that the deities generally possess the qualification for the knowledges of Brahman. //33//

Establishing the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṃgati*), he states the purport of the section: "Just as [the qualification] pertains to human beings.
He states the seed of the doubt: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
For what conscious being indeed would there not be a desire for eternal bliss from which all attachment to suffering has been wiped away?
On account of which [lack of qualification], a Śūdra would not be entitled [to Vedic study] due to the absence of need;
nor is there an absence of capacity for him regarding the knowledge of Brahman.
For capacity is of two kinds: innate and adventitious.
If it is argued that, in this regard, while the innate capacity for hearing and so forth is unimpeded for Śūdras just as it is for the twice-born,
they lack qualification because of the absence of such capacity due to the lack of Vedic study,
then alas!
It may be granted that, in the absence of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to those rites accomplished by fire due to the lack of fire;
however, since fire is not a means for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), why should those who have not maintained the sacred fires be excluded from it?
Nor is it correct to argue that they lack entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman because of their lack of entitlement to the means for its attainment, namely Vedic study (*adhyayana*).

For it is logical [to conclude] that since the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed as the locus for the oblation in the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," its specific nature is non-worldly (*alaukika*)— as it cannot be obtained from any source other than the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) enjoined by an independent scriptural statement— and since the *ādhāna* itself is prescribed as being connected only to the twice-born, the fire accomplished thereby is non-worldly and does not belong to a *śūdra*;
thus, a *śūdra* has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to rites accomplished by means of the *āhavanīya* and other such fires.
Furthermore, there is no extraordinary means for the knowledge of Brahman that would not be available to a Śūdra.
If it is argued that this is because of the restrictive rule regarding Vedic study, we say no; for that argument cannot withstand scrutiny.
That study might be restricted either to a human purpose,
such as the acquisition of wealth through receiving gifts and the like,
or to a ritual purpose.
For example, threshing in the injunction "one threshes the rice" is not for the sake of the sacrifice;
for the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" is not recited with reference to any particular sacrifice.
Just as, with reference to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is said, "One threshes the rice-grains";
and even that which is taught outside of a specific context (anārabhyādhīta) brings to mind the sacrifice by virtue of its inseparable connection with a ritual.
For study would be connected with a sacrifice only by means of a specific scriptural statement;
indeed, unlike the *juhū* ladle and other implements which are invariably connected to a sacrifice, the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is not so.
Therefore, the restriction is certainly not for the sake of the sacrifice.
Nor is it for the sake of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
for a human goal is that which proceeds dependent upon human desire,
such as a fruit or its means.
For even with respect to the means [of action], prior to the injunction, activity in its general form is based solely on human desire;
however, regarding the specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*), activity—both in its general and particular aspects—is entirely dependent upon the injunction.
Indeed, one who has not understood the distinctions among the instruments of action cannot engage in the specific procedures.
Therefore, because their activity is dependent upon an injunction, the subsidiary elements (aṅgas) serve the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha).
For the word "sacrifice" (kratuḥ) refers to the injunction by means of its object; that which is desired and made the object of that [injunction] is "for the purpose of the sacrifice."
Furthermore, neither study, nor private recitation (*svādhyāya*), nor the knowledge of its meaning has— prior to the injunction— a commencement dependent upon human desire,

by virtue of which it could constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Moreover, if the comprehension of meaning were restricted to being achieved through study alone, there would be a contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

Since that [knowledge] can be attained even without formal study—namely, by reading from books and the like—the fruit must be understood to arise from study alone, just as in the case of the injunction "gold is to be worn.

Consequently, because the injunction regarding study would lack restrictive force, a Śūdra would possess the capacity either through study or through reading from books and the like; thus, he too would be entitled to the knowledge of Brahman.
Let it be that there is no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman everywhere due to the absence of Vedic study;
however, it shall exist in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā,
because that [instruction] was imparted after addressing a Śūdra with the words, "O Śūdra, indeed, you have carried [the fuel]."

Furthermore, this word "śūdra" cannot be applied to a non-Śūdra through any etymological derivation of its constituent parts (*avayavavyutpatti*), because the conventional meaning of a whole word (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) is stronger than the meaning derived from its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*) due to its independence.

Therefore, just as a Niṣāda carpenter has the right to perform the *Iṣṭi* sacrifice despite not being a student (*anadhīyāna*) by virtue of the power of the scriptural injunction itself, so too it follows that a Śūdra will have the right to the Saṃvarga-vidyā. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
This being the case, we reply: there is no entitlement for a Śūdra because of his lack of Vedic study.

This is the intended meaning: although the injunction for study—"One's own Veda is to be studied"—is not recorded as being commenced with reference to any specific fruitful ritual action, nor is it connected to any category of things invariably related to a sacrifice, [it nevertheless establishes the necessity of study].
For the Veda (*svādhyāya*) does not have an invariable connection with a ritual (*kratu*), as do the ladle (*juhū*) and other such implements.

By the force of the term *prāṇavajra*, both the literal statement and the contextual framework are set aside; here, what is to be established is the fivefold internal and external wind (*vāyu*).

that which is asked is indeed the primary matter to be answered; that constitutes its context.

This is done to praise the rule that "for the *sāhana*, three *upasads* are to be performed," while [the twelve-fold number] is extended to all *ahīna* sacrifices by virtue of being their archetype (*prakṛti*), and is thus mentioned as a restatement (*anuvāda*), just like the *nivīta* and other such rules.

Therefore, even though the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) "ahīna," there is no displacement of the sentence "of the twelve [stotras] for the ahīna" from its context.
As for the displacement of the mantras for the invocation of Pūṣan and others— which are recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma— due to the force of their indicative power (*liṅga*),

Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of an option between the numbers three and twelve;

Because that [meaning] is understood from the context alone; however, in this case, since the intention is the connection with its own primary meaning, the aforementioned fault does not arise. As for the individual soul, since its liberation is caused by the direct realization of its own nature as the unconditioned, eternally pure, and enlightened Brahman, what purpose is served by the path beginning with light through the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman?
In this case as well, there is no difficulty for the knower of Brahman, because that [attainment] is logically possible for him.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate—provided that another interpretation is possible—to restrict the scriptural mention of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), which is employed without qualification, to something other than name-and-form consisting of the gross elements (bhūtākāśa).
Nor is it proper to interpret with some forced difficulty a characteristic of Brahman, such as its unimpeded power of manifestation, as belonging to something else;

for here the characteristic of Brahman, namely its status as a creator, is perceived most clearly in the passage: "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms."

Furthermore, since the individual soul (jīva) possesses the capacity to manifest names and forms by virtue of having the nature of Brahman, it is effectively Brahman itself that is said to be the manifester.

Thus, because the one who brings forth [the manifestation] and the intervening space are logically identical, the assumption of a difference in meaning—namely, that the bringer-forth is one thing and the intervening space another—is also untenable.
Consequently, the designation of the ether as "that which is between those two names and forms" becomes logically consistent.

Therefore, because it is designated as something different [from the individual soul], and likewise because of the designation, "That Brahman is that Immortal," it is established that the ether is indeed Brahman. //41//

First of all, the transmigrating self (saṃsāry-ātman), which is the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and is enveloped by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, is established for all people.

And since the scriptural passage beginning with "He who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" refers to that very self at its beginning, middle, and end, it must be intended as a restatement (anuvāda) of that [well-known self].
Thus, the transmigrating self itself is "great" in relation to something else.
Because saṃsāra is beginningless, it is called "unborn" (aja) due to its lack of a beginning;
however, there is no entity other than that which is to be established here as having the nature of being eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated.

This is not a case of actual difference; rather, this word "self" (ātman) denotes intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Therefore, because there is an absence of objects of distinction during the states of deep sleep and departure, one is embraced by the wise self (prājña-ātman) as its own intrinsic nature, whose cognition is withdrawn; thus, even though there is no difference, it should be understood through a figurative expression as if there were a difference, in the sense that "one knows nothing."
As they say: "The wise one is one whose wisdom is fully integrated.

Furthermore, words such as "individual soul" (*prati*) and so forth must be applied only to the transmigrating soul, because the world—consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects—is acquired through the karma of that soul and is its object of experience.
Therefore, it follows that only the transmigrating soul is being referred to here, and the Supreme Self is not what is being established.
This being the case, it is replied: "Because of the designation by distinction in deep sleep and departure" (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.42) is understood to carry over.

This is the intended meaning: Is there no Supreme Self other than the transmigrating soul, such that the statement, "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths," refers to the transmigrating self?

Or rather, since the Supreme Self (paramātman) is not mentioned here apart from the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī), and since the transmigrating soul is referred to at the beginning, middle, and end [of the passage], this [text] concerns the self of the transmigrator;
however, it is not that such a Self distinct from the transmigrator does not exist.

For hundreds of scriptural authorities (āgama) establishing its existence—such as "Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5) and "Because of the uniformity of the goal" (1.1.10)—have been demonstrated through a series of aphorisms.
Furthermore, even here there is no absence of mention of a Supreme Self distinct from the transmigrating soul,
because that [Supreme Self] is mentioned in the contexts of deep sleep and departure.

Nor is it appropriate to treat the mention of the Wise One (prājña) as the Supreme Self as being merely figurative— like the expression "the head of Rāhu"— by way of identity with the individual soul, when such a distinction is possible.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to explain the word *prājña*—which has a conventional usage (*nirūḍhavṛtti*) established for one possessing excellence of wisdom—as referring in any way to an ignorant person.
Nor is such excellence of wisdom, whose function is unrestricted, possible in anyone other than the omniscient one who has known everything that is to be known;
and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is not of such a nature.

Therefore, because the wise one, the supreme Self (prājña), is designated as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) during deep sleep and departure from the body, the state of that individual self— which is already established in the world through such passages as "this which consists of consciousness"— being the supreme Self is taught as something not previously known. Moreover, these statements do not have the mere restatement of the individual self as their sole purpose.
For verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition must be intent upon making known an object not previously apprehended; it cannot consist merely in a restatement of what is already known.

For this very reason, it is appropriate that the transmigrating soul be considered as the subject of restatement at the beginning, middle, and end [of the Upaniṣads] for the purpose of establishing its identity with the Supreme Self.
And thus, since the greatness and immutability of the omnipresent, eternal Self are possible, they will not be conceived as merely relative.
As for the mention of states such as being a Buddha and so forth in the middle [of the text],
it is not by this that the possession of states is intended to be expressed.

However, because the states possess the nature of arising and passing away, he intends to speak of the Supreme Self as distinct from them and devoid of states, upon considering the context of the subsequent passage. //42//

Therefore, it is established that the textual sequence beginning with "This which consists of consciousness" (yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ) is intended to establish the state of Brahmanhood for the individual soul (jīvātman), after first referring to that soul as already established by other means of knowledge. //43//

"The number five will be delimited by that [quality];
